Phase 1 of proposal 043 (`docs/proposals/043_real-port-addressing.md`, "Phase 1 (chart 2.7.0): per-port truth, no client-visible change"), on both registry backends. Nothing from Phases 2 to 4: no deprecation, no counter, and the legacy spellings (`:18081`, `:18082`, the bare name) keep working where they work on `main`. Fixes #1682 It also fixes the mixed-shape failures #1672 described (closed by the proposal): a pod with a raw-TCP declared port and an HTTP port now has both paths, on `etcd` and on `kubernetes`. ## What changed **The model.** What a service's ports are and what speaks on each is derived from the registry endpoints, per port. Nothing reads a protocol for a service as a whole: the capture reconciler no longer reads `aether.io/app-protocol`, and `PrimaryIsTCP` is gone. **The capture listener** has one HTTP chain and one route table per HTTP port number of the mesh (`cap_http_

`), plus `cap_http_other`, in place of one chain routed on `Host`. The port the client dialled selects the table; `Host` names the service. In the table of port P a service has a virtual host under every one of its names (mesh name, the `cluster.local` forms, the bare name when one namespace owns it), port-less and with `:P`, routed to the cluster of port P. No route of that table leads to another port. #1682 was the known-target route on the catch-all, which accepted any port of a `cluster.local` name and sent it to the default cluster; that route is removed. **Refusals.** An HTTP request that names a mesh service and no HTTP port of it is answered at once with `421` and `x-aether-error`: `port-mismatch`, `port-not-declared`, `port-not-http` or `port-required`. On the loopback listener too, where the port in `Host` is the port. **Clusters** are per (port, class): no h2 cluster for a port declared raw TCP, no default cluster for a service whose declared port is raw TCP, no raw-TCP alias for an HTTP port. **Routes.** A rule applies on every HTTP port of its parent Servic

issues.body:
With redirect-all capture, a call to a service by its `cluster.local` name and a specific port is routed to the service's default cluster, whatever the port, so it reaches the primary port.

Measured on kind, on main: a service with HTTP on 8080 (primary) and 9090. `http://<svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local:9090/` and `http://<svc>.<ns>:9090/` were answered by the container on 8080, 4 of 4, from two nodes. The mesh-domain name with the same port (`<svc>.<ns>.<mesh-domain>:9090`) reached 9090.

Cause, read in the code: the known-target route that pins a mesh service's `cluster.local` spellings ahead of the passthrough (`knownTargetAuthorityRegex`, added by #432 on 2026-06-28) accepts an optional `:port` and routes every match to the default cluster.

Consequence: for any multi-port HTTP service, a client that uses the Kubernetes name with a non-primary port silently gets the primary port's application. No error is raised.

A failing unit test exists from the review of PR 1677 (`TestReview1677_ClusterLocalPortSpelling`, not yet in the tree). Proposal 043 (PR 1681) removes the default cluster this depends on; this defect exists today and independently of it.

## #1679: a reverted roll that changes the worker count left the node with no listeners and a Ready pod

The surge pod does not hot-restart across a worker-count change (#1136): it asks the kept pod's Envoy to drain, waits the drain time, stops it, starts a fresh one. Deleted during that wait, it stopped where it was. The kept pod's Envoy closed its listeners and stayed LIVE on its admin.

**The surge pod** (`replacement.go`). Invariant: *a supervisor that has asked a predecessor to drain owns the node's listeners until its own Envoy has them.* Envoy cannot take a drain back, so "undo" does not exist; the supervisor finishes. A termination requested after the drain was sent is held back until its own Envoy is LIVE, then proceeds as for any pod terminated while it serves (it asks for a successor and the kept pod takes the node back). The hold is bounded (2 × drain time + 36 s, never more than the successor-wait budget, and the time it took comes off that budget). A termination requested *before* the drain is sent is obeyed at once and nothing is drained.

| | before | 0 to 3 s after | from 3 s |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| the listener | 200 | 200 | refused |
| `/ready` | LIVE | LIVE | LIVE |
| `/server_info` state | LIVE | not sampled | LIVE |
| `server.state`, `listener_manager.total_listeners_active` | 0, 1 | not sampled | 0, 1 |
| `listener_manager.listener_stopped` | 0 | 0 | **1** |

issues.body:
A new proxy pod that starts while a live predecessor's node heartbeat is stale starts Envoy at restart epoch 0. When the predecessor's epoch is not 0 mod 3, that start does not collide on the hot-restart domain socket: it unlinks and recreates the shared memory, dies on the admin bind, and leaves the "initializing" flag set. Every later hot restart from the healthy Envoy then exits with `previous envoy process is still initializing`.

Reproduced with real supervisors and the pinned Envoy (review of PR 1675): after the stray start, a following pod loops on that message and never attaches.

Consequence: the next roll's pod can never take over on that node (retries, then CrashLoop, while `maxUnavailable: 0` keeps the old pod) until the old proxy pod is deleted by hand. `retryBindCollision` assumes the collision is always on the domain socket, which holds only for some epochs. The trigger needs a live predecessor whose heartbeat has gone stale (a stalled supervisor, a slow node).

issues.body:
A proxy DaemonSet roll that changes the Envoy worker count (`proxy.concurrency`, or a CPU limit that changes it) and is reverted while the surge pod starts can leave a node with no listeners and a pod that still reports Ready.

Sequence, reproduced with two real supervisors and the pinned Envoy (review of PR 1675): the surge pod takes the worker-count path added by #1136 and asks the kept pod's Envoy to drain its listeners (`/drain_listeners?graceful`); the surge pod is then deleted (the roll was reverted) and receives SIGTERM during its drain-time wait; with its context cancelled it fails to stop the predecessor, reports it gone, and exits. The kept pod's Envoy has closed its listeners but stays LIVE on its admin, so the pod stays Ready and nothing restarts it.

Measured: after 25 s the kept pod is `ready=true`, admin LIVE at epoch 0, and its listener serves nothing.

Consequence: the node has no data plane until that proxy pod is deleted by hand, and readiness does not show it. It is the same reverted-roll scenario as the nightly failure fixed by PR 1675, for any roll that changes the worker count; that fix does not cover it, because the kept pod was never superseded. Main behaves the same way.

issues.body:
A pod whose primary port is raw TCP and which also declares an HTTP port (`endpoint.aether.io/protocol: tcp`, primary port 9000, `endpoint.aether.io/ports: "9000,8080=h1"`) cannot be reached over raw TCP through the mesh.

Measured on kind (etcd registry, SPIRE on) with the reproducer in `e2e/multiprotocol.sh` (PR #1671; outside its gate): `MP_TCP_PRIMARY=1 e2e/multiprotocol.sh up && e2e/multiprotocol.sh verify`, legs X1 to X3.

- raw TCP to the service on `:18082` and on `:9000`: no answer;
- HTTP to `:8080`: 200;
- HTTP to `:18081` and with no port: 502.

The calling proxy has no `cap_tcp_*` chain for the service, and the generated mesh Service is stamped `app-protocol: http`.

Inferred cause, not confirmed: the Service generator claims the Service for the first protocol it iterates (HTTP), so the capture reconciler reads the primary as not TCP (`registrar/internal/services/generator.go`, `agent/internal/capture/reconciler.go`, the `PrimaryIsTCP` computation) and builds no TCP floor; the HTTP path then targets the TCP primary port.

The mirror shape (HTTP primary with a TCP secondary) works and is what the nightly `multiprotocol` suite gates. Only the etcd backend was exercised.

agent_prs.body:
Closes #1641
Closes #1646

**Breaking for the length of an agent roll**: see "Mixed versions" below.

## What was wrong

Every caller-side route retried a `503` on another endpoint, for any method. A destination proxy answers `503` both when it never reached its application and when it had already sent the request and the application's connection then closed or reset before a response. The caller could not tell them apart, so a `POST` an application had received could be run a second time on another pod (#1641). For gRPC it was wrong the other way round: both kinds reach the caller as HTTP `200` with `grpc-status: 14`, and neither was retried (#1646).

## What is true now

The destination says what happened; the caller retries on that and on nothing else about the response. Status codes are unchanged.

**Destination.** Every inbound connection manager (mTLS TCP, cleartext, HTTP/3: one route builder) stamps `x-aether-outcome` on every response, overwriting anything the application set:

```
<code>;<flags>;<method>;<details>
%RESPONSE_CODE%;%RESPONSE_FLAGS%;%REQ(:METHOD)%;%RESPONSE_CODE_DETAILS%
```

`code` is the application's status, or `0` for a reply the proxy generated itself (what Envoy holds when response headers are finalised; measured). The grammar is documented in one place, `agent/internal/xds/proxy/outcome.go`, and is a wire contract between agent versions; a unit test spells the header name and the format out so that neither changes by accident.

**Caller.** `outboundRetryPolicy()` is `connect-failure,refused-stream,reset-before-request,retriable-headers` with ONE matcher on that header. `retriable-status-codes` is gone, and a test guards that it, `5xx`, `gateway-error` and `reset` never come back. The regex:

```
503;-;[ -~]*|0;(?:-;[ -~]*overload|(?:(?:U[FHO]|NC),?)+;[ -~]*|(?:(?:U[CFHOR]|NC|LR),?)+;(?:(?:GET|HEAD|OPTIONS|TRACE|PUT|DELETE);[ -~]*|[!-:<-~]+;[ -~]*e_refu[ -~]*))
```

1. `503;-;…`: a `503` with no failure flag, any method: the application
agent_prs.title: fix(agent): the destination reports each response's outcome in x-aether-outcome and the caller retries on that header alone, so a request the application had received is not replayed and an undelivered gRPC call is retried (#1641, #1646)

issues.body:
When the destination proxy cannot reach its local application (connect refused, no healthy upstream), it answers an HTTP request with `503`, and the caller's outbound retry policy (`retriable-status-codes: [503]`, `agent/internal/xds/proxy/route.go`) tries another endpoint. For a gRPC request the destination answers `200` with `grpc-status: 14` instead, which that policy never matches.

Measured on the pinned Envoy while working #1641 (PR #1645): a gRPC request to a destination whose application refused the connection came back `200` + `grpc-status: 14` and was not retried; the same failure for a plain HTTP request was retried on the other endpoint.

Consequence: a gRPC call that lands on a pod that has just terminated fails with `UNAVAILABLE`, where an HTTP call is carried over to another endpoint, so pod rolls are not hitless for gRPC unless the client retries itself. The retry policy would need the gRPC conditions (`retriable gRPC status` such as `unavailable`), with the same care about requests that had already begun (#1641).

issues.body:
`outboundRetryPolicy()` (`agent/internal/xds/proxy/route.go`) retries on `retriable-status-codes: [503]` with no method condition. When the destination proxy has already started sending a request to the application and the upstream connection is then terminated, it answers `503` with flag `UC`; the source proxy retries that on another endpoint, whatever the method.

Measured (access logs of an 8 h soak, joined by request id): 3 rows with `us_tx_beg_ms` set (the request had begun to be sent to the application) and `503 UC connection_termination` at the destination were answered `200` from a different pod at the source. Those were GETs; nothing in the policy would treat a POST differently.

Consequence: a non-idempotent request can be executed twice when an application closes the connection or dies after receiving it. `docs/workload-requirements.md` ("What the mesh retries for you") and the code comment say every retried failure happens before a request reaches an application; that holds for `UF` (connect failure) and not for a destination-synthesized `503 UC`.

A fix needs a choice: for example the inbound side marking a response "not sent upstream" so the source retries only those, or restricting the 503 retry to idempotent methods. Until then the documentation should say what is true.

agent_prs.body:
Closes #1635

## What was wrong

A service's h2 cluster, its TCP floor and its UDP floor share one load assignment, named after the service (`demo/db`). The HTTP default entry, the TCP floor entry and the UDP floor entry of the agent's cluster cache all name it, and exactly one is meant to hold it (proposal 037, "the bare-name CLA is owned by the HTTP default entry when the service has one, else by the `tcp:<fqdn>` entry"). When both listings are live there is one holder, not two equal ones: the HTTP entry holds it and the TCP entry holds none. The #1634 comment that said "two equal load assignments" was wrong and is corrected here.

Two paths gave the name two holders:

1. **Retention.** Ownership is decided while the refresh's passes run, when the map holds only entries built from a live listing. The retention step runs afterwards and re-inserted the entry of a listing that had gone with an *empty* load assignment under the same name. So: HTTP listing gone while TCP (or UDP) stays; the mirror in a single refresh (TCP gone, HTTP appears); both gone and one back.
2. **TCP and UDP.** The UDP pass asked only whether the HTTP entry held the name, so a service listed under TCP and UDP (and not HTTP) had two holders for as long as it was listed under both, with no retention involved.

go-control-plane keeps one resource per name, and which one is redrawn on every build.

## Measured on `main` (snapshot cache, 32 consecutive refreshes each)

Closes #1636

## What was wrong

A pod name is an RFC 1123 subdomain, so it may contain dots, and a dot is the separator of an Envoy stat name. The agent put the pod name into its per-pod stat names as it is. For a pod `web.external-7d9f` in `team-a`:

- `cluster.health_team-a_web.external-7d9f.membership_healthy` reads, to the bootstrap's stats exclusions (`^cluster\.health_[^.]*\.(…|external|…).*`), as cluster `health_team-a_web` and stat `external-7d9f.membership_healthy`. The exclusion matches, the gauge is never allocated, and the health gateway's `health_check` filter, which reads it, answers `503` for a healthy pod. The same for a second name label starting with `http1`, `http2`, `retry` or `assignment`.
- For every dotted pod the rest of the name stayed in the metric name, with `aether_pod="web"` and `aether_cluster="health_team-a_web"`.

## What changed

In a **stat** name the agent writes `~` for each dot of the pod name (`proxy.PodStatKey`):

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| listener `stat_prefix` | `inbound_team-a_web.external-7d9f` (and `…_h3`, `out_http_…`, `capture_…`, `capture_udp_…`) | `inbound_team-a_web~external-7d9f` (and the same four) |
| `tcp_proxy` / `udp_proxy` stat prefix | `in_tcp_team-a_web.external-7d9f[_<port>]`, `capture_udp_…` | the same with `~` |
| `health_` and `inboundready_` cluster stats | keyed by the cluster name | `alt_stat_name: health_team-a_web~external-7d9f`, set only when it differs from the name |

No resource is renamed: listener, cluster and filter chain names and the health gateway paths are what #1634 made them. A pod without a dot in its name gets byte-identical listeners and clusters (`TestPodWithoutADotKeepsItsStatNames`).

### Why this form

- **A chart-regex-only fix was rejected.** A regex has to tell where a dotted pod name ends and the stat begins, and `ssl`, `http2`, `external`, `default` are all legal labels of a pod name and names of Envoy stat subtrees. It could only be done with a list of every stat

    increase(aether_agent_xds_nacks_total{aether_xds_type_url="type.googleapis.com/envoy.config.listener.v3.Listener"}[1h])
  ) > 0

  sum by (job, node) (
    (aether_agent_xds_nacks_total{aether_xds_type_url="type.googleapis.com/envoy.config.listener.v3.Listener"} > 0)

agent_prs.body:
Closes #1624

## What is now true

The ACK tracker (`agent/internal/xds/ack`) keeps what a proxy holds **per xDS stream**. A stream is one connection of one proxy process: a hot restart has two for a while, and a proxy that reconnects opens a new one.

- What a proxy holds on a stream is what it stated in its first Listener request (`initial_resource_versions`), with every response it answered since, applied in the order it answered them. That is the proxy's own history, so nothing orders answers between streams: the send-order clock, the sent-order rules, the writing-stream field, `unconfirmed` and the close-time rules of #1559 have no counterpart here.
- Everything known through a stream goes with it when it closes. Nothing one stream says can change what another said.
- What the node holds is read off the open streams when a wait asks. A proxy counts from its Listener request on.

The two waits the CNI server makes:

| wait | answered when | failed when |
|---|---|---|
| `WaitListenerPresent` (pod ADD) | **one** proxy holds the listener at the version the agent publishes now, with nothing that adds or removes the name unanswered on its stream | **any** connected proxy's last answer about the name is a rejection of the published version |
| `WaitListenerAbsent` (pod DEL) | there is a proxy that has asked for its listeners, and **every** such proxy is known not to hold the listener: its statement has been answered, the name is not held, nothing about it is unanswered, and its last answer about it was not the rejection of an add | never by a rejection (see below) |

The published version is read from the snapshot cache (`ack.SnapshotVersions`, wired in `agent/internal/cmd/root.go`).

### Choices this makes, and why

- **Absent: every generation.** Each generation of a hot restart has its own sockets in the pod's network namespace.
- **Present: one generation answers, either rejecting fails.** This is a choice, not a proof that the listener serves; see the first limi

Closes #1584

## The defect

The node agent named everything it builds for one pod after the pod's **name** alone: `inbound_<pod>`, `inbound_<pod>_h3`, `outbound_http_<pod>`, `capture_<pod>`, `capture_udp_<pod>`, `app_<pod>_<port>`, `health_<pod>`, `inboundready_<pod>`. Its snapshot cache keys entries by network namespace, so two mesh pods of one name in two namespaces on one node (two StatefulSets called `web`, each with a `web-0`) produced two resources under each name.

go-control-plane keeps one resource per name. Which pod's it kept was decided by map order on every snapshot build, separately for listeners and for clusters. One pod had no listeners, and the other's inbound listener could route to an app cluster that dials the first pod's loopback. The CNI ADD/DEL acknowledgement waits and the liveness loop's health gateway paths were keyed by the same names.

Every per-pod listener name, cluster name, health gateway path, stat prefix and filter chain name is built from it:

| Before | Now |
|---|---|
| `inbound_<pod>`, `inbound_<pod>_h3` | `inbound_<namespace>_<pod>`, `inbound_<namespace>_<pod>_h3` |

| stat prefixes `out_http_<pod>`, `in_tcp_<pod>[_<port>]`; filter chains `in_…`, `in_tcp_…`, `in_h3_…` | the same with `<namespace>_<pod>` |

This is a breaking rename: no flag, no old-name fallback.

**A build

`OutboundListenerName` is `outbound_http_<pod>` and `InboundListenerName` is `inbound_<pod>` (`agent/internal/xds/proxy/listener.go`, `ingress.go`); the capture and QUIC listener names follow the same form. Closes #1620

## What was wrong

Since #1625 a snapshot build that could not hand a response to an open watch within its bound returns `cache.ErrWatchNotAnswered`, wrapped by every mutator. The snapshot is installed and is the one every later request is answered from. `agent/internal/cni/server` still treated that error as a build that failed: a CNI ADD was answered `Internal`, and the runtime tore down and retried a sandbox whose listeners were published.

## What is true now

Every caller of the snapshot cache in the CNI server passes the mutator's error through one helper (`snapshotInstalled`, `snapshotwatch.go`). For `errors.Is(err, cache.ErrWatchNotAnswered)` it logs a WARN, counts, and returns nil. Every other error is returned unchanged.

| Caller | Before, on the sentinel | Now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CNI ADD (`AddPod`) | `codes.Internal`, sandbox retried | `RESULT_SUCCESS`; the best-effort ACK wait still runs |
| CNI DEL (`removePodListeners`) | RPC succeeded (best-effort), ERROR `failed to remove listener` | RPC succeeds, WARN instead of the untrue ERROR |
| ghost sweep (`pruneOnePod`) | ERROR `failed to drop listener for pruned pod` | WARN instead of the untrue ERROR |
| surge takeover (`ReconcileStorage`) | step logged as `takeover step failed` | step succeeds |

Any other error keeps what it had: the ADD is `codes.Internal` with `failed to add listener: …`, the DEL and the sweep log their ERROR, the takeover step returns the joined error.

The build's own WARN (`snapshot installed, but an open watch was not answered from it`, with `snapshot_version`) precedes it.
- Metric: `aether.agent.cni.snapshot_watch_unanswered{aether.snapshot.caller}` (Prometheus `aether_agent_cni_snapshot_watch_unanswered_total{aether
agent_prs.title: fix(agent): a CNI ADD whose snapshot is installed succeeds although an open watch was not answered from it (#1620)

issues.body:
Since #1608 `generateSnapshot` does its bookkeeping for a snapshot whose `SetSnapshot` returned an error (the snapshot is installed; only answering an open watch failed), but it still returns that error. `AddPod`, and through it the CNI server, `RemoveCluster` and the other callers therefore report failure for state that is installed and served: a CNI ADD can fail and be retried although the pod's listeners are published.

- only an issue opened by `github-actions[bot]` (type `Bot`) under exactly the title counts; an issue anyone else opened under it is neither commented on nor closed, and does not stop the workflow opening its own;

An extra issue's report is copied to the older before the extra is closed, and the extra stays open if the copy fails (round three). The path that closes publish-verify issues counts the reports on the issue before and after its close and reopens it when a failure was written in between, and the missing-artifacts body is cut to fit the 65,536-character limit, saying how many lines were not shown (round four).

agent_prs.body:
Closes #1500

**This changes released artifacts once.** The first publish after it merges gives six binaries a new GNU build ID and five images a new digest (list below), with no change to their code. After that, renaming Bazel's output directory no longer changes any of them.

## What was wrong

Bazel builds each configuration under `bazel-out/<name>/`, and makes the name from the flags. A flag added to `.bazelrc`, a transition a rule gains or a Bazel upgrade can rename it with no change to any source.

Measured, on two builds of `//agent/cmd/agent` and `//agent/cmd/mesh-dns` whose only difference was `--platform_suffix=x1500` (it appends to the name of the target configuration's directory; the exec configuration, and so every tool, keeps its directory):

| | `k8-fastbuild` | `k8-fastbuild-x1500` |
|---|---|---|
| agent sha256 | `aee911f4…` | `41e796b7…` |
| mesh-dns sha256 | `c14a552e…` | `c14a552e…` |

The agent holds 19 strings that start with `bazel-out/k8-fastbuild/bin/`: one per generated `.pb.go` it links (14 from `//api`, 4 from go-spiffe, 1 from protoc-gen-validate). mesh-dns holds none. Each occurs once, in `.gopclntab`, the table a stack trace is printed from; the binary has no DWARF sections. The paths are 6 bytes longer under the second name, which shifts everything laid out after them: 20 million of the agent's 69 million bytes differ, though only 19 strings changed.

Why generated sources and no others: rules_go passes the compiler `-trimpath` for the sandbox's execution root. What is left is the path relative to that root, which is `agent/...` for a source file, `external/...` for a dependency, `GOROOT/...` for the standard library, and `bazel-out/<name>/bin/...` for a generated file. Nothing escapes the trim; the configuration name is inside what the trim leaves. The generated files carry no `//line` directives.

## The fix

`build --experimental_output_paths=strip` in `.bazelrc`. rules_go already declares `supports-path-mapping` on its compile act

Measured while doing #1427 (PR #1498): agent, identity-ready, uds-csi, cni, controller and registrar have different bytes, and so different GNU build IDs, when built in the command-line configuration and in the image index's configuration; the other eight released binaries are the same in both.

The standing decision from #1383 bounds it: OPA runs with `--watch`, and validating a policy is the job of whoever updates it, before the update. Nothing here validates, refuses or rolls back a policy. This is about seeing a policy that does not compile when it is applied, and about pinning in CI what it does at the restarts that follow.

## What changes

1. **A policy check** (chart `aether` 2.4.23, `proxy.authzSidecar.opa.policyCheck`, on by default with the OPA preset). One more pod, the Deployment `<release>-opa-policy-check`: the sidecar's image, the same ConfigMap mounted, and a readiness probe that runs `/opa check /policy/policy.rego`. Its pod template carries a checksum of the policy and its strategy is `Recreate`, so each policy change is judged by a new pod that mounts the ConfigMap as it is. With a policy that does not compile:
   - `kubectl rollout status deploy/aether-opa-policy-check` does not complete and the Deployment shows `0/1`;
   - the pod's `Unhealthy` event carries the compile error with file and line (measured 7 s after `helm upgrade` began);

   It takes no part in any request and no proxy pod is touched.

issues.body:
Since #1436 the OPA authz sidecar reloads its policy when the ConfigMap changes (`opa run --watch`), and validating a policy before applying it is the operator's responsibility. What a bad policy then does, measured:

- **Running sidecar:** the file is not loaded; the last good policy keeps deciding; no exit, no restart, health 200. Nothing changes that an operator would notice.
- **Any later sidecar restart** with the bad file in place: OPA exits 1 and crash-loops; the proxy keeps running and every authorization check is an error, so requests follow `failureMode` (403 on 18 of 18 with DENY).
- **Any later proxy pod replacement** (a roll, a node drain): the new pod never gets past the sidecar; the old pod serves with its own last good policy for its 155 s successor wait, then exits; after that the node has no proxy and requests fail to connect.

So the last good policy lives only in the running process, and the failure surfaces at an unrelated later event.

**Detection today:** only a log line at level `info` (`Processed file watch event.` with a non-null `err`, five lines per update). OPA's diagnostic endpoint has no reload metric and its status plugin is off; `/v1/policies` returns the loaded policy, which can be compared with the ConfigMap.

**Options:** a log-based alert on that line for the `authz` container; a small check (in the proxy pod's readiness, or an agent metric) that compares the loaded policy's hash with the mounted file and exports a mismatch; enabling OPA's status plugin if it reports bundle/load errors for file watches (to be checked). Not proposed: chart-side validation, which the owner decided against.

Reported by the OPA policy-watch work (PR #1436), not changed there. Measured on kind with OPA 1.21.1.

Part of #1514 (the edge, which is the title and the default; the control-plane case is left, see "Not fixed") and of #1543 (the script runs under Helm 4; the nightly job is not changed). #1542 is not touched; what was measured for it is at the end.

An agent wrote this pull request. Base: `da5198b2` (`main` merged in since, no conflict).

## What was reproduced

All on kind (Kubernetes v1.35.8), the real chart and images, before any change. Follow-ups to #1513.

| Issue | Helm 3.18.4 | Helm 4.2.0 (server-side apply) |
|---|---|---|
| #1514: `edge.enabled=true` at defaults, an upgrade, `helm rollback aether 1` | **fails**: `Error: no MeshConfig with the name "default" found`; release `failed` at revision 3; revision 1's manifest holds 1 MeshConfig, revision 2's none | rolls back (`resource exists on cluster but not in original release, using cluster state as baseline`) |
| #1515: a release that owns its namespace, the ownership annotations removed, an upgrade (the Namespace leaves the manifest, kept), `helm rollback` to the revision that holds it | **fails**: `Error: no Namespace with the name "aether-system" found`; release `failed`; namespace untouched (same UID, `Active`) | rolls back |

So #1515's "probably" is confirmed, for Helm 3. Both are the same Helm 3 behaviour as #1471 (`pkg/kube/client.go`, `Update`), and Helm 4.2.0 has neither.

## #1514: the edge's MeshConfig

A `pre-install` hook runs before the release's objects exist, so it cannot create the edge's MeshConfig in a namespace the same revision creates. It therefore stayed an object of the release, seeded once: in that one manifest, in no later one, still live.

The fix is the opposite of a hook: **render it on every revision**, for a release whose edge namespace this chart created. That is safe for this MeshConfig because the chart sets no field of its spec (`spec: {}` whatever the values):

- Helm 3 patches a custom resource with the difference between the previous manifest and the new
agent_prs.title: fix(chart, e2e): the edge's MeshConfig is in every revision's manifest, so helm rollback works to the revision that created the edge namespace (#1514, #1515, #1543)

issues.body:
#1513 makes the seeded MeshConfig a pre-install/pre-upgrade hook, so it is in no revision's manifest and `helm rollback` to the seeding revision works (#1471). A pre-install hook cannot create an object in a namespace the same revision creates, so in two cases the seed is still a release object on that one revision:

- the edge's MeshConfig with `edge.namespaceCreate=true`, the default once `edge.enabled=true`;
- the control plane's with `namespace.create=true`.

Measured on kind (Helm 3.18.4): with `edge.enabled=true` at defaults, `helm rollback <release> 1` fails with `no MeshConfig with the name "default" found` and leaves the release `failed`. With `edge.namespaceCreate=false` and an operator-made namespace it succeeds. The runbook section "Chart 2.4.24" has the way round.

No chart-only fix was found that neither deadlocks `--wait` nor risks operator edits. Routes: the controller seeds the edge MeshConfig, or the edge pod does not require the projected ConfigMap to start.

## What

Two issues, one pull request, because both are about `e2e/pressure/run.sh` saying only what it knows.

### #1578: a failed `kubectl` or `curl` call is neither an absent object nor a verdict

I went through every `kubectl` and `curl` call of the script, not only the pre-flights the issue names. Before this change a failed call was one of three things, depending on the call:

- **read as absence**: `get node` ("node not found"), `get job` (an API error let the run go on over a Job that might still be flooding), the age of the agent's series ("has no samples"), the first fetch of a collector's `/metrics` ("did not serve otelcol_* samples");
- **a silent exit 1**, which is this script's FAIL ("#662 is back"): every `x=$(kubectl ... 2>/dev/null)` under `errexit`, in the pre-flight, in the wait loops and in `verify_agent`. `{.items[0]...}` also fails on an empty list, so the moment between the old agent pod going and its replacement being created was a silent FAIL too;
- **a false statement**: a safety-ceiling abort said "job deleted" whatever the delete did, and cleared the flag that makes the cleanup trap try again.

One more, found on the way: `die` inside a `$(...)` handed its message to the caller's variable, so every `promq_req` abort ended the run without a word.

Now every call either gets an answer or ends the run with **exit 2** (INCONCLUSIVE) and the tool's own error on the terminal. Where absence is a legitimate answer it is read from a call that succeeded (`--ignore-not-found`, or a list or a jsonpath that came back empty).

agent_prs.body:
Closes #1544

A harness outside this repository pins a `version` of `test/harnesscontract/external-harness.yaml`. Until now a deployed mesh could not say which one it satisfies.

**The external-harness contract changed**: one new entry (`object.annotation.harness_contract_version`) and one new key on an existing object. Both are additions, so `version` stays 2.

## What a harness reads

```bash
kubectl -n aether-system get daemonset aether-agent \
  -o jsonpath='{.metadata.annotations.aether\.io/harness-contract-version}'
```

- It identifies the **contract**, not the build. Charts of different versions answer the same while the contract's `version` stays, and it says nothing about which images run.
- An empty answer is "not known", never a version: a chart older than 2.4.28, or one rendered from the source tree.

## How the value gets there

1. `//test/harnesscontract` exports `external-harness.yaml` to `//charts/aether` only.
2. The genrule `//charts/aether:harness_contract_version` reads the top-level `version:` line into `files/harness-contract-version`. It fails the build unless there is exactly one such line and it holds a positive integer.
3. Both packagings (`:aether`, `:aether_commit`) pass that file in `files`.
4. The helper `aether.harnessContractVersion` reads it with `.Files.Get`, and `agent-daemonset.yaml` writes it as an annotation on the DaemonSet's own metadata.

There is no literal anywhere. A contract bump edits nothing under `charts/`.

The annotation is optional in the template. A render of the source tree (`helm template charts/aether`, which the conformance action and one `ci.yaml` step run) has no generated file and renders no annotation.

## Upgrade

Chart `2.4.28` (main is at `2.4.27`). Nothing to set, nothing to do before upgrading.

- **No workload rolls for this change.** Every pod template is byte-identical before and after.
- The agent DaemonSet object's metadata gains one annotation.
- The `helm.sh/chart` label on each object's own me

issues.body:
Helm's `--wait` counts a DaemonSet as ready when `numberReady >= desiredNumberScheduled - maxUnavailable`. With the default `maxUnavailable: 1` on a one-node cluster that is zero pods, so `helm upgrade --install --wait` returns `deployed` for the prober chart (and for any aether DaemonSet on a single node) with no pod running — for instance when Pod Security refuses the pods.

The getting-started and runbook install steps should not present `--wait` as the check on a small cluster: follow it with `kubectl rollout status daemonset/…` (which waits for every pod) or the pod count the docs already show.

Found on kind (v1.35, Helm 3.18.4) while measuring upgrade safety for #1464.

issues.body:
`charts/aether/values.yaml` still describes `proxy.concurrency: 0` and `edge.concurrency: 0` as "one worker per core". Since #1452 the docs say what the pinned Envoy really does without `--concurrency`: the minimum of hardware threads, the process's CPU affinity and its OWN cgroup's CPU limit (rounded down, at least 1).

Three things an operator should be told where the values are documented:
- With `proxy.concurrency: 0`, changing `proxy.resources.limits.cpu` across a whole-CPU boundary changes Envoy's worker count, so that rollout is a drain and fresh start on every node instead of a hot restart. Set an explicit count whenever a CPU limit is set.
- Envoy reads only its own cgroup. A pod-level CPU limit with none on the proxy container leaves it at one worker per core while it is throttled (measured: 20 workers under a 1.5-CPU parent quota).
- `--concurrency 0` passed explicitly means one worker, not the default.

Fix: correct the two `values.yaml` comments and add the three notes to `docs/configuration.md`; consider a render-time warning (NOTES.txt) when a CPU limit is set and the count is 0. Needs a chart bump (comment change under `charts/`).

Reported by the worker-count work (PR #1452), not changed there because that task did not touch the chart.

Since #1453 the controller's caBundle injector reads them uncached and uses only `get` and `update`; no other controller code reads these kinds (checked by search). `list` and `watch` are cluster-wide reads of every webhook configuration in the cluster.

`TestCABundleInjectorNeedsOnlyGetAndUpdate` proves the injector works with `list`/`watch` refused. That `patch` is unneeded rests on the search, not on a test.

**Sequencing matters:** drop the verbs only in a chart release AFTER a controller image that contains #1453 is the one the chart pins. An older controller with `list`/`watch` removed hangs exactly as in #1431. Also consider `resourceNames` restricted to the two configurations the chart renders.

Reported by the injector fix (PR #1453), not changed there.

agent_prs.body:
Closes #1511

## The problem

After an agent restart the proxy already holds every pod listener. It states them in the `initial_resource_versions` of its first Listener request, go-control-plane finds them at the version it publishes and sends nothing for them, so nothing ever acknowledges them by name. For such a listener:

- `Tracker.WaitListenerPresent` ran to the caller's deadline (the CNI server's 2 s ACK wait on a pod ADD that is retried, or a pod re-added, after the restart);
- `Tracker.WaitListenerAbsent` returned at once, because the new agent knew of no listener to wait for.

## The change

Two things, the second forced by review of the first.

1. The tracker keeps what the **first** request of a type on a stream states, and reads the **first** response of that type against it. A stated name that response neither adds nor removes is recorded as held, at the version stated, when the proxy ACKs the response.
2. **Presence is for a version, not for a name.** The tracker records the version with every name: the one an acknowledged response carried, or the one the proxy stated. `WaitListenerPresent` is answered only when that is the version the agent publishes at the moment the wait looks. The node agent wires this with `SetPublishedVersion(ack.SnapshotVersions(snapshotCache, node))`, which reads the same per-resource version map go-control-plane computes its responses from.

Why the second: a pod's listeners are named after the pod (`outbound_http_<pod>`, `inbound_<pod>`). A same-named replacement publishes other content under a name the proxy already holds, so "the proxy stated this name" says nothing about the replacement. The same was already true on `main` of "the proxy once acknowledged this name" on an agent that did not restart; this change closes that too.

A rejection is read the same way: a NACK fails `WaitListenerPresent` only when the rejected version is the one published when the wait looks, so a predecessor's rejection or a rejected removal does

## #1619: one unread watch stalling every build. Not reachable with the pinned server

Read in the module source (`go-control-plane` v0.14.0) and held by tests that run the agent's cache under the library's own stream handlers.

`SetSnapshot` hands each open watch its response on a channel the stream owns and waits for room in it. There is always room:

- **Delta stream** (`pkg/server/delta/v3`): one channel for all types, capacity 20 (twice the resource types the library knows). A watch is answered once and removed. The stream opens the next watch of a type only when it handles the proxy's next request for it, and it empties the channel before it handles any request. So the channel holds at most one response per type that had a watch open, plus the answer to the request being handled: 7 for the six types the agent serves, 11 for a stream that watched every type the library knows.
- **State-of-the-world stream** (`pkg/server/sotw/v3`, the per-secret SDS streams): a new channel of capacity 1 for every request, and a watch is answered once. (The agent builds the server without the ordered-ADS option, whose stream shares one channel of capacity 10.)

A proxy that stops reading blocks the stream's goroutine in `Send`. That goroutine then takes no request, so it opens no new watch, and the build has nothing more to hand over.

The tests (`snapshot_watch_test.go`, all pass on `7fd7fd5d` too, which is the point):

| test | state | result |
|---|---|---|
| `TestABuildDoesNotWaitOnAProxyThatStoppedReading` | delta ADS, a watch open for each of the six types, the proxy takes no response, 39 builds that each change every type | the first build answ

Chart versions: **aether 2.4.25 → 2.4.26**, **prober 1.0.7 → 1.0.8**, **udsecho 2.0.3 → 2.0.4**. The external-harness contract is not changed.

**Not in this change:** #1560 (taken out after review, see "Taken out") and #1544 (see "Left out").

## What changes

### #1561: the node proxy's Envoy stats are `service.name=aether-proxy`

Where the backend maps `service.name` to `job` (Prometheus's OTLP ingestion does by itself; another backend may need the mapping made), their series gain `job="aether-proxy"`. Set in the **bootstrap** (`aether-proxy-config`), as a second resource detector of the OTLP stats sink, and not through the container's environment:

```yaml
          resource_detectors:
            - name: envoy.tracers.opentelemetry.resource_detectors.environment
              typed_config:
                "@type": type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.tracers.opentelemetry.resource_detectors.v3.EnvironmentResourceDetectorConfig
            - name: envoy.tracers.opentelemetry.resource_detectors.static_config
              typed_config:
                "@type": type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.tracers.opentelemetry.resource_detectors.v3.StaticConfigResourceDetectorConfig
                attributes:
                  service.name: aether-proxy
```

- The supervisor runs in the same container and builds its own resource from the same environment. Since #1564 a `service.name` in `OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES` no longer renames it, but `OTEL_SERVICE_NAME` still does, so nothing is added to the environment. **The proxy DaemonSet's pod template renders exactly as on `main`**, so the environment the supervisor builds its resource from is unchanged; a guard test pins every workload's `OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES` value and another fails on any `name: OTEL_SERVICE_NAME` entry in the render.
- Envoy merges detectors in the order they are listed and a later one ove

## #1549: a snapshot whose set returned an error is the one served

Checked in the module source (`go-control-plane` v0.14.0, `pkg/cache/v3/simple.go`): `SetSnapshot` stores the snapshot as its first step. It can return an error only after that, from answering the watches that were open: `respond` and `respondDelta` return `context.Canceled` when the context `SetSnapshot` was called with ends before the watch's channel takes the response. Its other error, building the version map, cannot happen for a snapshot whose map `fillVersionMap` already built (`ConstructVersionMap` returns at once on a non-nil map).

`generateSnapshot` returned on that error before the report of the snapshot. Now, whatever `SetSnapshot` returned:

- `logIdentityBindings`, `logInboundIdentityBindings` and `reportClusterPins` (the published gauge, its WARN and its counter) run, with the version of the installed snapshot. The pin report is of the build's own read of the cluster map. The two binding logs read the cache's maps when they run, on this path as after a `SetSnapshot` that returned nil, so a change a mutator made since the build read them is named under this version; a `SetSnapshot` that waits on a watch makes that window longer (review round 1, not changed here).
- The error is logged at WARN as `snapshot installed, but an open watch was not answered from it`, and is still returned, as `snapshot <v> is installed, but an open watch was not answered from it: …` instead of `failed to set snapshot: …`. Callers, the `Generated` metric and the span see an error as before.

Before, the skipped lines and the gauge were made up for by the next build, under that build's version.

Not changed: an open watch that was not answered stays open. It is answered by a later `SetSnapshot` unless its stream replaces or cancels it first.

agent_prs.body:
A workflow's rolling issue was found by a title search with no author check. The repository is public, so anyone could open an issue under one of those titles and have a workflow comment on it, read hidden markers from it and close it.

Closes #1568
Closes #1553
Closes #1532

## What is now true

**A workflow's rolling issue is the one it opened (#1532).** `scripts/rolling-issue-lib.sh` is sourced by `stuck-runs.sh`, `publish-verify-control-issue.sh`, `publish-verify-close-issue.sh` and the new `publish-verify-missing-issue.sh` and `e2e-report-failure.sh`:

- only an issue opened by `github-actions[bot]` (type `Bot`) under exactly the title counts; an issue anyone else opened under it is neither commented on nor closed, and does not stop the workflow opening its own;
- only what that account wrote is read back. This mattered for `stuck-runs`: its memory is a hidden marker, and a comment by anyone carrying `<!-- stuck-runs-uncancellable: <id> -->` made the watchdog stop counting that run;
- the issue is found by listing (`GET /issues?creator=…`), not by search, so there is no index to lag behind a create; two runs that still open one in the same moment are folded (the newer is closed as `not_planned`, its report becomes a comment on the older), and the memory `stuck-runs` reads back comes from the issue that won, never from the closed duplicate (review, round one). A duplicate whose close failed is closed by the next report, and a report written on an issue that was closed in that moment reopens it (review, round two). An extra issue's report is copied to the older before the extra is closed, and the extra stays open if the copy fails (round three). The path that closes publish-verify issues counts the reports on the issue before and after its close and reopens it when a failure was written in between, and the missing-artifacts body is cut to fit the 65,536-character limit, saying how many lines were not shown (round four).

**It is opened with a kind and an area lab
agent_prs.title: fix(ci): a workflow's rolling issue is the one it opened, and it is opened with labels (#1532, #1568, #1553)

issues.body:
The issues opened by `stuck-runs`, the e2e `report-failure` job and the publish-verify control script are created without labels, unlike the pin report added in #1558 (`enhancement`, `ci`, and a missing label fails the run). Give each a kind and an area label the same way.

- `e2e/helm-version.sh` pins one Helm 3 release (`v3.22.0`), one Helm 4 release (`v4.2.0`) and `HELM_DEFAULT_MAJOR` (`3`).

Five issues about the third-party image scanner and its scheduled report, in one change because they share two scripts and their tests. An agent wrote this.

## The scanner (`scripts/third-party-images.sh check`)

**#1525: YAML files are read with a YAML parser.** `scripts/third_party_images_yaml.py` (PyYAML) reads every `*.yaml` / `*.yml` file and hands the scan one record per scalar. The awk scan stays the only judge of what a reference is; it no longer reads YAML syntax in a YAML file.

- An alias is followed to its anchor and reported there. A block scalar behind node properties, a flow mapping broken anywhere, and a value on a later line are read.
- A file under a YAML name that no parser can read is a finding. The exception is a file that holds `{{`: a Helm template is not YAML until it is rendered, so it stays with the line reader, like a here-document. All 40 unparseable YAML files in the tree today are chart templates.
- What a string of a YAML file holds (a script, an embedded manifest, JSON) is still read line by line, as text in another language.
- Deleted from the awk reader: the fail-closed rule for YAML files (any `image:` after `{`, `[` or `,` is a flow key) and with it the false findings it charged for prose. The line reader's other YAML spellings stay, because here-documents, Go strings and Helm templates still need them.
- A reader that fails, or that does not answer for every file, is exit 2 with nothing checked.

On the real tree the old and the new scan agree line for line (`list` is identical: 36 references, 15 pins).

**Where the parser comes from.** Under Bazel the test runs `//scripts:third_party_images_yaml`, a `py_binary` on the PyYAML wheel the documentation site's lock already holds (hash-checked, no new pin, no `MODULE.bazel` change). In the `shell` job of `ci.yaml`, which runs `check` on the real checkout without Bazel, it is the runner's `python3` and its `yaml` module: not pinned, as `jq` and `curl` already are not for `outdated`. issues.body:
Since #1528 a cluster the proxy states but the agent has no record of becomes "held at unknown class", which withdraws the acknowledged gauge, unless the agent publishes that name now or the name belongs to a family known to carry no pin (per-pod, QUIC twin, UDP floor). A proxy that is rejecting updates and keeps a removed cluster of another non-pin family (`ew_ingress_*`, `authz_sidecar`) therefore withdraws the gauge until it accepts the removal. Conservative by design: a missing family costs a withdrawn gauge, never a low count.

**Narrowing:** export the "carries no pin of its own" predicates from `agent/internal/xds/proxy` in one place and have the tracker use them, with a test that every cluster family the agent can publish is classified.

issues.body:
After the proxy NACKs a cluster update, go-control-plane treats the rejected clusters as delivered and does not re-send them on that stream (measured on the pinned cache while doing #1483, PR #1504). The next ACK of an unrelated cluster change then moves `aether.agent.xds.acked_tls_clusters` to the newer snapshot's counts, although the proxy still holds the old version of the rejected cluster.

Example: cluster A is unpinned; the update that pins A is rejected; cluster B changes and is ACKed; the gauge then shows A pinned and `AetherProxyHoldsUnpinnedClusters` resolves.

Inferred from the measured cache behaviour and the tracker's code; not reproduced end to end. Present since #1479.

Fix direction: the acknowledged state must be kept per cluster (a NACKed resource stays at its last acknowledged version until a response carrying it is ACKed), not per snapshot.

agent_prs.body:
Closes #1506
Closes #1507

## What was wrong

`main-post-merge` (`main.yaml`) re-tests every push to `main`. It runs after the merge, so no ruleset can require it, and nothing consumed its result: a red run was seen only by whoever opened the Actions page (#1506). Separately, the header of `main.yaml` said `ci` was the only required status check; `proxy`, `codeql` and the code-scanning app's `CodeQL` are required too (#1507, checked against the rules of `main`).

## What this adds

- `.github/workflows/main-watch.yaml` (`main-post-merge-watch`): runs when a `main-post-merge` run completes, and by hand for a given run id (dry run by default).
- `scripts/main-post-merge-watch.sh`: all of the logic.
- `//scripts:main_post_merge_watch_test`: the script through a fake `gh`, and the workflow file held to its trigger, permissions and pins.
- `docs/runbook.md`: what the issue means and what to do, next to the paragraph on the post-merge run.
- `main.yaml`: the header comment names the four required checks. Comments only; no behaviour changes there.

A run that did not pass is recorded on **one** issue, "main-post-merge: a commit on main failed its post-merge run" (labels `bug`, `ci`, both of which exist): the commit, the run and the jobs that did not pass. The first failure opens it, later ones are comments. A commit is cleared when a re-run of its own run passes, and the issue closes when no commit recorded on it is failing.

## Decisions

A post-merge run tests only what its own merge reaches (bazel-diff against the first parent), and a merge that reaches nothing passes without running a test. ## #1555: what the pressure run's soak guard can honestly know

`preflight_no_soak` in `e2e/pressure/run.sh` looked for a `k6-soak-loader` DaemonSet and ran `pgrep -f 'soak/churn\.sh'`. Neither name is used any more, so the guard passed while a soak ran. `pgrep -f` also matches the command line of whatever waits on it.

The issue asks for a signal the external-harness contract names. I read `test/harnesscontract/external-harness.yaml` for one: it names **no identity for a load driver** (no ServiceAccount, label or priority class), and its `not_contract` section says the namespace, names and labels of a harness's workloads are the harness's own. So nothing in this repository can detect a soak, and this change does not invent a promise the contract does not make. The guard is now:

| Part | What it is | What it proves |
|---|---|---|
| `--no-soak-running` / `NO_SOAK_RUNNING=1` | Required for a real run. Checked before the cluster is asked anything. A `--dry-run` only warns. | Nothing the script verified: it is the operator's statement. |
| `SOAK_POD_SELECTOR` | Optional. Refuses while any pod in any namespace carries the selector. | As much as the selector. Unset (the default), no pod is looked for, and the script prints that. No default, because any default would be a guess. |
| Roll check | Refuses while a DaemonSet of the agent namespace is mid-roll (spec not observed, a pod not updated, a pod unavailable). | That no roll is in progress at that instant. A soak between two rolls passes it. |

Both checks fail closed (the old `kubectl ... >/dev/null 2>&1` read an API error as "no soak"). The `pgrep` is removed, not rewritten: a harness need not run on the machine the script runs on.

**This changes how the script is invoked:** a real run now aborts without `--no-soak-running`.

The limit is stated in the script header and in `e2e/pressure/README.md` ("The soak guard: what it can and cannot know").

Closes #1471

An agent wrote this pull request.

## What was wrong

The chart seeds the `default` MeshConfig once (a `lookup` skips it when one is live) and never renders it again, so that operators own it. As an object of the release it was in the manifest of the one revision that created it (normally the first; a later one when an upgrade found the object absent), in no later manifest, and still live (`helm.sh/resource-policy: keep`). `helm rollback` to that revision, `helm rollback <release> 1` on nearly every release, then fails:

```
Error: no MeshConfig with the name "default" found
```

**Measured** (kind, Kubernetes v1.35.8, Helm 3.18.4, the chart on `main`): install, an edit of the MeshConfig, upgrade, `helm rollback aether 1`. Revision 1's manifest holds one MeshConfig, revision 2's none; the rollback fails with the message above and leaves the release `failed` at revision 3; `helm rollback aether 2` then succeeds.

**Read in Helm 3.18.4** (`pkg/kube/client.go`, `Update`): for each object of the target manifest that is live, Helm takes the copy in the *current* manifest as the starting point of its patch and returns this error when there is none. `helm upgrade` does not hit it because it first adopts live objects that carry the release's ownership annotations; `helm rollback` has no such step. No hook ordering is involved.

## The fix

The seed is a Helm hook, `helm.sh/hook: pre-install,pre-upgrade`, so it is in no revision's manifest. The `lookup` guard is unchanged: the seed is rendered only when no MeshConfig is live.

- `pre-`, not `post-`: the agent pod stays in `ContainerCreating` until the controller has projected the MeshConfig into a ConfigMap, so under `--wait` a post-install hook would never run.
- `pre-upgrade` as well: an upgrade that finds the MeshConfig absent seeds it, as before.
- No rollback event. On a rollback Helm runs the hooks stored with the target revision, whatever is live; a seed with a rollback event would be created or applied
agent_prs.title: fix(chart, e2e): the seeded MeshConfig is a hook, so helm rollback to a release's first revision works (#1471)

issues.body:
The chart seeds the `default` MeshConfig on first install and guards it with `lookup` so later upgrades do not overwrite an operator's edits. The object is therefore in revision 1's manifest, absent from every later revision's manifest, and still live in the cluster. `helm rollback <release> 1` then fails:

```
Error: no MeshConfig with the name "default" found
```

Helm treats the object as one the target revision must create or patch, but the current revision does not own it. A rollback to any revision after the first works.

To decide: keep the seeded object out of Helm's ownership altogether (a hook, or `helm.sh/resource-policy: keep` with the object rendered on every revision while it is unmodified), or document that the first revision cannot be a rollback target.

Found on kind (v1.35, Helm 3.18.4) while measuring upgrade safety for #1464.

Closes #1462

## What was wrong

`e2e/soak/churn.sh` rolls `deployment/svc-1` … `svc-5` and scales `svc-5`, and the load addresses `svc-1` … `svc-4`, but no manifest for them was in the repository. A soak could not be set up from the repository alone, and a change to those workloads (the quiet start of #1461, for one) could not be reviewed. The pre-flight asked one thing of each of them: that it exists.

## What changes

- **`e2e/soak/svc.yaml`** defines the five: a Deployment and a ServiceAccount each, no Service (the registrar generates the mesh Service from the registered endpoints, as it does for `mixed-svc`). One multi-document file, like the other soak workloads. They are started quiet, the way `echo.yaml` is (#1395), and run the same two images by the same digests.
- **`churn.sh --preflight`** reads each of the five (one `get -o jsonpath` each) and refuses to start, naming the workload and the reason, when it is absent, has no replica, is not fully available or is mid-roll, has no `aether.io/managed` label on its pods, runs as a ServiceAccount other than its own name, has no readiness probe, or would not roll surge-first with `minReadySeconds` ≥ 10, a preStop sleep ≥ 10 s and a `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` of the sleep plus 2 s or more. On any of those it prints the `kubectl apply` that creates them. A server not started quiet is a `pre-flight note`, not a refusal: it costs log volume, it does not void a run.
- **`run.sh`**: the "no mesh Service for target(s)" line (the only check an `e2e`-mode run makes of the targets) now says where the workloads come from.
- **README**: step 0a of "Run" creates the workloads; "Files" describes `svc.yaml`.

### Why those checks

Each is a difference that would void a run and that nothing showed before T0:

| Difference | What it does to a soak |
|---|---|
| no replica | a roll of nothing is logged `ROLLED`; on `svc-5` the SHRINK aborts the run at T0+450m |
| not all replicas available | the run starts on a w

Closes #1491

Builds on #1490 (merged), which added the fourth reason, `tls_not_published`. The change is `e2e/soak/**` and one paragraph of `docs/runbook.md`.

## What was wrong

`e2e/soak/prober-grade.sh` failed its `UNPINNED` gate when `aether_agent_identity_cluster_unpinned_total` moved for any reason, and its text said `a TLS cluster was published without its server-identity pin`. Since #1479 and #1490 the counter is split by `reason`, and under two of the four (`trust_domain_unknown`, `tls_not_published`) the agent publishes **no TLS at all**. Every agent start is in that state for a moment, and the soak rolls the agents on purpose (T0+72 and the TRIPLE at T0+300). So a soak with no validation gap could fail this gate, with a text that was untrue.

## The verdict, per reason

| `reason` (the line's `class=`) | What the agent did | The gate |
|---|---|---|
| `no_namespace_metadata`, `pin_not_rendered` (`gap`) | published TLS that checks no server identity | **FAIL**, exit 1, on any movement of the counter and on any non-zero sample of the published gauge. The text names reason, count and nodes. |
| `trust_domain_unknown`, `tls_not_published` (`no_tls`) | published no TLS for those entries | reported with reason, count and nodes; **not a failure by itself**. FAIL only when the state stood for 300 s or more (below). A standing `tls_not_published` that the operator declared expected (`--expect-tls-not-published`) is reported and does not fail. |
| any other value (`unknown`) | an agent newer than the script | **FAIL** on any movement of the counter and on any non-zero sample of the gauge; the text says the script does not know the reason and names the two lists to add it to. |
| no `reason` label (`unlabelled`) | an agent from before #1424 | **FAIL** on any movement, with the text the gate always had, plus the count and the nodes. Its one series holds every reason, so the old rule is the only safe one. |

`UNPROVEN` (exit 2) still comes before `FAIL` (exit 1), in

`e2e/soak/prober-grade.sh` fails its UNPINNED gate when `aether_agent_identity_cluster_unpinned_total` moves for ANY reason, and its FAIL text says a TLS cluster was published without its server-identity pin. Since #1479/#1490 the counter is split by reason, and two of them (`trust_domain_unknown`, `tls_not_published`) are states in which the agent publishes no TLS yet: they are expected at an agent start, and a soak rolls the agents on purpose. So a soak can fail this gate, or report a failure whose text is untrue, on a run with no validation gap.

Decide the verdict per reason: `no_namespace_metadata` and `pin_not_rendered` fail; the two no-TLS reasons are reported (count, nodes, and whether they line up with the agent rolls in the churn log) without failing, or fail only when they persist past a bound. Fixtures for each, and the FAIL text must say which reason moved.

agent_prs.body:
## What was wrong

`.github/workflows/main.yaml` (the run after every push to `main`) has three jobs. What each does when an output it depends on was never set:

| Job | Depends on | An unset output, before this change |
|---|---|---|
| `diff` | nothing (no `if:`) | not applicable. Its own `steps.base.outputs.sha` being empty is the documented fallback to a full `//...` run, which widens the run |
| `test`, job level | `if: needs.diff.outputs.has_any == 'true'` | `'' == 'true'` is false: the job is **skipped and the run is green**, having built and tested nothing. This is #1501 |
| `test`, step `Unit tests` | `if: needs.diff.outputs.has_unit == 'true'` | already closed by #1493: the `impacted-lists` action runs earlier in the job and fails it when `has_unit` is not `true` or `false`. It only helps when the job runs at all |
| `refresh-pin-prs` | nothing: `if: always()`, no `needs`, reads no job output | not applicable |

## The fix

A new aggregate job `main` (`if: always()`, `needs: [diff, test]`) hands `toJSON(needs)` to `scripts/ci-gate.sh main`: a third rules table in the script that already decides the `ci` (#1486) and `proxy` (#1493) checks. It passes only when

- `diff` succeeded and wrote `true` or `false`, in those words, to `has_any`, `has_unit` and `has_integration`;
- `test` succeeded when `has_any` is `true` and was skipped when it is `false`;
- no job failed or was cancelled, and `needs` holds exactly the jobs the table names.

"Nothing impacted" is therefore three times `false` written by `diff`, never the absence of a value.

The script changes are what a workflow with no `changes` job needs: an empty `SWITCH` (nothing is switched off, the jobs always had to run), the list of `diff` outputs per table (`main.yaml` has no `has_e2e`), and the wording "runs on every push to main". The `ci` and `proxy` tables decide as before; their existing cases are unchanged and pass.

`refresh-pin-prs` is deliberately not in `needs`: it reads nothing another job write

agent_prs.body:
Closes #1483

## What was wrong

`aether.agent.xds.acked_tls_clusters{pin,reason}` is written when the proxy ACKs a cluster response. After an agent restart on a quiet node the gauge had no series until a cluster next changed.

The issue says the proxy "is owed no CDS response" in that state. That is not what happens on the wire, and it is where the fix is:

- go-control-plane answers the **first** wildcard request of a stream even when it has nothing to add and nothing to remove (`respondDelta`: "otherwise, envoy won't complete initialization").
- The proxy ACKs that empty response.

The pin history then gives that snapshot's counts to the gauge. When the stated versions differ, nothing changes: the difference is sent and the gauge moves on the ACK of that, as before. No claim is made without an ACK.

Three follow-ups to #1479 (the unpinned-cluster report). They are one pull request because they share one vocabulary: #1482 adds a `reason`, and the alert rules of #1481 and the runbook text of #1480 enumerate the reasons.

## What

### #1480: the NACK counters are seeded

`aether.agent.xds.nacks` and `aether.agent.xds.ack_wait_failures` were created by their first increment. A proxy that never rejected anything had no series, so "no NACKs" could not be told from "this agent reports nothing", and the runbook's published-versus-acknowledged reading of the SAN-pin gauges leans on that counter.

Both are now seeded at zero when the tracker is built, the way the unpinned counter is seeded per reason:

- `aether_agent_xds_nacks_total`: seven series per agent. One per resource type the agent serves (Listener, Cluster, ClusterLoadAssignment, RouteConfiguration, Secret, TypedExtensionConfig, each as its full `type.googleapis.com/…` URL) and `other`.
- `aether_agent_xds_ack_wait_failures_total`: four series (`present`/`absent` by `nack`/`timeout`).

The set of type URLs is closed. A NACK of a type outside it is counted under `other` and cannot open a series at runtime (nothing sends one today: the tracker only sees responses the agent's own server wrote). A test in the cache package holds the list to what a snapshot actually publishes, for the node proxy and for the edge, so a resource type added to the snapshot fails the build until it has a seeded series.

### #1482: no TLS published is not the validation gap

Before the node agent has its SVID nothing it publishes carries TLS (an HTTP cluster goes out bare, the TCP floor cluster is withheld). An entry whose endpoints carry no namespace was still counted and logged under `no_namespace_metadata`, the reason that otherwise means "TLS is served and checks no server identity".

**Choice: a fourth reason, `tls_not_published`**, not "do not count the entry while no TLS is published". Reaso

agent_prs.body:
Closes #1470

## What was wrong

`Supervisor.Run` started `watchConfig` on a goroutine and forked epoch 0 without waiting for that goroutine to create the fsnotify watcher and add the bootstrap directory to it. A bootstrap rewritten after epoch 0 had started and before the watch existed produced no event. The supervisor then did not hot-restart for it, and Envoy kept the old bootstrap until the next change.

The same gap is why `TestEnvoyChildSeesItsRestartEpoch/first_start_and_in-pod_hot_restart` failed once in CI ("config change did not trigger epoch 1" after 5 s): the test rewrites the bootstrap as soon as epoch 0 has recorded itself, and nothing guaranteed the watch was armed by then.

## What changes

- `Run` arms the watch itself, before the first fork (`armConfigWatch`: create the watcher, add the directory). Only the event loop (`watchConfig`) still runs on a goroutine. `inotify_add_watch` has returned before the fork, so every Envoy this supervisor starts reads the bootstrap after the kernel has started recording changes to it. A change is either read by that Envoy or reported.
- The first fork waits for the arming and nothing else (two system calls).
- A watch that cannot be set up behaves as before: the same two error lines, and the supervisor runs without the self-triggered hot restart. The watcher is now closed when adding the directory fails; it used to be closed by a `defer` in the goroutine.
- The cross-pod handoff, the bind-collision retry and the debounce are untouched. The watch is armed at the same point in `Run` where the goroutine used to be started, before `initStartEpoch`.

The issue offered a second option: compare the bootstrap against what epoch 0 was started with once the watch is armed. I did not add it. The supervisor never reads the bootstrap and keeps no hash or generation of it; a change is detected only by an fsnotify event, then debounced. With the watch armed before the fork there is no interval between "Envoy read the bootstrap"

issues.body:
`Supervisor.Run` starts `watchConfig` in a goroutine (`agent/internal/proxy/hotrestart/supervisor.go`, `go s.watchConfig(ctx, trigger)`) and forks epoch 0 without waiting for the watcher's `w.Add(dir)`. A bootstrap rewritten after epoch 0 starts but before the watch is armed produces no event, so the supervisor does not hot-restart for it until the next change.

This is also why `TestEnvoyChildSeesItsRestartEpoch/first_start_and_in-pod_hot_restart` is flaky: it failed once in CI on #1435 at `childenv_test.go:175`, "config change did not trigger epoch 1", after 5.06 s, and passed on re-run. A temporary 1 s sleep before `fsnotify.NewWatcher()` reproduces the same failure at the same line; 60 unmodified local runs had no failure.

Fix: arm the watch synchronously before the first fork, or compare the config against what epoch 0 was started with once the watch is armed. Either way the test then needs no timing margin.

## What changes

**#1459: the impacted targets are listed on the tree the test jobs build.**

- `diff` no longer checks out the pull request's head. It checks out what every other job of `ci.yaml` checks out: the run's commit, which on `pull_request` is the merge of the head into the base.
- `scripts/ci-merge-range.sh` (new) reads the range from that merge: its first parent (the base) to the merge itself. It refuses a checkout that is not the run's commit, and a merge whose second parent is not the pull request's head.
- `scripts/ci-impacted-targets.sh` refuses a `HEAD_SHA` that is not the commit checked out, and writes that commit next to the lists (`impacted_commit.txt`, part of the artifact).
- `.github/actions/impacted-lists` (new) is how `test`, `race`, `netns` and `integration` now get the lists: it downloads the artifact and runs `scripts/ci-impacted-lists.sh`, which fails when the lists were computed for another commit than the job's checkout.

**#1460: the `ci` check passes a skipped leg only when a job said so.**

- The `ci` job runs `scripts/ci-gate.sh` (new) on `toJSON(needs)` instead of the inline `contains(needs.*.result, 'failure') || contains(..., 'cancelled')`.
- `changes` must have written `control_plane=true` or `control_plane=false`. `diff` must have written `true` or `false` to each of `has_any`, `has_unit`, `has_integration` and `has_e2e`. Anything else, the empty string included, fails.
- Every job must then have ended the way those values say: run and succeed, or be skipped. "Nothing impacted" is `diff` writing `false` four times, and the job log says so (`decision: nothing impacted (diff wrote false to ...)`).
- A failed or cancelled job fails the check, as before. So does a job missing from `needs`, and a job in `needs` the script has no rule for.
- `scripts/ci-impacted-lists.sh` also fails on a missing list and on a `has_*` output that disagrees with its list. That closes the tw

issues.body:
Defence in depth after #1451, which made `scripts/ci-impacted-targets.sh` either set its outputs or fail:
- the `ci` aggregate accepts `skipped` jobs by design, so it relies on `diff` failing or setting outputs; it could require `has_any` to be exactly `true` or `false` whenever `diff` succeeded;

Closes #1443

## What was wrong

The supervisor's `--envoy-arg` startup check (`hotrestart.CheckExtraArgs`) had no table of Envoy's flags, so it could not tell a flag from a value. It compared every item with its reserved and once-only lists instead. Three consequences:

- **False refusals.** A value spelled like a refused argument was refused although Envoy takes it: `--service-node -c`, `--log-format --x=y`, `--service-cluster --service-cluster`.
- **A reserved flag could get through.** The pinned Envoy accepts a flag and its value in one item split by a space. `--envoy-arg="--socket-path @x"` and `--envoy-arg="--base-id 5"` matched no list entry as whole items, passed the check, and reached every fork. The first breaks every handoff; the second is a repeated flag, which Envoy refuses.
- **Anything not in the lists was passed through**: a misspelled flag, a stray word, a repeat of a flag the chart does not pass, a value flag with no value. Each fails at every fork instead of once at startup.

  - an empty item and a lone `-` are accepted and ignored;
  - everything after `--` / `--ignore_rest` is ignored;
  - an `h` anywhere in a single-dash item with no space is read as `-h`: `-xh` and `-lwhatever

**#1469, `e2e/soak/prober-grade.sh`.** The grade built its audit from the window query alone, and that query returns only the series that have a sample in the window. A series the query at T0 returned and the window query did not was in no line and no verdict:

- an agent that exported nothing for the whole window left the unpinned gate at `PASS` on the remaining nodes, exit 0.

It could not be fixed by adding every such series: the query at T0 answers with a series' *last* sample, up to five minutes old, so a pod replaced a few minutes before the run looks the same.

**The rule.** The grade asks two more instant queries at T0, `timestamp(<metric>)`, and goes by the age of the sample of each series that has none in the window:

| at most 120 s old (two export intervals) | alive at T0, silent for the window | in `PODS at_start`, a `GONE` line | `UNPINNED silent: node=… job=…`, gate `UNPROVEN`, exit 2, unless another series of the same node and job (a replacement pod) has samples in the window |
| older, or of unknown age | it had stopped before T0 | an `ENDED` line; no verdict | `UNPINNED ended: …`; no verdict |

issues.body:
The prober rate-limits its `AETHER_PROBE_FAIL` lines and closes each window with a `suppressed` summary. When the summary is flushed at shutdown, its `t` is the flush time plus one window (`p.fails.flush(time.Now().Add(failLogWindow))` in `prober/internal/prober/prober.go`, which passes a future `now` to force every open window closed, and `closeWindow` prints that `now`). The last line a prober writes is therefore dated 60 s after the pod stopped.

`e2e/soak/prober-grade.sh` tolerates it (a summary up to two minutes past the window end is treated as a boundary summary, #1458), but the line misleads anyone reading the log, and a log query bounded at the pod's stop time misses it.

issues.body:
`e2e/soak/prober-grade.sh` builds its audit from the range query over the window. A series that the T0 instant query returns but that has no sample inside the window is left out entirely:

- a prober pod deleted right after T0 is missing from `PODS at_start` instead of being reported `GONE`;
- an agent that exports nothing for the whole window does not make the unpinned-cluster gate `UNPROVEN`: the gate can report `PASS` from the remaining nodes.

A missing node is visible to a reader (`UNPINNED … nodes=N`, one line per node, `PODS at_end`) but not to the exit status, so the gate can pass on less than the fleet.

Not a one-line fix: the T0 instant query also returns a series whose last sample is up to five minutes old (the lookback), so "present at T0, silent in the window" is also what a pod replaced just before T0 looks like, and that ordinary case must not become exit 2. It needs a rule to tell the two apart (the age of the T0 sample, or expecting one unpinned series per node at the window's end, checked against the node list) and a fixture for each case, each seen red.

Raised in review of #1458, which introduced the audit.

#1363 removes the chart-version label from pod templates, but a deploy of a new commit still rolls every workload, because every image the chart pins by digest changes with every commit, whether or not its code changed.

**Why it matters:** every workload runs at least one of these images (the proxy DaemonSet through `install-supervisor`), so each deploy is a full roll including a hot restart of every node proxy, which is where the handoff stalls are (#1093, #1320).

**Options to weigh:** keep the commit out of the image config and the binary (record it as an OCI annotation on the index or as a referrer instead, so the manifest digest follows content); or stamp only a content-derived version. Either touches #837 and whatever reads the stamped version (`--version` output, build-ID checks, the published-artifact verifier that finds images by commit tag — tags are separate from digests and can stay). issues.body:
With the chart default `namespace.create=true` and the release stored in the namespace the chart creates (`-n aether-system`), a first install fails whichever way it is spelled:

| Command | Result |
|---|---|
| `helm upgrade --install … -n aether-system --create-namespace` | `namespaces "aether-system" already exists`; release left `failed`, namespace without pod-security labels |
| the same without `--create-namespace` | `create: failed to create: namespaces "aether-system" not found` (Helm stores the release record in the namespace before creating anything) |
| namespace created first with plain `kubectl create namespace` | `exists and cannot be imported into the current release: invalid ownership metadata` |

What works: pre-creating the namespace with Helm's ownership label and annotations (three `kubectl` commands), or `--create-namespace --set namespace.create=false` (the namespace then has no pod-security labels and they must be applied by hand), or storing the release in another namespace.

talos-main and every e2e script run `namespace.create=false`, which is why this was never seen.

**Decision needed:** default `namespace.create` to `false` and document creating and labelling the namespace (what we actually run); or keep the default and document the adoption pre-step; or have the chart apply the pod-security labels some other way.
