agent_prs.body:
Bottom of a three-PR stack for #1378 (every merge to main gives every image a new digest, so every deploy rolls every workload). This one removes the first of the two causes; the next removes the second; the third adds the CI check.

Part of #1378
Closes #1429

## What

Seven binaries (agent, mesh-dns, proxy-supervisor, uds-csi, controller, prober, registrar) linked the commit in as `Version`, through `x_defs` with `{STABLE_GIT_VERSION}`. Under `--stamp` each of them, and the image layer built from it, changed with every commit, including a docs-only one.

- `Version` is now the binary's own GNU build ID: the content-derived note `//bazel/buildid` already writes into every shipped binary, read from the running executable by a new stdlib-only package, `//common/buildinfo`. The seven `x_defs` are gone.
- The same seven components answer `--version` (#1429): build ID, main package, Go toolchain. They exit before starting anything. The stdlib-only probe binaries and the CNI plugin stay flagless.
- `charts/README.md` no longer says the chart's `appVersion` matches a version embedded in the binaries; the runbook gets "Which build is this binary".

## What reads `Version`, and what an operator loses

Read in the code, every use:

| Reader | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| OTel `service.version` (all seven) | `git describe` of the commit | the binary's build ID, 40 hex characters |
| uds-csi CSI `vendor_version` and its `starting` log line | the same | the build ID |

Nothing else reads it. No dashboard or alert in this repository refers to `service.version`.

What is lost: `service.version` no longer names a commit, so telemetry alone does not say which commit a pod runs. What replaces it:

- Two pods with the same `service.version` run byte-identical binaries; a value that changes across a deploy means that component's code changed.
- Commit to image: the `dev-<sha>` tag and the per-commit chart, which pins every image by digest.
- Image to commit: the signature's

## What changes

The supervisor's `envoy thread stall` line said an Envoy thread was starved and that the node was busy. It did not say who was on the CPUs, and #1320 and #1389 both stopped there. A line with a `[starved]` thread now also names the top CPU consumers on the node over the stall:

```
envoy thread stall epoch=210 pid=15 windowMs=1000 thresholdMs=200
  threads=["wrk:worker_0[starved] cpu=310ms runq=611ms blocked=0ms"]
  nodeBusyPct=99.1 ... nodePSICPUSomeMs=1010
  topCgroups="/podruntime/kubelet=1240ms /kubepods/burstable/pod0f3c1a2b-1111-4222-8333-444455556666=820ms /podruntime/runtime=180ms /=95ms"
  topCgroupsOverMs=1000
  topProcs="unavailable: /proc shows only this pod's PID namespace (no hostPID)"
  trackedEpochs=1 handoffPeer=-1
```

This line is an illustration of the format. It is not from a cluster: the change has not run on a cluster.

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `topCgroups` | `<cgroup path>=<n>ms`, largest first, at most `--stall-top-consumers` (5). CPU time from cgroup v2 `cpu.stat` `usage_usec`. Entries do not overlap: each excludes the cgroups below it that have their own entry; a pod is one entry; `/` is what was charged to the root cgroup itself after the listed cgroups below it are taken out (commonly kernel threads; a userspace task attached to the root is counted there too). |
| `topCgroupsOverMs` | The interval the figures cover: that line's stall, not the window, starting where the wait began. A runqueue wait is charged when it ends, so a 5 s wait is reported in the second it ended and a 500 ms wait seen 100 ms into a window began 400 ms before it. The start is inferred per starved thread (the tick the wait was seen on, minus the wait) and the consumers are taken from the last one-second sample at or before the earliest start. Two epochs starved in the same window each get their own interval from one sample. It is the interval actually measured. |
| `topCgroupsTruncated` | `true`, and only then on the line, when

`e2e/soak/prober-grade.sh --dir <run dir> --prometheus <URL>` (or `--prometheus-service <ns>/<svc>:<port>`, through the API server with the run's own context). The endpoint is a parameter and has no default.

- T0 is the churn driver's start line in the run's `churn.log`, the window 8 h. An e2e run has no churn log: `T_LOAD` + `DURATION_S` of `run.env`.
- Four instant queries, printed with the time each was evaluated at: each metric at T0, and `metric[<window>s]` at the window's end, which returns the raw samples.
- Per series the count is the sum of the steps between samples, starting from the value at T0. A series absent at T0 starts from 0. A sample below the one before it is a reset: the new value is counted whole and the reset is printed. A prober pod replaced mid-run is counted up to its last sample.
- Output: totals per tier and result with the success rate as the control, every non-success per tier, result and source node, each series born in the window, each reset, the pod set, a `PROBER verdict=` line and one `VERDICT` line. Exit 0 pass, 1 something to attribute, 2 unproven; 2 comes first, so a `FAIL` beside a count that cannot be trusted is exit 2.
- `--logs-file` or `--logs-url` adds the cross-check against `AETHER_PROBE_FAIL` lines (detail lines plus the `suppressed` counts). A `suppressed` summary carries the time its minute was closed, up to two minutes after the failures it counts; one closed within two minutes after either end of the window is printed as a boundary summary, left out of the sum, and the row is `UNPROVEN` when the counters lie between the two sums.

issues.body:
bash 5.2.21 drops a trapped signal that arrives while it is expanding a command substitution. It prints `trap: line 2: unexpected EOF while looking for matching ')'`, the handler does not run, and the script carries on. Seen 2 times in 1,680 timed TERMs, both in `out()`'s `$(date …)` in `e2e/soak/restart-watch.sh`; the process had no pending signal afterwards. It orphans nothing, but a single TERM can be ignored. Every trapping script in `e2e/soak/` (`churn.sh` too) has the exposure.

Options: avoid `$(…)` in the hot path of trapping scripts (`printf '%(…)T'` for timestamps needs no subshell); or document that stopping a soak script means sending TERM until it exits. PR #1417's test sends its in-command TERMs from the fake kubectl to avoid the bug.

Reported by the soak harness work (PR #1417), not changed there.

Exit 0 pass, 1 something to attribute, 2 unproven; 2 comes first, so a `FAIL` beside a count that cannot be trusted is exit 2.

## A failed probe's destination (#1391)

`aether_probe_requests_total` has no destination. Its `node` is the node the prober runs on, the source, and `target` is the name it asked for. A destination label would be a series per endpoint, so the metric stays as it is and its description now says that `node` is the source.

The client cannot name the destination either. On the mesh its connection ends at the node proxy of its own node, and the proxy adds no response header that names its upstream. So the `AETHER_PROBE_FAIL` line gets what the client does know, which costs no series:

| key | what it is |
|---|---|
| `dial` | the address of the last connect attempt (what the name resolved to); empty on a reused connection and when the lookup failed |
| `remote` | the far end of the connection the request was sent on: `127.0.0.1:18081` for liveness and reachability, the mesh Service address for mesh_dns. Never the pod that would have answered |
| `local` | this end of it, which is the access log's `downstream_remote_address` |
| `trace_id` | the trace id of the `traceparent` header the probe sent |

`trace_id` is the key to the proxies' own rows for that request:

```
log_name:aether_access_logs AND traceparent:"00-<trace_id>-"*
```

The source proxy's row has the endpoint it chose (`upstream_host`); a `reporter:destination` row on another node means the request arrived there. A probe that failed in `dns` or `connect` has no row, and `dial` is all there is. The runbook has the procedure ("Where a failed probe went").

All four keys are on every detail line, and empty for a probe that was never sent (`saturated`).

## What was wrong

When `proxy.concurrency` is `0` (the chart default) the supervisor passes no `--concurrency`, and at a cross-pod handoff it has to predict how many workers its own Envoy will run, to compare with the live predecessor's count. It predicted the number of online CPUs. The pinned Envoy does not do that. So a proxy with a CPU limit or a restricted CPU mask compared, say, 4 with a predecessor's 2, concluded the worker count had changed, and drained the predecessor and started fresh instead of hot-restarting, on every roll. The chart's default proxy resources have no CPU limit, so a default install was not affected; a deployment that sets `proxy.concurrency` explicitly was not affected either.

## Envoy's rule, read from the pinned source

`source/server/options_impl.cc`, `options_impl_platform_linux.cc` and `cgroup_cpu_util.cc` at the pin (`726d7ac`):

- Flag absent: `max(1, min(hardware threads, CPU affinity, cgroup CPU limit))`.
- Hardware threads: `std::thread::hardware_concurrency()`.
- CPU affinity: `CPU_COUNT` of `sched_getaffinity()` into one `cpu_set_t`. A failed call, a count of zero, or a count above the hardware threads is ignored.
- cgroup CPU limit: found through `/proc/self/mountinfo` and `/proc/self/cgroup`. A cgroup v1 hierarchy with the `cpu` controller wins over v2. v2 reads `cpu.max`, v1 reads `cpu.cfs_quota_us` and `cpu.cfs_period_us`. The result is quota / period rounded **down**, with a floor of 1. `max`, `-1`, a missing file and malformed content are all "no limit". Only the process's own cgroup is read, no ancestor. `ENVOY_CGROUP_CPU_DETECTION=false` (any case) in Envoy's environment turns this term off.
- `--concurrency N` is taken as `max(1, N)` whatever the mask or the limit. So `--concurrency 0` is one worker, not "use the default" (as #1433 measured). `--cpuset-threads` no longer changes anything.

agent_prs.title: fix(supervisor): the predicted worker count follows Envoy's own rule (cores, CPU affinity, cgroup limit) (#1442, #1444)

issues.body:
`agent/internal/proxy/hotrestart/concurrencychange.go` (`onlineCPUsPath`, `successorConcurrency`) assumes that without `--concurrency` Envoy runs one worker per ONLINE CPU. At the pinned Envoy the default is `OptionsImplPlatform::getCpuCount()`: the minimum of hardware threads, the process's CPU affinity and the cgroup CPU limit. Measured: under `taskset -c 0,1` on a 20-CPU machine Envoy ran 2 workers.

So with `proxy.concurrency: 0` (the chart default) and a proxy CPU limit or a restricted affinity, the supervisor compares a wrong count with the predecessor's, concludes the worker count changed, and (with hot-restart-on-concurrency-change handling) takes the drain-and-fresh-start path instead of a hot restart, on every roll. Not reproduced on a cluster. A deployment that sets `proxy.concurrency` explicitly is not affected.

Fix: compute the default the way Envoy does (affinity mask and cgroup v2 `cpu.max` as well as online CPUs), or read the running predecessor's actual count and compare against the explicit flag only. `docs/configuration.md` also says `proxy.concurrency: 0` gives "one worker per core"; correct it to the minimum of cores, affinity and cgroup limit.

Reported by the supervisor flag work (PR #1433), not changed there.

## #1434: what was actually wrong

The issue says the registrar has no anti-affinity or topology spread. It has: since #635 the registrar and the edge render a soft hostname spread, and the controller a preferred anti-affinity term about its own replicas. The cluster the issue was observed on carries that constraint on the registrar Deployment, and both replicas (same ReplicaSet, created 28 s apart in one rollout) were on one of five workers anyway. So the question became why a soft rule that is there loses.

Measured on kind (pinned v0.33.0 / Kubernetes 1.35.8, one tainted control plane plus workers). The pods are stand-ins: the chart's rendered `tolerations`, `affinity`, `topologySpreadConstraints`, labels, selector and rollout strategy, with one `pause` container. The three Deployments are rolled together, as a chart upgrade rolls them, twenty times per variant; the number is how many rollouts ended with both replicas of a Deployment on one node (controller / edge / registrar).

| Pod templates | 2 workers | 3 workers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `main` (measured at 2.4.18; #1436 did not touch these fields) | 8 / 5 / 10 | 1 / 0 / 5 |
| `main` without the controller's "off the registrars' node" term | 0 / 6 / 2 | 0 / 0 / 1 |
| `matchLabelKeys` added, that term kept (my first attempt) | 9 / 0 / 11 | 1 / 0 / 3 |
| **this PR**: `matchLabelKeys` added, that term gone | **0 / 0 / 0** | **0 / 0 / 0** |

1. **The controller's default affinity** preferred nodes without a registrar (#629). The scheduler applies a preferred anti-affinity term in both directions, so each new registrar was also pushed off the nodes holding a controller. Closes #1431

## The defect, reproduced first

The issue was read from code. Before changing anything I reproduced it in a test: the unfixed injector, on the client stack the controller-runtime manager builds (a real informer cache, the cache-backed client), against a small fake apiserver that answers 403 for every verb on `mutatingwebhookconfigurations`. Then I rotated the trust bundle and waited 8 seconds.

| Claim in the issue | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `inject()` never returns | Confirmed. The cached `Get` never reached the apiserver (0 `get` requests, 3 `list` attempts by the informer). |
| No `webhook caBundle injection failed` line | Confirmed. The injector's whole log was the one `injected SPIRE trust bundle into webhook caBundle` line for the validating webhook. |
| The validating webhook is not refreshed on a rotation | Confirmed. It still carried the pre-rotation bundle. |
| The `cache-sync` readiness check fails | Confirmed. `cache.WaitForCacheSync`, which that check calls, returned false. |

All four hold with controller-runtime v0.25.2. None was reproduced on a cluster.

## The fix

- **Reads are uncached.** The injector reads the two objects through the manager's API reader. That is two single-object GETs per pass, and a pass runs only on a trust-bundle change or a retry. No informer is created on either resource.
- **Every call is bounded.** One configuration's read and write share a 15 s context, so no reader can park the loop.
- **The two configurations are independent.** Each is read, written, reported and retried on its own. The old code returned on the first error, so a failing validating configuration also left the mutating one un-injected.
- **Failures are retried with backoff**, doubling from 1 s to 1 min. Before, a failure waited for the next trust-bundle rotation.
- **Failures are visible.** Each one logs `webhook caBundle injection failed` at ERROR with `kind`, `webhookConfig`, `reason` (`get`, `update`, `trust_bundle`), `retryIn` and the
agent_prs.title: fix(controller): the webhook caBundle injector cannot hang, and one webhook's failure does not stop the other's refresh (#1431)

issues.body:
`controller/internal/meshconfig/cabundle.go`: the injector runs on the leader, patches the validating webhook configuration, then does a `Get` on the mutating one through the manager's CACHED client. If that informer can never list (forbidden, as in #1411, or any unsyncable informer), the cached `Get` waits for the sync with no timeout and `inject()` never returns.

Consequences, read from the code (controller-runtime v0.25.2), not reproduced on a cluster:
- the injector's own `webhook caBundle injection failed` line is never logged; the only signal is client-go's reflector reporting the forbidden list;
- because the loop never comes back, the VALIDATING webhook's caBundle is written once and not refreshed on a SPIRE trust-bundle rotation while that leader lives;
- the `cache-sync` readiness check waits on every informer, so the leader replica should go NotReady.

#1426 removes the one known way into this state (the missing RBAC rule). The injector should still not be able to hang: read through the API reader, or bound the call with a timeout so it errors, logs and retries. Unit test with a client whose `Get` blocks.

Reported by the #1411 work (PR #1426), not changed there.

## What changes

The OPA preset's sidecar now runs `opa run --server --watch … /policy/policy.rego`, always (no value, no switch), and the `checksum/opa-policy` annotation from #1367 is gone from the proxy pod template. Changing `proxy.authzSidecar.opa.policy` changes the ConfigMap only: the running sidecars reload it and no proxy pod is replaced, so there is no Envoy hot restart for a policy change.

No validation is added, by the owner's decision: checking a policy before it is applied is the job of whoever updates it. The docs say so and give the commands.

**What an operator sees on upgrade:** with the OPA preset on, the upgrade to chart 2.4.19 rolls the proxy DaemonSet once (the annotation leaves the pod template and the sidecar gains `--watch`). With the preset off, or with a bring-your-own sidecar, the render is byte-identical to `main`. After that, a policy change is fleet-wide within about a minute and is **not staged**: there is no node-by-node roll to stop at a bad policy any more.

Chart `2.4.19` (`main` took 2.4.18 with #1426 while this was in progress).

`launchEnvoy` started every Envoy with `--use-dynamic-base-id`. With hot restart on, Envoy creates `/dev/shm/envoy_shared_memory_<base id * 10>` at startup and does not remove it when it stops. The dynamic base id is a random 28-bit number, so no later Envoy ever reuses the name and each file stays for good. `/dev/shm` is a tmpfs, so they are held in memory until someone deletes them or the machine restarts.

| `//agent/test/mtlspool:mtlspool_test`, before | 37 | 0 | 37 | 0 | **37** |
| `//agent/test/mtlspool:mtlspool_test`, after | 37 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| `//agent/test/envoy_validate:envoy_validate_test` | 14 | 12 (the other 2 are `--version`) | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| `//agent/test/envoyargs:envoyargs_test` | 88 | 86 (the other 2 serve with `--disable-hot-restart`) | 0 | 0 | 0 |

Every Envoy the test harness starts leaves a hot-restart shared-memory file behind in `/dev/shm` (`envoy_shared_memory_<base id>0`), and nothing removes it when the test stops Envoy. They accumulate without bound on a developer machine and for the life of a CI runner; a stress run (`--runs_per_test`, the flake-fix recipe) creates tens of thousands in a day. `/dev/shm` is a tmpfs, so they are held in memory.

**Probable source (not yet measured per target):** `agent/test/mtlspool/harness_test.go` starts every Envoy with `--use-dynamic-base-id`, which gives each one its own shared-memory region. Other candidates to measure: `envoy --mode validate` runs (`agent/test/envoy_validate`, `agent/test/envoyargs`) and the supervisor tests that start a real Envoy.

**Fix**
- Measure first: run each Envoy-starting test target once and count new `/dev/shm/envoy_shared_memory_*` files per target.
- Tests that are not about hot restart start Envoy with `--disable-hot-restart`: no shared memory at all, and many Envoys can still run in parallel (the only reason the dynamic base id is there). Confirm no test in the package depends on hot-restart behaviour.
- A test that does need hot restart records the base id Envoy chose and removes its file in cleanup.
- A guard: the harness's test run asserts the number of `envoy_shared_memory_*` files is the same after as before; red on today's code.

This pull request was written by an agent (Claude Code). It fixes #1411. It does **not** change anything for #1412 and does not close it: see "About #1412" below for why, and for what the owner needs to decide.

Three things depend on "the pod-mutating webhook exists":

|---|---|---|

With `controller.webhook.spire=true`, `namespaceInjection=true` and `injectPodNdots=false`, the controller is told to maintain the configuration's caBundle and has no permission to. ## What changed

**The restart watchdog leaves nothing behind (#1386).** `restart-watch.sh` waited between samples with `sleep N &`, `SLEEP_PID=$!`, `wait "$SLEEP_PID"`, and a trap that killed `$SLEEP_PID`. Two moments left the sleep running:

- a TERM just after them: the trap sends its kill and the sleep is sometimes still there.

The wait now has no child process at all: `read -t` on a private fifo, in two-second slices. TERM and INT are also trapped from the script's first line, so a `kubectl` call in the foreground is waited for instead of orphaned (this matters for `--preflight`, which had no trap).

Closes #1377

Test code only (`agent/test/mtlspool`). No production file changes and no test case is removed. Written by an agent.

## The flake

`freePort` listened on `127.0.0.1:0`, closed the socket, and wrote the number into Envoy's bootstrap. Between that close and Envoy's own bind the port belonged to nobody, so a test process running in parallel could be handed it. Every Envoy the package starts took its listener and admin ports this way.

Reproduced on unchanged `main` by running the built test binary 16 at a time. Three outcomes, all the same cause:

- Envoy logs `cannot bind '127.0.0.1:<port>': Address already in use` and exits; the test waits 30 s and reports `envoy never listened`.
- The same on `dest_h3`: the probe was TCP-only, and the HTTP/3 listener binds the number on UDP.
- The other process is another test's Envoy. Both set `SO_REUSEPORT`, so the bind succeeds, `listen()` fails (`cannot listen() errno=98`), and the wait for "something accepts on this port" is satisfied by the other test's proxy. The test then fails later with `no 200 through the source proxy`.

With listeners delivered over LDS the failed bind only rejects the listener and Envoy stays up. In the one such run seen, the port now belonged to another test's Envoy admin endpoint, and the test's first request came back `200` with the "Envoy Admin" HTML page.

## The change

- Every listener and the admin endpoint are configured with port 0 (`envoyPicksPort`), so the kernel assigns the port inside Envoy's own `bind`. The harness reads the admin address from `--admin-address-path` and each listener's bound address from the admin endpoint's `/listeners`. `freePort` and `waitListening` are gone.
- One launcher, `launchEnvoy`, replaces the four copies of the start-and-wait code (static bootstrap, ADS bootstrap, the QUIC selection harness, the cost harness).
- Startup waits end as soon as Envoy exits, and their message carries the end of Envoy's own output. A bind that fails now reports in un

issues.body:
`freePort` in `agent/test/mtlspool` listens on `:0`, closes, and hands the number to Envoy later. Another process can take the port in between. It probes TCP only, while the h3 listeners bind the same number on UDP.

**Measured** (PR #1370's new `TestAccessLogConnectionTiming`): with 4 parallel test jobs, 1 of 20 runs failed with `envoy never listened on 127.0.0.1:43965` after the 30 s wait; 30 of 30 serial runs passed. Every test in the package uses the helper.

Fix (test-only): let Envoy bind port 0 and read the bound port back (admin `/listeners`), or hold the listener and pass the fd; whichever the harness can do. Prove it twice: a stress run with zero failures and a mutation showing the test can still fail.

## The problem

The supervisor passes some Envoy flags itself on every fork. The pinned Envoy refuses a flag given twice (`PARSE ERROR: Argument: (--base-id) Argument already set!`). So an `--envoy-arg` that repeated one of them passed the startup check and then failed every fork. Only `--admin-address-path` was refused at startup.

## What changed

- **One list.** `agent/internal/proxy/hotrestart/envoyargs.go` holds the flags the supervisor passes, as constants, and a table `reservedEnvoyFlags` with what owns each one. `buildEnvoyCmd` and the `--mode validate` run now build their command lines from the same constants.
- **`hotrestart.CheckExtraArgs`** refuses each reserved flag in `--envoy-arg`, in the `--flag value` and the `--flag=value` spellings. The error names the flag and the supervisor option or chart value to change instead. `supervisorcmd.checkEnvoyArgs` calls it at startup, as before.
- **Reserved flags:** `-c` / `--config-path`, `--base-id`, `--restart-epoch`, `--drain-time-s`, `--parent-shutdown-time-s`, `--admin-address-path`, and `--mode`. `--mode` is on the list because the supervisor passes `--mode validate` when it checks a changed bootstrap.
- **`--concurrency` stays allowed once.** The chart passes it for `proxy.concurrency`. A second `--concurrency` is refused at startup with an error that names `proxy.concurrency`.
- **#1375.** `concurrencyArg` used to return the last of several `--concurrency` values, and its comment said Envoy's parser keeps the last. It does not. `concurrencyArg` now returns an error for a repeat (`errRepeatedConcurrency`) and the comment says what Envoy does. One existing test case (`--concurrency 2 --concurrency=3` gives 3) changed to expect that error.
- Docs: `docs/configuration.md` lists the reserved flags; `docs/runbook.md` points to it; the `--envoy-arg` help text says the same.

Nothing under `charts/` changed. No dependency was added.

Same approach as #1367: three helpers, `prober.selectorLabels` (unchanged), `prober.podLabels` (selector labels + `part-of` + `managed-by`, used by the pod template), `prober.labels` (pod labels + chart + version, used by object metadata). The DaemonSet, ServiceAccount and Namespace objects keep both labels.

The `aether.*.labels` helpers put `helm.sh/chart: aether-<version>` on every workload's **pod template**, not only on the workload object. Any chart version bump therefore changes every pod template and rolls every pod: 6 workloads by default, 7 with the edge. **Options**
1. Keep `helm.sh/chart` on the workload's own metadata and drop it from the pod template labels (selector labels are unaffected: `helm.sh/chart` must not be in a selector anyway). Pods then roll only when their spec changes.
2. Leave it and document that every upgrade is a full roll.

Check before choosing: whether anything selects or groups pods by that label (dashboards, the soak grader, the prober), and what the first upgrade does (it rolls everything once, to remove the label).

issues.body:
## Finding

`listener.<prefix>.udp.downstream_rx_datagram_dropped`, and the "Kernel dropped N datagram(s)" warning, over-report after a hot restart. Found while measuring #1332.

## Mechanism (read at the pinned Envoy)

The count comes from `SO_RXQ_OVFL`, which is cumulative for the lifetime of the **socket**. `UdpListenerImpl::packets_dropped_` starts at 0 in each **process**. A hot-restarted child inherits the parent's socket, so at its first read it reports the socket's whole history as new drops.

## Measured (kind, pinned proxy image)

- A roll with 743 real kernel drops (`/proc/net/udp`, `Udp: RcvbufErrors` in the pod netns): the stat read 1486, and the child logged 731 + 12 at parent exit.
- The next roll, with 0 real drops: the child still logged "Kernel dropped 273" and "21", and the stat read 294.

## Why it matters

- Any alert or soak gate on this counter fires on every proxy roll after the first real drop on that socket.
- It changes how the #1332 talos numbers read: the "17/8 on the child at exit" were lifetime totals of the two sockets, not drops during that handoff.

## Kernel truth to use meanwhile

`/proc/net/udp` drops and `Udp: RcvbufErrors` in the pod's network namespace.

## Options

- Do not gate or alert on this stat across a hot restart; use the kernel counters.
- A carried patch that seeds `packets_dropped_` from the socket's current `SO_RXQ_OVFL` value at inheritance. Whether to raise it upstream is the owner's call.

agent_prs.body:
Docs and one rule file. No behaviour change in any binary (the only Go edit is a comment in `registrar/internal/server/metrics.go`).

## #1322: the divergence expression

The runbook's expression counted hashes over the bare `aether_registrar_snapshot_content` selector. `content_hash` is a label, so a content change ends one series and starts another. The registrar stops exporting the old one, but OTLP has no staleness marker, so Prometheus returns it for the 5-minute lookback and every replica shows two hashes after every change.

It had a second fault: `aether_registrar_writebehind_queue_depth` is recorded only when an intent is queued or flushed. Until the first one the series is missing (it is missing on talos-main now), `and on() (max(...) == 0)` is empty, and the expression cannot be true at all.

New expression, in the runbook and as `AetherRegistrarSnapshotDiverged` in the new `docs/observability/registrar-alerts.yml`:

```promql
count by (job, revision) (
  count_values by (job, content_hash) (
    "revision",
    aether_registrar_snapshot_revision
    * ignoring (content_hash) group_right ()
    (
      aether_registrar_snapshot_content
      and
      (
        timestamp(aether_registrar_snapshot_content)
        == ignoring (content_hash) group_left ()
        max without (content_hash) (timestamp(aether_registrar_snapshot_content))
      )
    )
  )
) > 1
unless on (job) (max by (job) (aether_registrar_writebehind_queue_depth) > 0)
```

Closes #1350

## What was wrong

`downstreamIdleTimeout = 5 * time.Minute` set the downstream idle timeout of every HTTP connection manager the agent generates. The value was chosen for the mesh inbound, whose client is a peer proxy that idles its pools out at 30 s. On the listeners where the client is the pod's application, the rule is the opposite one: the server's idle timeout must exceed the client's, because HTTP/1.1 has no GOAWAY. A request written onto a kept-alive connection the proxy is closing at that instant is lost, and a client that does not retry on a reused-connection failure sees a reset (1 request in 270,000 in the issue).

## What this changes

Option 1 of the issue. `buildHTTPConnectionManager` no longer has an idle timeout of its own: every caller passes one, so a new listener has to say who its downstream is. Two Go constants in `agent/internal/xds/proxy/networkfilter.go`, no chart value and no flag:

- `peerFacingIdleTimeout = 5 * time.Minute`
- `appFacingIdleTimeout = time.Hour` (Envoy's default, now stated)

Nothing under `charts/` is touched.

agent_prs.body:
Closes #1329

## What

New registrar gauge `aether.registrar.snapshot.content_hash` (Prometheus: `aether_registrar_snapshot_content_hash`) whose **value** is the snapshot's content hash. One series per replica, no label that changes, so a content change moves the value and nothing is left in Prometheus's 5-minute lookback.

- **Value**: the first 13 hex digits of the 16-digit content hash, as an integer in `[0, 2^52)`. `snapshotversion.ContentHashValue` does the conversion, next to the existing version parser (no new parser: it takes the hash `ContentHash()` / `State.ContentHash` already yield).
- **Bit budget**: a float64 has a 53-bit significand, so every integer up to 2^53 is exact and 53 bits would fit. I kept 52 because it is a whole number of hex digits: `printf '%013x' <value>` is the start of the `<hash>` in a version string.
- **Collision**: two replicas serving different contents report the same value with probability 2^-52 (about 2.2e-16) per compared pair. It is a divergence check between a few replicas at one revision, not an identifier. The resume token still compares all 16 digits.
- **Where it is recorded**: in the existing `ObserveSnapshot` callback, from the same single `Snapshot.State()` read as the revision gauges, so the hash and revision of one collection always describe the same contents. The hash itself is still computed under the mutation lock; nothing new runs there.
- **Every version form**: clean `<rev>.<hash>`, dirty `<rev>+<hash>` and `hash:<hash>` all report the hash of what is served now.
- **kubernetes backend**: the gauge is reported (it names the contents), `snapshot_revision` is not, so the rule returns nothing there. Two replicas can differ briefly on that backend because health derives from each replica's clock, so it is for reading by hand and is not alerted on.
- **Old metric**: `aether.registrar.snapshot.content{content_hash}` is still exported, marked deprecated in its description, the code comment, the README and the runboo

issues.body:
Follow-up to #1322 (fixed in the rule by pairing on `timestamp()`, PR #1328). The root cause is that `aether_registrar_snapshot_content{content_hash}` carries the hash as a label: when the hash changes, the old series stops being reported but stays visible for Prometheus's 5-minute lookback, and the OTel Go SDK cannot send a staleness marker for an attribute set an observable gauge stopped reporting. A hash label on the revision gauge would have the same problem.

What would work: a gauge whose VALUE is the hash (the top 52 bits fit a float64 exactly), one series per replica, so divergence is `count(count_values(...)) > 1` with no staleness trick. It is a new metric plus a rule migration (runbook, `docs/observability/registrar-alerts.yml`, the GitOps rule and its promtool tests), keeping the old series for one release.

## 1. The tag listing retries like the other lookups (#1337)

`registry_all_tags` (`scripts/registry-lib.sh`) piped `curl -f` into a JSON reader, so an empty or non-JSON reply was a bare Python traceback and the walk carried on with whatever pages it had. Each page now goes through `registry__fetch_json`, the helper #1336 added:

| Answer | Handling |
| --- | --- |
| no HTTP answer, 408, 429, any 5xx, a 200 that is not JSON | retried (4 attempts, 2 s + 4 s + 8 s) |
| 401, 403, 404 | final, not retried |

A page that still fails is one line naming the URL and the status (`registry-lib: GET https://…/tags/list?n=1000 answered HTTP 503; giving up after 4 attempt(s)`). The pull token is passed as a header and is never part of that line. A listing that cannot be completed prints **nothing** and returns 1, so part of a listing is never readable as all of it.

| --- | --- | --- |
| before this PR | 13 | 12 × 5 s = **60 s** |
| the page retry nested under the 13 listings | 52 | 13 × 14 s + 60 s = **242 s** |
| this PR | 13 | **60 s** |

`registry_commit_tag` asks each page once (`REGISTRY_COMMIT_TAG_FETCH_ATTEMPTS`, default 1): its 13 listings are the retry. A listing that failed says so (`the listing FAILED: see the registry-lib line above`) in place of `scanned 0 tags`, which is what a pagination regression looks like (#875). Neither number includes the time curl itself spends on a request: there is no `--max-time`, before or after. The sign step stops at the first repository it cannot resolve, so 60 s is also t

agent_prs.body:
Closes #1334 (observation: #1324).

## What happened

A watch stream that ends before the `SNAPSHOT_COMPLETE` of its initial exchange, while the client holds no resume token, is followed by a second full resend. `endStream` only reports a dropped **non-empty** token (`watch_token_drops{reason="midbatch"}`), so the abandoned send was invisible: on the 2026-10-06 soak it showed only as 6 `resent` at an agent roll where 5 were expected.

## Mechanism (reproduced)

`TestWatchLoop_FilterChangeBeforeFirstSnapshotComplete` drives the real watch loop against the model registrar from #1266/#1303, holding stream 1 between its `FULL_SNAPSHOT` events and its marker:

1. `watchLoop` opens stream 1 with `lastVersion == ""` (`resumeFor` → `noToken`).
2. `SetServiceFilter` lands before the marker and cancels the stream.
3. `handleStreamError` returns the token unchanged (`""`); `endStream` returns early on `token == ""`, silently.
4. Stream 2 is opened with no token and no `partial_resume` → the registrar counts a second `resent`.

The outcome is correct (readiness is not announced on the abandoned half; the second resend clears and rebuilds the cache). The same change landing after the marker is `extended`/`current` (contrast cases in the same test).

Which dependency-set source fired on worker-04 is **not** established (debug logging was off). The takeover is one candidate, but the first connect was ~0.55 s before the node lock was acquired, which is long for an initial exchange; the informer-fed sources that land in an agent's first seconds (the mesh-Service projection's TCP services, GAMMA/L4 route backends) are at least as likely. The new INFO line carries what is needed to tell next time.

## Change

- `aether.agent.registry.watch_resends_abandoned{reason}` — a sibling of `watch_token_drops`, not a new label value on it: there is no token to drop, and the two never count the same stream (a stream is inside a batch only after its marker). `reason` is what ended the stream: `fi
agent_prs.title: feat(registry): count and log a watch resend abandoned before its first SNAPSHOT_COMPLETE (#1334)

issues.body:
From #1324. When an agent's first watch stream is cancelled before its first `SNAPSHOT_COMPLETE` (e.g. the dependency-set update at standby takeover re-asserts the filter), the token is still empty, so the next stream is a second full resend. `endStream` neither logs nor counts in that case (it only counts a dropped NON-empty token, `watch_token_drops{reason=midbatch}`), so the abandoned snapshot send is invisible: on the 2026-10-06 soak it showed only as 6 `resent` where 5 were expected.

Add a counter (e.g. `aether.agent.registry.watch_streams_abandoned{phase=initial}`) and an INFO line, document it next to `watch_token_drops` in the runbook, and consider whether the takeover can set the dependency set before the first stream opens so the abandoned send does not happen at all.

## Measured first (talos-main, read-only)

**cni-install CFS throttling: not readable from metrics.** There is no `container_cpu_cfs_*` and no `container_cpu_usage_seconds_total` series for `container="cni-install"` (nor `install-supervisor`) in the 45 h cAdvisor has been scraped, eight agent rolls included — the cgroup lives for under a second and never meets a ~60 s scrape. kube-state-metrics exports only `kube_pod_init_container_status_restarts_total` (no `..._state_started` yet). `kubectl` gives `startedAt`/`finishedAt` at 1 s resolution (all five live pods: 0–1 s) and no CPU time.

**Wall time, from the installer's own log timestamps (VictoriaLogs, 48 h, 40 agent starts = 8 rolls × 5 nodes):**

| first log line → last | |
|---|---|
| min / median / max | 496 ms / 598 ms / 802 ms |
| "running CNI installer" → "already installed and unchanged" (the byte compare) | 400–700 ms |
| every other gap between consecutive lines | ~0–10 ms or ~90–100 ms |

Every total is a multiple of ~100 ms and every gap is either nothing or a whole CFS period. That is the signature of a 100m quota (10 ms per 100 ms period) on a CPU burst: spend 10 ms, park until the next period. Five to eight periods bound the work at **50–80 ms of CPU (an inference, not a counter)**, so about half a second of every agent start was the quota. All 40 starts took #1123's "unchanged; not rewriting it" path; a start that rewrites the plugin was not in the sample.

What it does (`cni/internal/install`): Go start-up, a byte-for-byte compare of the plugin on the host against the image's, a few small conflist reads. No writes on that path.

**Edge `agent` container** (`aether-ingress`, 2 replicas, cAdvisor, 45 h): average 1.8m, busiest 5 minutes 4.4m. Live spec: no CPU limit, `GOMEMLIMIT` set, no `GOMAXPROCS` — so the Go runtime follows the node's core count.

## What happened

publish-verify run 37522284996 (`workflow_run`, commit `01391e0`) died in "Verify the signatures (every index and every child manifest)":

```
curl: (22) The requested URL returned error: 502
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
json.decoder.JSONDecodeError: Expecting value: line 1 column 1 (char 0)
##[error]could not obtain a pull token for aethermesh/proxy
```

quay.io answered **one pull-token request** with a 502. `registry_registry_token` piped `curl -fsS` into a JSON reader, which got an empty string. The run had already verified 27 manifests and the proxy index. The bot filed #1316 as "did not finish … UNVERIFIED"; the next three runs were green and nothing closed the issue.

## Fix (a): retry, and say what came back

`scripts/registry-lib.sh`, new `registry__fetch_json`, used by the pull-token, child-manifest and witness-tag lookups:

| Answer | Handling |
| --- | --- |
| no HTTP answer (no connection, timeout, truncated transfer) | retried |
| 408, 429, any 5xx | retried |
| 200 whose body is not the JSON asked for (empty, HTML, cut short, no `token`) | retried |
| any other 4xx (401, 403, 404) | final, not retried |

Four attempts, waiting 2 s, 4 s, 8 s (`REGISTRY_FETCH_ATTEMPTS`, `REGISTRY_FETCH_INTERVAL`). A lookup that still fails prints one line in place of the traceback:

```
registry-lib: GET https://quay.io/v2/auth?service=quay.io&scope=repository:aethermesh/proxy:pull answered HTTP 502; giving up after 4 attempt(s)
registry-lib: GET https://quay.io/v2/aethermesh/proxy/manifests/sha256:… answered 200 with a body that is not JSON (76 bytes, starts '<html>?<head><title>502 Bad Gateway…'); giving up after 4 attempt(s)
```

A token reply's bytes are never quoted (size only), and unprintable bytes in any quoted body are replaced.

## What the six lines are

`cni/internal/util/watcher.go` lines 119–121 and 135–137: the closed-`Errors` exit of `watchFiles` (`deliverError`'s `!ok` return and the `case err, ok := <-watcher.Errors` arm that calls it).

Found by diffing the `coverage-report` artifact of coverage run 37545139162 (main at `c4324313`) against a local `make coverage COVERAGE_FLAGS=--jobs=8`. The whole diff is nine lines; the other three (`meshdns/lameduck.go` 180–181, `common/signals/signals.go` 83) are covered locally and not on the runner, and are already in the runbook's timing-dependent list.

## Why the runner covers them and the workstation does not

It is a scheduling race, not privileges, a kernel feature, netns or `PATH`.

`Watcher.Close` closes `done`, then closes the fsnotify watcher, which closes its `Events` and `Errors` channels. The watch goroutine wakes with up to three ready `select` arms, and Go picks among ready arms at random. Which exit a `Close` takes depends on whether the goroutine runs before fsnotify has closed its channels.

| Where | Closed-`Errors` exit covered |
| --- | --- |
| GitHub runner, three coverage runs on main | 3 of 3 (hit counts 1, 2, 2) |
| Workstation, `bazel coverage --nocache_test_results --runs_per_test=10` | 0 of 10 |
| Workstation, plain `go test -coverprofile`, 20 CPUs | 11 of 30 |
| Workstation, same under `taskset -c 0-3` | 10 of 30 |
| Workstation, same under `taskset -c 0` | 0 of 30 |

The workstation's `make coverage` also reuses a cached test result (`//cni/internal/util:util_test (cached)`), so one draw is repeated until the package changes.

## The fix

Test-only; no production code changed and no test case removed.

`cni/internal/util/watcher_loop_test.go` (package `util`) runs `watchFiles` over an `fsnotify.Watcher` that is only its two exported channels, so exactly one arm is ready at a time:

- `Errors` closed: the exit this issue is about
- `Events` closed: its twin, decided by the same race
- `done` closed
- an fsnotify er

## Problem

`test/envoy_validate`, `test/envoy_validate/generate` and `test/mtlspool` imported `agent/internal/xds/{config,proxy,quicdemand}` from outside `agent/`. Bazel's `visibility` allowed it; Go's internal-package rule does not. So Bazel was green while `go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, gopls and CodeQL's traced build refused the three packages, and #1310 carried exclusion lists for them.

## Fix

The packages move under `agent/`, with `git mv` so history follows:

| Before | After |
| --- | --- |
| `test/envoy_validate` | `agent/test/envoy_validate` |
| `test/envoy_validate/generate` | `agent/test/envoy_validate/generate` |
| `test/mtlspool` | `agent/test/mtlspool` |
| `test/envoybin` | `agent/test/envoybin` |

## Problem

When coverage drops because of a BUILD-only change (a test target disabled or removed), no Go file changes. The gate's changed-files table reads `None of the changed files is in either report`, and only a component's delta hints at the cause (#1318's red demonstration: `agent` −7.99).

`scripts/coverage-compare.sh` adds a **Largest per-file drops** section:

- the files whose covered-line count fell most between baseline and head, whatever the diff touched;

| Total | Section |

Docs and one rule file. No behaviour change in any binary (the only Go edit is a comment in `registrar/internal/server/metrics.go`).

## #1322: the divergence expression

The runbook's expression counted hashes over the bare `aether_registrar_snapshot_content` selector. `content_hash` is a label, so a content change ends one series and starts another. The registrar stops exporting the old one, but OTLP has no staleness marker, so Prometheus returns it for the 5-minute lookback and every replica shows two hashes after every change.

It had a second fault: `aether_registrar_writebehind_queue_depth` is recorded only when an intent is queued or flushed. Until the first one the series is missing (it is missing on talos-main now), `and on() (max(...) == 0)` is empty, and the expression cannot be true at all.

New expression, in the runbook and as `AetherRegistrarSnapshotDiverged` in the new `docs/observability/registrar-alerts.yml`:

```promql
count by (job, revision) (
  count_values by (job, content_hash) (
    "revision",
    aether_registrar_snapshot_revision
    * ignoring (content_hash) group_right ()
    (
      aether_registrar_snapshot_content
      and
      (
        timestamp(aether_registrar_snapshot_content)
        == ignoring (content_hash) group_left ()
        max without (content_hash) (timestamp(aether_registrar_snapshot_content))
      )
    )
  )
) > 1
unless on (job) (max by (job) (aether_registrar_writebehind_queue_depth) > 0)
```

- The `timestamp()` filter keeps, per replica, the content series with the newest sample. A superseded hash is in the lookback but older.
- The multiplication and `count_values` label that series with the replica's revision, so hashes are counted per revision and a lagging replica is not compared.
- `unless ... > 0` is quiet only when a pending intent is actually reported.

On live Prometheus over the soak window (8 h to 2026-10-06T23:02:13Z, 15 s steps, 1,920 samples) the old expression's first two clauses return a samp

## What

On the 2026-10-06 8 h soak (first with cAdvisor), `aether-uds-csi` was CFS-throttled in **57.6 %** of the periods it ran in (20,248 of 35,169, 15 pods) against a `100m` limit, while using 11–23 CPU-seconds per pod over the whole run. It serves `NodePublishVolume`/`NodeUnpublishVolume`, on the start and termination path of every UDS pod. Same class as #1253 / #1260 (mesh-dns), same fix:

- **Removes the default CPU limit** of the uds-csi DaemonSet (`udsCsi.resources`).
- **Keeps the `5m` CPU request.** It is several times the measured average (23 CPU-seconds over 8 h is 0.8m) and it is reserved on every node whether or not a UDS workload runs there. It is small as a CFS weight under contention, but nothing measured so far shows the plugin waiting on a saturated node; the runbook says what to read (`cpu.pressure`) and when to raise it.
- **Pins `GOMAXPROCS=2`** through a new `udsCsi.goMaxProcs` (same shape as `agent.goMaxProcs` and `agent.meshDnsDaemon.goMaxProcs`). Go 1.25+ derives GOMAXPROCS from the CPU limit with a floor of 2, so under the old `100m` limit the daemon already ran with 2 Ps; without a limit it would scale to the node's cores, and so would the exec liveness probe (`/uds-csi --probe`, a second Go process in the same container every 30 s, which inherits the env var). 2 keeps today's runtime behaviour exactly. `0`/empty omits the env var.
- **Empty `limits.cpu` renders no limit.** uds-csi's template had the bug #1260 fixed for mesh-dns (`--set udsCsi.resources.limits.cpu=` rendered `cpu: ""`, which the apiserver rejects). #1260 fixed it inline; this PR moves that block into a shared `aether.resources` helper in `_helpers.tpl` and uses it from both DaemonSets. The mesh-dns render is unchanged (its three #1253 tests still pass).
- Memory is unchanged (16Mi/32Mi). This container sets **no GOMEMLIMIT**; `aether.goMemLimit` is not touched.
- QoS: already Burstable, stays Burstable.
- Chart `2.4.9 -> 2.4.10`.

agent_prs.body:
Two test-only fixes for port collisions between parallel test processes, both in tests from #1258. No production code changes.

## #1299: `TestOnFreshDNSAddrRetriesALostPort`
The test asserted **exactly one** retry. If another process also takes the next fresh port in the same window, the helper retries twice, which is correct behaviour, but the assertion failed. It now asserts:
- at least one retry,
- the returned address is not the held (stolen) port,
- the returned address is the last one tried.

## #1300: `TestReadyMarkerWrittenOnStartRemovedOnCancel`
The test waited with `udpAnswers(addr)`, which passes as soon as *something* answers on the address. A resolver from another test process, co-bound to that port through SO_REUSEPORT, can answer before this test's resolver has bound. The test now waits on **this resolver's own ready marker** (`waitStarted(errc, fileExists(marker))`), the `startReusePortServer` pattern from #1258. `udpAnswers` had no other callers and is removed.

I checked the rest of the package for the same wait shape. No other test waits by querying the address. `TestLameDuckHandsOffToACoBoundSuccessor` already waits on markers. `TestReusePortCoBind` does have a related exposure in its final *assertion* (not its wait): `assertResolves` on the shared address could reach another process's co-bound resolver, which has different records. It was left unchanged and was not seen in the stress runs below.

## Evidence
On a 20-core box (load about 2 at start) I ran, twice:
`bazel test --config=race //agent/internal/meshdns:all --runs_per_test=80 --test_arg=-test.count=20 --nocache_test_results --test_timeout=600 --local_test_jobs=40`
- Run 1: PASSED 80/80 (min 164.4 s, max 172.5 s).
- Run 2: PASSED 80/80 (min 164.8 s, max 171.0 s).
Bazel ran 20 shards at a time.

Temporary mutations, reverted and not committed:
- #1299 test, no port stolen (`if false && len(tried) == 1`): **FAIL**, `"1" is not greater than or equal to "2" — the lost port is retried`.
- #1

## Reproduced

The hazard in #1269 is real. `TestWatchLoop_MidBatchCutThenContentsReturn` (`registry/internal/registrar/watch_midbatch_test.go`) runs the real watch loop against a model registrar. The model names its contents `<rev>.<hash>`, classifies tokens with `snapshotversion.Compare`, stamps the version only on a batch's last event, and can cut a batch after any event. The interleaving:

1. The client is resent C0 = {a: 10.0.0.1, b: 10.0.1.1, c: 10.0.2.1} and holds V0 = `10.<h0>`.
2. Batch B1 = [REMOVED a/10.0.0.1, ADDED b/10.0.1.2] is committed (V1 = `11.<h1>`). The stream is cut after its first event, so the client has applied REMOVED a (unversioned) and still holds V0. `consumeStream` never adopts a version there, and `handleStreamError` returns `lastVersion` = V0 for EOF, cancel, drain and failure alike.
3. Before the reconnect, the contents return to h0.
4. The client reconnects presenting V0.

Results before this fix, in three variants:

| variant | how the contents return to h0 | registrar's answer | cache after the reconnect |
|---|---|---|---|
| ABA | B1's exact reversal is committed (`12.<h0>`) | `renamed` | `{b, c}`: a missing for good |
| peer replica | reconnect to a replica still at `10.<h0>`, which never got B1 | `current` | `{b, c}` |
| partial resume | the filter grows {a,b} → {a,b,c} while the stream is held at the cut, then the reversal | `extended` (sends c only) | `{b, c}` |

Nothing heals it. The agent's reconnect re-assertion re-registers its own local endpoints in the registrar; it does not touch the watch cache.

## Fix

`consumeStream` now tracks `inBatch`: whether a live event (after the initial exchange's marker) has been applied without a version since the last versioned event. Endpoint and catalog events both count. A batch's versioned last event, a version marker (#1241/#1267) or the initial `SNAPSHOT_COMPLETE` clears it. issues.body:
Raised by the adversarial review of #1266/#1267; **suspected from a code read, not reproduced**.

A watch stream cut in the middle of a batch leaves the batch's unversioned prefix applied to the agent's cache while its token is still the previous version (the #1203 rule: only the last event of a batch carries the version). Normally the next reconnect presents that older token, the content hash differs, and a resend heals the cache. If the registrar's contents *return* to the hash that token names — an ABA (a change and its reversal), or a peer replica whose snapshot never received a lost write-behind write — the registrar answers `current`/`renamed` and the applied prefix stays. Partial resume (#1266) inherits the same assumption.

**To do:** try to reproduce with a model-cache test (cut after event k of a batch, revert the content, reconnect). Candidate fixes: the agent discards its token when a stream ends after an unversioned event (it knows it applied events past its token), which costs one resend per mid-batch cut.

## What churned and why

`bazel mod show_extension @@rules_rust+//crate_universe:extension.bzl%crate` and `bazel mod explain rules_rust`:

```
<root> (aethermesh@_)
└───protobuf@36.2
    └───rules_rust@0.69.0
## Usage in protobuf@36.2 from https://bcr.bazel.build/modules/protobuf/36.2/MODULE.bazel:196
crate.spec(package="googletest", version=">0.0.0")
crate.spec(package="linkme", version="0.3.35")
crate.spec(package="paste", version=">=1")
crate.spec(package="quote", version=">=1")
crate.spec(package="syn", version="2")
crate.from_specs()
```

`crate.from_specs()` with no `cargo_lockfile`/`lockfile` resolves those open-ended specs against the live crates.io index every time the extension is evaluated. On a fresh `origin/main`, the first `bazel mod show_extension` rewrote `MODULE.bazel.lock` with `crates__syn-3.0.5 → 3.0.6` and `crates__unicode-ident-1.0.24 → 1.0.26`. main's lock was also already stale in two other entries (`system_python_extension` usagesDigest, `cu_nr` bzlTransitiveDigest), and CI never noticed because it ran in the default `update` mode.

Nothing in this repo builds Rust. rules_rust arrives only through protobuf, and a `build --nobuild //...` fetches `rules_rust+` and its toolchains but never `@crates`.

- **Pin it:** a `single_version_override` patch on protobuf's MODULE.bazel passes `cargo_lockfile` + `lockfile` to `crate.from_specs`. This backports upstream protobuf [e5deac314d](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/commit/e5deac314d) ("Provide pre-generated lockfiles for Protobuf Rust under Bzlmod"), which is not in a release yet. The lockfiles live in `//bazel/protobuf_crates`, so `CARGO_BAZEL_REPIN=1 bazel mod deps` writes them into the tree. With both set, rules_rust reports the extension `reproducible = True`: its 19 generated repos drop out of `MODULE.bazel.lock` entirely and evaluation never touches the crates.io index.

agent_prs.body:
## Problem (#1254)

A UDP forward to one upstream waited the full 2 s `forwardTimeout` on its first socket. For a pooled socket, the cold-dial fallback then waited **another** 2 s. With the single kube-dns upstream, one lost datagram cost at least 2 s, while the client gives up at 1 s and sends again (`timeout:1 attempts:3`).

## Design

Each upstream gets **one 2 s budget** (`forwardTimeout`, unchanged value):

| step | bound | behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| first try | **600 ms** (`forwardTryTimeout`) | pooled socket, or a fresh one when every slot is busy or pooling is off (as before) |
| one re-send | until **2 s** from the start | **only on a timeout**. The query is sent once more on a **freshly dialled** socket (new source port, so a new conntrack entry). The first socket **keeps listening**. The first reply from either socket is delivered and the other is read and dropped. |
| next upstream / SERVFAIL | | neither answered within 2 s |

- **Lost datagram:** about 600 ms + RTT, inside the client's 1 s window. Before: ≥ 2 s plus a dial.
- **Dead or black-holed upstream:** fails at 2 s with exactly one re-send. Before: 2 s + 2 s = 4 s per upstream with the pool. The budget is per upstream, so N dead upstreams cost N × 2 s (before: N × 4 s).
- **No answer is lost:** any reply that arrives within 2 s is still accepted, as before. The change can only make answers arrive sooner. The client's own retry is untouched: each client re-send is its own query with its own budget.
- **Only timeouts re-send.** ECONNREFUSED (ICMP unreachable), write errors and unparseable replies take the pre-existing path: the pooled socket is retired and the query gets one cold `fallback` dial, with no re-send.
- **One reply, pool not corrupted:** the late reply on the first socket is consumed by that socket's own read loop, so it is never left in the buffer for the next query on the slot. A pooled socket whose reply was only *late* is healthy and is **kept**. One that got nothing by 2 s is **re
agent_prs.title: fix(meshdns): re-send a timed-out forward once on a fresh socket inside the client's budget

Three scheduled sweeps in a row (37243212359, 37269704858, 37328769954) hit the 30-minute job limit during the cosign step and concluded `cancelled`. The issue step only reacted to `failure()`, so none of them reported anything, and the backstop verified nothing from 10-04 23:17 to 10-05 22:44.

agent_prs.body:
## What

Test-only. `startServe` in `agent/internal/udscsi/serve_test.go` now waits until both the CSI socket and the registration socket **accept a connection**, not just until their paths stat as sockets. No production code changes and no test case removed.

## Why

`startServe` deliberately pre-creates a **stale** socket file at the registration path, to exercise stale-socket startup. Its wait used `Probe`, which only stats the path. The stale file therefore satisfied the wait before `Serve` had removed it and listened, and the test's first RPC (not wait-for-ready) could:

- dial the dead stale socket: `connect: connection refused` (the #1273 CI failure), or
- catch the path between remove and listen: `connect: no such file or directory`.

Both `TestRegistration_GetInfo` and `TestRegistration_KubeletErrorEndsServe` go through `startServe` and had this shape. The other tests in the file (`TestListenUnix_RefusesToDeleteANonSocket`, `TestProbe`) dial nothing that `Serve` owns.

`accepts()` dials the unix socket and closes it. The kernel completes `connect()` as soon as `listen()` has run, before gRPC's `Accept`, so only `Serve`'s own listeners pass and the helper cannot block on the server.

## Proof

Stress: `bazel test --config=race //agent/internal/udscsi:udscsi_test --runs_per_test=400 --local_test_jobs=80 --test_arg=-test.run=TestRegistration --test_arg=-test.count=20 --test_arg=-test.cpu=1,4` (20-core workstation)

| | failed runs | errors |
|---|---|---|
| origin/main | **12 / 400** | 12 × `connection refused`, 1 × `no such file or directory` (both tests) |
| this PR | **0 / 400** | — |

The requested `bazel test --config=race //agent/internal/udscsi:udscsi_test --runs_per_test=100` has 0 failures. Lint (`fail_on_violation`) and `make format-check` are clean.

Closes #1273

agent_prs.body:
## What

The ext_authz sidecar (proposal 027) in the `aether-proxy` pod is now a **Kubernetes native sidecar**: an init container with `restartPolicy: Always`, after `install-supervisor` and before `proxy`, with a startupProbe on the authz socket. Chart **2.4.9**.

Closes #1275

## Why

`authz` was the second regular container. The kubelet starts regular containers in order and does not wait for one before starting the next, so `authz` started after `proxy`. When its image had to be pulled (7–13 s on talos-main, on the first roll onto OPA 1.21.1), the new Envoy took the node's listeners with nothing listening on the authz socket. Every check in that window was an `ext_authz` error, which is a 403 under `failureMode: DENY`. On deletion both containers got SIGTERM at once, so OPA closed its socket while the old Envoy was still serving (`successor_wait` after `kubectl delete pod`, and `drain_fallback`).

## Rendered pod spec (OPA preset on)

| | before (2.4.8) | after (2.4.9) |
|---|---|---|
| `initContainers` | `install-supervisor` | `install-supervisor`, `authz` (`restartPolicy: Always`, `startupProbe`) |
| `containers` | `proxy`, `authz` | `proxy` |

With the sidecar disabled (the default), the full `helm template` output is byte-identical to main's, apart from the randomly generated webhook certificates.

## The probe

`exec` of the stdlib-only `proxy-ready` binary, which `install-supervisor` already stages at `/opt/aether/proxy-ready`. The probe runs inside the sidecar's own container, which mounts the `supervisor-bin` volume read-only. `proxy-ready` gets a second mode, `--unix-socket=PATH`: it exits 0 only if a `connect(2)` to that AF_UNIX socket succeeds. It uses raw `syscall`, not `net`, so the binary stays small (#673). Why this option:

- **Port probes are out.** The pod is `hostNetwork`, so `httpGet`, `tcpSocket` and `grpc` probes reach whichever pod on the node holds the port (the same reason as #582). The proxy's own readiness probe already avoids them for

Seen on the talos-main upgrade to chart 2.4.8 (2026-10-05 19:30Z), the first roll with the new OPA image (`openpolicyagent/opa:1.21.1-envoy-static`, #1247), which fired `AetherAuthzCanaryErrors` (ext_authz error: 2 in 10m).

In every new `aether-proxy` pod the `authz` container started 7–13 s after the `proxy` container, because the kubelet starts containers in order and the new image had to be pulled (10.4 s on worker-01):

| node | proxy started | authz started |
|---|---|---|
| worker-03 | 19:29:50 | 19:30:03 |
| worker-04 | 19:30:18 | 19:30:29 |
| worker-01 | 19:30:46 | 19:30:57 |
| worker-02 | 19:31:16 | 19:31:23 |
| worker-05 | 19:31:44 | 19:31:53 |

On worker-01 the proxy answered two authz-canary requests in that window: `envoy_http_capture_http_ext_authz_error_total{node="main-worker-01"} = 2`, flat afterwards; ok/denied resumed 1:1 on all nodes. With `failureMode: DENY` those requests get a 403; a real route using the filter would see the same on every proxy roll that needs an image pull (and, to a lesser degree, on any roll).

**Fix options:** make the authz sidecar a native sidecar (init container with `restartPolicy: Always` and a startup probe on its socket) so it is up before the proxy container starts and outlives it on shutdown; or gate the proxy's readiness/hot-restart handoff on the authz socket accepting. Check the shutdown side too (sidecar exiting before the proxy drains). Add the ordering to the chart's `helm_template_test` and an e2e (there is none for ext_authz today).

agent_prs.body:
Stacked on the #1239 PR.

## Problem

`store_revision − aether_agent_registry_last_version` grew whenever the registrar's version moved and no batch reached the agent. That happens in two cases:
- a store revision that changes no contents, for example a write-behind flush landing in etcd after the RPC already applied the change (`<rev>+<h>` → `<rev'>.<h>`);
- a change to a service outside a filtered agent's watch filter.

The agent's cache was current in both cases, but its gauge and resume token stayed behind until an unrelated change. On the 2.4.5 soak the edge sat 81 revisions behind for 23 minutes, so the lag metric could not be alerted on.

## Fix: the preferred option (a version-only marker)

At the end of each sync cycle the syncer calls `Broadcaster.MarkVersion`. Every watcher whose channel was not last given the snapshot's current version receives a `SNAPSHOT_COMPLETE` carrying only that version. The watcher's last-sent version is tracked per watcher: its initial exchange, its last versioned batch event, or its last marker.

- **Consistent boundary (the #1203/#1205 rule).** `MarkVersion` holds `publishMu` for writing, so no publication is between its snapshot mutation and its broadcast. Every batch the current version includes is therefore already on every channel ahead of the marker, and a watcher that overflowed on one of those batches has already been closed. A filtered watcher holds the version for every service in its filter, which is what every token means. `TestMarkVersion_WaitsForAnInFlightPublication` is the negative: with a read lock instead of the write lock it fails ("MarkVersion ran while a publication was between its mutation and its broadcast").
- **Throttle.** One call per sync cycle. A burst of store writes is one debounced sync (200 ms), and a cycle that moved nothing sends nothing.
- **Never forces a resync.** A full channel skips its marker and is retried next cycle. A marker carries no event, so nothing is lost.

agent_prs.body:
## Root cause

`registry/internal/registrar/registrar.go` `watchLoop` (main at 65e473a4, lines 590-594) cleared the resume token whenever the filter generation moved:

```go
services, filterGen := r.assertFilter(streamCancel)
if filterGen != lastFilterGen {
	lastVersion = ""
	lastFilterGen = filterGen
}
```

`SetServiceFilter` bumps `filterGen` and cancels the live stream on every dependency-set change (a server-streaming RPC cannot change its filter in place). So every change re-opened `WatchEndpoints` with `last_version = ""`, which `Snapshot.resumeLocked` can only classify `resent`, shrink or growth alike. The registrar was not rejecting a good token: it never got one. Every TCP mesh service is always in every node's dependency set (`agent/internal/xds/cache/cache.go`), so a TCP service appearing or disappearing changes every node's set. That matches the soak: `resent` steps lined up with fleet-wide `service left dependency set`, and `current` never fired.

Clearing the token on a growth is necessary, because a growth needs content the agent lacks. On a shrink it was not.

## Fix

The agent now tracks `held`: the services whose cached endpoints are exactly what its resume token names. It is narrowed by every filter change (their entries are purged), set to the stream's filter at `SNAPSHOT_COMPLETE`, and emptied when a resend clears the cache. At each (re)open, `resumeFor` decides:

- **filter ⊆ held** (a shrink, or no change): send `last_version` as on any reconnect. The version names the registrar's whole snapshot, so a token that is current is current for any subset of the services it was earned on. The response is `current` or `renamed`.
- **filter ⊄ held** (a growth): `last_version` would be wrongly answered `current` while the added services are missing. It stays empty, and the token goes in the new `partial_resume {version, services: held ∩ filter}`. A registrar that knows the field sends only the missing services' endpoints, as unversioned `ENDPOINT_ADDED`

## What

**`e2e/kind-version.sh`** is the one place Kubernetes is set for every kind e2e surface, in the `e2e/etcd-image.sh` style (sourced, plain assignments):

```sh
KIND_VERSION="v0.33.0"
KUBECTL_VERSION="v1.35.8"
KIND_NODE_IMAGE="${KIND_NODE_IMAGE:-kindest/node:v1.35.8@sha256:07b2536e30b803ed61d1677a79df6115f798ce64c80f9e22f6ed45afd09323c0}"
```

The values are the ones #1246 pinned. They are not changed here.

- **The seven harnesses that create a kind cluster** (`eastwest-quic`, `l4routes`, `multicluster_{config,replicator,waypoint}`, `uds`, `uds-csi`) source the file and run `kind create cluster --image "$KIND_NODE_IMAGE" --config …`. The script-driven nightly jobs stop running the runner's default image (1.37). A local run stops running whatever the local kind defaults to.
- **Local kind binary check: refuse older, warn newer.** `kind_require_binary` runs before `kind create cluster`.
  - It refuses a kind binary **older** than `KIND_VERSION`. A node image is built for one kind release, and an older kind can fail to boot it minutes later, far from the cause.

Closes #1253

## What

mesh-dns is every managed pod's resolver and was CFS-throttled at steady state (25m request / 100m limit; ~24.5m average usage; `nr_throttled 16851 / nr_periods 193397` = 8.7 % on w05). This PR:

- **Removes the default CPU limit** and **raises the CPU request 25m -> 50m** (`agent.meshDnsDaemon.resources`). Same pattern as the agent (#1116) and the authz sidecar: request = scheduling reservation + CFS weight, no quota on a latency-critical path.
- **Pins `GOMAXPROCS=2`** via a new `agent.meshDnsDaemon.goMaxProcs` (same shape as `agent.goMaxProcs`). Go 1.25+ derives GOMAXPROCS from the CPU limit with a floor of 2, so under the old 100m limit the daemon already ran with 2 Ps. Without a limit it would scale to the node's cores, and the GC's background workers (25 % of Ps) with it, for a process whose work is a map lookup or a UDP round trip. Pinning 2 keeps today's runtime behaviour exactly. `0`/empty omits the env var.
- **Empty `limits.cpu` renders no limit.** The template now drops empty or null quantities instead of rendering `cpu: ""`, which the apiserver rejects. Non-map keys such as `claims` pass through.
- Memory is unchanged (32Mi/64Mi). This container sets **no GOMEMLIMIT** (it never used `aether.goMemLimit`), so nothing there changes.
- QoS: already Burstable (requests != limits), and it stays Burstable. Nothing in the chart or docs assumed Guaranteed, a LimitRange or a ResourceQuota for mesh-dns.
- Surge roll budget: the second pod per node now requests 50m instead of 25m.
- Chart `2.4.6 -> 2.4.7`.

### Rendered resources

Before (2.4.6):
```yaml
resources:
  limits:
    cpu: 100m
    memory: 64Mi
  requests:
    cpu: 25m
    memory: 32Mi
# no GOMAXPROCS env (runtime-derived from the limit: 2)
```
After (2.4.7):
```yaml
env:
  - name: GOMAXPROCS
    value: "2"
resources:
  limits:
    memory: 64Mi
  requests:
    cpu: 50m
    memory: 32Mi
```

- `aether_mesh_dns_cpu_r

rules_lint 2.9.1's `lint_buildifier_aspect` only visits `bzl_library` / `bzl_library_rule` targets and filegroups tagged `starlark` or `lint-with-buildifier`. `bazel query 'kind(bzl_library, //...) + attr(tags, "starlark|lint-with-buildifier", //...)'` returns **empty** for this repository.

Probe: a throwaway `bazel/lint/probe_dirty.bzl` with an unused `load` and no module docstring. Not committed.

- **Before:** `bazel build --config=lint --@aspect_rules_lint//lint:fail_on_violation //...` exit **0**. `bazel aquery --config=lint //... --output=summary` shows `AspectRulesLintBuf: 12`, `AspectRulesLintShellCheck: 26` and **no Buildifier mnemonic**. Run directly, buildifier flags both warnings with exit 4.
- **After:** `bazel run //:format.check` exit **1**, reporting `probe_dirty.bzl:1: module-docstring` and `probe_dirty.bzl:1: load`. The same probe under `proxy/bazel/` is caught too, without building the proxy workspace.

- **Wiring.** Lint rides the Starlark formatter through `format_multirun`'s `starlark_check_args` / `starlark_fix_args`, so it runs in a gate CI already requires and no CI job is added:

With no bzl_library targets, and BUILD files unable to be srcs of a target in another package, there was no idiomatic way to make it visit them.

agent_prs.body:
Closes #1252

## Problem
A mesh_dns probe whose name lookup was still in flight when its 2 s deadline fired was counted `timeout`, never `dns_timeout`. So "dns_* is zero" did not mean DNS was healthy, and a `timeout` did not say which phase ran out. #1240 had to infer the phase from access-log source-port order.

**Root cause, checked against the pinned SDK (go1.27.1):** `Transport.getConn` dials on `context.WithCancel(context.WithoutCancel(ctx))` (`src/net/http/transport.go:1596`). When the request context ends first, it returns `context.Cause(treq.ctx)` (`:1651`), a bare `context deadline exceeded` with no `*net.DNSError` in the chain. `TestTransportHidesResolutionStall` pins this. It fails if a future Go starts surfacing the DNSError.

## Fix
- Every probe carries an `httptrace.ClientTrace` (GetConn, DNSStart/Done, ConnectStart/Done, TLSHandshakeStart/Done, GotConn with `Reused`, WroteRequest, GotFirstResponseByte). The dial goroutine keeps firing hooks after `Do` returns, so `phaseRecorder` keeps everything under a mutex and the probe reads only a copied snapshot.
- `classifyFailure` = `classifyErr` + phase: a deadline in the `dns` phase becomes `dns_timeout`. A deadline in any later phase stays `timeout`.
- The `AETHER_PROBE_FAIL` line gains stable keys `phase, reused, conn_ms, dns_ms, connect_ms, tls_ms, write_ms, ttfb_ms` (`-1` = the phase never started; the phase the probe ended in is measured up to the failure). `phase` is one of `dns|connect|tls|write|first_byte|headers|conn_wait|response|""`.
- Dependencies: only stdlib `net/http/httptrace` was added.

## Metric contract
- `aether_probe_requests_total{tier,target,result}`: the name is unchanged and **the result value set is unchanged** (`success, http_error, connection_error, timeout, saturated, dns_error, dns_nxdomain, dns_timeout`). I did not add `connect_timeout`/`first_byte_timeout`. Each new value would be a new series per tier×target×pod. Splitting `timeout` would also silently change what existing
agent_prs.title: fix(prober): classify a probe deadline by the request phase it interrupted

issues.body:
Found investigating #1240.

`classifyErr` in `prober/internal/prober/prober.go` expects a resolution stall to surface as a DNS error. It cannot on this path: Go's `Transport.getConn` dials on `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` and returns `context.Cause` of the request context when the deadline fires, so a stalled lookup comes back as plain `context deadline exceeded` and is counted as `timeout`. So 'dns_* is zero' does not mean DNS was healthy, and a `timeout` does not say which phase ran out — #1240 needed a source-port-ordering inference over access logs to find out.

**Fix:** attach an `httptrace.ClientTrace` (DNSStart/DNSDone, ConnectStart/ConnectDone, GotConn, WroteRequest, GotFirstResponseByte), classify by the phase the deadline interrupted, and put per-phase milliseconds in the `AETHER_PROBE_FAIL` line. Prober chart bump.

## Problem

- **#1236**: tests that start the **resolver** on a `freeDNSPort` address can lose the port to another process between the probe and the resolver's own bind. They fail fast through `awaitBound`, but they still fail with `bind: address already in use`.
- **#1237**: `TestPooledConnRecycledAfterUpstreamRestart` required a single dead-upstream query to finish in `< forwardTimeout` (2 s) and saw 2.0007 s. That happens when the host drops the ICMP port-unreachable.
- **Also found by the stress for this PR** (same test as #1237): the upstream restart re-binds the freed port **by address**. It failed in **2 of 80** runs (`test upstream on 127.0.0.1:N/udp did not start: … address already in use`). That is far more often than the timing flake.

## Change (test-only)

**#1236: retry the first bind only**
- `onFreshDNSAddr(t, start)` starts the **first** resolver on an address from `freeDNSPort`. It tries a fresh port only when Start returned `EADDRINUSE` (`isLostPort`), at most `bindAttempts = 5` times. Any other error fails the test at once.
- `waitStarted` is `awaitBound` without the `t.Fatal`, so callers can see Start's error. `awaitBound` is now built on it, and its messages are unchanged.
- Callers: `TestReusePortCoBind`, `TestReadyMarkerWrittenOnStartRemovedOnCancel`, and `TestLameDuckHandsOffToACoBoundSuccessor`. In the lame-duck test the predecessor now waits for its ready marker before the successor starts. `reusablePort` is replaced by `onFreshDNSAddr`.

A failed attempt has nothing left running: its Start already returned, so the lame-duck test records no extra exit.

agent_prs.body:
Refs #1123. Part 1 of 4 of proposal 041 (the standby agent). Stack: **this PR** ← agent-ready probe ← chart ← e2e gate (`Fixes #1123`).

Nothing changes for a delete-then-create roll or a plain restart: the lock is free when the agent starts, so it owns the node as the manager starts and no takeover step runs. The surge strategy is turned on by the chart PR.

## What it does

**Node ownership** (`agent/internal/ownership`).
- The agent tries an exclusive `flock` on `/run/aether/agent.lock` (`--node-lock`) once, at process start, before local storage is read.
- **Free lock:** the agent owns the node.
- **Taken lock:** the agent is a **standby**. A goroutine blocks on the lock, and the kernel releases it the instant the owner's process dies, however it dies.
- **After acquiring the lock**, before announcing ownership, the standby:
  1. waits until no server answers on `xds.sock`/`cni.sock`. This covers an agent that predates the lock: the first surge roll onto this version.
  2. runs its takeover steps in order (below).

**Standby** builds everything a first serve needs: identity, registry watch, listeners from storage, capture projection, client certificates. It holds back:
- **Node sockets:** `xds.sock` and `cni.sock`. There is a new `SetBindGate` in `common/xds`, called between PreListen and bind.
- **Registry and storage writers:** the liveness loop, termination watch and ghost sweep. The SPIRE resubscription of stored pods still runs, because client certificates are a first-serve gate.
- **Node files:**
  - the observed-upstreams/QUIC-pairs file and the mesh-DNS snapshot (`SnapshotCache.SetNodeWriteGate`);
  - the conflist repair (`Reasserter.Owned`; it still *observes*, because readiness reads it).
- **Node and API writes:** the taint remover (`TaintRemover.Owned`) and the metrics port.
  - The metrics port is no longer bound by the manager. A runnable binds it once the node is owned, and retries `EADDRINUSE` for up to 30 s, never fatally. The kernel can hand ov
