## Root cause

Full analysis: https://github.com/bpalermo/aether/issues/1050#issuecomment-5875727632

On rev248 one proxy roll in ~60 wedged both Envoy epochs until the supervisor's liveness watchdog killed them. The two **main threads** deadlock over the hot-restart domain sockets:

- **Parent → child UDP forward.** After the child's `DrainListeners` RPC, every QUIC/UDP datagram the parent's workers read that no parent session owns is posted to the parent's main thread and sent to the child with a **blocking, timeout-less `sendmsg`** (`hot_restarting_parent.cc:60-85`, `hot_restarting_base.cc:84-143`). The child's UDP listeners stay paused until the parent exits, so for the whole `--parent-shutdown-time-s` window every packet of every new QUIC connection takes this path.
- **Child → parent stats.** On every 5 s stats flush the child calls `getParentStats`, a **blocking, timeout-less `recvmsg`** (`hot_restarting_child.cc:161-176`).
- When ~24 forwarded datagrams fill the child's queue just as it enters that `recvmsg`, the parent is parked in `sendmsg` and never reads the stats request. Admin, xDS and timers stop on both processes, and SIGTERM (a main-dispatcher event) cannot land on either.

## The fix: `--skip-hot-restart-parent-stats`, on by default

- New chart knob `proxy.hotRestart.skipParentStats` (default **true**) renders `--envoy-arg=--skip-hot-restart-parent-stats` through the supervisor's existing extra-args path (`buildEnvoyCmd`, which also feeds `envoy --mode validate`). The child then never makes the blocking stats call, so its half of the deadlock is gone.
- The flag exists at the pinned Envoy `726d7ac` (`source/server/options_impl.cc:85`, a TCLAP `SwitchArg`, read in `stripped_main_base.cc:125/142`). `agent/internal/xds/proxy` and `//test/envoy_validate` don't need to know about it: it is a command-line option, not bootstrap. `//agent/internal/supervisorcmd:TestFlagsCoverTheChartContract` still passes (the supervisor-side flag is `--envoy-arg`).

agent_prs.body:
Carries a patch on the 726d7ac pin that removes the hot-restart main-thread deadlock from #1050, as the real fix behind the `--skip-hot-restart-parent-stats` workaround shipped in rev250. Not proposed upstream from here; that is the maintainer's call (see "Upstreaming" below).

## The deadlock

Both halves are in Envoy as pinned (unchanged on `main` d0b811f):

- **Parent side.** After the child's `drainParentListeners()`, every UDP/QUIC packet no parent session owns is posted to the parent's **main thread** and sent to the child over the `_udp` AF_UNIX datagram socket with `RpcStream::sendHotRestartMessage`, which flips the socket to blocking and calls `sendmsg()` with no timeout. The child's inherited UDP listeners stay paused until the parent terminates, so all new QUIC traffic takes this path for the whole `--parent-shutdown-time-s` window.
- **Child side.** Every stats flush runs `mergeParentStatsIfAny → getParentStats → receiveHotRestartMessage(Blocking::Yes)` on the child's **main thread**, with no timeout, and reads nothing from the `_udp` socket while it waits. `duplicateParentListenSocket` (a listener added during the window) has the same shape.

Once the child's `_udp` socket queue is full, the parent's main thread is parked in `sendmsg()` and never reads the child's Stats request; the child's main thread is parked in `recvmsg()` and never drains the `_udp` socket. Each waits on the other for good: admin, xDS, timers and signal handling are dead in both processes, SIGTERM cannot land, and the workers keep serving. This path has existed since Envoy added UDP hot-restart forwarding (envoyproxy/envoy#29585, 2023); enabling h3 across many per-pod UDP listeners is what puts enough traffic through it to fill the socket.

## The patch (`proxy/bazel/patches/envoy-aether1050-hotrestart-nonblocking-forward.patch`)

Applied after 47743 (same files). Wire protocol unchanged: no proto change, `HOT_RESTART_VERSION` unchanged, so it hot-restarts across an unpatched paren

agent_prs.body:
## Mechanism

Details are in the [issue comment](https://github.com/bpalermo/aether/issues/1009#issuecomment-5869601110), which was read from the pinned Envoy 726d7ac. At a source-proxy hot restart, the draining parent stamps `Connection: close` on the 200. The HTTP/1.1 client (k6) reads the full Content-Length body and closes. The h3 upstream FIN is decoded a moment later, so `ConnectionManagerImpl::onEvent(RemoteClose)` → `resetAllStreams` flags the still-open stream `DC` with `response_code_details=downstream_remote_disconnect`.

This is cosmetic: `bytes_sent` equals the clean lines, the client closed the connection itself, and k6 counted every request as a success. h2 does not show it because nghttp2 delivers DATA+END_STREAM from one read. No Envoy config setting ends a stream on a satisfied Content-Length, so the fix is attribution rather than behaviour.

## Access-log fields (`agent/internal/xds/proxy/accesslog.go`)

| attribute | formatter |
|---|---|
| `upstream_rx_ms` | `%COMMON_DURATION(US_RX_BEG:US_RX_END:ms)%`, ending when the router decoded the upstream end_stream (`maybeEndDecode`) |
| `downstream_tx_end_ms` | `%COMMON_DURATION(US_RX_BEG:DS_TX_END:ms)%`, ending when the downstream codec finished encoding (`onCodecEncodeComplete`) |

`CommonDurationFormatter` renders `-` whenever either time point is unset. Reading the source, the race shows as **both** fields `-` together with a full `bytes_sent`, because `resetAllStreams` destroys and logs the stream before the FIN is decoded. A clean line has two numbers. A DC line with `upstream_rx_ms` set and `downstream_tx_end_ms` `-` is a different case: the upstream finished, then the response stalled on its way out. It gets attributed separately and is not the race.

## Grader rule (`e2e/soak/README.md`, "Benign `DC` at a source-proxy hot restart")

A `DC` line is **benign** only if **all** of these hold:
- `response_flags` is exactly `DC`
- `response_code_details` is `downstream_remote_disconnect`
- `response_

## Finding (rev242 proving QUIC soak, 2026-09-27)

The source proxies logged **74 `200/DC`** lines (svc-1 36, svc-2 38) plus 11 `0/DC` for k6 requests to the two QUIC twins, **only at the six proxy rolls** (~12 per roll), and **none** for the h2 destinations (svc-3, svc-4, echo, mixed-svc) at the same rolls. rev239's full run had none on any destination.

The k6 reconciliation shows these were **not client-visible**: k6's 1,154 failures are exactly the 1,060 `503/NC` (#1008) + 92 `504/UT` + 2 `503/UC` lines; every `DC` line was a request k6 counted as a success.

So on the QUIC path the draining proxy generation completes the response but records the downstream as gone, where the h2 path records a clean `-`. Most likely the h3 pool's drain during hot-restart handoff marks the downstream connection closed after the response has already been flushed (the response was delivered, k6 saw 200).

## Ask

Low severity, but it is a difference between the two paths at exactly the moment (#991, hot-restart handoff) we watch most closely, and `DC` is a flag the soak grade treats as a failure class. Either attribute it (which side closed, and at which handoff phase) and document it as a benign artefact of the h3 drain, or fix the flag. Until then the soak grader must join `DC` on `@` clusters against k6 before counting it.

Grader record: `project_soak_20260927_rev242_run`. Related: #1008, #991, #979.

agent_prs.body:
## Part A — #1046: the publish sign step exited silently

**What was wrong.** In "Sign published images (keyless)", under `set -euo pipefail`:

```bash
tag="$(printf '%s\n' "$tags" | grep -E -- "-${COMMIT}$" | head -1)"
if [ -z "$tag" ]; then echo "::error::no tag ending in -${COMMIT} ..."; exit 1; fi
```

On a miss grep exits 1, pipefail fails the substitution, and `set -e` ends the step **before** the `if`, so the step's own error line could never print. Publish run 36417203322 died that way with zero output.

**Fix.** The lookup moves into `scripts/registry-lib.sh` as `registry_commit_tag <repo> <token> <commit>`, next to `registry_all_tags`, so it can be tested offline:
- the grep is `{ grep -E -- "-${commit}$" || true; } | head -1`: a miss can't fail the pipeline, and the function doesn't depend on `set -e` (bash clears it inside `$(...)` anyway). Every outcome is an explicit return;
- **retry**: the same job pushed the tag seconds earlier and `tags/list` can lag, so it re-lists up to 13 times, 5 s apart (about 60 s; `REGISTRY_COMMIT_TAG_ATTEMPTS` / `REGISTRY_COMMIT_TAG_INTERVAL`). Each miss prints its scanned tag count;
- a final miss prints `::error::no tag ending in -<sha> in <repo> (scanned N tags); still absent after 13 listing(s) 5s apart -- refusing to sign …` and returns 1. The step does `if ! tag="$(registry_commit_tag …)"; then exit 1; fi`.

The "signed N of M images" accounting and the exact-reference handoff (`signed-images.txt`) to the verify step are unchanged.

Publish run https://github.com/bpalermo/aether/actions/runs/36417203322 (main 799acda, the #1043 merge) failed in "Sign published images (keyless)" with **no output at all**: the step's log is the `##[group]Run set -euo pipefail` line and, 0.6 s later, `Process completed with exit code 1`. publish-verify then filed #1045 (all 8 images published, none signed). The previous run at the same code (26ed7bc, 10:20Z) signed fine.

**Deterministic defect** (`.github/workflows/publish.yaml`, sign step):

```bash
tag="$(printf '%s\n' "$tags" | grep -E -- "-${COMMIT}$" | head -1)"
if [ -z "$tag" ]; then
  echo "::error::no tag ending in -${COMMIT} in ${repo} (scanned ${n_tags} tags); ..."
  exit 1
fi
```

When nothing matches, `grep` returns 1, `pipefail` makes the substitution fail, and `set -e` exits the step **before** the `if` runs. The "no tag ending in -COMMIT" error is unreachable, so the one failure the step was written to explain is the one it reports silently. Every other early path (`registry__host_ok`, `curl -fsS`, the python JSON helpers) prints to stderr, so the silent exit points at this line. (Same shape as [[feedback_pipefail_grep_q]] in my notes: a producer/consumer pipeline under pipefail.)

**Likely trigger, not proven:** the push step logged `quay.io/aethermesh/agent:dev-799acda…` at 11:44:37Z; the sign step listed tags at 11:45:05Z — 27 s later — and (per the theory) did not see it yet. Quay's `tags/list` can lag a push. Today the listing has 14 tags including the new one, and no `Link` pagination header, so pagination is not it.

1. `tag="$(printf '%s\n' "$tags" | { grep -E -- "-${COMMIT}$" || true; } | head -1)"` (or `set +e` around it) so the intended error line is reachable and prints the scanned tag count.
2. Retry the tag lookup for the just-pushed tag (e.g. up to 60 s, 5 s apart) before declaring it absent, since the same job pushed it seconds earlier. Resolving the digest by the exact tag the push step printed (it is in the lo

agent_prs.body:
## Part A — #1046: the publish sign step exited silently

**What was wrong.** In "Sign published images (keyless)", under `set -euo pipefail`:

```bash
tag="$(printf '%s\n' "$tags" | grep -E -- "-${COMMIT}$" | head -1)"
if [ -z "$tag" ]; then echo "::error::no tag ending in -${COMMIT} ..."; exit 1; fi
```

On a miss grep exits 1, pipefail fails the substitution, and `set -e` ends the step **before** the `if`, so the step's own error line could never print. Publish run 36417203322 died that way with zero output.

**Fix.** The lookup moves into `scripts/registry-lib.sh` as `registry_commit_tag <repo> <token> <commit>`, next to `registry_all_tags`, so it can be tested offline:
- the grep is `{ grep -E -- "-${commit}$" || true; } | head -1`: a miss can't fail the pipeline, and the function doesn't depend on `set -e` (bash clears it inside `$(...)` anyway). Every outcome is an explicit return;
- **retry**: the same job pushed the tag seconds earlier and `tags/list` can lag, so it re-lists up to 13 times, 5 s apart (about 60 s; `REGISTRY_COMMIT_TAG_ATTEMPTS` / `REGISTRY_COMMIT_TAG_INTERVAL`). Each miss prints its scanned tag count;
- a final miss prints `::error::no tag ending in -<sha> in <repo> (scanned N tags); still absent after 13 listing(s) 5s apart -- refusing to sign …` and returns 1. The step does `if ! tag="$(registry_commit_tag …)"; then exit 1; fi`.

The "signed N of M images" accounting and the exact-reference handoff (`signed-images.txt`) to the verify step are unchanged.

1. `.github/workflows/publish.yaml` sign step: tag lookup `grep | head` → `registry_commit_tag` (above).

issues.body:
Found while producing the kind evidence for #1043 (#1023 L4 observability).

The runbook's L4 observability section and a comment in `agent/internal/xds/proxy/egress.go` say a TLSRoute SNI chain routes to its backends' **TCP floor** clusters (`tcp_<ns>/<svc>`). On kind (`e2e/l4routes.sh`) the SNI chain actually routed to the backends' **per-port** clusters: the access-log record for `requested_server_name=alpha.l4tls.test` carries `upstream_cluster=tcp_aether-test/l4tls-a_9443`, and `/stats` shows `cluster.tcp_aether-test/l4tls-a_9443.upstream_cx_total: 47`.

The point the docs make still holds (there is no `tls_` key; TLSRoute traffic is counted under `tcp_` keys), only the word "floor" is wrong, and a LogsQL/PromQL filter written as `^tcp_<ns>/<svc>$` for a TLSRoute backend reads nothing — the `_<port>` suffix is needed.

Fix: say "per-port `tcp_<ns>/<svc>_<port>` clusters" in both places; adjust the example filters accordingly. Docs only.
issues.title: docs: TLSRoute SNI chains route to the backends' per-port tcp_ clusters, not the TCP floor (runbook + egress.go say "floor")

agent_prs.body:
Closes #1023

## What / why

Until now every L4 cluster (the TCP floor, its primary-port alias, every per-port TCP cluster and the UDP floor) passed the bare `<ns>/<svc>` service key as `alt_stat_name`. For a service that also serves HTTP, they all reported into the **same** `aether_cluster` series as the HTTP cluster, so an `ssl_fail_verify_san` tick could not be assigned to a cluster kind. The #1007 attribution had to rule HTTP out from access logs, and an L4 hop had no access-log record at all.

This PR:

- **Per-kind L4 stat keys** (`agent/internal/xds/cache/capture.go`, helpers in `agent/internal/xds/proxy/egress.go`):

  | cluster (config name) | `aether_cluster` |
  |---|---|
  | TCP floor `tcp:<fqdn>` | `tcp_<ns>/<svc>` |
  | TCP per-port / primary-port alias `tcp:<fqdn>:<port>` | `tcp_<ns>/<svc>_<port>` |
  | UDP floor `udp:<fqdn>` | `udp_<ns>/<svc>` |
  | HTTP default + aliases, QUIC twins | unchanged (`<ns>/<svc>`, `<ns>/<svc>@<ns>/<sa>`) |

- **A connection-level L4 access log**, on its own OTLP stream `log_name=aether_l4_access_logs` (`proxy/accesslog.go`, `attachL4AccessLog` in `proxy/capture.go`). It goes on every capture `tcp_proxy` chain: floor, per-port, TCPRoute-weighted, the any-port shim, TLSRoute SNI chains and the blackhole. It writes one record when a connection closes. It keeps every connection with a response flag, plus the HTTP log's success sample, and uses the same switch (MeshConfig `accessLogsEnabled`) and the same sink. It deliberately has no `reporter` attribute, so it cannot enter the collector's HTTP identity counters. It is not attached to the passthrough chain or to UDP (there is no per-datagram log).
- Tests: `test/envoy_validate/l4_observability_test.go` (real Envoy validation, including the chart's own tag regex run over the keys after sanitization), `cache/l4_stat_keys_test.go`, `proxy/l4observability_test.go`.
- `charts/aether` 1.0.2 → 1.0.3. Runbook sections "L4 stat keys and the L4 access log" and the L4-hop join; the two

issues.body:
## Gap (from the #1007 attribution)

The L4 data path cannot be graded or attributed today:

1. **Stat key collision.** Every L4 cluster (`tcp:` floor, primary-port alias, per-port) reports under the plain service key (`agent/internal/xds/cache/capture.go:413,1429,1440`), so `aether_cluster="aether-test/tcp-echo"` mixes them, and `"aether-test/mixed-svc"` also mixes with mixed-svc's HTTP cluster. A tick cannot be assigned to a cluster kind.
2. **No L4 access log.** `ssl_fail_verify_san` on an L4 hop has no source/destination/SAN record; the #1007 event had to be inferred from per-pod connection counters and the chain config.
3. **No gate.** The soak's `verify_san` gate reads the HTTP clusters only; the L4 ticks were graded "pre-existing" by hand for weeks.
4. **A cheap misdirection signal exists and is unused:** TCP-floor connections on pods that serve no raw-TCP port must be zero. They are non-zero today on svc-1..5, prober, k6 and udp-dialer — every one a #1007 landing.

## Ask

- Give L4 clusters their own stat key (`tcp:<ns>/<svc>[:port]`), keeping cardinality bounded (one key per cluster, not per endpoint).
- An L4 access log on the capture TCP chains (the existing OTLP access-log sink; fields: source pod, upstream cluster, SNI, `upstream_transport_failure_reason`, response flags), rate-limited to connection open/close.
- Soak gates: `verify_san` on L4 keys = 0 outside rolls; TCP-floor connections on non-TCP pods = 0. Seed both in the README's vacuous-gate list until seen red (#1007 gives the negative control).

Related: #1007, #911, 037.
issues.title: L4 observability: per-kind stat keys, an L4 access log, and two soak gates (verify_san on L4, zero TCP-floor connections on non-TCP pods)

agent_prs.body:
## Mechanism (#1041)

`aether_probe_requests_total{node="prober-h2mzs"}`: the prober's `node` label was its **pod name**. The chart's `OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES` (`k8s.node.name=$(NODE_NAME),…,k8s.pod.name=$(POD_NAME)`) was already correct. Two other things combined to overwrite it:

1. `newMeter` built the resource with `resource.WithHost()`. The prober pod does not use hostNetwork, so `host.name` is the pod name.
2. The talos collector's `transform/promote` set `node` from `host.name` **first**. It let `k8s.node.name` override that only for `aether.cluster` `agent_xds`/`otel_collector`, and its later backstop only fills an unset `node`.

This PR removes `WithHost()` from the prober. With no `host.name`, the collector's existing backstop already promotes `k8s.node.name`, so this PR on its own gives the prober the real node. The GitOps side, which fixes the precedence for every sender, is https://github.com/bpalermo/k8s-talos-main/pull/128.

**New `pod` datapoint attribute** on both instruments, taken from the resource's `k8s.pod.name`. Once `node` is the node, `pod` is what keeps per-pod anomalies apart, and it stops two prober generations on the same node from writing one series. The prober never stamps `node` itself.

## #1040 logging half: `AETHER_PROBE_FAIL`

Every probe that does not succeed prints one line to stdout. It mirrors the soak's k6 `AETHER_FAIL` (`e2e/soak/k6-mesh-soak.js`): a fixed marker, then one JSON object.

```
AETHER_PROBE_FAIL {"t":"…","tier":"mesh_dns","target":"echo.aether-test.aether.internal:18081","result":"timeout","err":"Get \"…\": context deadline exceeded","elapsed_ms":2000.4,"pod":"prober-h2mzs","node":"main-worker-01","n":1,"truncated":false}
```

- `elapsed_ms` is per failure, at 0.1 ms resolution. A 2 s `timeout` is distinguishable from a fast `connection_error`.
- `err` is the Go error string. For `http_error` it is `HTTP <status>`. For `saturated` it is "max in-flight probes reached; probe not sent".
- **Cap:** at most 20 detai

issues.body:
## Finding

`aether_probe_requests_total` (and the other prober series) carry `node="<pod name>"` (e.g. `node="prober-h2mzs"`), not the Kubernetes node. The chart sets `OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES=k8s.node.name=$(NODE_NAME),k8s.pod.name=$(POD_NAME)` correctly (`charts/prober/templates/daemonset.yaml`), so the `node` attribute is filled by the prober binary from the hostname (= pod name) or by the collector's attribute mapping; either way the exported label is wrong.

Consequence: a per-pod SLI anomaly cannot be placed on a node without the pod still existing (it did not, after the prober roll, on 2026-09-28), and every runbook query that groups the prober by `node` is grouping by pod.

## Ask

Export `node` = `k8s.node.name` (and keep the pod name under `pod`), with a `helm_template_test`/unit test that the resource attribute reaches the metric label. Update the runbook queries that use the prober's `node`.

Related: the mesh_dns timeout burst issue filed alongside this one; #210 (agent_xds stats collision, the same class of fleet-vs-instance labelling).

> **Stacked on #1035.** #1035 has not merged yet, so this PR's base is its branch, `fix/quic-pairs-no-readmit`, and the diff shows only #1036. When #1035 lands, GitHub retargets this PR to `main`. If that does not happen automatically, retarget it by hand.

## Mechanism

Envoy's ODCDS manager keeps **one subscription per cluster name for the life of the process**. Before this PR, the agent removed a twin the proxy had fetched on demand in two cases:

- the source ServiceAccount's last pod left the node (`pruneQUICPairsLocked`, `source_left_node`);
- the destination left the allow-list or the dependency set.

When that happens, Envoy drops the **cluster** and keeps the **subscription**. Every later on-demand request for the name is `already subscribed, skipping` inside the proxy and never reaches the agent. So when a pod of that ServiceAccount came back to the node (a Deployment roll does this all the time), its route selected a name Envoy would never ask for again. Every request then 503'd `NC` at the 2 s `on_demand` timeout until the proxy restarted. The soak's churn on talos rev245 would hit this.

This is now reproduced live, not only inferred. The forget control below is exactly the #1036 sequence: fetch, prune on source departure, source returns, request.

## Fix

The subscription is still open, so the control plane can push the twin again at any time and Envoy takes it **without a new request**. The agent therefore never forgets a pair Envoy has subscribed to.

**The ledger.** `agent/internal/xds/quicdemand/ledger.go` (new) adds `Ledger[K]`, which records which twins the proxy holds an ODCDS subscription for:
- every name it asked for on first use, including a refused one, because the subscription stays open either way;
- every name it re-subscribed on a fresh stream.

It lives in `quicdemand` so the live gate runs the agent's ledger, not a copy of it. That is the same reason #1035 put the classifier there.

issues.body:
## Finding (from #1035's live gate)

Envoy's ODCDS manager (`XdstpOdcdsSubscriptionsManager`, `od_cds_api_impl.cc`) keeps one singleton subscription per cluster name for the life of the proxy process. When the server removes a cluster that was fetched on demand, Envoy drops the cluster and keeps the subscription. Every later on-demand request for that name logs `ODCDS-manager: resource … is already subscribed to, skipping` and sends nothing. The request 503s `NC` at the 2 s `on_demand` timeout, and so does every request after it, until the proxy restarts. `//test/mtlspool` `TestOnDemandQUICSubscribedTwinsServedAfterAgentRestart/strand_control` shows this: `status=503 … in 2.000384001s`, and no CDS request reaches the control plane.

#1035 handles this for agent restarts: re-subscribed twins are served. #1032's removal-evidence pruning (`pruneQUICPairsLocked`) has the same exposure, and it is not fixed:

1. A pair's twin was fetched on demand, so the proxy holds a live subscription for it.
2. The source ServiceAccount's last pod leaves the node, so the pair and its twin are pruned. The subscription stays.
3. A pod of the same ServiceAccount is scheduled on the node again while the proxy lives. The arm names the twin again, the request routes to it, Envoy skips the fetch, and it 503s at the timeout, forever.

A destination that is delisted and then re-listed has the same exposure.

This is inferred from the mechanism; the source-return sequence was not reproduced separately.

## Ask

- Add a live repro in `//test/mtlspool`: fetch the twin, prune it, return the source, request.
- Candidate fix: the agent tracks the twin names the proxy holds a live on-demand subscription for, on the current stream (first-use and re-subscribed names), and re-admits such a pair when it becomes valid again.

Related: #1020, #1032, #1033, #1035.
issues.title: quic: a pruned on-demand twin is stranded if its source ServiceAccount returns to the node — Envoy never re-requests a subscribed ODCDS name (503 NC forever)

## Why

The first talos deploy of #1032 (rev245 = 1.0.2-6ad804b, 2026-09-28 03:00Z, an agent roll from an agent that had built SAs × destinations twins) logged this on **every** node:

```
east-west QUIC fan-out quic_clusters=24 observed_pairs=24 local_identities=12 allow_listed_services=2
                       18/18/9, 28/28/14, 20/20/10, 20/20/10
```

`observed_pairs == local_identities × 2` everywhere. The demand scoping delivered no reduction, and because pairs prune only when their source leaves the node, the fan-out was persisted for good.

## Mechanism

On an agent restart the running Envoy opens a fresh delta stream and re-states its inventory in the stream's first CDS request. #1032's observer admitted a pair for every `quic:` name in it: `RestoreQUICTwin` on `initial_resource_versions` (the "held twins on a fresh xDS stream re-admit their pair" rule), and `ObserveQUICTwin` on `resource_names_subscribe`. The twins the previous agent had built up front came back as observed pairs, and were persisted to `ObservedUpstreams.quic_pairs`.

- **Twin held only through the wildcard.** Delivered by CDS, with no on-demand subscription behind it (this is how the pre-#1020 agent's up-front twins arrived). agent_prs.body:
> **Do not merge until #1022's talos proof is in** (#1028 deployed, and the TCP-floor landing counter reads zero on the patched proxy). With this change alone, a node-proxy socket leaked into a pod netns (the #1022 defect) would leave through the correct endpoint's ORIGINAL_DST from a pod IP and **succeed silently**. The stray `in_tcp_<pod>` landings are the only signal that shows #1022, and this change would switch them off. That is why this PR is a draft.

## What was wrong

The capture listener set `use_original_dst: true`. In Envoy, that listener **field** adds two things:

1. **A second copy of the `original_dst` listener filter** (`listener_impl.cc` `buildOriginalDstListenerFilter`). aether already configures that filter explicitly, first in the list.
2. **The restored-destination handoff** (`active_tcp_socket.cc:240-267`). When a connection's restored local address matches another listener, Envoy hands the connection to "the listener bound to that address" via `getBalancedHandlerByAddress`. The lookup is keyed by the address **string** alone (`connection_handler_impl.cc:122`, wildcard fallback `:425-433`), and the string carries no netns.

Every pod's inbound listener binds `0.0.0.0:18008` inside its own netns, so each new pod overwrites the previous entry. Any connection a capture listener accepted with original destination `*:18008` therefore ran through the inbound filter chains of **whichever pod was added last**. That listener presented its own SVID and failed the client's SAN check. This is the "always the newest pod on the node" landing from #1007.

## The change

- **`UseOriginalDst: false`** on the capture listener (`agent/internal/xds/proxy/capture.go`).
- **The explicit `original_dst` listener filter stays, first in the list.** It is the thing that sets `localAddressRestored()`. It is also all the ORIGINAL_DST passthrough needs: `original_dst_cluster.cc:51` reads the downstream local address only `if (connection->connectionInfoProvider().localAddre

issues.body:
## Finding

`envoy_cluster_ssl_fail_verify_san_total` ticks on the **L4 TLS clusters** of the soak's `tcp-echo` and `mixed-svc` services, including inside windows with **no roll of any kind**. It is present on every recent build and predates QUIC and TPROXY:

| window | tcp-echo | mixed-svc |
|---|---|---|
| 2026-09-23 (3 days before rev239) | 136 | 44 |
| rev239 8 h soak (2026-09-26, no QUIC) | 13 | 8 |
| rev242 8 h soak (2026-09-27, QUIC on svc-1/2) | ticks, incl. the 12:30–14:00Z no-roll window | ticks |

The HTTP services (`svc-1..5`) do not tick outside proxy rolls, so this is not the #829 session-resumption class (fixed in #834, verified zero on rev227) and not #638's roll-adjacent burst. The runbook's "Attributing an `ssl_fail_verify_san` event" section covers only those two shapes.

## What is different about these two services

Both carry a TLSRoute / TCP-floor leg (proposal 037 multiprotocol): the client dials a TLS port, the capture listener SNI-routes it, and the upstream cluster is the mesh mTLS cluster for that service. The SAN check that fails is the **client-side** check on the outbound mTLS hop, so either (a) the destination's inbound chain for the L4 port presents a different SVID than the URI SAN the source pins, or (b) the source pins the wrong SAN for L4 clusters (the pin is derived from the Service's ServiceAccount; `mixed-svc` carries two ports on one SA, `tcp-echo` predates 037 — see `e2e/soak/README.md` on its doubled `tcp_` chain name).

## Mechanism

`Network::Utility::execInNetworkNamespace` (`source/common/network/utility.h` ~383 at the pinned `726d7ac`) records the namespace to return to by opening `/proc/self/ns/net`. In a multi-threaded process `/proc/self` resolves to the **thread-group leader**, which is the main thread. `setns(CLONE_NEWNET)` moves only the calling thread.

The main thread enters pod namespaces briefly and often: health-check connects every 5 s per local pod, and listener socket creation. If a worker calls the helper (every `app_<pod>` connection) during one of those windows, it "restores" itself into that pod's netns and stays there until its next call. While it is stuck, its host-intended upstream sockets are created inside the pod. Redirect-all capture then diverts them to the pod's capture listener, and #1007's `use_original_dst` handoff passes them to the newest pod's inbound `:18008` listener, where the client's SAN check rejects them. That is the working explanation for #1007's cross-pod L4 landings. The talos proof below is what confirms or refutes it.

`/proc/self/ns/net` is the only place in the Envoy tree that saves and restores a netns this way. I grepped for `/proc/self`, `ns/net` and `setns`, and every `setns` call site is inside this helper.

`proxy/bazel/patches/envoy-aether1022-exec-in-netns-thread-self.patch` is the third entry in `single_version_override(patches=…)`. It is applied after #47743 and #47740, and `git apply --check` passes on the three in order at `726d7ac`.

- **`utility.h`:** opens `/proc/thread-self/ns/net`. On `ENOENT` (kernels older than 3.17) it falls back to `/proc/self/task/<gettid()>/ns/net`. The error message names whichever path failed.
- **`utility_test.cc`:** `ExecInNetnsTest.Basic`'s expected path string follows the new spelling.
- **New `test/common/network:exec_in_netns_thread_test`**, in the patch's BUILD hunk.

## Problem (#991)

On the rev242 soak (0.95.3, `cb79180`) the old `aether-proxy` pod was deleted **mid-handoff** on 22 of 30 node-rolls: its supervisor logged `termination requested mid-handoff` and recorded `shutdown_branch{branch="handoff"}`. A successor that wedges before going LIVE would have left the node on the 155 s `drain_fallback` rather than on an old pod that is still Ready.

Nothing in the supervisor or the chart changed between rev239 and rev242. What changed is the successor Envoy's fork → `starting workers` time under load: **2.2–3.5 s on rev239, 3.2–6.0 s on rev242** (one outlier at 31 s). That broke two assumptions:

On 2026-09-27 two unrelated PRs went red the same way and passed on a plain re-run:

The #995 log is the useful one. The repository cache was **already** restored, as an exact hit, 1.9 GB:

Two unrelated PRs went red on 2026-09-27 in the same way: #979's `test` job (`gazelle++go_deps+com_github_go_openapi_swag: fetch_repo: … Get "https://proxy.golang.org/…/@v/v0.29.2.info": net/http: TLS handshake timeout`) and #995's `netns` job (`gazelle++go_deps+org_golang_google_genproto_googleapis_api: fetch_repo: google.golang.org/genproto/googleapis/api@…`). The BuildBuddy remote cache covers actions, not repository fetches, so every job that has to populate the Go module repos re-downloads from proxy.golang.org and inherits its flakiness.

## Verdict: test race, not a code race

**What raced.** `TestNodeSVIDRedeliveryCountsUnchanged` takes its push baseline (`pushesBefore`) once `bundle_updates{own,initial}` reaches 1. But `refreshWorkloadBundle` records that counter **before** it calls `pushSecrets`. Interleaving on the failing runs:

1. Initial wake (`runIdentityRefresh` goroutine): `refreshNodeSVID` → `svid_updates{node,initial}` → push #1 `{agent:v1, vc:0}`.
2. Same wake: `refreshWorkloadBundle` bumps gen, records `bundle_updates{own,initial}=1` …
3. Test goroutine: counter is 1, reads `gen()` (already bumped) and `len(store.snapshot()) == 1`.
4. Bridge goroutine: … `pushSecrets` → push #2 `{agent:v1, vc:1}`.
5. Redelivery: correctly classified `unchanged`, no bump, no push. The test then sees 2 pushes vs baseline 1 → "an unchanged node SVID must not push".

Evidence: all 21/300 failing runs on `main` carry the same payload — the 2nd push is `{…/aether-agent:1 validationContexts:1}`, i.e. the **initial wake's bundle push**, not a push caused by the redelivery (which would carry the same state as push #2 and would have been collapsed by the `publishedGen` check anyway).

**Why production is not affected.** Refresh is already serialised: its only callers are `Start` (one synchronous `refreshIdentity`, then `go runIdentityRefresh`, so there is a happens-before) and the single `runIdentityRefresh` loop, which handles the `Updated()` wake and the 30 s tick in one `select`, one at a time. No two refreshes run concurrently, so there is no "both see nothing served yet" window. On top of that, `pushSecrets` drops a push whose generation is already published.

The test now waits for the observable effect of the initial wake's last push, the **served generation** (`publishedGen == gen`; `publishedGen` is written only after `SetSecrets` returns, under `pushMu`), before it takes the baseline. The "must not push" / "must not bump" assertions are unchanged.

The assertion that failed is the production invariant, not test plumbing: a byte-identical node SVID redelivered by SPIRE must classify as `unchanged` and must NOT push a new snapshot generation. ## Mechanism

1. `proxy.QUICClusterFrom` cloned the h2 base, so every `quic:` twin kept the base's `eds_cluster_config` (the bare-service EDS name, `ads: {}`).
2. Envoy's delta-ADS `WatchMap` deduplicates subscription interest per (type_url, resource name).
3. A twin added **after** its base is subscribed (a new ServiceAccount's first pod on the node) therefore adds nothing to `resource_names_subscribe`: no request goes out.
4. The control plane correctly sends nothing (the resource did not change), so the twin warms for the full 15 s `initial_fetch_timeout`. Every request from that SA to that destination is `503/NC`.
5. On talos rev242 this caused 1,060 client-visible 503/NC in 11 s at k6 start, with `envoy_cluster_init_fetch_timeout_total{aether_cluster="aether-test/svc-1@aether-test/default"}` = 1 on every node. This is #842's mechanism (SDS, fixed in #865), this time on EDS.

## Fix

- `proxy.QUICClusterFrom` sets the twin's `eds_cluster_config.service_name` to the twin's own cluster name. The config source is still `ads: {}`, on the same stream.
- New `proxy.QUICLoadAssignmentFrom(base, twinName)` publishes the base's `ClusterLoadAssignment` under the twin's name. Endpoints, named endpoints and policy all come from the base, including the health status aether writes and all locality/metadata. The endpoint slice elements are shared, not deep-cloned: CLAs are never mutated after build. A test pins the CLA descriptor's field set, so a new upstream field cannot be dropped silently.
- `cache.entryTwinsAndVhost` returns the twin CLAs from the same pass that produces the twins, so a new twin and its CLA always ride the **same snapshot**. They are emitted in sorted-identity order and re-sorted with every other CLA, so identical inputs produce byte-identical output.

This follows the pattern the per-port clusters already use: a cluster that must not share EDS membership gets its own EDS name.

## Why not a separate `api_config_source` (the #865 shape)

A separate source

## The gap

#1000 hot-fixed #999: `check_signature` in `scripts/verify-published-artifacts.sh` step 5 was handed the proxy repo's **tag list** where it takes the pull **token**. The offline harnesses never saw it because their fake registries accepted **any** `Authorization: Bearer …` value. A wrong token and the right one looked the same.

- **`scripts/check-registry-lookup.sh`** (the `curl` fake): the fake now issues one token, `fake`, from the token endpoint (`/token` for ghcr.io, `/v2/auth` for quay.io, unchanged). ## Mechanism

`aether_agent_spire_svid_updates_total{aether_spire_identity="node",aether_spire_update="unchanged"}` is seeded at 0 on every node (#717), but `refreshNodeSVID` in `agent/internal/spire/bridge.go`:

- returned early on an SVID whose chain+key equal the one served (`// unchanged; avoid a no-op snapshot bump`) **without recording anything**, and
- classified every other update with `initialOrRotated(firstServe)`.

So the node `unchanged` series could never move, and a gate reading zero there was vacuous. The pod path already classifies by comparing bytes, and its `unchanged` does move (SPIRE re-sends every SVID fleet-wide at a JWT-key prepare).

## Fix

The node path now classifies the same way as the pod path: the first serve is `initial`, a different chain+key is `rotated`, and the same chain+key is `unchanged`. `unchanged` is counted and still returns early, so there is no snapshot bump and no push.

`unchanged` is counted only when SPIRE actually **delivered** the SVID. That means the refresh was woken by the source's `Updated()` channel, which go-spiffe's watcher fires on every Workload API X509 response (`OnX509ContextUpdate` → `triggerUpdated`), changed or not. The 30s backstop tick re-reads a cached value and is not a delivery. Counting it would add about 2/min/node forever, so the counter would track the ticker instead of redeliveries. This matches the pod path, which counts Broker responses and not polls. `refreshIdentity`/`refreshNodeSVID` now take a `delivered` flag that `runIdentityRefresh` sets on the `Updated()` wake.

**Own-bundle path:** checked; it does not have this problem. `bundle_updates` seeds only `initial`/`rotated` (for `own` and `federated` alike), so no `unchanged` series exists that could sit at a meaningless zero. I added a comment at its early return saying so.

**Docs:** `docs/runbook.md` now says node `unchanged` is real, spells out what it counts (deliveries only, never the backstop re-read), and adds a paragraph: a zero

agent_prs.body:
Refs #846. Prerequisite for the next 8 h soak — without it the run reproduces the same unexplained residual.

## Why

The rev226 soak ended with **~510 k6 failures that had no access-log line at any proxy**, and the harness could not say what they were. k6's text summary aggregates across tags, so `error_code` never reaches the output: a refused dial during a proxy roll, a DNS failure during a mesh-dns roll, and a 4xx below the access log's `accessLogMinStatus` are indistinguishable. Those are three different defects with three different owners.

## What it adds

Eight per-class counters (`dns`, `conn`, `tls`, `timeout`, `proto`, `http_4xx`, `http_5xx`, `other`) and a summary that prints them — plus the line the classes exist to serve:

```
classified=N of http_req_failed≈M
```

**N < M means a failure mode `classify()` does not recognise**, and that gap is the finding, not an error. A non-zero `other` says the same thing one level down.

## Two details that make it correct rather than merely present

- **They have to be `Counter`s.** Each VU runs its own JS context, so a module-level object tally is per-VU and never aggregates — and `handleSummary()` runs in yet another context that would see none of it. k6 aggregates by metric *name*; ordinary variables it does not. This is the kind of thing that silently reports zero.
- **`classify()` keys on the documented hundreds ranges**, not individual `error_code` constants. A wrong constant would file failures under the wrong defect, which is worse than filing them under `other`. Two deliberate deviations: timeouts match on the error *string* first (they surface under more than one range), and `1211` is dial-time DNS so it joins DNS rather than TCP.

`handleSummary` writes **stdout only**. A summary file would add a filesystem failure mode (the runner drops to uid 12345) to the very last step of an 8 h run, and this repo has lost soak summaries more than once. `kubectl logs` is what actually collects it.

## Verification

Closes #985

## Problem

`scripts/verify-published-artifacts.sh` paged through **every** tag of each repository (`ghcr_all_tags`) and grepped for the tags it expected. A tag listing is not a snapshot. The 2026-09-27 ~11:24Z sweep overlapped a publish and reported cni-install's d526bf2 signature `MISSING` while the tag was there (`FAIL: 1 of 260`). A re-run minutes later passed 260/260.

## Fix: look each expected tag up by name

Every coordinate the verifier checks has a name it can compute. So it now asks for each one directly with `HEAD /v2/<repo>/manifests/<tag>` (`ghcr_tag_exists`), accepting the OCI and Docker index and manifest media types:

| answer | meaning |
|---|---|
| 200 | present (`ok`) |
| 404 | `MISSING`, but only beside a **witness** (see below) |
| anything else (401/403/429/5xx, timeout, no connection) | exit 2, inconclusive. Never reported as missing or as present |

- **Image tag**: `<release_tag default>-<sha>`. The prefix is read from `bazel/img/go_multi_arch_image.bzl` as of that commit, the same way chart versions are read. If it can't be read, the verifier exits 2.
- **Signatures**: both layouts (`sha256-<d>.sig` for cosign 2, `sha256-<d>` for the cosign 3 bundle) are looked up by name every time, so `both` is still caught (`ghcr_signature_layout_direct`). If either lookup goes unanswered, the verifier exits 2.
- **Witness**: a 404 is reported `MISSING` only when a tag the same repository lists (`ghcr_any_tag`, one `n=1` page) answers 200 to the same lookup. A repository that lists nothing, or a lookup that 404s a tag the registry just listed, exits 2 instead of producing a wall of false `MISSING`. This is a real risk: ghcr 404s a manifest HEAD whose Accept header it doesn't match (`dev` → 404 with no Accept header, 200 with one). The witness replaces the old `(scanned N tags)` diagnostic.
- **Output**: the shape consumers read is unchanged (`ok`, `MISSING <repo>:<tag>`, `PASS: N artifact(s)` / `FAIL: M of N`). Each commit also prints `chec

Found while building #930's expected-red control (PR #983).

A `scripts/verify-published-artifacts.sh --recent` run at ~11:24Z on 2026-09-27 reported `FAIL: 1 of 260` — the one miss was the cni-install signature tag for d526bf2 (`sha256-217b6449…`). issues.body:
`verify-published-artifacts.sh` is the gate that catches a commit whose publish run was cancelled at queue time and pushed nothing (#880). It has never been shown to fail on purpose.

## Why this surfaced now

`1e31e3a` (#924) published unsigned images — a genuine, naturally-occurring red input. The scheduled sweep caught it and filed #929, then **went green on its own** three runs later without anything being fixed:

```sh
RECENT_WINDOW="${RECENT_WINDOW:-24 hours ago}"
RECENT_GRACE="${RECENT_GRACE:-2 hours ago}"
```
<sub>`scripts/verify-published-artifacts.sh:88-89`</sub>

The commit aged out of the window. That is right for a backstop — a rolling window is what stops it alarming forever about a commit nobody will republish — but it means the one red input we had was temporary, and we are back to a gate whose failure path is asserted rather than demonstrated.

## What is and is not already covered

The script does guard against the *empty-input* flavour of vacuity, and deliberately:

- an empty `--recent` window falls back to the newest commit old enough to have published, "so a scheduled run ALWAYS checks something real and is always capable of failing (#853)"
- an empty repo list is rejected, since the list is shared with the signer

Both stop the script passing while checking **nothing**. Neither shows it fails when it checks **something that is genuinely missing**. Those are different claims, and only the second is the one #880 rests on.

## The shape of a fix

`verify_commit` takes any commit-ish, so a fixture does not need the sweep to happen to catch something:

```
scripts/verify-published-artifacts.sh <commit-ish> [<commit-ish>...]
```

Options, roughly in order of preference:

1. A unit-ish test that drives `verify_commit` against a commit with no published artifacts and asserts exit 1 plus the `MISSING …` lines — the negative control, run every CI pass, no registry round-trip needed if the GHCR query is seam-able.
2. Name `1e31e3a` explicitly as a perman

`publish.yaml` signs with `cosign sign --recursive` (the index **and** each per-arch child), but records one index digest per repo in `signed-images.txt`, and `cosign verify` has no `--recursive` (v2.4.1 and v3.0.6 both lack it). So the verify step checked 8 index signatures and never looked at the 16 per-arch manifests, which are what a node actually pulls.

- **Enumeration:** `ghcr_index_children` in `scripts/ghcr-lib.sh` does a GET on `/v2/<repo>/manifests/<index digest>` (OCI index / Docker manifest-list Accept) and parses `.manifests[].digest` with python3, the same way the rest of the lib parses JSON. The runner does not need crane or oras. Every entry is returned; buildx `unknown/unknown` attestations would be checked too rather than filtered out. A non-index, an empty list or a malformed digest is a **failure**, not an empty success.
- **`scripts/verify-image-signatures.sh`** runs `cosign verify` on each index ref **and on every child**, using the same identity regexp and issuer as before. It checks everything before it fails, so a single run names every bad manifest. Exit codes: 1 = something did not verify, 2 = could not check (including a walk that found no children).
- **`publish.yaml`**: the verify step now runs that script over `signed-images.txt`.
- **`publish-verify`** gets two changes:
  - The registry sweep (`verify-published-artifacts.sh`) now requires a signature tag, in exactly one layout, for every child as well as the index. That is 36 coordinates per commit, up from 20.
  - A new cosign pass (the same SHA-pinned installer, v4.1.2 -> cosign v3.0.6) verifies every resolved index and child. Unverified manifests are added to the rolling issue.
- **`scripts/check-index-children.sh`** plus a CI step: 7 hermetic cases for the walk. I mutation-tested it: letting an empty `manifests` list through turns the check red (`FAIL index with zero children: accepted, printed []`, exit 1).

issues.body:
## The gap

`.github/workflows/publish.yaml` signs with `--recursive`, which covers the index **and every child manifest**. But it records only one digest per repo:

```
publish.yaml:199   echo "ghcr.io/${repo}@${digest}" >> signed-images.txt
publish.yaml:235   cosign verify \
publish.yaml:241   done < signed-images.txt
```

and **`cosign verify` has no `--recursive`** — not in v2.4.1, not in v3.0.6. So the verify step checks eight index digests and nothing else.

## Why it matters

The per-architecture manifests are exactly what a puller receives when they pull by an arch-specific digest, which is what any node actually does. Those manifests are signed and never checked, so the verification step does not cover the artifact anyone consumes.

It is not a signing failure — the signatures exist and are correct. It is a coverage gap in the check, which makes the green signal narrower than it reads. Same family as #853, #882 and #906: a gate that passes while covering less than it appears to.

## Fix

Enumerate the children from each index and verify each one, the way the signer already walks them. Two details worth knowing before writing it:

- buildx-produced indexes carry extra `unknown/unknown` attestation manifests (SBOM/provenance). `--recursive` signs those too and they verify fine, so they are harmless — but a naive child count will not equal the platform count. rules_img indexes carry only the real platforms.
- `scripts/ghcr-lib.sh` (#913) already resolves index digests and per-repo tags, so the walk probably belongs there rather than inline in the workflow.

Prove it can fail before trusting it: a verify loop that silently iterates zero children would be the same defect one level down.

## Provenance

Pre-existing; not introduced by the cosign v3 upgrade (#924), which left it untouched and flagged it. Found while checking a peer session's claim that aether "already verifies each child" — **I repeated that claim before checking it, and it is wrong.**

🤖 Generate

## Root cause

The issue suspected the 1s production debounce, but `newStoreTestCache` already sets `observedFlushDebounce = 10ms`. The real cost sits behind the debounce: `writeObservedUpstreams` → `file.WriteFileAtomic` fsyncs the temp file and then the parent directory. On a loaded workstation disk (the output base is on `/mnt/md0`) those two fsyncs alone can take longer than the tests' 2s `Eventually` budget. So the tests went red 6/6 locally and green in CI.

## Fix (test-only)

`waitObservedFlush(t, c)` waits on the store's own completion order instead of polling the file against a deadline:

- `flushObservedUpstreams` holds `observedWriteMu` across both `takeObservedSnapshot` and the write. `takeObservedSnapshot` is what disarms the timer and clears `observedDirty`.
- Once `observedFlushTimer == nil && !observedDirty` (read under `depMu`), the pending change has been taken by a flush that holds, or already released, `observedWriteMu`. Acquiring `observedWriteMu` then returns only after that write has landed.
- The only bounded wait (`flushFireWait = 30s`) covers **scheduling a 10ms timer**, not I/O. After it, the tests read the file with strict assertions.

No production change and no new seam: the helper reads existing unexported fields from the in-package test. The tests still go through the real debounce timer; they don't call `FlushObservedUpstreams()` to short-circuit it. `eventuallyWait` is removed.

`publish` runs once per **push** to `main`, for the push's head commit. gh-stack #963 merged #959, #962, #964, #965 and #966 atomically: five squash commits in **one** push whose head was `4930733`. `publish` ran for `4930733` and published it completely. `d74d77a`, `690dbb5`, `937a8fd` and `ef44437` were never the tree of any publish run, so they have no artifacts by construction, and nobody can pin a deploy to them. Found while writing the east-west QUIC e2e (038 PR 8), on #956.

`ApplyQUICClusterSelection` rewrites every route on the allow-listed service's vhost whose action is `cluster: <its h2 cluster>` into the matcher cluster specifier. - extend the selection to `WeightedClusters` too (each weighted arm gets its per-source twin) and retire the carve-out.

issues.body:
Found while writing the east-west QUIC e2e (038 PR 8), on #956.

`proxy.QUICClusterFrom` is a `proto.Clone` of the h2 service cluster, so every per-source `quic:<fqdn>@<ns>/<sa>` twin keeps the h2 cluster's `alt_stat_name` (`<ns>/<svc>`). All twins and the h2 cluster therefore report under one `cluster.<ns>/<svc>.*` stat tree: `upstream_rq_total`, `upstream_cx_*`, outlier/health counters and everything Prometheus scrapes are summed across h2 + every source's twin. Only `upstream_cx_http3_total` shows that any QUIC happened, and nothing attributes it to a source.

Consequences:

**Fixes #932.**

`UDPLoadAssignment` clone-and-patched the service's **shared** bare-name load assignment, rewriting exactly two fields (protocol, port) and carrying everything else through `proto.Clone`. For a waypointed endpoint that is wrong in a way the rewrite cannot fix.

`src`'s address for a remote-cluster endpoint **is not the pod**. The HTTP path rewrote it to the destination *node's* IP plus the east/west tunnel port (proposal 019) and marked it with waypoint subset metadata. Rewriting only the port left the node IP in place, so the datagram went to a host that was never the backend — silently, because the UDP floor has no transport socket and nothing asserts the reply.

## Why drop rather than fix the address

There is no correct address to substitute. The tunnel is a TCP mTLS SNI forwarder with **no datagram counterpart**, so a waypointed backend is genuinely unreachable over the UDP floor.

Dropping makes that legible: the service ends up with no routable endpoint, which is exactly what `udp_no_healthy_backend` counts and logs (#937). So a waypoint-only service now **reports itself** instead of delivering to the wrong machine — the two fixes compose.

## Two other fields stop surviving

| field | why |
|---|---|
| `Metadata` | the `udp:` cluster sets no `LbSubsetConfig`, so an `envoy.lb` subset key is inert — and an inert subset key on a cluster that does no subset LB invites someone to think it is load bearing |
| `HealthCheckConfig` | it opts an endpoint out of an **active** health check, and this cluster has none, so it describes a mechanism that does not exist here |

`Priority` is flattened to 0: without the locality-priority set the HTTP path builds, a lone endpoint left at a non-zero priority is a cluster whose only host sits in an empty fallback tier, which Envoy will not use.

## What deliberately still survives

`HealthStatus`. Before #936 it was meaningless here — a TCP probe of a UDP port could only ever fail, which was #931. Now the probe

**Fixes #931.** Fourth of the series, and the one that actually closes the bug.

## The mechanism

aether builds each pod's liveness probe as a bare `tcp_health_check` against its **application** port. A UDP workload listens on a UDP socket and nothing else, so that connect can never succeed:

```
tcp_health_check{} on health_<pod> fails forever
  -> health gateway 503 on /healthz/health_<pod>
  -> combineLiveness: "the application decides; the gate never rescues it"
  -> endpoint.Health = HEALTH_UNHEALTHY
  -> endpointHealthStatus stamps UNHEALTHY into the service CLA
  -> UDPLoadAssignment's proto.Clone carries it into the udp: cluster
  -> HealthyPanicThreshold: 0  =>  empty healthy set
  -> udp_proxy drops the datagram
```

Silently, at every step.

Measured on a live cluster before the fix. nft counters in three netns showed the datagram reaching Envoy's `:18001` socket while the upstream forward stayed at **0** everywhere, and udp_proxy's own counter read `downstream_sess_rx_datagrams: 1` after **four** datagrams arrived — it counts only once a session exists, and a session needs a host. Repointing the UDPRoute at a healthy backend made the forward appear with nothing else changed.

## The fix, and what it does not claim

`NewAppHealthProbeCluster`'s `tcp bool` becomes a protocol. A bool had no room for a third state, which is why the gap existed at all.

A UDP pod is probed at the mesh inbound port, which does answer a TCP connect. **Be precise about the strength of that:** it asserts the pod is up and its proxy is serving, *not* that the application is reading datagrams. The UDP floor deliberately bypasses the inbound hop, so a wedged UDP listener on a live pod still reads healthy.

It is chosen because it is the only thing about a UDP workload we can actually check — a datagram probe needs a per-service request payload and a per-service notion of a valid reply, and there is no sensible default for an arbitrary UDP protocol. The strong per-pod assertion stil

## The change that matters is one annotation

`deploy_l4echo_workload` derives the registry protocol from the listener mode instead of hardcoding `"tcp"`:

```bash
local protocol="tcp"
[ "$mode" = "udp" ] && protocol="udp"

Derived rather than a sixth parameter, because every `--mode=udp` workload must register `"udp"` and every other mode must not — deriving makes the two impossible to get out of step.

The comment block explaining the old workaround is rewritten. It had described, accurately for its time, that the UDP workloads register `"tcp"` because `"udp"` was not accepted and the TCP classification supplied what the UDP path needed. **That explanation was load-bearing evidence for #931 — it wrote the lie down without noticing it was a bug.**

✓ 40/40 datagrams answered by l4udp-a, 0 by the weight-0 backend

issues.body:
The UDP floor (proposal 018 Phase 3b) cannot deliver a datagram to any backend that speaks only UDP on its application port — which is every real UDP service. `udp_proxy` receives the datagram and drops it with **no log, no NACK, and no stat**.

This is the cause of the `l4-routes` T3.1 failure in #927. Reproduced locally in kind and isolated to a single variable.

## The chain

1. Aether active-health-checks each backend's **application port** with a bare `tcp_health_check: {}`.
2. A UDP-only workload (here `l4echo --mode=udp`, bound to UDP 9001) has nothing listening on **TCP** 9001, so the check can never pass. Envoy marks the endpoint `failed_active_health_check: true` and the service EDS goes `UNHEALTHY`.
3. `UDPLoadAssignment` (`agent/internal/xds/proxy/egress.go:421`) clones that load assignment to rewrite address/port for the plaintext UDP hop — and `proto.Clone` carries `health_status` across verbatim.
4. `NewUDPServiceCluster` sets `HealthyPanicThreshold: 0`, which **disables panic routing**. With the default 50% Envoy would have routed to the unhealthy host anyway; at 0 it refuses.
5. `udp_proxy` has zero healthy hosts, so it never opens a session and silently discards the datagram.

Step 3 is a category error on its own: the source EDS describes readiness of the **mesh inbound `:18008` TCP hop**, and the UDP floor deliberately bypasses that hop entirely — the function's own doc comment says so ("the UDP floor has no inbound mTLS proxy, so udp_proxy reaches the application port directly"). Inheriting that verdict applies one port's health to a different port on a different protocol.

## The proof

nft counters in three netns (client pod, node host, backend pod), one datagram at a time.

**Backend `l4udp-a` — UDP-only, `udp:` cluster `UNHEALTHY`:**

```
pod netns   A-client-send-preNAT   (udp dport 18081)  3
pod netns   D-postNAT              (udp dport 18001)  3   <- CNI REDIRECT fired
pod netns   B-delivered-local      (udp dport 18001)  3   <- reached E
issues.title: UDP floor blackholes every UDP-only backend: a TCP health check on the app port marks it UNHEALTHY, and udp_proxy drops the datagram with no stat and no log

issues.body:
## What happens

`e2e/multiprotocol.sh` waits for its workload with:

```bash
k rollout status deployment/mp-e2e-svc --timeout=120s
# The registrar generates the mesh Service; the agent needs its endpoints.
sleep 15
```

A fixed sleep is not enough. On rev237, three consecutive runs against an unchanged cluster gave:

| run | http_18081 | http_portless | tcp_9000 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **FAIL** `got=[]` | PASS | PASS |
| 2 | **FAIL** | PASS | PASS |
| 3 | PASS | PASS | PASS |

Same build, same cluster, same script. The failure is `got=[]` — an empty body, i.e. the dial produced nothing rather than a wrong answer.

## Why it only surfaced now

It was masked by the name collision in #918. Until that was fixed the script created a Deployment called `mixed-svc`, and the soak harness (`e2e/soak/multiprotocol.yaml`) keeps a **permanently warm** mesh Service of that exact name in the same namespace. So the e2e's client was dialling a service that had existed for a day: generated Service, built clusters, propagated EDS, already in the node's demand set.

Renaming the ephemeral workload to `mp-e2e-svc` made the e2e genuinely cold for the first time, and the race it had always had became visible.

Two accidents cancelling out is worse than either alone: the e2e was passing *because* of the bug that destroyed the soak's workload.

## Why a sleep cannot be right here

The step is waiting on a chain of independent asynchronous events — registrar observes the pods → generates the mesh Service → agent observes it → builds clusters → EDS propagates → the capture listener can route. None of that has a bounded duration, and it is slowest exactly when the cluster is busy, which is when the e2e is most likely to be run.

The dialer's own startup numbers say the same thing: a brand-new service loses its first few dials while registration settles, and that was measured at ~2-3 dials, not zero.

## Fix

Replace the sleep with a bounded readiness poll on the observable the test actually
issues.title: e2e/multiprotocol.sh: fixed 'sleep 15' races a cold mesh Service — 2 of 3 runs failed http_18081

issues.body:
## What happened

Running `./e2e/multiprotocol.sh` on talos-main destroyed the long-lived soak workload `mixed-svc`, and nothing said so.

Both harnesses use the **same workload name in the same namespace**:

| file | `mixed-svc` | lifetime |
|---|---|---|
| `e2e/multiprotocol.sh` (#901) | creates it | **deleted by its `cleanup` EXIT trap** |
| `e2e/soak/multiprotocol.yaml` (#902) | defines it | long-lived; drives the 037 Phase 4 evidence |

So the e2e's normal, correct teardown removes the soak's workload. Same for the ServiceAccount.

## How it presented

Not as an error. The e2e printed `multi-protocol e2e: PASS` and exited 0 — it had genuinely passed. The damage only showed up in the dialer tally:

```
before:  {"cycles":11180, "port_ok":11169, "port_fail":11,   ...}
after:   {"cycles":14020, "port_ok":11179, "port_fail":2841, ...}
```

2,830 consecutive failures on the `mixed-svc:9000` leg — the per-port path proposal 037 exists to provide — while `mesh_fail` and `prim_fail` (which target `tcp-echo`, untouched) stayed flat at 3 and 16. `mp-dialer` kept running and kept reporting; nothing alerted.

## Why it matters beyond the noise

That leg is one of the three chains whose traffic makes `cap_tcp_anyport_*` reading zero *mean* something. Phase 4's gate is a conjunction: the neighbouring chains must demonstrably carry traffic **and** the shim must stay flat. With `mixed-svc` deleted, the first half silently stops holding while the second half keeps reading zero — which is exactly the state that looks like evidence and is not.

An 8h soak started after an e2e run would have graded Phase 4 against a dead leg.

## Fix

Give the e2e's ephemeral workload a distinct name (`mp-e2e-svc` or similar) so it cannot collide with the soak's long-lived one. The e2e is right to clean up after itself; it is wrong to clean up something it did not create.

agent_prs.body:
Closes #911.

## The bug

Proposal 037 Phase 2 gave every TCP-primary service `destination_port`-qualified floor chains (`:18082` and the primary port), and design (d) gave **every** service `destination_port` chains for its non-primary raw-TCP ports. Envoy resolves `destination_port` **first** and `server_names` third, so an SNI chain matching only `prefix_ranges + server_names` lost outright — it never reached the tier where its SNI would have won.

From that commit, a TLSRoute on such a service was **Accepted, generated correct-looking config, and was inert on both mesh spellings.** Nothing errored.

Its only surviving path was the 037 any-port shim — so TLSRoute traffic was incrementing `cap_tcp_anyport_<svc>.downstream_cx_total`, the exact counter **Phase 4's removal is gated on**. The bug quietly contaminated the evidence for deleting the chain that was carrying it.

## The fix

Let Envoy's own precedence apply instead of working around it: give each SNI chain a `destination_port`-matched twin for every port something else claims. The two then tie on tiers 1 and 2, tier 3 decides, and the chain carrying `server_names` wins. No ordering hack, no special case.

The unqualified chains are **retained** — they still serve every port nothing claims, which was the only spelling that worked before this fix.

`claimedTCPPorts()` derives the port set from **both** producers (`buildCaptureTCPPortFilterChain` and `tcpPrimaryFloorChains`), with a test pinning that, so a third producer cannot silently reopen this on a new port.

## The comment that made it easy to miss

It said the TLS chains were *"inserted first so Envoy evaluates server_names+IP before the destination-IP-only floor chain"*. True in outcome when written, **wrong in mechanism** — and when 037 added a `destination_port`, the wrong mechanism stopped predicting the outcome. Filter chains are selected by specificity tiers, never by list position. Rewritten to say so.

Found while writing #868's TLSRoute e2e leg. Filing separately per one-issue-per-finding — this is a control-plane reachability limit, not test debt.

This is a **code-read conclusion, not an observation**: the harness that would confirm it (#868's T2 leg) has not been run against a cluster yet. It is filed now because it determined a design decision in that harness, and because the Phase 4 coupling below is the kind of thing that is cheap to notice now and expensive to notice later.

## What the code does

`BuildCaptureTLSRouteFilterChains` (`agent/internal/xds/proxy/l4route.go:121-157`) gives each SNI chain a match of `prefix_ranges: <ClusterIP>/32` + `server_names` — and **no `destination_port`**.

Proposal 037 Phase 2 then gave every TCP-primary service `destination_port`-qualified floor chains (`tcpPrimaryFloorChains`, `agent/internal/xds/proxy/capture.go:514`):

* `cap_tcp_<svc>_18082` — the well-known TCP mesh port;
* `cap_tcp_<svc>_<primaryPort>` — the service's own port;
* `cap_tcp_anyport_<svc>` — portless, the deprecation shim.

Envoy resolves `destination_port` **first** and falls back to the portless bucket only when **no** chain claims the exact port. The repo says so itself, in `buildCaptureTCPPortFilterChain`: *"Envoy evaluates destination_port ahead of prefix_ranges"*.

So for a service with a TLSRoute attached:

| the client dials | chain selected |
|---|---|
| `VIP:18082` | `cap_tcp_<svc>_18082` — the **floor**. SNI chains never considered. |
| `VIP:<primaryPort>` | `cap_tcp_<svc>_<primaryPort>` — the **floor**. SNI chains never considered. |
| `VIP:<any other port>` | portless bucket → SNI chain wins on `server_names`, else the any-port shim |

1. **TLSRoute does not work on the mesh's own spellings.** `:18082` is the well-known TCP spelling proposal 037 introduced precisely so a raw-TCP client has an unambiguous address, and a service's primary port is the other obvious one. A TLSRoute is accepted, gets `Accepted=True`, produc

Closes #904.

## What was wrong

`otelslog`'s `convertValue` matches only the **predeclared** scalar types in its fast-path type switch, and its `reflect` fallback covers only `Struct`, `Slice`/`Array`, `Map`, `Pointer` and `Interface` kinds. A protobuf enum is a *named* `int32`, so it matches neither and falls through to:

```go
return attribute.StringValue(fmt.Sprintf("unhandled: (%s) %+v", t, v))
```

`%s` of the `reflect.Type` gives `registryv1.Service_Protocol` and `%+v` gives `PROTOCOL_TCP` — reproducing the live rev235 VictoriaLogs value byte for byte.

The consequence is not cosmetic: `protocol:PROTOCOL_TCP` matches nothing and returns an **empty result rather than an error**, indistinguishable from "no TCP endpoints were listed". Same vacuous-gate shape as #853 / #882, sitting in the etcd registry's endpoint-listing path.

Eight `.String()` calls, matching the style of the sites that already get it right (`etcd.go:394`, `registrar/internal/server/sync.go:147`, `agent/internal/cni/server/ghostsweep.go:436`):

| File | Sites |
| --- | --- |
| `registry/internal/etcd/etcd.go` | 6 (the ones in the issue) |
| `registrar/internal/server/server.go` | 1 — `ListAllEndpoints`, `req.GetProtocol()` |
| `registrar/internal/server/broadcaster.go` | 1 — the slow-watcher force-resync line, `event.GetType()` |

The two registrar sites are new — found by the sweep, not in the issue. The broadcaster one is three characters from its own sibling metric, which already does `event.GetType().String()`, so the log line and the counter disagreed.

Closes #906.

## The finding

`make format-check` was **red on `main`**. `e2e/multiprotocol.sh` landed in #901 with two-space indentation against shfmt's tabs, with `ci` and `proxy` both green, and sat unformatted.

The cause: **no job ran the formatter.** `ci.yaml` had twelve jobs — `changes`, `diff`, `chart-version-bump`, `deps-audit`, `shell`, `envoy-api-parity`, `proxy-pin`, `test`, `race`, `integration`, `e2e`, `ci` — and none invoked `//:format.check`. The only reference to it in the entire repo was the `Makefile` target.

So the repo had formatters configured in `bazel/format/BUILD.bazel`, a documented `make format-check` in CLAUDE.md, and nothing that made either matter.

## Why this is the #853 family

A check that exists, is documented, and never runs. Its greenness carried no information because it was never capable of turning red — the same shape as the shellcheck aspect that linted zero files (#853) and the counter whose zero meant nothing because it was unseeded (#882).

One detail worth recording, because it is what made this easy to miss: the **`shell` job did shellcheck that exact file**, and passed. Lint coverage was real; format coverage was absent. A green `shell` job is not evidence a file was formatted.

Modelled on `shell`, including its anti-vacuity discipline. It asserts **the set of languages the formatter actually ran**, not merely the exit code — `//:format.check` prints one `Formatted <language>` line per configured language and exits 0 regardless of how much it inspected, so a language quietly dropped from `bazel/format/BUILD.bazel` would otherwise leave this job green while checking less than it claims.

Added to the required `ci` aggregate gate. `control_plane` matches `**`, so it runs on any non-proxy change.

`e2e/multiprotocol.sh` uses two-space indentation; shfmt wants tabs. It landed in #901 (b087cd1) with `ci` and `proxy` both green, and nothing objected.

## Cause

**No CI job runs the formatter.** `.github/workflows/ci.yaml` has twelve jobs — `changes`, `diff`, `chart-version-bump`, `deps-audit`, `shell`, `envoy-api-parity`, `proxy-pin`, `test`, `race`, `integration`, `e2e`, `ci` — and none of them invokes `//:format.check`. The only reference to it anywhere in the repo is the `format-check` target in the `Makefile`. `grep -rln 'format.check\|format_check\|//:format' .github/workflows/ Makefile` returns the Makefile alone.

So the repo has formatters configured (`bazel/format/BUILD.bazel`: gofumpt, buildifier, shfmt, buf), a documented `make format-check` in CLAUDE.md, and nothing that makes either matter.

## Why this belongs with #853 and #882

This is the same family as the vacuous gates already tracked here: a check that exists, is documented, and never runs. #853 was a shellcheck aspect that linted zero files. #882 was a counter whose zero meant nothing because it was never seeded. This one is a formatter that no pipeline invokes.

The tell is identical in all three: the green signal was never capable of turning red, so its greenness carried no information.

Note the asymmetry that let it hide — the `shell` job DOES run shellcheck on `e2e/multiprotocol.sh` (it is in an `sh_library`), and shellcheck passed. Lint coverage was real; format coverage was absent. Easy to conflate the two and assume the file was checked.

## Fix

1. Reformat the offending file so `main` is clean.
2. Add a `format-check` job to `ci.yaml` and make it part of the required `ci` gate.
3. Prove the new job can fail before

issues.body:
Found while planning #868's e2e coverage. Filing separately per one-issue-per-finding — this is a control-plane correctness limit, not test debt.

## What the code does

`GenerateUDPCaptureListener` (`agent/internal/xds/proxy/l4route.go:186-206`) builds **one UDP listener per pod** whose `RouteSpecifier` is a bare `Cluster`:

```go
var primaryCluster string
for _, svc := range slices.Sorted(maps.Keys(udpRoutes)) {
	if backends := udpRoutes[svc]; len(backends) > 0 {
		primaryCluster = backends[0].Cluster
		break
	}
}
```

So for UDP:

1. **Backend weights are ignored entirely.** `common/l4project` resolves and defaults weights (including `weight: 0` as drain, #492), and then the UDP path takes `backends[0]` and discards the rest. A `UDPRoute` with a 90/10 split silently sends 100% to one backend.
2. **Multiple UDPRoute-backed services on a node collapse onto one cluster.** The loop takes the first non-empty service over the sorted key list and `break`s. A second service's UDPRoute is accepted, projected, and then silently has no effect on that pod's listener.

The code says so itself — *"This is the minimal viable control-plane shape"* — and the sorted-key iteration is there for determinism (#135), not for correctness of the selection. Nothing tracks the gap.

## Why it matters

The failure is **silent on both sides**: the `UDPRoute` is accepted by the API, the projector produces the right weighted backends, and the data plane quietly ignores them. There is no NACK, no warning, and no stat that distinguishes "weights applied" from "weights discarded" — so the first symptom is traffic in the wrong place.

It also means **a `UDPRoute` e2e cannot assert backend selection**, which is why this surfaced: #868 originally scoped a "UDPRoute picks the right backend" test, and that test would fail by design rather than find a bug.

## Scope note

`weight: 0`-as-drain is meaningful for TCP and TLS and was a real shipped bug there (#492). For UDP it currently cannot be honoured

| bootstrap | shape |
|---|---|
| `capture_tcproute_bootstrap.json` | capture listener whose per-ClusterIP floor chain is a `weighted_clusters` `tcp_proxy` over two backends, 75/25 |

agent_prs.body:
Closes #880.

## The hole

`publish.yaml` serialises on `concurrency: { group: publish-main, cancel-in-progress: false }` (#692). That protects the **running** publish, and it stays exactly as it is. What it does not do is make the queue a queue: GitHub holds at most **one** pending run per concurrency group, so a merge that lands while a publish is running is cancelled by the *next* merge before it starts a single job. The run ends `cancelled` — grey in the Actions UI, not red — having pushed nothing. `f332061` (#875) was lost that way on 2026-09-20.

Nothing noticed. That is the whole bug, so the fix is a check that notices.

## What this adds

**`scripts/verify-published-artifacts.sh`** — asks the registry, not GitHub. Per commit it checks **20 coordinates**:

| what | how |
| --- | --- |
| 4 charts | `charts/{aether,crds,prober,udsecho}:<X.Y.Z>-<full sha>` — all four are commit-addressable (crds/prober/udsecho carry `version: "X.Y.Z-{GIT_COMMIT}"`; aether gets it from `//charts/aether:aether_commit`) |
| 8 images | a tag ending in `-<full sha>` in each published repo |
| 8 signatures | the index digest of each of those images, present as `sha256-<hex>.sig` in the same repo |

Properties that matter:

- It **never asks whether a workflow exited 0.** A run that exited 0 having pushed nothing, a run cancelled at queue time, and a run that never existed all give the same answer: MISSING.
- **Read-only.** Every request is a GET or a HEAD. Nothing in it can push, retag or delete — the release workflow stays the only publisher.
- Chart versions are read from `charts/*/Chart.yaml` **as of that commit**, so a commit that bumped a chart is checked against the version it actually published under. Every commit-ish is expanded to 40 characters **by git**; no sha is assembled by hand.
- Anonymous GHCR pull token by default, so it runs from a workstation with no credentials: `make check-published [COMMIT=<sha>]`.

`classify()` tested the HTTP status only inside an `error_code === 0` branch. k6 sets a **non-zero** `error_code` for an HTTP error response, so those status tests were unreachable for every response they were written for:

On its first real run (rev231, 2026-09-20/21) it worked — the reconciliation was exact on all five runners — but the 4 failures it found all landed in `other`, and **`other` cannot be resolved into anything actionable from what the run produces.**

## Evidence

```
{"counts":{"dns":0,"conn":0,"tls":0,"timeout":0,"proto":0,"http_4xx":0,"http_5xx":0,"other":4},

## The gap

`e2e/soak/k6-mesh-soak.js` does pass the disambiguating detail as tags:

```js

  endpoint: url,
  code: String(res.error_code || 0),
  status: String(res.status),
});
```

with the stated intent: *"The exact code/status rides along as a tag so the raw output can still resolve a class down to a specific error when one needs chasing."*

But the run keeps no raw output. `handleSummary` reads `data.metrics[metric].values.count`, which is aggregated across tags, and it returns `{stdout: ...}` — which **replaces** k6's default summary. So the only artefact is the per-class count. The tags exist during the run and are discarded at the end of it.

The comment is therefore true only in a configuration we do not run: there is no `--out` sink, deliberately (the runner drops privileges, and this repo has lost soak summaries to filesystem writes before — see the note in `handleSummary`).

## Why it matters

agent_prs.body:
Closes #883. Closes #884.

Three fixes to the document a workload author reads to learn how to address the mesh.

## The port-stripping claim was inverted (#883)

It said *"A `:port` on the authority is stripped before routing"*. The data plane does the opposite — `strip_any_host_port` is off, and three places assert it must stay off. The authority's port is **part of the vhost domain match**; if it were stripped, proposal 005's per-port routing couldn't work at all.

Wrong on the exact axis proposal 037 turns on, so a reader starting here would have started from the inverse of the truth.

## The ODCDS timeout was stale (#884)

Documented as 5s; `onDemandClusterTimeout` is 2s. Now stated relative to the constant and named, so the next change makes the doc's staleness findable by grep.

## The 037 client contract was undocumented

The annotation table listed **neither** `endpoint.aether.io/protocol` **nor** `endpoint.aether.io/ports`, despite both being registration facts a workload author has to set. Both are now in the table, with the suffix grammar.

Adds the resolution table — `http://`, `https://`, `:18081`, `:18082`, `:<port>` — and the reason the two mesh ports exist:

> HTTP demuxes on the **authority header**, which carries its own port as a string — so `http://<svc>/` is unambiguous without one. Raw TCP has no authority; its only demux key is the 5-tuple.

That asymmetry is intrinsic to the protocols, not to this mesh, and it's why TCP gets a well-known port of its own rather than the bare name changing meaning depending on a service's primary protocol.

Also records that `:18082` does **not** need redirect-all while a dial to a service's own application port does, and that an unregistered port is REJECTed by kube-proxy rather than silently forwarded.

Docs only.
