issues.body:
## Summary

`docs/workload-requirements.md:194` documents the on-demand (ODCDS) timeout as **5s**. The code uses **2s**.

## Evidence

Doc:

> *under the mesh domain* fail after the 5s on-demand timeout; anything [...]

Code — `agent/internal/xds/proxy/httpfilter.go:27-32`:

```go
// onDemandClusterTimeout bounds how long a request to a not-yet-distributed
// cluster is paused while ODCDS fetches it from the node-local agent. With
// the leading-edge reload + catalog-gated RPC fill, a legitimate cold warm
// completes in tens of milliseconds, so this bound is purely the ghost
// cap: requests for catalog-rejected services fail when it expires.
onDemandClusterTimeout = 2 * time.Second
```

It is applied at `httpfilter.go:50` as the on-demand filter's `Timeout`.

## Why it matters

Minor on its own, but it is a number an operator would use when setting a client-side timeout or when judging whether a hang is aether's ghost cap or something else. A client timeout tuned to the documented 5s would never observe the real 2s failure, and someone triaging a stall would look 2.5x too far out.

## Fix

Change the doc to 2s, or better, state it relative to the constant and name it (`onDemandClusterTimeout`), so the next change to the constant makes the doc's staleness findable by grep.

Found incidentally while checking a different claim in the same file (the authority-port statement, filed separately). The file has not been audited.

issues.body:
## Summary

`docs/workload-requirements.md` — the client-facing contract for addressing mesh services — states:

> A `:port` on the authority is stripped before routing.

The data plane does not do this. The authority port is a **first-class routing key**.

## Evidence

`strip_any_host_port` is set nowhere in the tree, and three separate places assert it must stay off:

- `agent/internal/xds/proxy/filterchain.go:27` — "strip_any_host_port stays OFF: the authority port is a first-class routing [key]"
- `agent/internal/xds/proxy/filterchain_test.go:59` and `edge_test.go:82,284` — `assert.False(t, hcm.GetStripAnyHostPort(), ...)`
- `agent/internal/xds/proxy/edge.go:123,166,203,375` — the edge uses `ignore_port_in_host_matching` specifically *instead of* `strip_any_host_port`, because the latter "would mutate the :authority for the whole [request]"

And the routing depends on the port being present. `BuildOutboundClusterVirtualHost` (`agent/internal/xds/proxy/route.go:275-281`):

> The default-port cluster passes two domains (portless FQDN + FQDN:defaultPort) so both spellings reach it; a non-default port cluster passes the single FQDN:port. The authority port is meaningful (strip_any_host_port off), so exact-domain precedence keeps a ported authority from matching the portless default vhost (spike-verified).

So `<svc>.<ns>.<domain>:8080` reaches the `:8080` per-port cluster **because** the authority carries `:8080`. If the port were stripped as documented, per-port routing (proposal 005) could not work at all.

## Why it matters

This is the document a workload author reads to learn how to address the mesh. It describes port-agnostic addressing, which would lead someone to conclude the port they put in a URL is decorative — when in fact it selects the upstream cluster. Someone debugging why `<svc>:8080` and `<svc>:9090` behave differently would be reading a doc that says they cannot.

It also mis-states the shape of the system in a way that matters for design work: pr

Closes #878.

## The bug

`ListEndpoints`/`ListAllEndpoints` returned nil for every `PROTOCOL_TCP` query, so a pod annotated `endpoint.aether.io/protocol: tcp` was accepted at registration and silently dropped on read. On the **chart-default** backend that means `Accepted=True` on the user's TCPRoute and no endpoints, with nothing said anywhere.

The blanket return was a workaround, and its own comment admitted as much. The actual cause was a layer down: **`podToEndpoint` never read the protocol annotation.** Every managed pod therefore looked like an HTTP endpoint, and answering a TCP query with that same set made every mesh service collapse to a TCP-only entry — `LoadClustersFromRegistry` overwrites the HTTP cluster and GAMMA `cap_http` vhost with a vhost-less `tcp:true` entry, and captured requests 503'd with `no_healthy_upstream` (#430). Suppressing the TCP listing hid the symptom; reading the annotation removes the cause.

## What changed

Both listings filter on the protocol each pod declares, **in both directions**. Returning HTTP pods under TCP is #430; returning TCP pods under HTTP is the same bug mirrored, and would put a raw-TCP pod behind an h2 cluster.

The "a service is HTTP or TCP, never both" invariant is untouched and still holds, because every pod behind one ServiceAccount carries the same annotation. `RequireProtocolDisjoint` keeps passing — and now has a call site where **both maps are non-empty**, which is the only shape in which it can fail. Its existing call site runs the loop body zero times; that is now noted in place rather than left to look like coverage.

`podToEndpoint` never read `endpoint.aether.io/ports` either. `Ports` was nil on every endpoint this backend returned, so **proposal 005's per-port EDS membership has never worked here** while working fine on the write-based backends. Nobody had hit it, but it is the same defect wearing a different hat.

agent_prs.body:
The `replicator` suite intermittently fails step 3's **negative** assertion — `client(a)` must stop reaching `echo` once region-b's mirror expires from etcd-a. The registry half is provably fine (mirror expires at **0s**, b's origin data persists); what flakes is the **data path outliving the registry state**, and today that failure says nothing beyond "still 200".

That matters more than a loose budget suggests. The withdrawal path is **watch-driven end to end** — a's registrar syncs off the etcd watch with the 5s poll as a mere backstop (`registrar/internal/server/sync.go`, `registry/internal/etcd/etcd.go`), and the agent pushes xDS off the resulting broadcast. Designed latency is sub-second plus debounce, so exceeding 30s is ~2 orders of magnitude off the designed path, not a marginal overrun.

Widening the window would bury one of three materially different causes, so this instruments the hops instead. **No timeout, retry budget, or production code is touched.**

## `dump_failover_state()` — on the failure path, before `die`

| Section | Discriminates |
|---|---|
| **registry** — region-b keys in both etcds | re-printed at failure time so the log is self-contained |
| **registrar** — two greps of a's logs: watch establish/re-establish + lease/leader/mirror lines, then the sync cadence | **(1)** the watch lapsed and we degraded to the 5s poll, vs **(2)** a replicator leader-election / mirror-stream gap |
| **agent** — snapshot rebuilds + dependency-set transitions for `echo`, plus `aether_agent_snapshot_*` metrics | first half of **(3)** |
| **envoy** — the `echo` cluster's hosts from admin `/clusters` | proves or clears **(3)** outright |

Two registrar greps rather than one because the chart runs everything with `--debug`, so per-cycle chatter would otherwise crowd the rare decisive lines out of any single tail.

**(3)** is the consequential one: hosts still present would mean cross-cluster failover latency is bounded by something other than the origin-heartbea

agent_prs.body:
Closes #597.

## It was never a flake in the sense everyone assumed

The replicator e2e went red on 09-18 and 09-19 after **sixteen** consecutive green runs. The decisive datum: **09-17 and 09-18 built the same commit `0459c2a4` with opposite outcomes**, so no bisect could ever have found it. Both standing hypotheses — an intermittent stall, and a 30 s budget that is too tight — predict exactly that pattern, which is why more observation could not separate them.

Neither is the cause.

```sh
mirror_present() {
    docker exec ... etcdctl get --prefix ... --keys-only 2>/dev/null | grep -q .
}
```

Stderr is discarded and the pipeline's status is **grep's**. A `docker exec` that could not start, or an `etcdctl` that timed out, produces no output — and is therefore **indistinguishable from "the keys are gone"**. Step 3's expiry loop breaks on the first "gone", so a single hiccup on a contended runner (two kind clusters, 2× SPIRE, 2× etcd on `ubuntu-latest`) made the harness declare the mirror expired *while it was still there*, and start its 30 s stopwatch **up to ~29 s before the event it claims to measure**.

Reconstructed from the 09-18 logs, the mesh withdrew in **~150 ms**. The harness was timing the wrong interval.

## What changes

- **`mirror_state()`** replaces the boolean with three values — present / absent / **read failed**. Read failures are loud on stderr, carry `--command-timeout=5s`, and can never mean "absent". **Only a successful read that finds nothing may anchor the stopwatch.**
- **The origin-data check had the same defect somewhere worse**: a failed read made it report *"region's ORIGIN data vanished from its own etcd"* — a spurious hard failure asserting data loss. Now distinguished.
- **Step 3 measures instead of only judging.** Samples at ~1 s rather than 6×5 s and prints `AETHER_METRIC replicator_withdraw_seconds` on **every** run, pass or fail. Budget stays 30 s; the cap is 120 s so a run that blows the budget still yields a *number*. A red r

The `replicator` job in the `e2e` workflow intermittently fails at step 3/4 on the **negative** assertion:

2. Envoy retaining the endpoint after an empty/updated EDS response lo

agent_prs.body:
Closes #842.

Replaces the per-identity `transport_socket_matches` + `transport_socket_matcher` on every mesh cluster with **one** transport socket whose `custom_tls_certificate_selector` resolves the client certificate per connection, and drops `connection_pool_per_downstream_connection`.

Both halves are the same mechanism — the source SPIFFE ID in a downstream-shared filter-state object — so they ship together. Removing the flag without the hashable key re-opens the #831 leak, and it fails **open**.

## The filter state

Mesh-originating chains stamp a third object, under the name Envoy's `filter_state_override` upstream certificate mapper hardcodes (`envoy.tls.certificate_mappers.on_demand_secret`), with the `envoy.hashable_string` factory.

That factory is the whole point: `set_filter_state`'s default `envoy.string` builds a `Router::StringAccessorImpl`, which is not `Envoy::Hashable`, and `CommonUpstreamTransportSocketFactory::hashKey` folds a shared filter-state object into the upstream pool key only behind a `dynamic_cast` to `Hashable`.

`aether.source.spiffe_id` keeps being stamped **for one release**: it is what a pre-#842 cluster's matcher reads, so rollback stays hitless (the dual-key overlap #815 used), and it is the access log's `source_spiffe_id`. Retiring it and the netns copy together is a follow-up.

## The cluster

```
custom_tls_certificate_selector:
  envoy.tls.certificate_selectors.on_demand_secret
    config_source:      ads (the agent's own stream)
    certificate_mapper: ...upstream_certificate_mappers.filter_state_override
                          default_value: <node SVID>
    prefetch_secret_names: [<node SVID>]
```

issues.body:
Split out of #831, which established (PR #841) that aether is not exposed to the
cross-source certificate leak *because* every node-proxy mesh cluster sets
`connection_pool_per_downstream_connection: true`.

That flag is a mitigation, not a design. It buys correctness by giving every
downstream connection its own upstream pool, which means the node proxy **cannot
multiplex** streams from different source pods onto a shared upstream HTTP/2
connection. On a node with many pods talking to the same service that is a real
and permanent cost: one upstream connection per downstream connection, one
handshake each, and no h2 stream concurrency benefit across sources.

The root cause is narrow and fixable upstream. `set_filter_state`'s default
`FactoryKey: "envoy.string"` builds a `Router::StringAccessorImpl`
(`source/common/router/string_accessor_impl.h`), which implements `StringAccessor`
only. `CommonUpstreamTransportSocketFactory::hashKey`
(`source/common/network/transport_socket_options_impl.cc:47-53`) folds a
downstream shared filter-state object into the upstream pool hash **only** if
`dynamic_cast<const Hashable*>` succeeds. Envoy already ships a hashable variant
(`envoy.hashable_string` → `HashableString`); the `set_filter_state` config has no
way to ask for it for an inline literal.

Two shapes, either of which is enough:

1. a `hashable: true` knob on `FilterStateValue` that selects the hashable string
   factory, or
2. upstream a `Hashable` string filter-state factory registered under a name the
   control plane can put in `factory_key`.

With that, `aether.source.spiffe_id` lands in the pool key and pools separate by
*identity* rather than by *connection* — which is the correct granularity: pods
sharing a ServiceAccount could then share upstream connections, and pods that do
not, could not. `connection_pool_per_downstream_connection` could come off every
mesh cluster.

aether already carries Envoy patches (`proxy/`), so this is tractable here before
it lands upst

agent_prs.body:
Closes #724.

## Why

`proxy-release` comments on the rolling tracking issue on **every** run. #727 removed the hand-off that was built for, so since then every comment has ended with *"Nothing to do here"* — and has been correct **13 times out of 13**, which is every pin PR the flow has ever produced:

| | |
|---|---|
| `chore/proxy-image-bump-*` PRs, all time | **13** |
| merged | **13** |
| needed a human | **0** |

A thread whose every entry says there is nothing to do buries the rare entry that does not, and it sits in the open-issue list competing with work that is actually blocked.

## What changes

The tracker becomes an **escalation** thread. A single new step writes to it, only when the run genuinely needs somebody:

- auto-merge could not be armed;
- a superseded `chore/proxy-image-bump-*` PR was left open;
- `RELEASE_PAT` is expiring (<30d), expired, rejected or unparseable;
- the run fell back to the #703 manual hand-off (the comment then carries the `gh pr create` one-liner).

On the happy path nothing is written — the run summary is the whole record. **Silence now carries information:** an empty thread means every release since went through untouched.

## Two traps this had to avoid

1. **Closing the issue would not have worked.** The resolve step *created* the issue when it was missing, so the next release would simply have opened a new one. It now only finds an already-open issue; the escalation step creates one on demand.

Rolling tracker for the `proxy-release` -> chart-pin hand-off (#703).

agent_prs.body:
Addresses item 1 of #812.

## The problem

A surging edge roll needs room for an extra 400m pod. On rev214 that pod was preempted by the proxy DaemonSet on a node at 84 % CPU requests and **wedged the roll outright**; later rolls escaped it only because the surge pod happened to land elsewhere.

That is a rollout whose success depends on cluster headroom at the moment it runs. A release process should not have that property, and "it worked last time" was luck rather than design.

## The change

With **≥ 2 replicas**, the default becomes `maxSurge: 0, maxUnavailable: 1`. This removes the scheduler from the rollout path entirely — no new pod has to be placed for the roll to proceed. The soft hostname spread already on this Deployment keeps replicas apart, so at least one is serving behind the LB throughout.

A briefly degraded ingress beats a stuck one, and a stuck roll is what we actually observed.

With **exactly 1 replica** the old `maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0` is kept, because a single replica cannot roll without either a surge or an outage window, and surging is the better of the two. That is the kind/e2e shape rather than a production one — and a flat change would have turned every single-replica roll into a full ingress gap, which is why this is conditional rather than a one-line edit.

`edge.rollingUpdate` overrides both branches for a cluster with spare headroom that would rather surge.

## Verification

Rendered on all three paths:

| `replicaCount: 2` (default) | 0 | 1 |

| `edge.rollingUpdate` set explicitly | honoured verbatim | |

Fixes #859.

## What broke

`mesh-http` and `gateway-http` have failed every nightly run since 2026-09-13. The conformance tests **pass** — `gateway-http` has *zero* failing subtests — and the job still reports `--- FAIL`, with no report artifact (`No files were found with the provided path: .../gateway-http-report.yaml`):

       can't generate report: the test suite is currently running
```

## Why

`a2d72e1` (#751) bumped `GATEWAY_API_VERSION: v1.6.1 → v1.6.2`. Upstream v1.6.2 deleted this from the tail of `ConformanceTestSuite.Run()`:

```go

	suite.lock.Lock()
	suite.running = false
	suite.results = results
	suite.lock.Unlock()
```

and replaced it with a cleanup registered *inside* `Run`:

```go
	t.Cleanup(func() {
		suite.lock.Lock()
		suite.running = false
		suite.lock.Unlock()
	})
```

Register the report write as a `t.Cleanup` **before** `cSuite.Run`. Cleanups run LIFO, so ours fires after the suite's own (registered later, inside `Run`): `running` is already clear.

This also closes a second, latent bug the old call site had: `Run` returns before its parallel subtests finish (the run log shows `=== CONT …` lines *after* the report error), so even without the flag the report was being rendered mid-flight. A cleanup on the parent test is guaranteed to run after every parallel subtest completes.

`writeReport` now records failures with `t.Errorf` instead of `require`, because a `FailNow` inside a cleanup would skip the suite's remaining cleanups (its base-resource teardown).

agent_prs.body:
Closes #853.

## The defect

`.bazelrc` has run the shellcheck aspect on every `--config=lint` build since it was added, and it has never read a line of this repository's own shell.

The issue diagnosed it as "the root workspace declared no `sh_*` target". That is one step off, and the real shape is worth recording because it is what made this invisible for so long. The repo **has** always had an `sh_binary` — `//:gazelle`, from the `gazelle` macro — so `bazel query 'kind("sh_(binary|library|test)", //...)'` was never empty. But `filter_srcs` (`lint/private/lint_aspect.bzl`) keeps only srcs that are source files in the main repo:

```starlark
return [s for s in rule.files.srcs if s.is_source and s.owner.workspace_name == ""]
```

`//:gazelle`'s only src is the **generated** `//:gazelle-runner`, which that discards. So the aspect was handed zero files. `make lint` was green because it had no input — indistinguishable from green because the shell is clean.

## What changed

**Five `sh_library` targets**, one per shell-bearing package: `//scripts`, `//bazel`, `//e2e`, `//e2e/pressure`, `//e2e/soak`, each `glob(["*.sh"])`. No symlink bridge — unlike #848 these files are not behind `.bazelignore`, so the targets sit in their own packages directly.

Per-directory rather than one target, for two reasons. A glob cannot cross a package boundary, so a single `glob(["**/*.sh"])` under `//e2e` would stop dead at `//e2e/udsecho`'s `BUILD.bazel` and cover less than it appeared to — the same class of silent under-coverage this PR exists to end. And a per-directory target keeps the lint failure label pointing at the directory the script lives in. `//scripts:check_proxy_shell_lint` (#848, one file) becomes `//scripts:scripts_shell` (all seven); only `//scripts:all` was ever referenced, so nothing depended on the old name.

`.bazelrc` has run the shellcheck aspect on every `--config=lint` build since it was added:

```
build:lint --aspects=...,//bazel/lint:linters.bzl%shellcheck,...

## What it would take

`//scripts:check_proxy_shell_lint` is the one-file precedent added by #848; widening its `srcs` to `glob(["*.sh"])` and adding the same target under `e2e/` and `bazel/` is the mechanical part. ## The gap

`proxy.DownstreamTransportSocket` set `RequireClientCertificate: true` with a validation context carrying **no SAN matchers at all**. The handshake therefore proved one thing: the trust bundle signed *something*. Any certificate that bundle chains to satisfied it, workload SVID or not.

The inbound HCM then stamps that certificate's URI SAN into XFCC with `SANITIZE_SET` (`ingress.go:231-235`), and RBAC/ext_authz decisions key on the result. So the property every XFCC-derived rule assumes — "this value came off a verified workload identity" — was never actually established.

## The fix

The destination cannot pin a *specific* ServiceAccount; in a mesh any workload may legitimately call, and identity-level authorization belongs in RBAC/ext_authz. It can require the certificate to be **structurally a workload SVID**. Every mTLS inbound chain now carries a combined validation context with one `match_typed_subject_alt_names` entry:

layered over the same SDS-rotated trust bundle as before.

Split out of #831. Independent of the pooling question that issue raised (refuted,
PR #841) — this one stands on its own and is still open.

`proxy.DownstreamTransportSocket` (`agent/internal/xds/proxy/transportsocket.go:35-49`)
sets `RequireClientCertificate: true` with a validation context carrying **no SAN
matchers at all** — trust-bundle membership only. Every mesh workload in
`aether.internal` satisfies it, including certificates that are not workload SVIDs
at all.

The inbound listener then stamps XFCC `SANITIZE_SET` from that peer certificate
(`ingress.go:231-235`), so whatever URI SAN the peer presented is propagated to the
application and to any ext_authz/RBAC decision as though it had been meaningfully
verified. The destination has verified only "some cert this trust bundle signs".

The fix does not require knowing which ServiceAccount may call — any mesh workload
legitimately may. It requires the certificate to be **structurally a workload
SVID**: a `match_typed_subject_alt_names` entry with `san_type: URI` and a prefix
matcher on `spiffe://<trust-domain>/ns/`, which rejects a node SVID, an
infrastructure identity, or anything else whose SPIFFE path is not

Split out of #837, which added OCI provenance labels to every published image.

For the seven Bazel-built images, `rules_img` writes the labels at **index level and on each per-platform descriptor**, so `crane manifest <index>` answers directly.

`aether-proxy` is different: its multi-arch index is assembled by `docker buildx imagetools create` in `proxy-release.yml`, **outside Bazel**. The per-platform manifests and configs carry all five provenance keys, but the index itself carries **no annotations at all** — confirmed on the published artifact for both arches.

So anyone asking "which Envoy is in this proxy image?" has to hop to a platform-specific manifest first. That is a smaller version of the original problem: the answer exists but the obvious query does not return it, and a tool walking index annotations gets nothing rather than the truth.

## Fix

An extra `crane`/`buildx` step in `proxy-release.yml` to set index-level annotations matching the per-platform ones. Deliberately out of scope for #845, which stayed inside Bazel.

Worth noting the related asymmetry found at the same time: the top-level index for the Bazel images had no annotations before #845 either, and `agent:dev` carries only `org.opencontainers.image.base.*` inherited from distroless.

The node's egress listener routes over RDS for `out_http`

config **only when `len(vhosts) > 0`** — unlike the edge and capture route

with nothing to publish (the local-only fallback `loadInitialRegistryConfig`
takes when the registry cannot serve endpoints inside its 15 s budget) therefore
published no route config at all.

The issue says "no `initial_fetch_timeout` anywhere, so Envoy does not wait".
**Envoy waited, and it waited exactly 15 s** — that field's default is 15 s, and
the measured w02 timeline is a ~15 s wait, not a zero-length one:

| event | timestamp | Δ from LDS |
|---|---|---|
| new-epoch LDS `update_time` | 16:08:50.558Z | — |
| first `404 NR` | 16:09:05.214Z | **+14.656 s** |
| last `404 NR` | 16:09:08.032Z | +17.474 s |
| first `out_http` RDS update | 16:09:08.123Z | +17.565 s |

issues.body:
`kill -TERM` on the soak churn driver does not stop it — **it makes it fire the next roll early.** The signal you send to stop the tool causes the opposite of what you asked.

Hit for real on 2026-09-19 while killing an accidentally duplicated driver before the rev226 soak. The TERM produced an unscheduled `ROLLED aether-test/deployment/svc-1` at 23:10:32Z while the process carried on running.

## Cause

`e2e/soak/churn.sh:125`:

```bash
trap restore_shrink EXIT INT TERM
```

`restore_shrink` (`:114-124`) **returns rather than exiting**. So on TERM, bash runs the handler, the handler returns, the in-flight `sleep` inside `waituntil` has already been interrupted by the signal, and control falls straight through to the next `roll`. The driver keeps running, one roll ahead of schedule.

This reads in the logs as "the tool ignored my signal", which sends you debugging the wrong thing — the tool did not ignore it, it did the opposite. Those need different debugging, which is the real cost.

## Fix

Keep `EXIT` as the idempotent safety net and make the interactive signals actually terminate:

```bash
trap restore_shrink EXIT
trap 'restore_shrink; exit 130' INT
trap 'restore_shrink; exit 143' TERM
```

`restore_shrink` is already idempotent — it clears `SHRINK_PREV` before scaling — so the EXIT trap firing again after an INT/TERM handler is harmless.

## Sibling footgun, same family

`pkill -f "soak/churn.sh"` matches **the issuing shell's own command line** and kills that too, because the pattern appears in the command being run. Same for `pgrep -cf`, which is why a count of running drivers reads one too high. Match on PID, or anchor the pattern to the absolute script path.

Both of these are cases where **the safety action causes the harm**, which is what makes them worth documenting rather than just fixing.

## Also worth adding to `e2e/soak/README.md`

- Stop the driver with `kill -9 <pid>`, not `kill`/`pkill`.
- Before launching, check for an existing driver by **abso

issues.body:
You cannot determine which Envoy commit a running `aether-proxy` contains — **neither from the process nor from the image**. Two symptoms, one gap.

Surfaced while investigating #829, where knowing the exact Envoy build mattered for whether a runtime guard's behaviour was in play.

## Symptom 1 — the runtime gauge does not match the pin

`envoy_server_version` reads **3121738** = `0x2FA24A` → hex string `2fa24a`, identically on all five proxy nodes. Envoy derives that gauge from the first six hex digits of its build SCM revision.

Our pinned Envoy is `1.40.0-dev.20260904.13144fb.envoy` — first six digits `13144f` = 1250383. **They do not match and are not close.**

Most likely reading: the gauge is stamped from the **`proxy/` workspace's own** SCM revision rather than Envoy's, since we build Envoy as a bzlmod dependency and the stamping takes the driving repo. If so the gauge will report the driving repo forever, and no amount of reading it will ever answer "which Envoy is this".

## Symptom 2 — the image carries no provenance either, and one annotation is actively misleading

Decoded from the published index (`aether-proxy@sha256:caa471b6…`, arm64 config blob — amd64 may differ):

- **No labels at all.** No `org.opencontainers.image.revision`, no version, no build metadata.
- `created` is `1970-01-01T00:00:00Z`; history entries are `bazel bu…`. Fully reproducible, zero-timestamp output — deliberate and good.
- The manifest's **only** annotation is `org.opencontainers.image.source = https://github.com/GoogleContainerTools/distroless`, **inherited from the distroless base**. That is worse than absent: anything walking image annotations for provenance gets a confident wrong answer pointing at Google's repo rather than ours.

Confirmed repo-wide: there are **no `org.opencontainers.image.*` labels on any image we publish**, so this is not specific to the proxy — the proxy is just where it bites, because it is the one image whose contents come from a third-party pin.

agent_prs.body:
Fixes #836. Fixes #832.

Both were found while investigating #829, both live in the upstream-TLS /
server-identity-pinning path, and both touch the same two files
(`agent/internal/xds/proxy/transportsocket.go`, `agent/internal/xds/cache/mtls.go`)
plus the same test harness — so they ship together rather than as two PRs that
would conflict with each other.

## #836 — the readiness probe gets its own TLS context

`inboundready_<pod>` built its transport socket with `UpstreamTransportSocket`,
the same helper every mesh cluster uses. That probe dials each local pod's mesh
inbound **inside that pod's netns** every 5 s, so its TLS peer is always a pod
on this node presenting that pod's SVID — the one certificate that must never
turn up in an unrelated cluster's handshake. In #829 it did: mesh clusters
resumed from a session the probe had created and were handed a local pod's
certificate, which is exactly why the leaked identity was always a source-node
neighbour.

The probe now builds its own `UpstreamTlsContext`
(`proxy.InboundReadyProbeTransportSocket`) carrying its **own**
`max_session_keys: 0`.

**Why #834 does not make this redundant.** #834 set `max_session_keys: 0` on the
shared mesh builder, which removes the slot everywhere — correct, and it should
stay. But it is a *global switch*, and it is one someone may legitimately
reverse: upstream envoy#45982 scopes the upstream session cache by SNI, and once
that is in force for our config, resumption for mesh traffic becomes defensible
again. The moment that happens, the probe would silently be back inside the same
cache as application traffic. What this change adds is the **boundary**: the
probe's TLS state is not reachable by application traffic regardless of what the
mesh path does. The two changes have different lifetimes.

The SAN pin (`[]string{podSpiffeID}`) and the empty SNI are unchanged — both are
load-bearing and the reasons are restated at the new function.

## #832 — an unpinned cluster is no longer silent
agent_prs.title: fix(agent): give the readiness probe its own TLS context, and make an unpinned cluster loud (#836, #832)

issues.body:
The `inboundready_<pod>` readiness-probe cluster shares a client-side TLS session cache with mesh application traffic on the same node proxy. A health check therefore deposits a session — and with it a peer certificate — into a cache that serves application requests.

That is a boundary violation on its own terms, independent of the defect it happened to cause.

## Why this is separate from #834

#829's fix (#834) sets `max_session_keys: 0` on every upstream builder, which removes the slot everywhere. That is correct and should land. But the two changes have different lifetimes:

- **#834 is a fix.** It also forecloses upstream session resumption as a future option for mesh traffic, and it silently reopens this class the moment anyone re-enables resumption for a good reason.
- **This is a boundary that should have existed anyway.** A readiness probe's TLS state has no business being reachable by application traffic, regardless of whether resumption is on.

## What the probe actually is

`agent/internal/xds/proxy/cluster.go:492`:

```go
TransportSocket: UpstreamTransportSocket(nodeSpiffeID, validationContextName, []string{podSpiffeID}, "" /* no SNI: the no-SNI h2 chain */),
```

It dials each local pod's inbound listener **inside that pod's netns**, on a 5 s health-check interval. Its peer is therefore always a pod on this node, presenting that pod's SVID. In #829 that is exactly what leaked: the probe's session carried a local pod's certificate, and every mesh cluster that then resumed from the shared slot was handed it. The observed "the leaked identity is always a source-node neighbour" rule is a direct consequence of what this cluster talks to.

## Proposed fix

Give the probe its own TLS context so its session state cannot reach mesh clusters, or simply never resume on it — `max_session_keys: 0` scoped to this cluster specifically, which is correct permanently and not merely while #834 stands. A health check gains nothing from resumption: it runs every 5 s again
issues.title: The inboundready probe shares a TLS session cache with mesh traffic; it should have its own

issues.body:
When the agent's trust domain is empty, a mesh cluster is published with **no server-identity pin at all**. The handshake then proves only trust-domain membership — any workload in `aether.internal` satisfies it. Nothing asserts the window, counts it, or logs it.

This is a silent authentication downgrade whose only trace today is a code comment.

## The path

`agent/internal/xds/cache/mtls.go:107-113` — when `st.trustDomain == ""`, `sanURIs` stays nil.

`agent/internal/xds/proxy/transportsocket.go:117-121` — the `len(sanURIs) == 0` branch emits a plain `ValidationContextSdsSecretConfig` with **no `match_typed_subject_alt_names`**.

The comment at `mtls.go:103-106` acknowledges this as the deliberate lesser evil versus emitting `spiffe:///ns/…` with an empty trust domain — which is the exact failure that took down rev222 (#815/#819: SDS names nobody serves, endpoints demoted permanently, no alert). Choosing the unpinned form over the unservable one is right. Shipping it **silently** is not.

The bound is "one snapshot", but nothing enforces or observes that bound, so a window that lasts longer than intended looks identical to one that does not happen at all.

## Why it matters beyond the window

Combined with any path that puts a foreign endpoint in a cluster's load assignment, an unpinned cluster turns a would-be rejection into a **clean handshake and a delivered request**, with nothing logged or counted anywhere. That is the fail-open direction; the pin is what makes these failures loud. See #829, where the pin is what caught the problem.

## Fix

1. At `mtls.go:107-113`, when `st.trustDomain == ""`, emit a WARN once per snapshot naming the affected clusters, and increment `aether.agent.identity.cluster_unpinned`. **Seed the counter at zero** — an unseeded zero reads as a false zero, which this repo has been bitten by before.
2. Extend `trustdomain_test.go`, which already covers the empty-trust-domain path, to assert the counter and the WARN rather than only the a

agent_prs.body:
Closes #818. Two small leftovers from turning the canary on, batched because every prober chart release re-rolls the prober DaemonSet and resets the SLI counters — so this lands deliberately right after a graded soak rather than before one.

## Spread the target

Both `authz-echo` replicas **and** the `authz-canary` client landed on main-worker-01, the densest node. That put the entire canary path — source proxy and destination — behind a single node's proxy, so a roll of that one proxy reads as "authz down" rather than as the roll it is. That is exactly the distinction the canary exists to make.

Soft `topologySpreadConstraints` on hostname with `ScheduleAnyway`, matching the harness `echo` deployment. Deliberately soft: spreading is worth having, but never worth leaving the canary unscheduled, because **an unscheduled canary is indistinguishable from a broken one**. Spreading the target is sufficient — no anti-affinity on the client is needed.

## Stop printing `allow=000000`

`curl` already prints `000` for `%{http_code}` on a connect failure, so the `|| echo 000` appended a second one and every FAIL line read `allow=000000`. Now the code is captured and defaulted only when the capture is genuinely **empty** — which is what a killed curl produces, as opposed to a failed one.

## Verification

`helm template` renders clean with `authzCanary.enabled=true`; both changes confirmed in the rendered output. Chart `0.4.1` → `0.4.2`.

Note the chart version carries a `{GIT_COMMIT}` placeholder substituted at release time, so `helm template` against the tree needs a concrete version — rendered against a temp copy with the placeholder replaced.

issues.body:
Two small leftovers from turning the canary on (talos-main, prober rev13 = 0.4.1, 2026-09-19). The canary itself works: `allow=200 / deny=403` since 16:36:5xZ, and `ext_authz` statistics exist for the first time.

1. **No spread:** both `authz-echo` replicas AND the `authz-canary` client landed on main-worker-01 — the densest node, and a single node's proxy now carries the whole canary path (source and destination), so a w01 proxy roll reads as "authz down". Add the soft `topologySpreadConstraints` (hostname, `ScheduleAnyway`) the harness `echo` uses, and a preferred anti-affinity between the client and nothing in particular is needed — spreading the target is enough.
2. **Cosmetic:** on a connect failure curl already prints `000` for `%{http_code}` and the script's `|| echo 000` appends a second one, so the FAIL line reads `allow=000000`. Capture the code and default it only when empty.

Batch with the next prober chart change: every prober chart release re-rolls the prober DaemonSet and resets the SLI counters.

For the runbook / an alert (exact names as exported):
- `envoy_http_capture_http_ext_authz_{ok,denied}_total{node}` — the filter on the capture HCM (stat prefix `capture_http`); `error`, `timeout`, `failure_mode_allowed` appear only once non-zero (Envoy's OTLP sink flushes used counters only).
- `envoy_cluster_ext_authz_{ok,denied}_total{aether_cluster="aether-test/authz-echo", node}` — per destination cluster.
- Healthy canary: `ok` and `denied` each grow at ≈0.2/s on the node hosting the client; an alert is `increase(…ext_authz_ok_total[10m]) == 0` or any growth of `…_error_total` / `…_timeout_total` / `…_failure_mode_allowed_total`.

agent_prs.body:
## Verdict: the mechanism is **CONFIRMED**, the exposure is **REFUTED**

#831 was derived from source reading. It is now demonstrated, against the pinned
`aether-proxy` Envoy, in both directions.

**Confirmed, in Envoy.** Every link the issue names is real. The source SPIFFE ID
is stamped with `set_filter_state`'s default `FactoryKey: "envoy.string"` →
`Router::StringAccessorImpl`, which is not `Envoy::Hashable`, and
`CommonUpstreamTransportSocketFactory::hashKey`
(`source/common/network/transport_socket_options_impl.cc:47-53`) folds a downstream
shared filter-state object into the upstream pool hash **only** behind a successful
`dynamic_cast<const Hashable*>`. The identity that selects the client certificate
contributes **zero bytes** to the pool key. Under h2 the consequence is exactly as
severe as the issue's follow-up comment says.

**Refuted, for aether.** The chain breaks at the link the issue did not examine:
*"Pools are keyed by cluster + host and are shared across source identities on the
node proxy."* They are not. Every mesh cluster the node proxy builds sets
`connection_pool_per_downstream_connection` (`proxy.NewServiceCluster` /
`NewTCPServiceCluster`, via `SnapshotCache.perDownstreamConnectionPool()` =
`!c.edge`), and Envoy mixes the downstream connection id into the hash in **both**
pool paths — `cluster_manager_impl.cc:2189` (HTTP) and `:2317` (TCP),
`ConnectionImplBase::hashKey` → `addIdToHashKey(hash, id())`. One pool per
downstream connection, and a downstream connection is one pod, so there is nothing
to share. The edge passes `false`, correctly: one identity cannot leak into itself.

`docs/runbook.md` already carried this as a *derived* note. This PR upgrades it to
a demonstrated one, and closes the gap that made #831 plausible in the first place:
nothing said the flag was load-bearing **security** configuration where someone
tuning connection pooling would look.

## The evidence, both ways

The harness (`//test/mtlspool`) runs the real pinned p

issues.body:
The source workload's SPIFFE ID is stamped into filter state but does **not** contribute to Envoy's upstream connection-pool hash key. Two pods on the same node with **different ServiceAccounts** talking to the same upstream share one connection pool, so whichever source happened to create the connection supplies the client certificate that every later request rides — including requests from the other workload.

The destination does not catch it, stamps the wrong identity into XFCC, and any RBAC or ext_authz decision keyed on source identity then authorizes the **wrong workload**.

This predates today's changes. It is **not** a regression from #815 (the previous netns-path key was also `envoy.string`); release two made it neither better nor worse. Found while investigating #829, which it is not the cause of.

## The chain

1. `agent/internal/xds/proxy/networkfilter.go:175` stamps the source identity with `FactoryKey: "envoy.string"` → Envoy constructs a `Router::StringAccessorImpl`.
2. `source/common/router/string_accessor_impl.h:8` — `StringAccessorImpl : public StringAccessor` only. It does **not** implement `Hashable`.
3. `source/common/network/transport_socket_options_impl.cc:47-53` — `CommonUpstreamTransportSocketFactory::hashKey` folds a downstream-shared filter-state object into the hash **only if** `dynamic_cast<const Hashable*>` succeeds.

So `aether.source.spiffe_id` contributes **zero bytes** to the pool hash. Pools are keyed by cluster + host and are shared across source identities on the node proxy.

## Why the destination cannot catch it

`agent/internal/xds/proxy/transportsocket.go:35-49` (`DownstreamTransportSocket`) sets `RequireClientCertificate: true` with a validation context carrying **no SAN matchers** — trust-domain membership only. Any workload in `aether.internal` satisfies it. agent_prs.body:
Closes #824.

Every identity field in an access-log line was something the control plane baked
into the emitting pod's own config, so a line could say who it THINKS it is but
never who the other end actually proved to be. Validating #815 release two needed
exactly that — "did any workload's traffic arrive as the node agent's identity?" —
and the answer had to be inferred from a match counter and from OPA's view of the
source's own claim.

Each hop now logs the one peer it verified:
- reporter=destination (the per-pod inbound listener): `downstream_peer_uri_san`
  = %DOWNSTREAM_PEER_URI_SAN%, the CALLER's SPIFFE ID as validated against the
  mesh trust bundle.
- reporter=source (outbound_http, capture_http): `upstream_peer_uri_san` =
  %UPSTREAM_PEER_URI_SAN%, the server certificate the destination proxy
  presented — the client-side view of the #638 cross-wiring, which today only
  shows up as envoy_cluster_ssl_fail_verify_san telling you SOME peer failed.

Split by reporter because each side has exactly one interesting peer and the
other operator renders "-" on every line. Both render "-" when the hop is not
mTLS, so SPIRE-off output is unchanged apart from one extra "-" field.
Cardinality is bounded by the number of ServiceAccounts.

Also closes a hole in the validation gate that this change walked straight into:
//test/envoy_validate never enabled access logging, so the entire access-log
config — ~30 substitution operators, the DYNAMIC_METADATA and FILTER_STATE specs,
the filter tree — had never been through a real Envoy config loader. The node
bootstrap now carries it (plus the otel_collector cluster the logger names).
Verified non-vacuous: replacing an operator with a bogus one fails the gate with
`error initializing configuration`, and both new operators pass against the
pinned 1.40.0-dev binary.



## Why now
Validating #815 release two, the destination-side check the plan called for could not be run at all — this is the instrument that was missing. It also a

issues.body:
Found validating #815 release two (rev225, 2026-09-19).

Release two changed how an outbound connection's client certificate is selected. The authoritative check — on the DESTINATION side, which verified identity did each request arrive with — could not be run: the OTLP access-log format (`agent/internal/xds/proxy/accesslog.go`) has no peer-identity field. There is no `%DOWNSTREAM_PEER_URI_SAN%`, no XFCC, and `source_netns` is source-side only (destination lines carry `-`). The validation fell back to the OPA decision log's `metadataContext.filterMetadata["aether.source"].spiffeId`, which is what the SOURCE proxy claims, not what the destination verified, plus the `match_count` no-match counter.

Proposal: add the verified peer URI SAN to inbound (destination-reporter) access-log entries — `%DOWNSTREAM_PEER_URI_SAN%` — and, symmetrically, `%UPSTREAM_PEER_URI_SAN%` / the presented local cert's URI SAN on the source side. Cardinality is per ServiceAccount, the same as the identities already in `aether_stats`. It turns "did any workload's traffic arrive as the node agent's identity" into one LogsQL query, which is the failure signature for #815's matcher and for #638/#686.
issues.title: access logs carry no verified peer identity, so 'which client identity did the destination see' cannot be answered

agent_prs.body:
Release one of three for #815. **Do not deploy without the live validation below** — it changes what HEALTHY means.

## Why
Every local pod ADD/DEL rewrites every mesh cluster on the node (the per-source upstream-mTLS matcher is keyed by the source pod's **netns path**). Under delta xDS each rewritten cluster re-warms for the 15 s EDS initial-fetch timeout and the swap drains every upstream connection pool on the node — measured live: 24–33 clusters warming for exactly 15 s per pod ADD. That is the 8-hour soak's SHRINK episode (18 timeouts on `echo`) and the prober timeouts after service rolls. The end state keys the matcher by the source pod's **SPIFFE ID** (per ServiceAccount, byte-stable). That switch is only safe once every originating listener already stamps the new filter-state key — otherwise `OnNoMatch` = node identity = the wrong client certificate (#686). Hence:

- **Release one (this PR):** listeners stamp BOTH keys; the cluster matcher is untouched (pinned by `TestClusterMatcherStillKeyedOnNetns`).
- **Release two:** switch the matcher input to `aether.source.spiffe_id`.
- **Release three:** drop the netns key.

## Part A — both filter-state keys
`aether.source.spiffe_id` (literal inline string, `shared_with_upstream: ONCE`, same read-only/skip semantics as the netns key — the matcher input only sees SHARED filter state) on the five per-pod originating chains: outbound HTTP, capture HCM, capture TCP floor, capture TCPRoute, capture TLSRoute. Correctly NOT stamped: `cap_passthrough`, the UDP capture listener (no filter chains), inbound, the waypoint tunnel, edge. Fixed filter order; omitted only when the trust domain is still empty (pre-SPIRE startup → exact pre-#815 bytes).

**One-time cost:** every mesh pod's outbound/capture listener changes bytes once on rollout (the netns key is set unconditionally today, so the new one is too — including SPIRE-off clusters). In-place filter-chain update with a drain.

## Part B — HEALTHY now requires an mTLS handsha

agent_prs.body:
Fix forward for #819 (release one of #815), which failed its live validation on talos-main and was rolled back (rev222 → rev223, 2026-09-19). `main` has been undeployable since; this makes it deployable again. **Deploy only with the live validation at the bottom.**

## Root cause of the outage — a lock-ordering hoist widened a nanosecond race into a ~700 ms one
The node agent's trust domain is late-bound (#740). `LoadListenersFromStorage` filled `c.listeners` under `listenerMu` and only afterwards recorded `c.trustDomain` — so for the duration of the load the cache held a complete listener map together with an **empty** trust domain. Pre-#819 the regeneration paths read `c.trustDomain` at the point of use, *inside* `listenerMu`, so the losing window was a few instructions wide and was never hit. #819 hoisted that read *above* the blocking `Lock()` ("read before taking listenerMu"), so any regeneration that merely **queued** on the lock during the load sampled `""`, waited, and then rewrote every per-pod listener from it: `spiffe:///ns/<ns>/sa/<sa>`.

On main-worker-03 the gamma reconciler's first `SetServiceChainFilters` fired 416 ms into the 710 ms load:

```
17:31:21.608 listener.go   generating listeners                  ← load starts
17:31:22.024 gamma.go      service chain filters updated         ← INSIDE the load
17:31:22.218 snapshot .1   secret=spiffe://aether.internal/…     ← correct
17:31:22.318 listener.go   generated listeners count=16          ← load ends
17:31:22.423 snapshot .2   bound_spiffe_id=spiffe:///ns/…        ← all 15 chains broken
```
w01 and w02 had the same event land *after* the load; w05 had it inside and won the race. Envoy subscribed to five SDS names nobody serves (`envoy_sds_spiffe_ns_*_init_fetch_timeout_total` = 1 each), the inbound listeners came up with no certificate, the new TLS probe could never pass, and four endpoints were demoted and never re-promoted.

agent_prs.body:
Release two of three for #815. Release one (#819 + #821) is live and validated on talos-main (helm rev224, `0.92.27-0f2b6c4`). **Deploy only on top of release one, with the live validation at the bottom.**

## The defect
Every local pod ADD/DEL rewrote **every** mesh cluster on the node: the per-source upstream-mTLS `transport_socket_matcher` keyed its `exact_match_map` on the source pod's **netns path**, unique per pod. Under delta xDS each rewritten EDS cluster re-warmed for the full 15 s EDS `initial_fetch_timeout`, and the warming→active swap destroyed the old `ClusterEntry` on every worker, draining every upstream connection pool on the node. Measured on talos-main rev224 (5 s resolution): one new pod → 20–24 clusters warming for 15 s; two on one node → 30 for 30 s; nodes with no new pod → 0. That handshake storm is the latency after a service roll and the 8-hour soak's largest error episode.

## The change
The matcher always *selected* per ServiceAccount — the `transport_socket_matches` entry name **is** the SPIFFE ID — so keying the map by identity loses nothing and makes the Cluster proto byte-stable across pod churn within a ServiceAccount. Release one made every mesh-originating chain stamp `aether.source.spiffe_id` (`shared_with_upstream: ONCE`); this reads it. The `FilterStateInput` key becomes `aether.source.spiffe_id`, the map is keyed by source SPIFFE ID (sorted, de-duplicated), `on_no_match` stays the node identity. The listeners keep stamping BOTH keys — dropping the netns key is release three.

| event | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| pod ADD/DEL, ServiceAccount already on the node | every cluster re-warms 15 s | **nothing** |
| rolling update, replacement lands on the same node | every cluster, twice | **nothing** |
| FIRST pod of a ServiceAccount arriving on a node / LAST one leaving | every cluster | every cluster, once |
| registry change to a cluster | that cluster | that cluster |

So the svc-4 4 → 8 burst that measured 30 clusters for 30 s

agent_prs.body:
The query shipped with #822 returns a FALSE ZERO on a live cluster, twice over
(caught during the rev225 validation by a Prometheus check from the platform side):

- the family is `envoy_cluster_match_count_total` — Prometheus' OTLP ingest moves
  "total" to the end; `envoy_cluster_total_match_count` does not exist;
- on a node agent the matcher's `on_no_match` identity is the AGENT'S OWN SVID
  (`spiffe://<td>/ns/aether-system/sa/aether-agent`), not
  `spiffe://<td>/node/<node>`, so the `/node/` selector matches nothing.

Runbook: corrected query (by node and cluster), what healthy looks like (0 over a
quiet window; during a pod ADD the increments sit entirely on that service's own
cluster), and where to read the identity from (`served node SVID`). It also claimed
a destination-side access-log cross-check that does not exist — the OTLP access log

Release three was planned as "drop `aether.network.network_namespace` from the listeners". Evaluated against the code and the pinned Envoy (1.40.0-dev, `13144fb`), it is a net loss. **This closes it as a decision rather than implementing it.** Documentation only — Go comments and Markdown, no generated bytes change, no chart change, nothing to deploy.

## What it would have bought
On a *listener* the netns entry carries no per-pod state: its value is the constant format string `%FILTER_STATE(envoy.network.network_namespace:PLAIN)%`, byte-identical on every chain of every pod. All of #815's churn lived in the *cluster* matcher, which release two (#822) fixed. Removing the listener entry would not reduce churn, re-warm or `cluster_modified` by one count. It saves ≈240 bytes per mesh-originating filter chain (≈0.5–1 KB per pod) and one format-string evaluation per new downstream connection. That is the entire benefit.

## What it would have cost
- **Rollback, permanently — the decisive one.** While the listeners stamp both keys, a proxy matches correctly against clusters from *either* side of release two, which is what makes a downgrade below `0.92.28` hitless. **This issue used that once already**: release one was rolled back on talos-main on 2026-09-19 (rev222 → rev223 = `0.92.26`). A release-three listener stamping only the SPIFFE ID, facing a pre-release-two netns-keyed cluster, matches nothing → `on_no_match` → the pod presents the agent's own SVID (`spiffe://<td>/ns/aether-system/sa/aether-agent`; not `spiffe://<td>/node/<node>` — #825). Trading the rollback path and a permanent version floor for ~240 bytes is a bad trade.
- Another full-fleet deploy that re-keys and drains every per-pod filter chain (listeners only — clusters would be untouched, so no `warming_clusters` wave and no pool drain; cheaper than release two, still not free).
- An access-log schema migration: `accesslog.go`'s `source_netns` is the copy's only remaining reader.

## Observation
The agent already detects the condition and only observes it: `agent/internal/xds/cache/inboundidentitybinding.go` logs WARN `inbound chain references a secret absent from the snapshot`. A pod's inbound listener is generated at CNI ADD; its SVID arrives later over the SPIFFE Broker stream (1.7–7.6 s under load, 60–391 ms on a quiet cluster), so every pod start publishes a chain whose secret does not exist yet.

## Why it matters
8-hour soak, 2026-09-19, rev218: the harness scaled `aether-test/svc-5` 4→0→4. Restore at 07:03:01Z → that WARN on w01/w04/w05 at 07:03:03Z (`…/sa/svc-5`) → **18 prober timeouts** fleet-wide at 07:03:20–22Z (w05 9, w03 4, w02 3, w01 1, w04 1) — 43 % of the run's errors and its largest episode. The victims were requests to **`echo`, not svc-5**: access logs show only `DC`/`downstream_remote_disconnect` from the prober (263–1440 ms) with the paired `DR`/`http2.remote_reset` at echo; no `UF`/`UH`/`URX`/`UO`/`NR`; upstream hosts on three nodes. So it is not "traffic to a pod without a certificate" — something on the node stalls unrelated requests for a moment. The 20 s gap between the WARN and the timeouts is unexplained.

The same WARN fires on a plain agent restart (3× for one pod, 0.1 s after its resubscribe, 2026-09-19 12:09:58Z).

main-worker-05's prober timed out 1.5–2.5 min after 4 of 18 service Deployment rolls in that soak (svc-5 ×2, svc-1, svc-4): client-side deadline expiries again, on the hottest proxy (812m CPU vs 506m on w01). 9 of the run's 42 timeouts.

Listener warming on an absent SDS secret and what it blocks; CDS/EDS ordering under SotW ADS when an upstream TLS context's secret is absent; one full snapshot regeneration per pod ADD **and** per SVID arrival (N pods → ≥2N SetSnapshot calls); the demand-scoped dependency set dropping and re-adding

Fixes #766.

Three sites logged ERROR for a retry that is expected to fail once and heals by
itself, so "zero ERROR lines" stopped being a usable bar for deploy and soak
grading. Each keeps ERROR for the case where the excuse no longer holds.

- xDS initial snapshot (the edge): the edge does not hold its first snapshot for
  identity, so with no SVID yet it cannot handshake with the registrar, exhausts
  the 15s budget and starts local-only — at ERROR, on every healthy roll. It now
  gets a severity-only view of its identity (SetIdentityWatch): WARN while the
  SVID is pending, and the background retry escalates to ERROR once if identity
  arrives and three more loads still fail. With the SVID in hand the ERROR is
  unchanged. The node agent is unaffected (it holds for identity first).
- Broker subscribe (the agent): Unavailable is WARN until the subscription has
  been failing for 2 minutes (the readiness dwell), then ERROR. A restarted agent
  resubscribes before its own SVID has landed, and a SPIRE agent restart removes
  the socket for ~35s: both cost one ERROR per managed pod per attempt and healed
  in seconds at zero prober cost.
- Pod termination (the agent): the failed DRAINING mark has a fallback and is
  WARN. The fallback failing too stays ERROR — a terminating pod remains
  selectable — unless this agent's SVID is pending, when no registry call could
  have succeeded. The message said "CNI DEL will retry"; since #798 a DEL does not
  retry against an agent that is down, so it now names the real owners: the pod's
  CNI DEL or the next ghost sweep.



Tests: `local_only_severity_test.go` (WARN while pending, single escalation after identity, ERROR unchanged otherwise), `bridge_unreachable_severity_test.go` (WARN→ERROR ladder), `TestHandlePodTerminatingFallbackSeverity`. No chart change.

registry unavailable for initial snapshot; starting with local-only config and retrying in background

Found by the 30-minute soak on talos-main rev217 (0.92.24-9fc27c8), 2026-09-18.

## Symptom
`aether_agent_spire_broker_reference_not_found_total{node="main-worker-02"}` climbs at ~2/min and never stops (29 at 19:40Z, 38 at 19:45Z; every other node 0). The agent log repeats a Broker subscribe failure for `aether-test/svc-3-79c5b9bdf5-sr558` — SPIRE answers `NotFound … pod not found on agent node`. That pod no longer exists in the API server.

Data-path cost: zero (prober 0 errors on w02, no listener references the pod). It is a goroutine + a gRPC call every ~30 s, per leaked pod, for the agent's lifetime — and it permanently poisons the `reference_not_found` counter, which proposal 036 uses as a signal.

## Mechanism
1. The TRIPLE churn step rolled agent + proxy + svc-3 together. The svc-3 pod's CNI DEL landed while w02's agent was down; since #798 that DEL returns without the agent, so the agent never ran `RemovePod` for it.
2. The new agent loaded the pod from storage and `runResubscribeStoredPods` resubscribed it (the pod was still in the API server, Terminating, so the liveness GET passed).
3. The ghost sweep then did its job: `aether_agent_ghost_sweep_orphans_pruned_total{node="main-worker-02"}` = 1. But `pruneOnePod` (agent/internal/cni/server/ghostsweep.go) removes the storage entry and the listener and **never calls `spireBridge.UnsubscribePod`**. `RemovePod` (pod.go) is the only teardown path that does.
4. The bridge classifies `NotFound` as transient (correct at CNI ADD, where the kubelet pod list lags), so the orphaned subscription retries at max backoff forever.

So this is not a stale storage entry — storage is clean. It is a leaked subscription. It predates the Broker API (the delegated bridge leaked the same way, silently, because SPIRE's delegated API just never answered); the Broker API's explicit `NotFound` plus the new counter made it visible, and #798 made the trigger (DEL without the agent) routine rather than rare.

issues.body:
## Why

The node agent mints per-pod SVIDs through SPIRE's proprietary **Delegated Identity API** on the agent **admin socket**, authorised by `authorizedDelegates`, with **hand-built selectors** (`agent/internal/spire/bridge.go` `PodSelectors`: `k8s:ns`, `k8s:sa`, `k8s:pod-name`, `k8s:pod-uid`). That has three costs: (1) registration entries keyed on any other selector (pod labels, container image, sigstore) never match, because the delegate — not SPIRE — decides the selector set; (2) the admin socket is an all-or-nothing capability (any selector → any identity on the node); (3) it is SPIRE-specific and drags `github.com/spiffe/spire-api-sdk` into the module for one package.

The **SPIFFE Broker API** (spiffe/spiffe#340, merged 2026-06-16) standardises exactly this role: a broker presents a *workload reference*, the SPIFFE provider attests the referenced workload itself, and the broker is authenticated by mTLS with its own SVID and authorised by SPIFFE ID (optionally RBAC-scoped through a Kubernetes SubjectAccessReview).

Everything required is already in the versions we run: SPIRE agent **1.15.2+** implements it (`experimental.broker`; talos-main runs 1.15.3), Helm chart **spire-0.30.2** (what GitOps pins) exposes `sockets.broker`, `brokerAPI.brokers.<key>` and `workloadAttestors.k8s.brokerAPI`, and go-spiffe **v2.8.1** (pinned in go.mod) ships the stubs at `exp/proto/spiffe/broker`.

This is a **replacement, not an opt-in**: the goal is to delete the delegated path, the admin-socket plumbing and the `spire-api-sdk` dependency.

## Design decisions (made here so the PR does not re-litigate them)

- **Reference type:** `KubernetesObjectReference{type:{plural:"pods", group:"core"}, key:{namespace,name}, uid}` — both key and uid, so SPIRE verifies the UID of the pod it resolved (spec §3.1.3). `pod_reference_scope` stays `agent_node` (kubelet pod-list fast path; a node agent only ever brokers local pods). `WorkloadPIDReference` is not used.

Found by the rev214 deploy validation (2026-09-16). worker-03 ran **12 m 47 s without an aether-agent** during the helm upgrade; the data path on the node never broke (proxy kept serving, prober 0 errors), but the node was unmanaged for that whole time and three alerts fired.

Chain: worker-03 sat at 89 % CPU requests (a tenant workload, `clj-grpc-soak/grpc-jvm`, requests 1 full core) → the aether-edge Deployment's `maxSurge: 1` placed a third edge pod there → the `system-node-critical` aether-proxy DaemonSet pod **preempted** it → the evicted edge pod's CNI DEL failed 42× because `/run/aether/cni.sock` was gone with the old agent pod → a Pod stuck in Terminating still counts its CPU request → the new aether-agent pod could not be scheduled to restore the socket. Circular; broken by force-deleting the wedged edge pod (all three pods scheduled 5 s later). The precondition is still live (84 % after the tenant left some load), so this recurs on the next deploy.

Three independent fixes, any one of which breaks the loop:
1. **CNI DEL must not depend on the agent socket being up**: when the socket is absent, the plugin should succeed the DEL locally (remove the netns/redirect state it owns, leave a tombstone the agent's ghost sweep already knows how to reconcile — #245/#641 machinery) instead of failing; a failed DEL keeps the pod Terminating forever, which is strictly worse than a stale registration.
2. **Edge rollout should not surge onto a node that cannot hold it**: `maxSurge: 0, maxUnavailable: 1` for the edge (it has 2 replicas and MetalLB fronts them), or a `topologySpreadConstraint`/anti-affinity that keeps the surge pod off nodes with an aether-proxy pending preemption.
3. **Agent priority**: the agent DS should carry the same `system-node-critical` priority as the proxy so it can preempt what blocks it (today the proxy can, the agent cannot).

Also: the deploy brief's "cluster is quiet" premise was wrong — check `kubectl top nodes` / requests before rolling.

issues.body:
Found by the rev214 deploy validation (2026-09-16, record `validate-rev214.md`, memory `project_deploy_20260916_rev214.md`).

**Before #785** (measured 2026-09-15 on rev213): `kubectl delete pod aether-proxy-*` took 21–23 s, the old Envoy kept serving until the DaemonSet's surge replacement hot-restarted it, and the prober saw **zero** errors on that node. That was the *accidental* effect of the #771 bug: the broken probe always chose the wait-for-successor branch.

**After #785** (rev214, 2 samples on worker-04/05): the probe works, the admin reports LIVE at our own epoch, so `handleShutdown` takes the drain branch and calls `s.shutdown()` (bare SIGTERM to Envoy — Envoy does not drain listeners on SIGTERM). Termination 1.5–2.3 s, the replacement logs `no live predecessor; starting fresh at epoch 0`, and the node has **no Envoy for 7.95 s / 8.11 s** → **130 / 126 prober `connection_error`s** and `AetherProberLivenessErrors` **pages** (CRITICAL 03:02:55→03:07:55Z). Same path as node drain, eviction and preemption.

**Root cause of the design:** for a DaemonSet with `maxSurge` and a transparent-capture node proxy, "no handoff in progress" on SIGTERM does not mean "nobody is coming" — the replacement is created within ~1 s and hot-restarts us. The right policy is the pre-fix behaviour made *deliberate and bounded*: on SIGTERM, if no successor is live yet, **wait for one up to the grace budget** (#785's `--termination-grace`-derived budget, 155 s at the chart default), hand off when it arrives, and only fall back to a real graceful drain (admin `/drain_listeners?graceful` + `--drain-time`, then SIGTERM) when the budget expires (node shutdown, scale-down, DaemonSet delete — no successor will ever come).

**Fix:** in `agent/internal/proxy/hotrestart/supervisor.go` `handleShutdown`: drain-immediately only when the successor wait is *impossible* (no surge configured / explicit flag), otherwise wait-bounded-then-drain; the fallback drain must be graceful, not a bare SIGTERM

Phase A2 of #772.

### fix(registry/etcd): wait for the watch loop before closing the client (#772)

R1 in the 2026-09-15 races review, and the only production data race the
detector found (`--config=race --runs_per_test=3` failed 2 of 3 runs on
`//registry/internal/etcd:etcd_test`).

`Close` cancelled the watch context and then immediately nil'd `r.client`
and `r.watchCancel` without waiting for `watchLoop` to exit. `watchLoop`
checks `ctx.Done()` and *then* dereferences `r.client` to re-establish the
watch (etcd.go:200), so beyond the unsynchronised write/read pair there was
a real nil-deref panic window on shutdown. `Close` was also unguarded, so
two Closes raced each other.

- `watchLoop` now takes a `done` channel and closes it on return.
- `Close` cancels, waits on `done`, and only then closes the etcd client.
  The wait needs no context of its own: the loop honours cancellation on
  both select arms and clientv3 closes the watch channel when the watch
  context is cancelled, so the loop returns promptly and unconditionally.
- `Close` no longer nils `client`; a post-Close call now fails with etcd's
  "client closed" error instead of panicking, and there is no unsynchronised
  write left for a concurrent reader to trip over.
- `Close` is idempotent via `sync.Once` (with the result memoised so every
  caller sees the same error).
- `Initialize`'s plain writes are documented as safe: every field the loop
  reads is written before the `go` statement that is itself the
  happens-before edge.

Regression test `TestEtcdRegistry_CloseRacesWatchLoop` uses the package's
existing testcontainers etcd fixture: it churns registry writes to keep the
watch busy while three goroutines call `Close` concurrently, ten rounds.
Verified it reproduces: against the old `Close` the test fails with
`WARNING: DATA RACE` on the first round; with the fix
`bazel test //registry/internal/etcd:etcd_test --config=race` passes.

Phase A7 of #772. Refs #597 (kept open: it is about the e2e harness's data-path withdrawal, which this does not measure) and #599.

### fix(registrar): bound the origin-heartbeat lease grant on a peer (#772) (#597)

The replicator's per-peer mirror loop could park forever on its very first
RPC. `startLease` grants the origin-heartbeat lease with the replicator's
long-lived context, and that is the one call in the loop that cannot use a
lease-scoped context, because the lease does not exist yet. Every other peer
RPC runs on `connCtx`, which the keepalive watchdog cancels when the lease
dies — the grant has no such rescue.

clientv3 does not bound it either, and the field name suggested otherwise:

  * `Config.DialTimeout` does NOT bound connection establishment. Client
    creation has been non-blocking since etcd #21832 (client/v3@v3.7.1
    config.go:36-44 says so outright), so `clientv3.New` returns before a
    byte has crossed the wire.
  * `grpc.WaitForReady(true)` is a default call option (options.go:29,62),
    so an RPC to a peer that accepts the connection and then says nothing
    waits rather than failing fast.

Net effect against an unresponsive peer: `LeaseGrant` blocks, `runPeer`
never comes back around, `aether_replicator_mirror_connected` stays false
for that peer and nothing retries until the registrar is restarted.

The fix gives the grant — and only the grant — a deadline, reusing
`DialTimeout` as the peer-connect budget it was always meant to be. The
`KeepAlive` stream deliberately keeps the unbounded context: it must live as
long as the connection, and its loss is the signal that redials.

`DialTimeout` is left at its 5s default in production (`registrar/internal/
cmd/root.go:343` sets none of the tuning fields). Lowering it, as was
originally proposed, would be a regression rather than a hardening: clientv3
derives the first keepalive's deadline from it as `DialTimeout+1s`
(lease.go:193), so a 500ms dial timeout would also cut the first-keepali

### fix(common/file): fsync the file before the rename and the directory after (#772)

S23: `AtomicWriteReader` renamed the temp file into place without fsyncing it,
and neither it nor its sibling `WriteFileAtomic` ever fsynced the parent
directory. The rename is atomic for readers, but atomicity is not durability:
after a power cut the destination can come back zero-length, or the directory
entry can be rolled back entirely. That path writes the mesh-DNS record
snapshot (`meshdns/server.go:438`) and the CNI conflist
(`cniconflist/reassert.go:255`, `cni/internal/install/cniconfig.go:101`) — the
two artefacts whose loss took the fleet out on 2026-08-29 (#645), on a cluster
with four power incidents on record.

- `common/file/file.go`: collapse `WriteFileAtomic` and `AtomicWriteReader`
  onto one `writeAtomic` body. The bug existed precisely because two
  near-identical copies drifted and only one of them synced; there is now one
  place to drift from. Both fsync the temp file before `Close`/`Rename` and
  fsync the destination directory after the rename, and a failure of either is
  returned rather than swallowed. Temp-file naming, permissions (0600 default
  for `WriteFileAtomic`, explicit mode for `AtomicWrite*`) and the
  `FADV_DONTNEED` hint are unchanged; the hint now runs after the fsync, where
  it actually evicts (it only drops clean pages).
- `common/file/dirsync_unix.go` / `dirsync_windows.go`: new `syncDir`, keeping
  the package's platform-file structure. Opening the directory O_RDONLY and
  fsyncing it is the portable POSIX form. A filesystem that does not implement
  it (EINVAL/ENOTSUP/ENOSYS/EPERM/EACCES) is best-effort — the added durability
  is not worth failing a CNI conflist write over — while real I/O failures
  (EIO, ENOSPC) surface. No-op on Windows, which cannot open a directory.

### fix(registry): hand out copies of the cached endpoint slices (#772, A3/S2)

The registrar client's watch goroutine mutates a service's endpoint slice in
place: `upsertLocked` overwrites `eps[i]` when an endpoint's IP already exists,
`removeLocked` left-shifts the tail over the hole. Both `ListEndpoints` and
`ListAllEndpoints` handed out that same slice — `ListEndpoints` returned the
cache's own slice header after dropping the RLock, and `ListAllEndpoints`
copied the map but aliased every value.

Consumers read them on another goroutine: `agent/internal/xds/cache/cluster.go`
builds CDS/EDS from both, and its cold-path RPC-fill appends into what it read.
This is not only a detector finding — a reader ranging the backing array while
the left-shift runs can see one endpoint twice and skip another, so it corrupts
EDS content.

- `registry/internal/registrar/registrar.go:385` and `:414`: `slices.Clone` the
  slice(s) under the read lock before returning.
- State the ownership contract in both method docs: the slice/map is the
  caller's copy, the `*registryv1.ServiceEndpoint` elements are shared and must
  be treated as immutable (no consumer mutates them today — the only in-place
  writes are the two cache mutators, which swap the pointer rather than edit the
  message — so a shallow copy is sufficient and a `proto.Clone` per endpoint is
  not paid on the xDS rebuild path).
- Note the in-place rewrite at `upsertLocked`/`removeLocked` so the coupling is
  visible from the mutating side too.

### fix(storage,cni): storage owns its values — deep-copy across the boundary (#772, A3/S1)

`agent/storage`'s RWMutex protects the map, not the values, so `GetAll` and
`GetResource` handed every caller the cache's own pointer. Two goroutines then
touched the same proto with nothing ordering them:

  - `agent/internal/cni/server/termination.go:114` — `cur.Terminating = true`,
    written in place by the termination watch under `lifecycleMu`;
  - `agent/internal/cni/server/liveness.go:95` — `pod.GetTerminating()`, read by
    the 5s liveness tick holding no lock at all (it released storage's RLock
    inside `GetAll`).

`AddResource`'s own `protojson.Marshal` is a third concurrent reader of the same
value. The type's doc claimed the implementation was "safe for concurrent
access", which was true of the map and false of everything it contained.

Fixed at the source (option (a) of the two the review offered) rather than by
making the two call sites copy-on-write: the contract now is that the cache owns
its values and every message crossing the boundary is deep-copied — `AddResource`
caches a clone of what it is given, `GetResource`/`GetAll`/`loadAll` return clones
of what they hold. Callers own what they get back and may mutate it freely; to
persist a change they write it back with `AddResource`, which is exactly what
termination.go already does. Documenting immutability instead would have left
every future `GetAll` consumer one in-place write away from the same bug, with no
test able to catch it.

The cost is real but small, and was measured rather than assumed
(`BenchmarkGetAll`/`BenchmarkGetResource`, added here, on a record carrying the

### fix(agent): make SPIRE bridge SDS publication monotonic (#772) (A6a)

`pushSecrets` was build-then-publish with no serialisation: it snapshotted
`b.secrets` under `mu`, released it, and called `store.SetSecrets` — a
whole-map replace. Four independent goroutines reach it (the bundle stream,
every per-pod SVID stream, the node-SVID refresher, and `UnsubscribePod` off
the CNI DEL path), so two overlapping pushes — an SVID rotation racing a
bundle update, or a `Updated()` wake from #740's bridge changes — could land
the older set on top of the newer one. Last writer wins, and a just-arrived
secret disappears from the SDS snapshot until something else pushes. That is

### fix(proxy-supervisor): probe the admin endpoint on a detached ctx at shutdown (#771) (#772)

handleShutdown has exactly one call site — `case <-lp.ctx.Done()` in
restartLoop.run — so the context it is handed is ALWAYS already cancelled by
controller-runtime's signal handler. It passed that context straight into the
epoch-identity probe (adminLiveAtEpoch -> adminServerInfo ->
context.WithTimeout on an already-cancelled parent), so http.Client.Do failed
with "context canceled" in microseconds without ever opening a socket.
`!adminLiveAtEpoch(...)` was therefore true on every SIGTERM regardless of
Envoy's actual state, and the "termination requested mid-handoff; waiting for
successor" branch was taken unconditionally — including when Envoy was LIVE at
our own epoch and no successor existed, in which case Envoy was never drained.

Measured on talos-main (issue #771 reproduction): both sampled pods recorded
`aether_supervisor_admin_probes_total{probe_endpoint="server_info",
result="unreachable"}` exactly once in a 2d21h lifetime — at their SIGTERM —
while `result="live"` was still climbing +10/30s on the same series and
`envoy_server_state` was 0 (LIVE). The mid-handoff line was logged 194ms/195ms
after the delete, 4.3-6.3s before any successor Envoy started.

Fix: run the probe on a context detached from the caller's, keeping its values
but not its cancellation, bounded by shutdownProbeTimeout. This is the same
trap and the same idiom as common/telemetry/setup/lifecycle.go's
DetachedTimeout (issue #662). The branch semantics are unchanged: admin LIVE at
our epoch -> drain; not LIVE at our epoch (a successor has taken the admin
port) -> leave Envoy alone for the successor's parent-shutdown protocol.

NOT match". So `'!proxy/**'` matched `agent/...`, `docs/...`, `charts/...` —
every file — and the whole filter was true for any change whatsoever.
`control_plane` has never once evaluated to `false` since it was written, and
every proxy-only PR has been paying for `diff` (bazel-diff + Java + full
history), `chart-version-bump` and `deps-audit` for nothing.

v4 ships `predicate-quantifier: 'some-with-excludes'` for exactly this: a file
counts when at least one positive pattern matches and no negated pattern does.
Set it. This is the same fix C1 applied to `proxy.yml` in 17ac1f3.

Scope of the exclusions — deliberately still just the proxy workspace:

### fix(proxy-supervisor): probe the admin endpoint on a detached ctx at shutdown (#771) (#772)

handleShutdown has exactly one call site — `case <-lp.ctx.Done()` in
restartLoop.run — so the context it is handed is ALWAYS already cancelled by
controller-runtime's signal handler. It passed that context straight into the
epoch-identity probe (adminLiveAtEpoch -> adminServerInfo ->
context.WithTimeout on an already-cancelled parent), so http.Client.Do failed
with "context canceled" in microseconds without ever opening a socket.
`!adminLiveAtEpoch(...)` was therefore true on every SIGTERM regardless of
Envoy's actual state, and the "termination requested mid-handoff; waiting for
successor" branch was taken unconditionally — including when Envoy was LIVE at
our own epoch and no successor existed, in which case Envoy was never drained.

Measured on talos-main (issue #771 reproduction): both sampled pods recorded
`aether_supervisor_admin_probes_total{probe_endpoint="server_info",
result="unreachable"}` exactly once in a 2d21h lifetime — at their SIGTERM —
while `result="live"` was still climbing +10/30s on the same series and
`envoy_server_state` was 0 (LIVE). The mid-handoff line was logged 194ms/195ms
after the delete, 4.3-6.3s before any successor Envoy started.

but not its cancellation, bounded by shutdownProbeTimeout. This is the same
trap and the same idiom as common/telemetry/setup/lifecycle.go's
DetachedTimeout (issue #662). The branch semantics are unchanged: admin LIVE at
our epoch -> drain; not LIVE at our epoch (a successor has taken the admin
port) -> leave Envoy alone for the successor's parent-shutdown protocol.
