issues.body:
Found by the 2026-09-15 codebase review (dead-code sweep, chart mutation rendering).

`charts/aether/values.yaml:386` documents `proxy.authzSidecar.failureMode` as an ALLOW/DENY switch, but the only consumer in the templates is a single `{{- if eq .Values.proxy.authzSidecar.failureMode "ALLOW" }}`. `Allow`, `allow`, a trailing space, or a YAML-quoted value with whitespace all fail the comparison and the ext_authz filter renders with `failure_mode_allow: false` — i.e. **fail-closed on an authorization control**, with no error, no warning, and nothing in `helm lint`.

Fix (one PR, chart patch bump):
1. Normalise before comparing: `{{- if eq (upper (trim (toString .Values.proxy.authzSidecar.failureMode))) "ALLOW" }}`.
2. Reject anything else at render time: `{{- if not (has (upper (trim …)) (list "ALLOW" "DENY")) }}{{ fail "proxy.authzSidecar.failureMode must be ALLOW or DENY" }}{{ end }}`, or add `charts/aether/values.schema.json` with an `enum` for the key (schema validation is the more general fix and also covers the other string-enum values in the chart — worth a look at `registrar.registryBackend`, `edge.config.*`).
3. `//charts/aether:aether_template_test` gets a case for `failureMode: allow` (lower case) that must render `failure_mode_allow: true`, and one for `failureMode: maybe` that must fail.

Not exploitable on talos-main today (`proxy.authzSidecar.enabled=false`, enabled-inert), but it is the kind of default that bites at the worst time.

## Why

The `dynamodb` registry backend implements only the base `registry.Registry` interface (register / unregister / list). Everything the registrar has gained since June is etcd-only: watch-driven sync (`ChangeNotifier`, #174, the fix that closed the last-old-exit skew), the cross-cluster config plane (`ConfigExporter` / `ConfigImporter`, proposal 026), `ServiceExporter`, and the multi-region mirror (proposal 006). Nobody runs it, and it no longer meets the propagation-time requirement.

Discriminator 1 from #638: make the source-side identity binding observable, so the next soak can confirm or kill the hypothesis rather than reasoning about it after the fact.

## The hypothesis under test

> During proxy startup an outbound cluster serving requests from pod A is briefly handed the client-cert SDS secret of co-located pod B, until the next snapshot push re-binds it. The 4.25s / 14.7s / 5.29s burst durations are the time-to-next-push, not a timeout.

## What reading the generator already settles

The binding is **not** per-cluster, and the secret name is **not** independently chosen.

Every mTLS-injected outbound cluster gets the same two pieces of config from `proxy.InjectUpstreamMTLS`:

1. `transport_socket_matches` — one entry per unique local SPIFFE ID (plus the node identity), **named by that SPIFFE ID**, whose transport socket fetches the SDS secret of **the same name** (`upstreamTransportSocketMatchesNamed` passes `id` as both the match name and `tlsCertificateSecretName`).
2. `transport_socket_matcher` — an `exact_match_map` from the source pod's netns (the `aether.network.network_namespace` filter state, `SharedWithUpstream: ONCE`) to one of those names, built from `c.localWorkloads`.

So:

* **"A cluster's match presents a secret it is not named for" is structurally impossible** — the socket name and the SDS name are the same Go string. The literal mismatch the issue asked for cannot be constructed at `transportsocketmatch.go:89`.
* **The whole (source pod → cluster → secret) binding collapses to one node-wide index**: `localWorkloads[netns] → SPIFFE ID`. It is byte-identical on every outbound cluster on the node.

That second point is itself evidence: it is exactly the field fingerprint. One wrong identity presented toward five distinct clusters within one time slice, "a node-wide constant per time slice, not per-endpoint", is what a wrong entry in this single index looks like. A per-cluster or per-endpoint SDS bug could not produce it.

Envoy's `default_validator.cc:332` prints `verify cert failed: SAN matcher, certificate SANs are [...]` for the certificate it is **validating** — the one the **peer** presented.

Every one of these binaries initializes its dependencies **before** starting the

## Summary

The node agent's startup **hard-depends on the OTel collector accepting exports**. When the collector is shedding (`data refused due to high memory usage`), the agent's export blocks past its startup deadline, the startup context is cancelled, SPIRE Workload API source creation fails, and the process exits 1 — so the agent crash-loops and the node loses its xDS control plane. A telemetry backend under memory pressure should never be able to stop the data plane from starting.

Observed live on talos-main during the 2026-09-02 soak (rev189/0.91.3-d22cf05), on 3 of 5 nodes during a rolling restart:

```
starting aether agent
exporter export timeout: rpc error: code = Unavailable desc = data refused due to high memory usage
ERROR failed to shutdown telemetry: context canceled
Error: failed to create SPIRE Workload API source: context canceled
```

Kubelet on the same nodes: `Readiness probe failed: .../readyz: context deadline exceeded` → `Liveness probe failed` → `Container agent failed liveness probe, will be restarted`.

Restart counts at 06:08Z: w05 0, w01 0, w03 1, w04 2, **w02 5 and still `0/1 CrashLoopBackOff`** — i.e. it does not reliably self-recover while the collector stays saturated; worker-02 sat with no agent for minutes. It recovered only after the soak load was torn down and collector pressure fell.

The collector saturation had an external cause (see context below), but the coupling is ours:

1. **Blocking startup on a telemetry export** makes an observability component a hard dependency of the data plane. The agent programs Envoy; if it cannot start, that node's mesh config goes stale and new pods on it get no listeners.
2. **The failure is correlated across the fleet.** Every agent exports to the same collector, so a shedding collector can take out *every* node's agent at once — precisely during a rolling restart, when they all start simultaneously. This is the same class of fleet

agent_prs.body:
Fixes #736. Option 1 from the issue, with the process's own lame-duck stamp instead of the pod name — no collector/GitOps change is needed for it to appear.

## Mechanism

A lame-duck exit is a **once-per-process event, emitted at the end of the process's life**. With the exported label set `{node, job, reason}`, each mesh-DNS generation increments its own fresh process-local counter to 1 and exits; the successor starts at 0 and, when it later exits, also reaches 1. Prometheus therefore sees one series go `1 → 1 → 1`, which is not a counter reset, so `increase()`/`rate()` over a window spanning several rolls report ~0. The #729 validation (10 rolls) had to count its 50/50 `successor` exits from raw per-roll snapshots.

## The attribute

Both instruments now carry `instance` — the 64-bit random identity stamp the process already mints for successor detection (`newInstanceID`, `lameduck.go`):

- `aether.mesh_dns.lame_duck.exits` (the counter)
- `aether.mesh_dns.lame_duck.duration` (its `_count` is a counter with exactly the same defect)

The stamp is exactly one value per generation and is never reused, so each generation is its own series and each exit a genuine `0 → 1` rise. It is also the value already logged as `instance=` on the `lame duck started` / `successor observed` lines, so the metric joins straight to the logs of the generation that emitted it.

Exported label set as Prometheus will see it:

```
aether_mesh_dns_lame_duck_exits_total{node, job, reason, instance}
aether_mesh_dns_lame_duck_duration_seconds_{bucket,sum,count}{node, job, reason, instance}
```

`reason` stays a **closed** set (`successor|deadline|signal`) — the tests fail on anything else. `instance` is the only unbounded-in-time dimension, deliberately.

## Cardinality

One series per generation per node: bounded by DaemonSet roll frequency (≈31 rolls per 8h soak across 5 nodes), and the series age out with the generation rather than accumulating.

Closes #729.

## The mechanism (from #726 Phase 1)

`aether-mesh-dns` rolls with `maxSurge: 1 / maxUnavailable: 0`, `SO_REUSEPORT`, readiness `initialDelaySeconds: 1`, **no preStop and no drain**. The DaemonSet controller deletes the predecessor the instant the successor passes its first readiness probe, the kubelet SIGTERMs it, and `Server.Start` closed the UDP + TCP sockets immediately on `<-ctx.Done()`.

While both sockets are in the reuseport group the kernel hashes each arriving datagram at one of them. Anything already steered into the departing socket's queue is **silently discarded** by `close()`. #726 measured exactly that: a 5.106 s hole (12:30:40.841Z → 12:30:45.947Z) in one prober's mesh-domain access log, 16 timeouts, and **zero** non-200 responses anywhere in Envoy — the requests never reached the data plane. One lost datagram, amplified because Go's resolver singleflights by name, so every concurrent lookup of that name waited out the same retransmit.

#728 shrank the client-side cost (`options timeout:1 attempts:3`, `dns_timeout` now reachable). The datagram loss itself was untouched, and that is this PR.

## Design as implemented

**1. Lame duck on SIGTERM** (`agent/internal/meshdns/lameduck.go`). On SIGTERM the resolver:
- removes its pod-local ready marker (so `mesh-dns-ready` reports NotReady) and stops the wedge watchdog, so nothing can restore the marker,
- **keeps the UDP + TCP listeners serving**,
- closes them only when a successor is observed serving, `--lame-duck-max` elapses, or a second signal arrives,
- then closes and exits 0.

**2. Successor detection is evidence, not a timer.** The resolver answers a reserved identity name — `_instance._aether.<mesh-domain>` **TXT**, TTL 0 — with 64 random bits minted at process start. The stamp is random rather than pid-derived on purpose: predecessor and successor each run as **pid 1** in their own container, so a pid stamp would make them indistinguishable and every window would run to its deadlin

## Summary

#726's Phase-1 analysis (see its comment) found the root of the per-roll prober timeout bursts: on an `aether-mesh-dns` DaemonSet roll (`maxSurge: 1`, `maxUnavailable: 0`, `reusePort: true`, readiness `initialDelaySeconds: 1`, **no preStop, no drain**), the predecessor's SO_REUSEPORT socket is closed the moment the successor passes its first probe. Any datagram the kernel had already queued to the predecessor is discarded. The client (stock resolv.conf, `timeout:5`) retransmits after 5 s, and Go's resolver singleflights by name, so one lost packet stalls every concurrent lookup of that name for 5 s — a 5.1 s hole in the mesh-domain path's access log on 2026-09-06 12:30:40–12:30:45Z, 16 prober timeouts, zero non-200 responses anywhere in Envoy.

#728 shrinks the blast radius from the client side (`options timeout:1 attempts:3` injected by the pod-mutating webhook; the prober now classifies resolution failures as `dns_timeout`). The **datagram loss itself is untouched** by #728.

## Ask

In `agent/cmd/mesh-dns` / `agent/internal/meshdns/server.go`: on SIGTERM, keep serving for a lame-duck window (e.g. until `terminationGracePeriodSeconds - 2s`, or until a successor is observed answering on the same port — both sockets are in the reuseport group, so a self-query that returns the successor's `envoy_server_version`-style identity or a generation stamp would do) and only then close the socket; add `preStop` sleep + a matching `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` in the chart so the kubelet does not race it. This drains the predecessor's queue instead of discarding it. Note the residual: the instant of `close()` on a reuseport socket can still drop a datagram queued between the last `recvfrom` and `close` — a kernel-level race not fully closable from userspace (eBPF `sk_reuseport` steering would be the complete fix); the lame-duck window reduces the exposure from "every roll" to "a sub-millisecond race".

Validation: ≥10 mesh-dns rolls under prober load, raw per-ser

Detected **15** data clump(s) in **15** cluster(s) that should be refactored. Please extract the shared variables into a dedicated class or parameter object and update all usages accordingly.
<details>
<summary>How to refactor data clumps</summary>

# Refactoring Strategies for Each Data Clump Type

## 1. General Principle

All data clumps follow the same core idea:

> Recurring groups of variables should be transformed into an explicit abstraction.

Typical refactorings:

- Extract Class
- Introduce Parameter Object
- Preserve Whole Object
- Optional: Inheritance instead of composition

However, the applicability depends on the data clump type and its directionality.

---

## 2. Data Clump Types and Refactoring

### 2.1 Field–Field Data Clumps (Bidirectional)

**Definition:**
A group of fields appears in multiple classes.

**Refactoring Strategy:**

- Extract shared fields into a new **class** (preferred over an interface)
  (e.g. class Address with street, city, zip)
- Replace duplicated fields with a reference to this class
- If a suitable class already exists, **reuse it** instead of creating a new one

**Alternative:**

- Use inheritance:
  - Move shared fields into a superclass

**Key Property:**

- Bidirectional
  → Refactoring can start from either class

**When to use what:**

- Reuse existing class → if a matching class already exists (most preferred)
- Extract Class → if the data represents a meaningful concept and no suitable class exists; **use a class, not an interface**
- Inheritance → if classes share a structural identity

**Note on classes vs. interfaces:**

> Prefer generating a **class** over an interface for the extracted data clump type.
> Classes can carry behaviour, be instantiated directly, and are easier to evolve.
> Only use an interface when you explicitly need a structural contract without implementation.

## Was
Der Quellcode von [freekrai/directus-extension-upsert](https://github.com/freekrai/directus-extension-upsert) (MIT, © 2023 Roger Stringer) steckt jetzt als neuer Endpoint `upsert-endpoint` direkt im `directus-extension-rocket-meals-bundle`. Eine separate Extension ist nicht mehr nötig.

```
POST /upsert/:collection
{ "filter": { "key": "test2" }, "body": { "key": "test2", "value": "abc" } }
```
Findet `filter` einen Eintrag, wird er mit `body` aktualisiert, sonst wird `body` neu angelegt. URL und Antwortformat (`success`, `msg`, `code`, `data`) entsprechen dem Original.

### Upsert im `ItemsServiceHelper`
Extensions können dieselbe Logik ohne HTTP-Umweg nutzen:
```ts
const { id, created } = await myDatabaseHelper.getFoodsHelper().upsertByFilter({ alias: 'pizza' }, { alias: 'pizza', price: 3 });
```
Das bestehende `upsertOne` (Directus-Upsert über den Primärschlüssel) bleibt unverändert. `upsertByFilter` legt neue Einträge wie `createOne` mit `status: published` an, akzeptiert wie alle anderen Helper-Methoden `optsCustom` (z. B. `disableEventEmit`) und lehnt einen leeren Filter ab, damit nicht ein beliebiger Eintrag überschrieben wird.

## Abweichungen zum Original
- **Rechte:** Das Original sucht mit einer rohen Knex-Abfrage und umgeht damit die Leserechte. Diese Version nutzt `ItemsService.readByQuery` mit der Accountability des Aufrufers: Lesen, Anlegen und Aktualisieren unterliegen alle den Directus-Policies.
- **Filter:** Einfache Werte werden zu `_eq` (wie im Original). Zusätzlich gehen `null` (→ `_null`) und fertige Directus-Operator-Objekte (`{ "_in": [...] }`).
- **Fehler** gehen per `next(error)` an Directus. Im Original war es `throw` im async-Handler, also eine unbehandelte Rejection.
- `data` enthält `{ id }` des betroffenen Eintrags statt `null`. Ein fehlender Filter liefert HTTP 400 statt 200, unbekannte Collections liefern 404.

## Dateien
- `src/upsert-endpoint/index.ts`: Endpoint

New module `rsna/competitive/weight_average.py`. It builds an **inference-only** uniform average of epochs 6–10 from ONE completed fixed-ten-epoch `frozen_base_delta` run. Epoch 10 stays the primary comparison.

**LoRA is averaged in effective-delta space, not by averaging factors:**
```
mean_k(s·B_k·A_k) = (s/5)·[B_6..B_10]·[A_6;..;A_10]     # s = alpha/sqrt(r)
```
- This is stored as concatenated factors: rank `5r`, scaling `s/5`, using the same `ResidualLinear` forward.
- There is no SVD and no truncation.
- `dense_suffix_delta_v1` deltas and learned head/pool tensors are linear, so they are averaged directly (in float64, then cast back).
- Non-floating learned tensors must be bitwise equal across epochs.

- `run.json` must be completed, non-diagnostic and have no gold.
- Every snapshot must be a regular file whose SHA/size matches its record.
- Each snapshot must be its bound `epoch, next_update=0` boundary.
- All five must have the same binding (source, config, fold, seed, fitting supervision, base, code).
- All five must have the same `model_storage` (frozen-base hashes and learned graph).
- Step counters must equal `epoch × updates_per_epoch`.
- Only `(6,7,8,9,10)` and the `(10,)` identity control are accepted.
- Refused: buffers outside the encoder, extra learned encoder tensors, and other adapter methods.

**Output format and refusals:**
- Output is `epoch_weight_average_inference_v1`: `optimizer_boundary: False`, string `schema_version`, no optimizer/RNG/scaler/`binding`.
- `load_checkpoint`, `restore_checkpoint_model` and `FrozenBaseDelta` all refuse it. `apply_candidate` freezes the model, so the applied model cannot resume training.

agent_prs.body:
## Why I'm doing:

Before taking the planner lock, `QueryAnalyzer.ExternalTablesOnlyVisitor` resolves the external tables a statement reads. This keeps connector metadata loads out of the internal lock. To tell a table from a CTE, it put every name of a with clause in scope for the whole clause, including inside each CTE's own definition. The analyzer does not see it that way. A CTE is in scope only after its definition, so a same-named table inside the definition is the table:

```sql
-- current catalog and database: a JDBC catalog that has a table tbl0
WITH tbl0 AS (SELECT * FROM tbl0)
SELECT * FROM default_catalog.test.t0 JOIN tbl0 ON true;
```

The pre-pass skipped the inner `tbl0` as the CTE. The analyzer then fetched the JDBC table's metadata while holding `t0`'s lock, so DDL on `t0` waited for the connector.

## What I'm doing:

- The external-table pre-pass brings a CTE's name into scope after its definition, as the analyzer and the planner lock collection (`PlannerMetaLocker.TableCollector`) do, instead of putting all names in scope up front.
- WITH RECURSIVE, where the analyzer brings a CTE into scope after its anchor, is handled in #84444, stacked on this PR. Until then the pre-pass takes a self-reference in a recursive member for a table, and looks it up in the current catalog before the lock. That is one extra lookup outside the lock; the analyzer still reads the CTE, because it resolves a CTE name before a table.

Test in `StatementPlannerExternalTablesLockTest`: a JDBC table named like a CTE, read inside that CTE's definition, with blocking JDBC metadata. The lock is not taken while the lookup blocks, and the analyzer reuses the pre-resolved table. This test fails without the change.

Observability: the signal reviewed was the `blocking_call_under_lock` violation reported by `BlockingCallValidator`, which flags a connector request made under an FE metadata lock. It does not change. A same-named external table inside a CTE definition no longer triggers

agent_prs.body:
## Why I'm doing:

With spilling, `SELECT DISTINCT ... LIMIT n` can return fewer than `n` rows, a different number from run to run. On a 96-bucket table where each of 4096 keys sits in two rowsets of its tablet, `pipeline_dop = 1` and `spill_mode = 'force'`, `count(*)` over `SELECT DISTINCT c0 FROM t1 LIMIT 100` is 80 instead of 100, and `LIMIT 1000` gives 543. Both spillable distinct operators are affected (the default sort-based one and `spill_partitionwise_agg = true`); without `LIMIT`, or without spilling, the result is right.

## What I'm doing:

Fixes #84386

`AggregateDistinctBlockingSinkOperator::push_chunk` stops its input once a countdown shared by all drivers of the node reaches zero, and decrements it by how much this driver's hash set grew (`enable_pipeline_share_limit`, added in #42449). The spillable subclasses empty the hash set on every spill, so a key that comes back after a spill is counted again: the countdown reaches zero while fewer than `limit` distinct keys have been kept, and the sink stops reading. In the repro each key is in two rowsets of its tablet, so with every chunk spilled each key is counted twice.

The spillable group-by sinks already turn the shared limit off for this reason (`spillable_aggregate_blocking_sink_operator.cpp`, #55455; `spillable_partitionwise_aggregate_operator.cpp`, #60216); the two spillable distinct sinks never did. This PR sets `enable_pipeline_share_limit = false` in `prepare()` of `SpillableAggregateDistinctBlockingSinkOperator` and `SpillablePartitionWiseDistinctSinkOperator`, the same line the group-by sinks have. The per-driver `size >= limit` check stays: it only counts the keys in the live hash set, so stopping on it still leaves at least `limit` distinct keys, and the `LimitOperator` after the source trims the output.

Cost: with spill enabled but never triggered, DISTINCT + LIMIT at `pipeline_dop > 1` no longer stops all drivers once together they reach the limit; each stops at `limit` keys of its own.

issues.body:
### Steps to reproduce the behavior (Required)
```sql
CREATE TABLE t1 (c0 STRING, c1 BIGINT, c2 BIGINT) DUPLICATE KEY(c0)
  DISTRIBUTED BY HASH(c0) BUCKETS 96 PROPERTIES ("replication_num" = "1");
INSERT INTO t1 SELECT generate_series, 4096 - generate_series, generate_series FROM TABLE(generate_series(1, 4096));
INSERT INTO t1 SELECT * FROM t1;

SET pipeline_dop = 1;
SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT DISTINCT c0 FROM t1 LIMIT 100) tb;   -- 100

SET enable_spill = true;
SET spill_mode = 'force';
SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT DISTINCT c0 FROM t1 LIMIT 100) tb;   -- 80, 87, 80 on three runs
```

### Expected behavior (Required)
100: `t1` has 4096 distinct `c0` values, so `DISTINCT ... LIMIT 100` returns 100 rows whether or not the aggregation spills.

### Real behavior (Required)
With `spill_mode = 'force'` the query returns fewer than 100 rows, and a different number on each run:

| Settings | Result |
|---|---|
| defaults | 100 |
| `enable_spill = true, spill_mode = 'force'`, `pipeline_dop = 1` | 4.1.8: 80, 87, 80; main b42bd332486: 80, 80, 80 (three runs each) |
| same, without `LIMIT` (`count(*) FROM (SELECT DISTINCT c0 FROM t1)`) | 4096 (correct) |
| same, `pipeline_dop = 0` | 100 in the run we did |

So it is a wrong result, not an error: the limited, spilled DISTINCT drops rows. It reproduces in the SQL-tester case `test/sql/test_agg/T/test_bucket_agg` (`select count(*) from (select distinct c0 from t1 limit 100) tb;`) under the same two variables.

Found by running SQL-tester with randomized result-invariant session variables (#83805); the failing settings were narrowed down to `enable_spill` + `spill_mode` by dropping one variable at a time.

### StarRocks version (Required)
Reproduced on `allin1-ubuntu` 4.1.8-b16342f, on main 82286961d16 (2026-11-18) and on main b42bd332486 (2026-11-24, built without starcache, single FE + single BE).

agent_prs.body:
## Why I'm doing:

With `enable_recursive_cte = true`, `RecursiveCTEAstCheck` runs before analysis to decide whether a statement goes to the recursive CTE executor. Since #82970 the pre-analysis `AstTraverser` also visits the SELECT list, so the checker now sees table references inside projection subqueries. The checker pushes every CTE on a name stack (the parser marks every CTE as an anchor) and treats any matching name as a self reference, so a valid ordinary nested CTE is rejected:

```sql
WITH a AS (
    WITH t0 AS (SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t0) AS n)  -- inner t0 is the base table t0
    SELECT n FROM t0
)
SELECT n FROM a;
-- ERROR: Doesn't support multi-level recursive CTE
```

## What I'm doing:

Keep the projection traversal from #82970 and make `RecursiveCTEAstCheck` follow the same CTE scope rules as `QueryAnalyzer`:

- A CTE is a recursive candidate only under `WITH RECURSIVE` with a `UNION` definition. It is visible only in its recursive members, not in its anchor (as in `tryProcessRecursiveCte`).
- An ordinary CTE enters the scope after its definition; CTE names are scoped to the query that defines them, so inner CTEs shadow outer ones. Names are compared exactly, like the analyzer's scope lookup.
- A recursive reference made while another recursive definition (anchor included) is open is still rejected as a multi-level recursive CTE.

```
WITH RECURSIVE q AS ( <anchor> UNION ALL <recursive members> )
                      ^ q not visible     ^ q visible -> recursive
                      nested recursive CTE in either part -> multi-level, rejected
```

Observability: reviewed the checker's error path and the executor dispatch in `StmtExecutor`; no new signal is needed, the existing error message is kept.

Fixes #84402

issues.body:
### Steps to reproduce the behavior (Required)

```sql
SET enable_recursive_cte = true;
CREATE TABLE t0 (v1 INT) DUPLICATE KEY(v1) DISTRIBUTED BY HASH(v1) PROPERTIES ("replication_num" = "1");

WITH a AS (
    WITH t0 AS (SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t0) AS n)
    SELECT n FROM t0
)
SELECT n FROM a;
```

### Expected behavior (Required)

This is an ordinary (non-recursive) nested CTE. A CTE is not visible inside its own definition, so the inner `FROM t0` refers to the base table `t0`, and the query should succeed.

### Real behavior (Required)

```
Doesn't support multi-level recursive CTE
```

With `enable_recursive_cte = false` the query succeeds.

### Analysis

`RecursiveCTEAstCheck` runs before analysis when `enable_recursive_cte` is on. Since #82970 the pre-analysis `AstTraverser` also visits the SELECT list, so the checker now sees the table reference in the scalar subquery. The checker treats every CTE as a recursion candidate (the parser marks every CTE as an anchor) and only compares names against a stack, so the base-table reference is taken as a self reference of the inner CTE at depth 2.

### StarRocks version (Required)

main, and branches that contain #82970 (4.2, 4.1).

## Why I'm doing:

A `SELECT` without `FROM` that reads a rollup through `[_SYNC_MV_]` in one scalar subquery, and another table in another scalar subquery, fails during planning. Retrying does not help:

```sql
SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM r1 [_SYNC_MV_]) = (SELECT count(*) FROM t_ref);
-- ERROR 1064 (HY000): A table the statement reads was dropped or replaced while it was being planned, please retry
```

A `[_SYNC_MV_]` relation names a materialized index, not a table. So `PlannerMetaLocker` resolved `r1` as a table name and found nothing. `QueryAnalyzer`, however, finds the base table by the index name and copies it (`copyOnlyForQuery`) while analyzing:

- On the fast path, that copy is taken without the base table's lock (the known violation "2-g").

agent_prs.body:
## Why I'm doing:

`[_SYNC_MV_]` reads a materialized index by its name: `SELECT * FROM r1 [_SYNC_MV_]`. A synchronous materialized view's name is unique in its database, because `CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW` checks the other tables' indexes. A rollup's name is not: `ALTER TABLE ... ADD ROLLUP` checks only its own table. So two tables of a database can each have a rollup named `r1`.

`Database#getMaterializedViewIndex` returns the first visible index of that name it meets while iterating the database's table map, which is a hash map keyed by table id. So which table such a read gets is not determined, and it can change without the statement changing:

- when another table of the database gets a rollup of that name;
- when a rollup of that name becomes visible.

Seen on a cluster: adding `r1` to a second table switched `SELECT * FROM r1 [_SYNC_MV_]` from reading one table to reading the other, with a different schema and different rows.

## What I'm doing:

- `Database#getMaterializedViewIndexes` (replacing `getMaterializedViewIndex`) returns every visible rollup or synchronous materialized view of the name, with its table. `LocalMetastore#getMaterializedViewIndexes` wraps it. Like the lookup it replaces, it leaves out the base index of each table (#84330) and other sessions' temporary tables (#84313). So a table named like the rollup, or another session's temporary table with a rollup of the name, does not make a valid read ambiguous. The session's own temporary tables count, because one can be created with a rollup and read through `[_SYNC_MV_]`.
- `QueryAnalyzer#resolveTable`, for a `[_SYNC_MV_]` relation, rejects a name that more than one table has:

  ```
  Duplicate rollup name 'r1': more than one table has a rollup of that name
  ```

  A name that one table has is read as before.

Only `[_SYNC_MV_]` reads change. Creating a rollup, and the optimizer's choice of an index for a query on the base table, are unchanged.

issues.body:
### Steps to reproduce the behavior (Required)

A rollup's name is unique only in its table (`ALTER TABLE ... ADD ROLLUP` and `CREATE TABLE ... ROLLUP` check the table, not the database), so two tables of a database can each have a rollup of the same name. `[_SYNC_MV_]` reads a materialized index by its name alone:

```sql
CREATE TABLE t_a (k1 INT, k2 INT, v1 INT) DUPLICATE KEY(k1, k2) DISTRIBUTED BY HASH(k1) BUCKETS 1
    ROLLUP (r_shared (k2, k1)) PROPERTIES ('replication_num' = '1');
CREATE TABLE t_b (k1 INT, k2 INT, v1 INT) DUPLICATE KEY(k1, k2) DISTRIBUTED BY HASH(k1) BUCKETS 1
    ROLLUP (r_shared (k2, k1)) PROPERTIES ('replication_num' = '1');
INSERT INTO t_a VALUES (1, 10, 100), (2, 20, 200);
INSERT INTO t_b VALUES (3, 30, 300);

SELECT k2, k1 FROM r_shared [_SYNC_MV_] ORDER BY k2;
```

### Expected behavior (Required)

The read is ambiguous, because two tables have a rollup named `r_shared`, and there is no syntax to say which table's rollup to read. The statement should fail with an error that names the tables, so that the user can rename one of the rollups (`ALTER TABLE ... RENAME ROLLUP`).

### Real behavior (Required)

The statement succeeds and reads one of the two rollups:

```
30	3
```

Here it read `t_b`'s rollup. Which one it reads is not determined: `Database#getMaterializedViewIndex` returns the first visible index of that name that it meets while iterating the database's table map, a hash map keyed by table id. So the same statement can switch to the other table without being changed. This can happen when another table gets a rollup of that name, or when a rollup of that name becomes visible. On a cluster, adding a rollup named `r1` to a second table switched `SELECT * FROM r1 [_SYNC_MV_]` to that table, which has a different schema and different rows.

A synchronous materialized view does not have this problem: `CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW` rejects a name that another table's index already has. Only rollups can share a name.

agent_prs.body:
## Why I'm doing:

`[_SYNC_MV_]` was added in #22419 to read a synchronous materialized view directly: `SELECT * FROM <mv_name> [_SYNC_MV_]`. A synchronous materialized view is an index of its base table, not a table, so it cannot be read by name otherwise. Rollups are the same kind of index and are read the same way.

`Database#getMaterializedViewIndex` matches the name against every visible index of every table, and that includes each table's base index, which is named after the table. Nothing in #22419 intended this: its description, examples and tests are all about synchronous materialized views. The base index matches only because the lookup iterates every visible index. The result:

- A table name with the hint reads the table itself: `SELECT * FROM t [_SYNC_MV_]` is `SELECT * FROM t`.
- A table and another table's rollup can share a name, because `ADD ROLLUP` checks only its own table. Then `x [_SYNC_MV_]` matches both the table `x` and the rollup `x`. Which one the read gets depends on the iteration order of the database's table map, which is a hash map keyed by table id.

## What I'm doing:

- `Database#getMaterializedViewIndex` leaves out the base index of each table, so `[_SYNC_MV_]` matches only rollups and synchronous materialized views.
- The javadoc of `Database#getMaterializedViewIndex` and `LocalMetastore#getMaterializedViewIndex` says so.

A table name with the hint now gets "Unknown table", the error a name that matches no index already gets. Read a table by its name, without the hint.

issues.body:
### Steps to reproduce the behavior (Required)

`[_SYNC_MV_]` reads a synchronous materialized view or a rollup by its name. A table and another table's rollup can share a name, because `ADD ROLLUP` checks only its own table.

```sql
CREATE TABLE t_x (k1 INT, k2 INT, v1 INT) DUPLICATE KEY(k1, k2) DISTRIBUTED BY HASH(k1) BUCKETS 1 PROPERTIES ('replication_num' = '1');
CREATE TABLE t_y (k1 INT, k2 INT, v1 INT) DUPLICATE KEY(k1, k2) DISTRIBUTED BY HASH(k1) BUCKETS 1 ROLLUP (t_x (k2, k1)) PROPERTIES ('replication_num' = '1');
INSERT INTO t_x VALUES (1, 10, 100), (2, 20, 200);
INSERT INTO t_y VALUES (3, 30, 300);

SELECT * FROM t_x [_SYNC_MV_];
SELECT * FROM t_y [_SYNC_MV_];
```

### Expected behavior (Required)

`[_SYNC_MV_]` was added in #22419 to read a synchronous materialized view directly. It matches only rollups and synchronous materialized views:

- `t_x [_SYNC_MV_]` reads the rollup `t_x` of `t_y`.
- `t_y [_SYNC_MV_]` fails with "Unknown table": `t_y` has no rollup of that name. The table is read by its name, without the hint.

### Real behavior (Required)

The lookup also matches each table's base index, which is named after the table:

- `t_y [_SYNC_MV_]` reads the table `t_y`.
- `t_x [_SYNC_MV_]` matches both the table `t_x` and the rollup `t_x` of `t_y`. Which one it reads depends on the iteration order of the database's table map, which is a hash map keyed by table id.

`Database#getMaterializedViewIndex` iterates every visible index of each table, and that includes the base index.

agent_prs.body:
## Why I'm doing:

A temporary table is visible only in the session that created it. A plain read of its name from another session fails with "Unknown table". But a `[_SYNC_MV_]` read of its rollup from another session reads the other session's data:

```sql
-- session B
CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE tmp_secret (k1 INT, k2 INT, v1 INT) ENGINE=olap DUPLICATE KEY(k1, k2)
    DISTRIBUTED BY HASH(k1) BUCKETS 1 ROLLUP (r_tmp_secret (k2, k1)) PROPERTIES ('replication_num' = '1');
INSERT INTO tmp_secret VALUES (7, 77, 777);

-- session A, same database
SELECT k2, k1 FROM r_tmp_secret [_SYNC_MV_];   -- returns 77, 7
SELECT count(*) FROM tmp_secret;               -- ERROR: Unknown table
```

This was reproduced on a shared-nothing cluster built from `main`. `Database#getMaterializedViewIndex` looks the index name up in `idToTable`, which holds the temporary tables of every session. A name lookup finds a temporary table only through the session that created it. The same goes for a temporary table's base index, which is named after the table: another session's temporary table can also be what an `x [_SYNC_MV_]` read finds.

## What I'm doing:

- `Database#getMaterializedViewIndex` and `LocalMetastore#getMaterializedViewIndex` take the reading session's id, and leave out the temporary tables of other sessions. The session's own temporary tables stay, because one can be created with a rollup and read through `[_SYNC_MV_]`.
- `QueryAnalyzer#resolveTable` passes `session.getSessionId()`.
- The index-name parameter is renamed to `indexName`. It matches any materialized index: the base index, a rollup or a synchronous materialized view.

Tests: `CreateSyncMaterializedViewTest#testSelectFromRollupOfAnotherSessionsTemporaryTable` uses two sessions. One session creates a temporary table with a rollup, and reads the rollup through `[_SYNC_MV_]`. The other session's read of the rollup fails with "Unknown table". The test fails without the change.

issues.body:
### Steps to reproduce the behavior (Required)

A temporary table is visible only in the session that created it. It can be created with a rollup, which `[_SYNC_MV_]` reads by name.

Session B:

```sql
CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE tmp_secret (k1 INT, k2 INT, v1 INT) ENGINE=olap DUPLICATE KEY(k1, k2)
    DISTRIBUTED BY HASH(k1) BUCKETS 1 ROLLUP (r_tmp_secret (k2, k1)) PROPERTIES ('replication_num' = '1');
INSERT INTO tmp_secret VALUES (7, 77, 777);
-- keep the session open
```

Session A, in the same database:

```sql
SELECT k2, k1 FROM r_tmp_secret [_SYNC_MV_];
SELECT count(*) FROM tmp_secret;
```

### Expected behavior (Required)

Session A cannot see session B's temporary table, so both statements fail with "Unknown table".

### Real behavior (Required)

The read by table name fails as expected:

```
ERROR 5502 (42602): Getting analyzing error. Detail message: Unknown table 'db.tmp_secret'.
```

But the `[_SYNC_MV_]` read of the rollup returns session B's data:

```
77	7
```

`Database#getMaterializedViewIndex` looks the index name up in `idToTable`, which holds the temporary tables of every session. A lookup by table name, by contrast, finds a temporary table only through the session that created it. A temporary table's base index is named after the table, so `tmp_secret [_SYNC_MV_]` from another session can also reach it.

### StarRocks version (Required)

Reproduced on a build from main.

agent_prs.body:
## Why I'm doing:

`ARRAY_CONTAINS_ALL(CASE WHEN c0 IS NOT NULL THEN [1, 2] END, ARRAY_SORT([2, 1]))` crashes the BE with SIGSEGV in `ArrayContainsAll<TYPE_INT, false>::process` (#84127). Reproduced on 3.5, 4.0, 4.1 and main.

`array_contains_all` / `array_contains_seq` build a hash state in `prepare()` from an argument that is a constant literal there. An argument that is only computed to a constant, such as `array_sort([2, 1])` or `array_distinct([...])`, is not constant in `prepare()`, but arrives as a `ConstColumn` at runtime. `process()` took its constant-input path for any `ConstColumn` and read the state:
- with no state at all, it dereferenced a null pointer (the crash in the issue);
- with a state built from the other argument (one literal, one computed constant), it returned a "both constant" result that `prepare()` never computed, so the answer could be wrong instead of a crash.

## What I'm doing:

`prepare()` records which arguments the state was built from. `process()` unpacks any other constant argument into a full column before it is used, so only the arguments the state really describes take the constant path.

Tests:
- BE UT `ArrayFunctionsTest.array_contains_all_computed_const_argument`: both functions with two computed constants, one computed constant and a column (either side), one literal and one computed constant (either side), and two literals (the prepared result is still used). With the fix reverted the test crashes.
- SQLTest `test_array_contains_all_computed_const`: the two queries from the issue on the year-partitioned table, plus `array_contains_seq` and the literal/computed-constant mixes. It kills the BE on main and passes with the fix.

Observability: not applicable, the change only removes a crash and a wrong constant result.

Fixes #84127

agent_prs.body:
## Why I'm doing:

`col IN (NULL, NULL)` is NULL for every row, so a WHERE filter should keep nothing. Instead every row passes (#84124). `IN (NULL)` is not affected, because the FE rewrites it to `col = NULL` and folds that to NULL. An IN list with at least one non-NULL value is not affected either.

The IN predicate is pushed into the scan unchanged. When the scan normalizes it, the NULL is removed from the value list and the value set is left empty. `ColumnValueRange::add_fixed_values(FILTER_IN, {})` reads an empty set as "no constraint" and resets the range to the full range. The predicate is then marked as pushed down, so it is dropped. A NOT NULL column ends up with no filter at all, and a nullable column keeps only an `IS NOT NULL` filter. The same happens on a low-cardinality dictionary VARCHAR column, which goes through the same code.

## What I'm doing:

When no value is left in an IN list once NULL is removed, empty the column range and mark the predicate as normalized. `col NOT IN (..., NULL)` is already handled this way. What happens next depends on where the predicate is:
- In the top-level AND, the empty range ends the scan (EOF).
- Inside an OR, such as `(col IN (NULL, NULL) AND x) OR y`, the builder is not the root, so it returns "not push down". The OR is left in place and evaluated as an expression, which keeps the `y` rows. I did not return EndOfFile directly from the normalizer, because an error from a child builder under OR is propagated and would end the whole scan.

The DATE path already checked for an empty value set. But it only assigned `Status::EndOfFile` to a local status that was never returned, so the predicate was evaluated row by row. Its result was correct, but the scan was not skipped. It now empties the range in the same way.

Tests:
- BE UT in `olap_scan_prepare_test.cpp`:
  - `IN (NULL, NULL)` on INT and on DATE ends the scan;
  - `(c1 IN (NULL, NULL) AND c1 = 1) OR c1 = 2` and `c1 IN (NULL, NULL) OR c1 = 2` do not end the scan

The predicate is then marked as pushed down, so it is dropped. A NOT NULL column ends up with no filter at all, and a nullable column keeps only an `IS NOT NULL` filter. The same happens on a low-cardinality dictionary VARCHAR column, which goes through the same code.

## What I'm doing:

When no value is left in an IN list once NULL is removed, empty the column range and mark the predicate as normalized. `col NOT IN (..., NULL)` is already handled this way. What happens next depends on where the predicate is:
- In the top-level AND, the empty range ends the scan (EOF).
- Inside an OR, such as `(col IN (NULL, NULL) AND x) OR y`, the builder is not the root, so it returns "not push down". The OR is left in place and evaluated as an expression, which keeps the `y` rows. I did not return EndOfFile directly from the normalizer, because an error from a child builder under OR is propagated and would end the whole scan.

The DATE path already checked for an empty value set. But it only assigned `Status::EndOfFile` to a local status that was never returned, so the predicate was evaluated row by row. Its result was correct, but the scan was not skipped. It now empties the range in the same way.

Tests:
- BE UT in `olap_scan_prepare_test.cpp`:
  - `IN (NULL, NULL)` on INT and on DATE ends the scan;
  - `(c1 IN (NULL, NULL) AND c1 = 1) OR c1 = 2` and `c1 IN (NULL, NULL) OR c1 = 2` do not end the scan

```sql
CREATE TABLE t_in (k INT, v SMALLINT NOT NULL, w SMALLINT NULL)
DUPLICATE KEY(k) DISTRIBUTED BY HASH(k) BUCKETS 1 PROPERTIES ("replication_num" = "1");

### Expected behavior (Required)
`v IN (NULL, NULL)` is NULL for every row (the projection above shows that), so the WHERE filter keeps no rows and both counts are 0.

### Real behavior (Required)
Every row passes the filter. It happens when the IN list holds two or more NULLs and nothing else; `IN (NULL)` and an IN list with a non-NULL value are correct. The predicate is pushed into the scan unchanged (`PREDICATES: 2: v IN (NULL, NULL)` in EXPLAIN), so the storage-layer IN predicate seems to treat an all-NULL value list as "no filter".

Reproduced on `allin1-ubuntu` images: 3.5.21-85fccf8, 4.0.18-bebaa45, 4.1.8-b16342f. Not checked on main.

## Why I'm doing:

`SELECT COUNT((NOT 5) OR NULL) FROM t` returns the table's row count instead of 0 (#84119). `RewriteSimpleAggToMetaScanRule` answers `COUNT(<constant>)` from tablet metadata, and it only rules out a NULL literal as the argument. A column-free expression that has not been folded yet passes that check although it is NULL at runtime. Examples are `(NOT 5) OR NULL` and `CAST(5 AS BOOLEAN) = false OR NULL`. The result is wrong with the default configuration. Adding a `WHERE` clause disables the rewrite, so the bug only shows on queries without one.

`RewriteSimpleAggToHDFSScanRule` has the same check, so a COUNT on an external table can be answered from file row counts in the same way.

## What I'm doing:

Both rules now rewrite `COUNT(<arg>)` only when the argument is a non-null literal (`ConstantOperator` that is not NULL). `COUNT(*)`, `COUNT(1)` and the other literal forms keep the rewrite. An argument that uses a column is projected to a column reference first, so the existing column check still covers it.

Tests:
- FE UT:
  - `AggregateTest.testSimpleAggRewrite`: `COUNT(1)` still uses MetaScan; `COUNT((not 5) or null)` and `COUNT(cast(5 as boolean) = false or null)` do not.
  - `HiveScanTest.testHiveRewriteSimpleAggToHdfsScan`: the same argument is not rewritten to `___count___`.
  
  With the fix reverted, both new assertions fail.
- SQLTest `test_count_null_constant_expr`: covers the two expressions from the issue, the same count with a `WHERE` clause, `COUNT(NULL)`, `COUNT(1)` / `COUNT(*)`, and a non-null constant expression. It fails on main (`COUNT((NOT 5) OR NULL)` returns 3 instead of 0) and passes with the fix.

Observability: I reviewed EXPLAIN, which shows `MetaScan` when the rewrite applies. No change was needed: queries that are no longer rewritten show the normal `OlapScanNode` / HDFS scan.

issues.body:
`SELECT COUNT(<expr>) FROM t` without a `WHERE` clause returns the table's row count when `<expr>` references no column and evaluates to NULL but is not a NULL literal at planning time, for example `(NOT 5) OR NULL`. The correct result is 0. `RewriteSimpleAggToMetaScanRule` rewrites such a `COUNT` into a metadata row count because it only rules out a literal NULL argument.

### Steps to reproduce the behavior

```sql
CREATE DATABASE cnt_repro;
USE cnt_repro;
CREATE TABLE t (id INT, v INT) DUPLICATE KEY(id) DISTRIBUTED BY HASH(id) BUCKETS 1
PROPERTIES ("replication_num" = "1");
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, 10), (2, NULL), (3, 30);

SELECT (NOT 5) OR NULL FROM t LIMIT 1;               -- NULL
SELECT COUNT((NOT 5) OR NULL) FROM t;                -- 3   (wrong, expected 0)
SELECT COUNT((NOT 5) OR NULL) FROM t WHERE id > 0;   -- 0   (correct)
SELECT COUNT(NULL) FROM t;                           -- 0   (correct)

SET enable_rewrite_simple_agg_to_meta_scan = false;
SELECT COUNT((NOT 5) OR NULL) FROM t;                -- 0   (correct once the rewrite is off)
```

`EXPLAIN SELECT COUNT((NOT 5) OR NULL) FROM t;` with the rewrite on shows the count answered from metadata:

```
  2:AGGREGATE (update finalize)
  |  output: sum(rows_id)
  ...
  0:MetaScan
     Table: t
     <id 6> : rows_id
```

`CAST(5 AS BOOLEAN) = false OR NULL` behaves the same way. `5 = 0 OR NULL` does not: it is folded to a NULL literal before the rule runs.

### Expected behavior

`COUNT(<expr>)` counts the rows where `<expr>` is not NULL, so `SELECT COUNT((NOT 5) OR NULL) FROM t` returns 0, with or without a `WHERE` clause.

### Real behavior

Without a `WHERE` clause it returns the number of rows in the table (3 here).

### Root cause

`fe/fe-core/src/main/java/com/starrocks/sql/optimizer/rule/transformation/RewriteSimpleAggToMetaScanRule.java:296-303` accepts a `COUNT` whose argument uses no column as long as the argument is not a NULL literal:

agent_prs.body:
## Why I'm doing:

A BE on main crashed with SIGSEGV in a spill restore IO task:

```
PC: starrocks::spill::SpillEventObservable::notify_source_observers()
    starrocks::spill::SpillerReader::trigger_restore<IOTaskExecutor,
        ResourceMemTrackerGuard<weak_ptr<QueryContextLifetime>, weak_ptr<SpillerReader>>>::{lambda}
    starrocks::workgroup::ScanExecutor::worker_thread()
```

A restore task completes through `SpillerReader`'s raw `Spiller*`: `complete_io()` decrements the spiller's in-flight IO count and notifies its source observers. The guard type in the stack pins only the query context and the reader. Three call sites restore with that guard: the partition-wise aggregate and distinct source operators, and the spillable NL join chunk stream. Every other spill site uses `TRACKER_WITH_SPILLER_*_GUARD`, which also pins the spiller.

`Aggregator::close()` resets the spiller when the driver is finalized. If the query is cancelled or times out while a partition restore is still in flight, the task's completion runs on a freed `Spiller`. Reproduced on an ASan + fail-point build (`spill_restore_sleep`, partition-wise agg with `query_timeout` hit during restore):

```
ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-free
WRITE of size 8 ... thread T833
  #1 starrocks::spill::Spiller::decrease_in_flight_io() compute_env/spill/spiller.h:228
  #2 starrocks::spill::Spiller::complete_io<SpillerReader::trigger_restore<...>>
  ...
  #10 starrocks::workgroup::ScanExecutor::worker_thread()
freed by thread T690 here:
  ...
  #12 starrocks::Aggregator::close(starrocks::RuntimeState*) exec/aggregator.cpp:831
previously allocated by thread T486 here:
  #9  starrocks::spill::SpillerFactory::create(...)
  #10 starrocks::pipeline::SpillablePartitionWiseAggregateSinkOperatorFactory::create(int, int)
```

In release builds the freed memory is reused, and the next step (`notify_source_observers()`) dereferences a garbage observer pointer, which is the crash above.

issues.body:
### Steps to reproduce the behavior (Required)

Needs a BE built with `ENABLE_FAULT_INJECTION=ON`. The fail point only makes the race window wide; without it the crash depends on timing.

1. Create and load a table:
   ```sql
   CREATE TABLE t0 (c0 int, c1 varchar(20)) DUPLICATE KEY(c0)
   DISTRIBUTED BY HASH(c0) BUCKETS 1 PROPERTIES("replication_num"="1");
   INSERT INTO t0 SELECT generate_series, generate_series FROM TABLE(generate_series(1, 1000000));
   ```
2. Slow down spill restore IO:
   ```sql
   ADMIN ENABLE FAILPOINT 'spill_restore_sleep';
   ```
3. Run a spilled partition-wise aggregation that times out while its partition restore tasks are in flight:
   ```sql
   SELECT /*+SET_VAR(query_timeout=20,pipeline_dop=1,new_planner_agg_stage=3,spill_mode='force',
            enable_spill=true,spill_partitionwise_agg=true,spill_operator_min_bytes=1024,
            spill_mem_table_size=1024) */
          count(*), sum(murmur_hash3_32(c1, cnt))
   FROM (SELECT c1, count(*) cnt FROM t0 GROUP BY c1) t;
   ```
4. Wait about 25s for the sleeping restore tasks to finish.

### Expected behavior (Required)

The query fails with a timeout and the BE keeps running.

### Real behavior (Required)

The BE crashes when the in-flight restore task completes.

## Why I'm doing:

When the database does not exist, `REFRESH EXTERNAL TABLE` reports the database name as an unknown table:

```
mysql> REFRESH EXTERNAL TABLE default_catalog.db_c.tbl_d;
ERROR 5502 (42602): Getting analyzing error. Detail message: Unknown table 'db_c'.
```

Other statements report the same situation as an unknown database:

```
mysql> SELECT * FROM db_c.tbl_d;
ERROR 5501 (3F000): Getting analyzing error. Detail message: Unknown database 'db_c'.
mysql> SHOW TABLES FROM db_c;
ERROR 5501 (3F000): Getting analyzing error. Detail message: Unknown database 'db_c'.
mysql> DESC db_c.tbl_d;
ERROR 5501 (3F000): Getting analyzing error. Detail message: Unknown database 'db_c'.
```

`RefreshTableStatementAnalyzer` passes `ErrorCode.ERR_BAD_TABLE_ERROR` with `dbName` when `getDb` returns null. It is the only analyzer under `sql/analyzer` that does this; the others use `ERR_BAD_DB_ERROR`.

## What I'm doing:

- Use `ErrorCode.ERR_BAD_DB_ERROR` when the database is missing in `RefreshTableStatementAnalyzer`. The error becomes `ERROR 5501 (3F000): Unknown database 'db_c'`.
- Add `RefreshTableStmtTest#testRefreshTableUnknownDbOrTable` covering the missing-database and missing-table cases.
- Add SQL-Tester case `test/sql/test_refresh_external_table/T/test_refresh_external_table_unknown_db`.

Observability: no metric or log change; only the user-facing error code, SQLSTATE and message for this case change.

agent_prs.title: [BugFix] Report Unknown database when REFRESH EXTERNAL TABLE targets a missing database (backport #83995)

agent_prs.body:
## Why I'm doing:

When the database does not exist, `REFRESH EXTERNAL TABLE` reports the database name as an unknown table:

```
mysql> REFRESH EXTERNAL TABLE default_catalog.db_c.tbl_d;
ERROR 5502 (42602): Getting analyzing error. Detail message: Unknown table 'db_c'.
```

Other statements report the same situation as an unknown database:

```
mysql> SELECT * FROM db_c.tbl_d;
ERROR 5501 (3F000): Getting analyzing error. Detail message: Unknown database 'db_c'.
mysql> SHOW TABLES FROM db_c;
ERROR 5501 (3F000): Getting analyzing error. Detail message: Unknown database 'db_c'.
mysql> DESC db_c.tbl_d;
ERROR 5501 (3F000): Getting analyzing error. Detail message: Unknown database 'db_c'.
```

`RefreshTableStatementAnalyzer` passes `ErrorCode.ERR_BAD_TABLE_ERROR` with `dbName` when `getDb` returns null. It is the only analyzer under `sql/analyzer` that does this; the others use `ERR_BAD_DB_ERROR`.

## What I'm doing:

- Use `ErrorCode.ERR_BAD_DB_ERROR` when the database is missing in `RefreshTableStatementAnalyzer`. The error becomes `ERROR 5501 (3F000): Unknown database 'db_c'`.
- Add `RefreshTableStmtTest#testRefreshTableUnknownDbOrTable` covering the missing-database and missing-table cases.
- Add SQL-Tester case `test/sql/test_refresh_external_table/T/test_refresh_external_table_unknown_db`.

Observability: no metric or log change; only the user-facing error code, SQLSTATE and message for this case change.

Fixes #83996

issues.body:
### Steps to reproduce the behavior (Required)
1. Make sure database `db_c` does not exist.
2. `REFRESH EXTERNAL TABLE default_catalog.db_c.tbl_d;`
3. Compare with `SELECT * FROM db_c.tbl_d;`, `SHOW TABLES FROM db_c;` or `DESC db_c.tbl_d;`

### Expected behavior (Required)
A missing database is reported as an unknown database, like other statements do:
```
ERROR 5501 (3F000): Getting analyzing error. Detail message: Unknown database 'db_c'.
```

### Real behavior (Required)
`REFRESH EXTERNAL TABLE` reports the database name as an unknown table:
```
mysql> REFRESH EXTERNAL TABLE default_catalog.db_c.tbl_d;
ERROR 5502 (42602): Getting analyzing error. Detail message: Unknown table 'db_c'.
mysql> SELECT * FROM db_c.tbl_d;
ERROR 5501 (3F000): Getting analyzing error. Detail message: Unknown database 'db_c'.
mysql> SHOW TABLES FROM db_c;
ERROR 5501 (3F000): Getting analyzing error. Detail message: Unknown database 'db_c'.
mysql> DESC db_c.tbl_d;
ERROR 5501 (3F000): Getting analyzing error. Detail message: Unknown database 'db_c'.
```

Root cause: `RefreshTableStatementAnalyzer` calls `ErrorReport.reportSemanticException(ErrorCode.ERR_BAD_TABLE_ERROR, dbName)` when `getDb` returns null. It should use `ERR_BAD_DB_ERROR`. It is the only analyzer under `sql/analyzer` that reports a missing database this way.

 - main, branch-4.2, branch-4.1 and branch-4.0.

agent_prs.body:
## Change

Follow-up to #3760, #3774 and #3798 for #3743, the GTK grid with large local results.

- **Before:** after a background sort or filter, `RowStore` still built one `Slot` per row. On a 1M-row result that is a 1M-element vector, rebuilt on every sort.
- **Now:** the order is kept as one index vector (`SourceOrder`). Row objects are created only when GTK asks for an item, and are weakly cached.
- **Edits and inserts:** replacing a row in place keeps the compact form (`object_rows`). A splice that changes the row count switches back to the slot form (`materialize_source_order`).
- **Selection:** prepared orders of 10,000 or more rows carry a position index. Restoring the selection after a sort looks up each selected row directly, instead of scanning the whole order.

This finishes the work preserved on `wip/fix/gtk-large-sort-apply-3743`. **Review fixes:**
- the WIP removed a vendored mongodb line that `main` needs (`verify_hostname: _`); `main`'s vendor files are kept;
- it dropped the early return for an empty selection, which made every sort walk the whole order. The early return is restored.

**Reviewed:** every reader of `slots` in `row_store.rs`, including item, n_items, cells, search, find, the draft id and the source value/index readers, handles the compact form. Every writer of `slots` also sets or clears `source_order`.

`changelog.d/gtk-large-sort-lazy-rows.changed.md`

issues.body:
Problem: `apps/linux/app/src/ui/grid/local_sort.rs` (`sorted_source_indices`) and `local_filter.rs` run synchronously; neither file has a spawn call. A sort or filter over a result near the 1 million row limit blocks the GTK main loop. #674 fixed the selection restore cost only.
Wanted: Run the index computation off the UI thread with a cancel token and a stale-result check, and show a busy state.
Acceptance:
- Sorting 1 million rows keeps the main loop responsive (no frame gap over 100 ms, measured with the existing GTK harness, or Unknown if no harness fits).
- A second sort during the first cancels the first; the grid never shows an older result.
Why now: spool-backed whole-result operations (ADR 0029) make big local results common.
Lane: UX
Size: M
Severity: low

Code references (read on `main` 2026-11-22): `apps/linux/app/src/ui/grid/local_sort.rs`

Found in the 2026-11-22 review of research notes against `main`. Not scheduled.

One PR for the GPUI UI coherence audit (#4002). It fixes the layout, button, shared-part, colour, wording and guardrail findings, adds every bundled colour theme to Settings, and changes the grid Export button to open the file export with a format choice.

Closes #3996
Closes #3997
Closes #3998

## Layout (#3996)
- **Home and status bar:** Home counts no longer show 1 when the count is 0. The status bar follows the active tab: a query tab shows its connection, not the last table. The theme name is gone from the footer.

issues.body:
Found in the 2026-11-25 GPUI UI audit. UI copy is inconsistent.

- **Title Case among sentence case:** "Quick Start", "Database Types", "New Query", "Connection Status", "Command Palette", "Query History" (`home_page.rs:99-244`); "Table Data" next to "Summary" (`query_pane.rs:344`); "Import Connections…" and "Export Connections" (`chrome.rs:572`); "Open Home"; "Foreign Key Peek:" with a colon (`fk_peek_ui.rs:48`).
- **One action, several names:**
  - New query: "New query", "New Query", "New query tab".
  - Saving a query: "Save" (`query_pane.rs:89`), "Save query as favorite".
  - Export: "Export CSV", "Export current page or selection as CSV", "Export to a file…".
  - The Connections button has id `new-connection`.
- **Shortcut text uses two formats.** The palette shows `ctrl-f` and `ctrl-enter`; the editor hints show `Ctrl+Enter`. "Go to last edit (Ctrl+Alt+-)" puts the shortcut inside the label.
- **Palette groups tell you nothing.** Almost every command is in "Workspace". Several labels explain themselves in parentheses: "Reconnect and refresh the table list (closes other tabs)", "Disconnect (close this window and open a clean one)".
- **Status message tone varies.** 14 end with a period and about 246 don't. Cancellation is worded three ways ("Cancelled the import", "Export cancelled; no file was created", "The export was cancelled.").
- **Spelling mixes British and American:** "Colour", "Behaviour", "cancelled" next to "favorite", "organization", "Minimize".
- **The status bar shows the theme name** ("light" / "dark"), which isn't useful information.

### Proposal
- Sentence case everywhere except product names.
- One name per action, shared by palette, toolbar, menu and button.
- One shortcut format, rendered by `Chord::label`.
- Palette groups by object: Table, Query, Connection, View, App.
- One spelling, with American as the default unless docs say otherwise.
- Status messages without a final period.
- A copy test over palette, tooltip and button strings, w

issues.body:
Found in the 2026-11-25 GPUI UI audit. Colour roles are used inconsistently.

- **Blue is used as decoration, which DESIGN.md forbids** ("Blue is not decoration"):
  - the active tab icon and underline (`chrome.rs:850,864`);
  - splitter hover (`chrome.rs:690`, `query_pane.rs:196`);
  - diagram key markers (`diagram_ui.rs:227`).
  The row-details links (`detail_panel.rs:276`) and foreign-key cells use `info`, while other clickable text is plain. Decide on one link role.
- **Errors use two colours.** `warning` for query errors (`query_pane.rs:442`), audit errors (`audit_page.rs:144,154`) and Home history failures (`home_page.rs:240`). `destructive` for history failures (`history_view.rs:195`), save errors (`save_ui.rs:447`) and form errors (`connection_form.rs:127`). Errors should be `destructive` and warnings `warning`.
- **Colours ignore the theme:**
  - text input selection is a fixed `rgba(0x5b8cff55)` (`text_input.rs:797`);
  - the placeholder is `hsla(0,0,0.7,0.45)` (`text_input.rs:597`);
  - the scrim is `rgba(0x00000088)`.
- **Dark theme inverts header emphasis.** Column types read brighter than column names.
- **The connection colour has two shapes:** a dot in the sidebar and tabs, a square swatch in the form.

### Acceptance
- Every colour comes from a theme role; no `rgb(0x…)`, `rgba(0x…)` or `hsla(` outside `theme.rs`.
- A contrast test over both themes for text on each surface, button text at rest, hover and pressed, selection and status tints (as BarSQL `theme_files.rs` and dbdelve `theme/mod.rs` do).

issues.body:
Found in the 2026-11-25 GPUI UI audit. The UI checks are weaker than they look.

- **`scripts/check-ui-patterns.py` stops reading a file at the first `#[cfg(test)]`** (line 41), even an indented one. So it never checked `chrome.rs` past line 248 (toolbar, sidebar, tabs, settings, Home), `text_input.rs` past 111 or `grid_table.rs` past 1302. Its px rule also misses expressions like `px(8.0 + 14.0 * depth)`.
- **Nothing ratchets** raw colours, `rounded_*`/`shadow_*` outside a dialog helper, `text_xs`/`text_sm` (37 uses of `px(TEXT_SMALL)` alongside `text_xs` in `grid_table.rs:520` and FK peek), `cursor_pointer()` outside helpers (a sign of a hand-built button), `theme.info` outside an allowlist, or `ghost(…, "")`.
- **No contrast or keyboard-coverage tests.** dbflux fails on any clickable id without a keyboard path (`bolt::keyboard_coverage`). BarSQL and dbdelve test text and button contrast in every theme.
- **`docs/ui-design.md` is silent on:** one shared constructor per job, bar height = control height + padding, truncation order, focus rings only after keyboard input, elevation order, dialog button order and minimum width.

### Proposal
1. Fix the `#[cfg(test)]` cut-off so only `mod tests` blocks are skipped, and re-baseline.
2. Add the ratchets above, at a zero baseline where possible.
3. Add a contrast test over both themes, and a keyboard-coverage test per surface (every clickable id has a keyboard path).
4. Add the peer-derived rules to `docs/ui-design.md`. A UI PR attaches light and dark screenshots at 1500 and 760 px.

agent_prs.body:
Closes #3952 and #3953. These are the last two of the six peer-adoption issues; #3976 has the other four.

**Stacked on #3976**: the GPUI sidebar sizes reuse #3976's connection-info fetch. Merge #3976 first; GitHub then retargets this PR to `main`.

## #3952: table sizes and full-scan chips
- **New optional call**: `Connection::table_sizes(_controlled)`. The trait default returns `Unsupported`.
  - `PolicyGuard` forwards it as a governed, audited metadata read ("TABLE SIZES").
  - `bookie-agentd`'s session wrapper forwards it.
  - SQLite and DuckDB report no sizes and are listed in their stop-class contracts.
- **Catalog reads per engine**, each capped at 10,000 rows:
  - **PostgreSQL**: `relpages` from `pg_class` for the table, its TOAST table and its indexes. These are catalog statistics, so the read takes no locks; only tables the user can SELECT, with temp and TOAST schemas excluded.
  - **MySQL/MariaDB**: `information_schema.tables` data + index length, for base tables.
  - **SQL Server**: `sys.partitions` + `sys.allocation_units` used pages. Unlike `dm_db_partition_stats`, this needs no special permission.
  - **ClickHouse**: active `system.parts` bytes on disk.
- **Shared index** (app-services `table_sizes`): `SizeIndex` looks sizes up by schema and name, falling back to a unique name when the sidebar has no schema. `size_label` formats in B, KiB, MiB, GiB and so on.
- **Both sidebars**: sizes show as a muted label, loaded once per connection in the background. A failure only means no sizes are shown.
- **Plans**: `explain_plan::full_scan_rows` flags Seq Scan and Parallel Seq Scan nodes of 1,000 rows or more, using actual rows when known. It shows as "Full scan of ~N rows" in the GPUI plan view and the GTK plan tree.

## #3953: closed drafts and last edit
- **Store**: app-services `closed_drafts` holds closed query SQL in `closed-drafts.json`.
  - Blank SQL and drafts over 256 KiB are skipped, an immediate repeat is collapsed, and at most 20 are kept.
  - Reo

issues.body:
Two schema and plan hints from BarSQL (BAR-44) that help a DBA:
- The sidebar shows table sizes from the catalog (PostgreSQL, MySQL/MariaDB, SQL Server, ClickHouse) without waiting on locks.
- A query plan shows a "Full scan" chip on whole-table reads of 1,000 rows or more.

BookiE has a plan misestimate flag (#3830) but neither of these.

### Proposal (our own implementation)
- Catalog size reads per engine in the drivers: `pg_total_relation_size` with a lock timeout, `information_schema.tables` data and index length, `sys.dm_db_partition_stats`, `system.parts`. They load lazily and are bounded, and a failure shows nothing rather than an error.
- Sizes are shown muted next to table names, in both frontends.
- In app-services `explain_plan`, flag sequential or full scans over a row estimate threshold as a chip in the GPUI plan view and the GTK plan tab.

issues.body:
The GPUI connection form shows every field at once. Peers keep the core fields first and put the rest away:
- TablePro opens on the core fields and puts SSL, tunnels, appearance and advanced options behind disclosures. A section opens by itself when a field inside it fails validation.
- BarSQL fills the form from a pasted or typed connection URL, maps each driver's TLS settings, and copies a connection back as a URL without its password.

The GTK app can already parse and copy connection URLs. GPUI cannot.

### Proposal (our own implementation)
- Open on name, engine, host, port, database, user and password. SSL/TLS, SSH tunnel, environment and colour, and advanced options become collapsible sections.
- When validation fails inside a collapsed section, open it and focus the field.
- A "Paste connection URL" action fills the form through the shared URL parser in app-services, which GTK already uses. "Copy as URL" leaves out the password and any secrets.
- The headless tests cover the disclosure state, validation reveal, URL round trip and password exclusion.

issues.body:
## Problem

In a GPUI query tab, the Prod approval bar is only rendered inside the grid pane. `query_pane.rs` `result_body` shows the grid pane only when the active run succeeded and the view is **Table Data**. In every other state the approval request is invisible:
- the active run failed;
- the Messages, Summary, Chart or Plan view is open;
- the tab has no runs yet.

The write then waits unseen for `APPROVAL_TIMEOUT` (120 s), and the request is denied.

It fails closed: nothing is written. But a Prod write in a transaction looks hung ("Running in the transaction…"). While it waits, Commit, Roll back and closing the tab are all refused.

## Reproduce (acceptance run 2026-11-24, `c081dd0b7e`)

1. Connect a saved PostgreSQL connection with environment **Prod**.
2. In a new query tab, run any failing statement (e.g. `BEGIN; UPDATE …`, refused by policy).
3. Click **Begin transaction**, then run `UPDATE t SET c = c WHERE id = 1`.
4. No approval bar appears. The server shows the session `idle in transaction` after the impact `SELECT count(*)`. After 120 s the statement is denied.
5. Run a `SELECT` first, so a result grid is shown, then the same UPDATE: the bar appears ("This write needs your approval", Deny / Approve once).

The approval bar also did not appear on the table tab while the request was pending.

## Expected

A pending approval is always visible in the window that owns the request, whatever the result view: a top-level bar or an overlay, not part of the grid pane.

## Evidence

`bookie-research/evidence/acceptance-2026-11-24/`:
- `s2-a` … `s2-g`: invisible;
- `s2-i`: visible once a grid is shown.

Refs #3890, ADR 0057.
issues.title: GPUI: Prod approval bar is invisible unless the query tab shows a result grid

agent_prs.body:
## Change

Fixes #3843. GPUI table tabs now have a WHERE bar that sends the filter to the server, as GTK's filter strip, dbx and BarSQL do. Before this, GPUI's only filter ran over the rows already loaded, so on a large table it silently searched one page.

- **The bar:** an always-visible monospace input (`WHERE …`) with Apply (also Enter) and Clear, plus a chip showing the current sort. The palette commands "Filter this table on the server (WHERE)" and "Clear the server WHERE filter" do the same.
- **Shared path:** the text goes into `FilterSet.extra_sql` and through the shared `app-services::browse_query::BrowseTarget` (the same path the GTK browse uses), via the guarded query runner. Nothing is concatenated in GPUI. MongoDB and Redis refuse it ("WHERE filters need a SQL database").
- **Sort and count:** both respect the WHERE (`load_table_where_controlled`, `count_table_rows`, which now reports "… rows matching the WHERE filter").
- **Late results:** a result is dropped when the session, table or view changed meanwhile, or when unsaved edits block a reload. A bad WHERE keeps the previous grid and reports the server error.
- **Per table:** the filter is kept per table and restored when switching tabs.
- **Client-side filters:** the existing client-side Find and Filter are now labelled "Find in loaded rows" and "Filter loaded rows".

## Changelog fragment

None: GPUI only (ADR 0052).

`server_filter_ui_tests` (first commit, written before the fix) loads `orders` with a 2-row cap, then applies a WHERE that matches a row beyond the loaded page and expects it to appear. It also checks that a bad WHERE keeps the grid and reports, and that Clear restores the unfiltered table. On the old code the matching row is never found.

issues.body:
## Problem

The GPUI filter row (`apps/gpui/src/render.rs` `grid_filter_row`, `find_filter.rs` `apply_filter` -> `parse_predicate` -> `source.filter`) filters only the rows already loaded into the grid. On a table larger than the loaded rows it silently searches part of the table. `LiveTable::load` / `LiveSession::load_table_sorted_controlled` take no filter.

GTK sends the filter to the database: `apps/linux/app/src/ui/filter_strip.rs` edits a `bookie_core::FilterSet` (rules and raw `extra_sql`), and browsing goes through `crates/app-services/src/browse_query.rs` (`BrowseTarget { filter, .. }`, `build_filter_where`) and the policy-guarded read path.

## Repro

1. Open a SQLite table in GPUI with more rows than are loaded (for example load `orders` with `max_rows = 2`).
2. Filter for a row beyond the loaded ones (`id = 6`).
3. Result: no match, although the table has the row.

## Expected

- Table tabs show a WHERE row (monospace input, Apply on Enter, Clear) and a chip with the current sort.
- Applying reloads the table from the server with `FilterSet.extra_sql` through the shared browse query and the same guarded read path; the exact row count respects the filter.
- A bad WHERE reports the database error and keeps the previous grid; a late result never replaces a newer load.
- Find and the predicate filter stay client-side and are labelled as working on loaded rows.
issues.title: GPUI: table filter runs on loaded rows only; send WHERE to the server like GTK

## Change

Closes #3803. Part of the GPUI parity work before the preview is promoted (#3684).

Before: GPUI created every `DatabaseService` with `UnknownHostKey::Refuse` and no prompter, so a built-in SSH connection to a host missing from known_hosts failed with the host-key-refused error and offered no way to trust it. GTK asks.

Not in scope: GTK's system OpenSSH backend (askpass prompts) is not wired into GPUI.

Adds ledger rows for the two other parity gaps (#3804 server messages, #3805 MCP settings).

GPUI parity gap before the preview is promoted (#3684).

GTK installs a host-key prompter (`DatabaseService::enable_builtin_ssh_prompter`): an unknown built-in SSH host key opens a trust-on-first-use dialog with the host, key algorithm and fingerprint; Trust records the key in known_hosts, Cancel refuses. agent_prs.body:
Closes #850.

- Queries, statements and session statements now drop the running request on Stop or timeout, send a TDS Attention through `cancel_query`, and report `Cancelled` or `TimedOut` only after the server acknowledges. A missing acknowledgement stays `OperationOutcomeUnknown` and retires the handle.
- The vendored Tiberius drain now keeps reading when SQL Server finishes the cancelled request in one message and acknowledges Attention in the next; the old drain stopped at the first end of message and failed.
- `supports_server_cancellation()` is now true. Catalog reads and transaction batches still retire the handle on interruption.
- Real SQL Server tests: cancelled read, lock-blocked write left unchanged, session keeping its temp table. Full MSSQL integration target passes (68 tests).
- ADR 0005 and the user docs are updated.

Decision to review: a multi-statement autocommit batch keeps statements that finished before Attention; this is documented in known limitations.

issues.body:
The accepted cancellation ADR and current docs say SQL Server cannot send TDS Attention because Tiberius exposes no API. This branch uses Tiberius 0.13, whose public `Client::cancel_query()` API sends Attention and drains the acknowledgement: https://docs.rs/tiberius/0.13.0/tiberius/struct.Client.html#method.cancel_query

BookiE currently still reports `supports_server_cancellation() == false` and retires the connection after interruption. The new API alone does not prove our mutex/session lifecycle can cancel the active request safely, so keep the capability false until a real SQL Server test proves the whole path.

Acceptance:
- A controlled query interruption sends Attention on the active client and observes the server's cancellation acknowledgement before reporting `Cancelled` or `TimedOut`.
- The connection/session is usable afterward, with no partial result returned.
- A write is reported as terminal only when the server confirms cancellation; otherwise the result remains `OperationOutcomeUnknown` and the handle is retired.
- Tests use a real SQL Server fixture and include a read and a write.
- Update ADR 0005 and user-facing docs to the verified result.

agent_prs.body:
Closes #3508. From the 2026-11-19 audits of #3513 and #3520 (findings A1 and A3), now including the delete path.

**A1: the write session is re-validated.** The cached `WriteSession` was frozen at open and never evicted, so a connection flipped to read-only or production elsewhere was still written through, and a dropped connection blocked every later save or delete.
- `ReadSessionStore::saved_connection_stamp` serializes the saved connection (no secrets: those live in the keyring). `WriteSession` stores it at open; `is_current()` compares it before each save or delete and reopens on a difference.
- `finish_save` keeps the cached session only after a successful save and drops it after any failure. Test `a_write_the_guard_denies_...` now asserts the eviction and fails without it (checked).

**A3: an approval prompt in GPUI, and #3508.**
- `app-services::approval_prompt`: `ChannelApprovalSink` sends the request to the window and waits for Deny or Approve once. A timeout (120 s), a cancelled operation, a dropped answer or a closed window all deny. Wrapped in `ReviewableApprovalSink`, so a statement over 16,384 characters or with invisible or direction-changing characters is denied before any prompt (#3508). The GTK app now installs the same wrapper outermost, above the remembering sink, so a remembered grant cannot approve an unreadable statement.
- Prompt bar in the save-bar slot: rule, reason, connection, environment, class, any preview or exact row count, and the full SQL; Deny is first. An abandoned question disappears and the next queued one is shown.
- It lives in `app-services` because ADR 0041 forbids `apps/gpui` from depending on `bookie-policy` (the boundary check enforced that).

**Local checks:** 156 GPUI tests (new: two prompt tests, the eviction assertion), 5 new sink tests, `cargo clippy -p bookie-app-services -p bookie-policy -p bookie-app --all-targets -- -D warnings` and GPUI clippy clean, function-size, crate-boundaries, panic-sites, comment-lines, `

issues.body:
## What

After #3504, a person cannot approve SQL that is longer than `MAX_APPROVAL_SQL_CHARS` or contains invisible or direction-changing characters, but only because the GTK approval dialog disables its approve buttons (`apps/linux/app/src/services/gtk_approval.rs`).

The guard applies the same rule only to agents: `resolve_authorization` in `crates/policy/src/guard.rs` (around line 310) turns `RequireApproval` into `Deny` with rule `agent_sql_not_reviewable` when `principal` is `Principal::Agent` and `!sql_is_reviewable(sql)`. For `Principal::Human`, an unreviewable statement reaches whatever `ApprovalSink` is installed.

## Why it matters

Any other human-facing approval sink has to repeat the rule by hand. The GPUI frontend is gaining a write path (ADR 0052 item 5, #3505) and will need its own approval prompt; a CLI or another frontend would be the same. A sink that shows a truncated preview, or approves without checking `sql_is_reviewable`, would let a person approve a statement whose tail they never saw. That is the situation #3504 closed for GTK.

Today the exposure is closed for the read-session store used by GPUI, because its `DatabaseService` uses `DenyApprovalSink`, which refuses everything that needs approval.

## Suggested direction (for the policy lane to choose)

- A decorator sink in `bookie-policy` that denies a request when `!sql_is_reviewable(&request.sql)` before delegating, so every frontend that installs it gets the rule; or
- the same check in the guard for humans, with the GTK dialog keeping its explanatory text for the denial.

Either way, add a test that an unreviewable statement does not reach the inner sink.

## Related

#3504 (GTK dialog fix), #3505 (writable read session), ADR 0052 item 5.
issues.title: Human approval of unreviewable SQL is enforced only in the GTK dialog, not in the guard or a shared sink
