issues.body:
## O que acontece

`scripts/check-validate-parity.sh` reprova no Windows (Git Bash / MSYS2) com uma mensagem que **acusa o CLI**:

```
validate parity (script_integrity FIFO): .../siu-fifo-go.json did not accuse
  'could not be read' for the FIFO fixture — obtained: []
```

Os três CLIs estão certos. O que não existe é a fixture.

## Medição

`mkfifo` (linhas 487–488) sai com **exit 0** e o `ls -l` mostra `prw-rw-rw-`. O que ele grava no NTFS, porém, é um **atalho do Windows**:

```
$ [ -p "$P/.claude/settings.json" ] && echo "test -p : SIM, e FIFO"
test -p : SIM, e FIFO                      <- visao do MSYS

$ python -c "import os; print(os.listdir(...))"     # Python nativo do Windows
['settings.json.lnk']                      <- nao existe 'settings.json'

$ cygpath -w "$P/.claude/settings.json"
C:\...\.claude\settings.json.lnk           <- o proprio cygpath resolve para o .lnk
```

O `mkfifo` do MSYS emula FIFO com um arquivo `.lnk` de 130 bytes, `mode=100444`, resolvido apenas por processos MSYS-aware. **Go, Node e Python compilados para Windows não são MSYS-aware**: para eles, `.claude/settings.json` simplesmente **não existe**.

Daí o `[]`. Reproduzido nos três, com a fixture exata do gate:

```
--- go     : 0 violacoes, 0 warnings   regras presentes: []
--- node   : 0 violacoes, 0 warnings   regras presentes: []
--- python : 0 violacoes, 0 warnings   regras presentes: []
```

Config ausente não é config ilegível. Não acusar é o comportamento correto.

## O produto já está certo — e o comentário dele já diz por quê

`internal/validator/regularfile_windows.go` argumenta exatamente isto, e antes de eu medir:

> *"A path under a project or `$HOME` directory on an NTFS/ReFS volume cannot, in practice, resolve to a named pipe the way a POSIX path can resolve to a FIFO via `mkfifo(1)`."*

Está correto. O que o comentário não alcança é a consequência para o **gate**: se o caminho não pode virar FIFO no Windows, então a fixture que o gate monta para exercitar esse ca
issues.title: check-validate-parity: a fixture de FIFO não materializa no Windows, e o gate acusa o CLI por isso

issues.body:
## O buraco

A **Regra Dura de Paridade** exige que toda mudança de comportamento entre nos 3 CLIs. O gate que a sustenta, `scripts/check-cli-parity.sh`, compara **comandos de primeiro nível** — o `--help` da raiz. **Subcomando divergente passa em silêncio.**

Falsificado nas duas direções, em worktree isolado, com `req list` removido **só do Node**:

```
[defeito plantado]  cmd.command('list')  ->  cmd.command('list-REMOVIDO-PELA-SONDA')
                    'list' desaparece do `trackfw req --help` do Node

check-cli-parity.sh         exit 0   "CLI parity smoke checks passed"      <- CEGO
check-subcommand-parity.sh  exit 1   "✗ req: 'list' faltando no runtime node"

[controle, arvore intacta]
check-cli-parity.sh         exit 0
check-subcommand-parity.sh  exit 0   "Subcommand parity checks passed"
```

O controle importa tanto quanto o defeito: um gate que reprovasse sempre também "pegaria" o caso plantado.

## Superfície não coberta hoje

```
adr       3 subcomandos
req       4 subcomandos
roadmap   5 subcomandos
```

**12 subcomandos** cujo conjunto nenhum gate compara entre runtimes. E o `docs/cli-parity.md` tem a tabela de comandos de primeiro nível com `yes/yes/yes` por runtime, mas **nenhuma tabela equivalente para subcomando** — a checagem por linha de tabela `comando subcomando` devolve 1.

## Isto já mordeu, e não é hipótese

O comentário do nosso gate registra o que motivou escrevê-lo:

> *"`req move` faltou nos três e `req list` faltou no Python sem nenhum gate avisar."*

## O gate

issues.body:
Encontrado auditando critérios de aceite antigos do meu fork, verificando um AC que afirmava
*"o gate **falha** com o CRLF reintroduzido — não-vacuidade verificada, não assumida"*. Fui falsificar
e o AC estava errado.

## O gate

`scripts/check-python-writes-lf.sh` existe para garantir que o CLI Python nunca escreva com
`newline=None` — que no Windows traduz `\n` para CRLF. A linha que decide é:

```bash
if 'newline' in call: continue
```

**Ele verifica se o argumento existe. Não verifica o valor.**

## Medido — duas mutações no mesmo sítio

`pypi/trackfw/generators/adr.py:105`, `with open(filepath, 'w', encoding='utf-8', newline="\n")`:

| mutação | gate |
|---|---|
| **remover** `newline=` | `exit 1` ✅ pega |
| trocar para `newline="\r\n"` | **`exit 0`** 🔴 **não pega** |

O caso que o gate existe para impedir — arquivo saindo com CRLF — passa, desde que escrito
explicitamente.

## Tamanho da exposição

```
81 sitios com `newline=` em pypi/trackfw
79 deles com newline="\n"
```

Qualquer um dos 79 virando `"\r\n"` — por merge, por editor, por engano — não é acusado.

## Por que isto importa mais do que parece

O comentário do próprio gate diz por que ele nasceu:

> *"arquivo novo que vier de lá chega sem newline. Este gate pega no merge."*

Ele pega **a omissão**, que é o vetor do merge. Mas o AC que eu estava auditando afirmava cobertura
do **CRLF reintroduzido**, e a diferença entre as duas coisas nunca foi medida — foi assumida. É a
forma que a sua Regra Dura de Reconciliação nomeia, agora no lado do gate: *o artefato afirma mais do
que mediu*.

## O que não estou propondo

**Não** digo que a correção é comparar o valor com `"\n"`. Pode haver sítio legítimo com outro
`newline` — não varri isso. E há a escolha entre exigir `"\n"` literal ou proibir `"\r\n"`, que têm
alcances diferentes.

**Não há PR meu.** O gate é seu, byte a byte idêntico ao do upstream (`git diff HEAD upstream/main`
vazio nesse arquivo).

## Nota de método

🔴 Minha **primeira** falsificação nã

issues.body:
Complementa a recomendação 2 registrada no #337:

> *"Nenhum gate cruza a versão do CHANGELOG com os 5 sítios de bump — os testes atuais afirmam formato (`trackfw <semver>`), não valor."*

Medi em `upstream/main` `a3988d1`. O resultado **refina** a frase em vez de só confirmá-la: o cruzamento **existe**, mas tem um único ponto de execução, que é o momento da tag. Entre uma release e outra, a divergência atravessa tudo o que roda num PR.

## Onde o cruzamento existe

`trackfw release tag` é o único sítio que lê os cinco sítios e o CHANGELOG juntos:

- `internal/commands/release.go:104-108` — as 5 checagens: `version.go`, `npm/package.json`, `pypi/pyproject.toml` e as duas ocorrências em `pypi/trackfw/__init__.py`;
- `internal/commands/release.go:425-429` — pré-condição 4: `CHANGELOG.md` do commit-alvo tem a seção `## [<versão>] - YYYY-MM-DD`.

Então a divergência **é pega**, mas só quando alguém vai gerar a tag. A essa altura o bump já foi mesclado, e a correção vira outro PR.

## Onde ele não existe

| superfície | o que lê | por quê não pega |
|---|---|---|
| `trackfw validate` | — | nenhuma regra em `internal/validator` cita `CHANGELOG`, `package.json` ou `pyproject.toml` |
| `scripts/check-ci-workflow-pin-parity.sh:230` | só `internal/version/version.go` | por construção; o comentário em 225-228 declara que os outros sítios *"são mantidos em lockstep manualmente"* |
| testes de `release` nos 3 runtimes | mapa de arquivos em memória com `9.9.9` | `release_test.go:17,75-87`, `release.test.js:7,81`, `test_release.py:19,81` — nunca leem o repositório real |
| testes de versão (`version_test.go`, `version.test.js`) | a saída do CLI | afirmam `^trackfw [0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+$` e `version` ≡ `--version` — formato, não valor |

## Medição por efeito

Plantio em bytes, só a string de versão (guarda: exatamente as linhas planejadas mudaram), `CHANGELOG.md` intacto no topo em `7.6.0`. Controle e divergência no **mesmo** worktree, mesmo método, falhas comparadas **por nome**

O projeto tinha **duas fontes de verdade** para metadado de REQ, e cada comando escolhia uma:

roadmap: "" no frontmatter       27 REQs      ← o que o arquiteto media
"no linked Roadmap" no validate  57 REQs      ← o que o produto media
```

Vincular quatro REQs editando o frontmatter **não as tirou** da lista do `validate`. O mesmo mecanismo, no outro campo, é o **#306**: `req list` lia o `status:` do **corpo** e contradizia o `validate`.

## A causa raiz — mais sutil do que a hipótese

`validateREQsHaveRoadmap` usava `extractRefPath`, que **exige sufixo `.md`**. Efeito: 21 REQs com o frontmatter corretamente preenchido continuavam sendo acusadas de órfãs.

issues.body:
## O achado

`trackfw req list` **não lê o `status:` do frontmatter.** Ele extrai o status de uma linha do
**corpo** — `> Date: … | Status: <status>` —, e o resultado pode contradizer o frontmatter que o
`validate` usa.

Idêntico nos três runtimes, então **não é quebra de paridade**: é o contrato que está assim.

## Falsificação — duas fixtures de controle

Duas REQs criadas do zero, com o **mesmo** frontmatter e corpos diferentes:

```yaml
# controle A
---
name: REQ-2026-09-09-zz-a
status: Done
---
# REQ: A
```

```yaml
# controle B
---
name: REQ-2026-09-09-zz-b
status: Done
---
# REQ: B

> Date: 2026-09-09 | Status: WIP
```

Medido:

| runtime | controle A | controle B |
|---|---|---|
| Go | `unknown` | `WIP` |
| Node | `unknown` | `WIP` |
| Python | `unknown` | `WIP` |

**Os dois declaram `status: Done` no frontmatter.** A reporta `unknown`; B reporta `WIP`.

E o `validate` **não acusa** a contradição — passa com `✓ No violations found`.

## O caso pior: prosa do corpo virando status

No meu acervo, duas REQs rendem isto:

```
REQ-adr-wizard-e-list-2026-06-11.md      <status>` (regex ou strings.Split).
REQ-req-wizard-e-list-2026-06-11.md      <status>`.
```

A string vem de uma linha de **descrição** dentro do corpo, que por acaso descreve o próprio
extrator:

```
- **Status**: da linha `> Date: … | Status: <status>` (regex ou strings.Split).
```

Ou seja: o extrator se auto-capturou ao ler uma REQ que documenta o extrator. As duas declaram
`status: Done` no frontmatter.

## Denominador, para dimensionar sem exagerar

No meu acervo de **66 REQs**, a coluna do `req list` diverge do frontmatter em boa parte dos casos
antigos — o corpo daqueles arquivos usa `> Criado em: … | Status: WIP | Agente: Apolo`, escrito
quando o trabalho começou e nunca atualizado, enquanto o frontmatter foi mantido.

🔴 **Não estou afirmando um número para o seu acervo.** O meu tem 28 REQs herdadas do seu `docs/req/`
de junho, então a distribuição aqui não é representativa. O que afirmo é o

Dois testes em `internal/discover/discover_test.go` **morrem no setup** num Windows sem o privilégio de criar symlink, e a falha se apresenta como qualquer outra reprovação:

    discover_test.go:941: symlink C:\...\vitima.txt C:\...\.github\workflows\trackfw-validate.yml:

--- FAIL: TestWriteCIWorkflow_NeverWritesThroughDanglingSymlink (0.00s)
    discover_test.go:978: symlink C:\...\does-not-exist-yet C:\...\trackfw-validate.yml:
        A required privilege is not held by the client.
FAIL	github.com/kgsaran/trackfw/internal/discover	7.099s
```

O sítio:

```go
if err := os.Symlink(victim, workflowPath); err != nil {
    t.Fatal(err)
}
```

`os.Symlink` está no **arranjo**, não na asserção. Sem `SeCreateSymbolicLinkPrivilege` (Developer Mode desligado, processo não elevado) ele falha, e `t.Fatal` transforma "não consegui montar o cenário" em "o teste reprovou".

## O repositório já sabe que isso é dependente de privilégio — em outro arquivo

`internal/integrations/manager_test.go:217`, listado na [#279](https://github.com/kgsaran/trackfw/issues/279):

```
"symlink creation is privilege-dependent on Windows"
```

E `internal/generators/update_test.go:35`, da mesma lista:

```
"guarda de escrita atraves de symlink nao exercitada..."
```

**Os dois sítios do `discover_test.go` não têm guarda nenhuma.** A #279 mediu 9 skips de classe plataforma em 4 arquivos que a #269 não tocou; `internal/discover/discover_test.go` não está nem numa lista nem na outra — é um quinto arquivo, com dois sítios da mesma classe, e sem sequer o skip que os outros têm.

## Por que isto é da família da #274, num eixo novo

A #274 separou **suíte que não carregou** de **teste que reprovou**. Aqui há um terceiro estado que produz o mesmo observável:

```
o teste reprovou                        <- a conclusao que o FAIL publica
nao consegui montar o ce

## O defeito

`trackfw update harness` **reescrevia** o script do guard e reportava `updated=0`.

```
alvos cujo path é o script do guard:  ZERO
```

O script era escrito como **efeito colateral** do alvo de fiação, e a contagem só enxergava a fiação — que não mudou, e por isso saía `skipped`. **Não era contador que erra às vezes: era caminho escrito e nunca contabilizado.**

| estado | relatório | efeito real |
|---|---|---|
| desatualizado (macOS) | `updated=9 skipped=18` | conteúdo novo: 561 → 580 linhas |
| já em dia (macOS, ao vivo) | `updated=0 skipped=27` | **reescrito**: mesmo sha, mtime +160s |
| `--dry-run` (Windows, autor do issue) | `updated=0 skipped=33` | nada |

🔴 O `updated=9` veio de arquivos de **fiação**. O script mudou nos dois primeiros casos e **não foi contado em nenhum** — o número não é impreciso, **mede outra coisa**.

## A correção

Alvos próprios `git-branch-guard-script` e `credential-guard-script`, nos 3 CLIs. O `credential-guard` foi **medido** com o mesmo padrão, não presumido — mesma causa, mesmo ML.

**Verificado após a correção:**

```
já em dia     • git-branch-guard-script: skipped     mtime NÃO muda   ← idempotente
adulterado    ✓ git-branch-guard-script: updated     sha restaurado
```

🔴 **O critério que mais pesou não foi a contagem, foi o controle:** um alvo que conta certo e **para de escrever** seria **pior que o defeito** — a correção do guard da 7.5.0 deixaria de chegar às máquinas, **em silêncio**. Adulterei o arquivo e confirmei que o comando restaura.

## O que acontece

`scripts/check-gates-falsify.sh` aborta no Windows (Git Bash / MSYS2), antes de chegar às provas:

```
OK   [falsify/artifact-parity/req-content-drift]
cp: cannot create regular file '/tmp/trackfw-falsify.P7R5cS/s8-mod/bin/trackfw': File exists
```

A linha é a 543:

```bash
T8_MOD="$WORK/s8-mod"
cp -r "$ROOT_DIR/." "$T8_MOD"
```

Copia a **árvore inteira**, e com ela o `bin/` — que está no `.gitignore` (linha 1, `/bin/`; e `*.exe` na linha 3).

## Mecanismo, falsificado nas duas direções

O erro não é do `cp -r`. É especificamente o par `foo` / `foo.exe`: o fallback de `.exe` do MSYS faz o segundo parecer já existir depois que o primeiro é copiado.

Em fixture isolada, com arquivos de 1 byte:

| conteúdo do diretório copiado | exit |
|---|---|
| `trackfw` + `trackfw.exe` | **1** — `cannot create regular file … File exists` |
| só `trackfw` | 0 |
| `alpha` + `beta.exe` (sem colisão de nome) | 0 |

O terceiro caso é o controle que importa: dois arquivos, um deles `.exe`, **sem** compartilhar o nome-base — passa. O que quebra é a colisão, não a presença de um `.exe`.

Numa árvore Windows os dois convivem sem esforço: `make build` produz `bin/trackfw` (`go build -o $(BUILD_DIR)/$(BINARY)`), e um `go build ./cmd/trackfw` avulso produz `trackfw.exe`. O próprio `.gitignore` já reconhece que o par coexiste — as linhas 4–7 listam `trackfw-bin` **e** `trackfw-bin.exe` para npm e pypi.

## O defeito mais fundo não é a colisão

A colisão é só o sintoma que torna isto visível. O problema é a linha 543 copiar **conteúdo ignorado pelo git** para dentro da fixture: o resultado do gate passa a depender do que o desenvolvedor tem no `bin/`, que por construção o git não vê e o CI não reproduz.

Aqui `bin/` pesa **37 MB** — copiados a cada execução, para uma fixture que precisa de `cmd/`, `internal/` e `go.mod`, não do binário.

Um projeto por runtime, cada um inicializado pelo próprio — a mesma forma da fixture do Cenário 3 de `check-update-parity.sh`. `MINGW64_NT-10.0-26200`, binários da árvore em `fac76a0`:

| runtime | `\` na saída de `update --json` |
|---|---|
| Go | **0** |
| Node | **0** |
| Python | **16** |

issues.body:
Adotei a **v7.3.0** como base de um repositório consumidor e rodei os três CLIs, as três suítes e os gates num Windows 11 (Git Bash, Python 3.12, Node 22, console cp1252). Apareceram sete defeitos, todos com a mesma origem: **a 7.3.0 nunca foi exercitada em Windows**. Na CI Linux nenhum deles se manifesta.

Abro consolidado porque eles se encadeiam — corrigir um revela o próximo — e porque o mapa completo é mais útil que sete issues soltas. Todos foram corrigidos no meu fork e posso abrir PRs se você quiser, separados ou juntos.

Caminhos com meu usuário estão como `C:\Users\<user>`.

---

## 1. `pypi/trackfw/cli.py` — `UnicodeEncodeError` no console cp1252

`--help`, `status` e `validate` morrem antes de imprimir qualquer coisa:

```
UnicodeEncodeError: 'charmap' codec can't encode character '\u2192' in position 98
```

A descrição do parser tem `ADR → REQ → ROADMAP → kanban`. O console Windows padrão entrega cp1252, que não representa `→`. Go e Node escrevem bytes UTF-8 direto e não consultam codepage.

**Correção:** reconfigurar `sys.stdout`/`sys.stderr` para UTF-8 no topo de `main()`, com `newline="\n"` para não emitir CRLF onde os outros dois emitem LF. Guardado por `getattr(stream, "reconfigure", None)` — testes substituem stdout por objetos sem esse método.

---

## 2 e 6. Os três runtimes ignoram `$HOME` no Windows

`os.UserHomeDir()` (Go, **28 sites** em `internal/`), `os.homedir()` (Node, **25** em `npm/src`) e `os.path.expanduser` (Python) leem `%USERPROFILE%` no Windows.

```
node   os.homedir()      com HOME=/c/tmp/fake  ->  C:/Users/<user>
py     expanduser("~")   com HOME=/c/tmp/fake  ->  C:/Users/<user>
```

**Nenhum teste consegue isolar a home.** Os testes fazem `t.Setenv("HOME", t.TempDir())` — 97 call sites só no Go — e no Windows isso não isola nada. Uma execução de `go test ./...` nesta máquina escreveu **dentro da home real**: um ADR em `~/.trackfw/adr/`, o `integrations-manifest.json`, dois scripts de guard, e tocou os seis arquivos de config

issues.body:
`req_has_adr` e `req_has_roadmap` detectam marcador vazio comparando com **uma literal**, e a literal é exatamente o que o template emite. **Cinco de sete grafias naturais de "vazio" passam.**

Medido no **seu próprio acervo**: o gate acusa 11 REQs sem ADR. São **69**.

## O mecanismo

`internal/validator/validator.go`:

```go
func contentHasMarker(content string, markers []string) bool {
	for _, marker := range markers {
		if strings.Contains(content, marker) &&
			!strings.Contains(content, marker+" \n") &&
			!strings.Contains(content, marker+" \r\n") {
			return true
		}
	}
	return false
}
```

A vacuidade é reconhecida **só** como `marcador + exatamente um espaço + newline`. Qualquer outra grafia de vazio é lida como preenchida.

Plantei sete grafias e rodei o binário:

```
ADR:          (sem espaco)       PASSA   <- vazio nao detectado
ADR:          (um espaco)        reprova
ADR:          (dois espacos)     PASSA   <- vazio nao detectado
ADR:\t        (tab)              PASSA   <- vazio nao detectado
ADR:\r\n      (CRLF sem espaco)  PASSA   <- vazio nao detectado
ADR: \r\n     (CRLF um espaco)   reprova

`python3` aqui é o App Execution Alias da Microsoft Store — o default de quem instala pela Store. Corrige o #237. Um arquivo, 8 linhas.

## O que muda

`sys.stdout.reconfigure(encoding="utf-8", errors="replace", newline="\n")` no heredoc da linha 516 — o único ponto do script que imprime `evidence`/`failures` do barrier, que contêm os tokens de status do roadmap.

Esse `python3 -` não passa pelo `main()` do CLI, então não recebe o `_force_utf8_output`. Mesmo mecanismo do item 4, em outro script.

## Por que `newline="\n"` junto

Não é cosmético aqui. O bloco grava em `CORPUS_LINES_FILE`, que a **linha 542 hasheia** para o `corpus/non-reclassification`. Sem `newline` explícito o Python emitiria CRLF no Windows, e o hash mudaria por plataforma pelo mesmo motivo que a codificação mudaria:

```
mesma linha de evidence
  utf-8    d0f5dfc074b8697c  (82 bytes)
  cp1252   UnicodeEncodeError em '\u2b1c'
```

O crash era o sintoma barulhento; corrigir só o encoding deixaria o hash instável entre sistemas — falha silenciosa.

## Medição

Windows real, Git Bash:

```
antes    10 checks OK, morria no 11º
depois   45 checks OK, 0 UnicodeEncodeError
```

Deixei fora de propósito: não quis misturar uma correção verificada com um diagnóstico que ainda não fiz.

Fixes #237

agent_prs.title: fix(probe): run.ps1 nao roda no Windows PowerShell 5.1, e o item 2 emite REPRODUCED sem medir

issues.body:
A sonda da camada 2 (`scripts/windows-repro/run.ps1`, do #221/#226) **não executa no shell padrão do Windows**. São três defeitos independentes, e o segundo produz **falso positivo** — o pior modo de falha para um instrumento de medição.

Todos têm a mesma forma: o script só funciona no ambiente onde foi escrito. Os 10 steps do `windows-probe.yml` usam `shell: pwsh` — PowerShell 7 — que lê UTF-8 sem BOM, tem `ArgumentList` e roda com `RUNNER_TEMP` definido. Os três defeitos são invisíveis lá e certos fora de lá.

Medido em `Windows PowerShell 5.1.26100.9278`, `PSEdition=Desktop`, `CLR 4.0.30319`, numa máquina Windows real.

---

## 1 — Sem BOM, o arquivo não parseia

`run.ps1` é UTF-8 sem BOM e contém 30 em-dashes. O Windows PowerShell 5.1 lê `.ps1` sem BOM como **ANSI (cp1252)**:

```
UTF-8 do em-dash:  e2 80 94
lido como cp1252:  U+00E2  U+20AC  U+201D
                                    ^ aspa dupla tipográfica
```

O tokenizador trata `U+201D` como delimitador de string. A string fecha no meio e o parse morre **antes da primeira linha executar**:

```
+ $x = "traco ─?" aqui"
+                 ~~~~~
Token 'aqui"' inesperado na expressão ou instrução.
```

Provado por execução, arquivo mínimo com um em-dash:

```
sem BOM : <nada — ParserError>
com BOM : ok: traco — aqui
```

## 2 — `RUNNER_TEMP`, e este mente

`$env:RUNNER_TEMP` só existe dentro do GitHub Actions. Fora dele é `$null` — e no PowerShell 5.1:

```powershell
Join-Path $null "item2-fake-HOME"   ->   []      # string vazia, SEM erro
```

O item 2 então compara a saída dos 3 runtimes contra `""`. Como nunca são iguais:

```powershell
$item2Verdict = if ($goIgnoresHome -or $nodeIgnoresHome -or $pyIgnoresHome) { "REPRODUCED" } else { "ABSENT" }
```

**REPRODUCED incondicional** — inclusive numa árvore onde o defeito já esteja corrigido. Medido: com `RUNNER_TEMP` ausente, o item 2 emite `REPRODUCED` com o detalhe todo em branco:

```
HOME= (deliberadamente diferente)
Go   os.UserHomeDir()      ->
Node os.ho

## Summary

Writing the docs in #192 against the code surfaced places where websec reported success it had not earned. This PR fixes them, pins each with tests that fail on the previous code, and aligns the docs. It is the content of **0.22.0**: [migration notes](docs/MIGRATING-0.22.0.md).

### Fail-open / false-negative
- **`run <subdir> --diff` and `gate <subdir>` passed every finding.** Git paths are relative to the repo root, but findings are relative to the target. Both now scope correctly from any subdirectory.
- **`security/` was never scanned** while the run reported complete. It had been on the skip list since the initial commit. Only websec's own output directories are skipped now, detected by their contents. Source inside the remaining build-output directories is reported as a `skipped_directory_code` gap.
- **`--only <dir>` matched nothing.** A directory now selects every file under it, on path-component boundaries. An entry that selects nothing becomes a `scope_missed` gap, and the run prints **REQUESTED SCOPE NOT ANALYZED**.
- **An explicit `--graph <missing>` was silently ignored.** It is now an execution gap. Graphs get their own 64 MiB read cap; real graphify graphs exceed the 2 MB source cap.
- **A failing OWASP Noir read as absent.** The run now reports the failure (`routes.noir` plus a `route_engine` gap), and `doctor` has a route-engine section.

### Exit-code contract (0 clean · 1 findings · 2 usage · 3 incomplete)
- Usage errors exit `2`, not `1`. This covers a bad target, `dynamic`/`calibrate` argument errors, and malformed JSON inputs.
- `dynamic` gates on dynamic evidence only, and a confirmed leak wins over an incomplete run.
- `calibrate` that measured nothing exits `3`.
- `attest` never projects a partial run.
- `gate` outside a git repo without `--only` exits `3`.

### Suppression and misc
- **`.websec-ignore` path patterns** now match path components. During the transition, findings matched only by the old substring rule stay suppresse

issues.body:
## Summary
`websec init` proposes `tests/` as a scope glob ("test code (6 files)"). The generated file's own header recommends `fingerprint:` acknowledgements over path globs because a glob hides future findings too. For secrets in particular, a `tests/` glob would hide a real credential committed to a test later.

## Suggestion
When the only findings under a test directory are test-fixture secrets (already downgraded to LOW by hygiene), propose fingerprint acknowledgements for those specific findings (with a placeholder reason and expiry) instead of the directory glob — or at least add a comment on the proposed glob warning that it also suppresses future secrets.

Field note: on a small Node app this produced the better outcome when done by hand (each fixture password acknowledged by fingerprint with an expiry; a new secret in `tests/` still gates).
issues.title: websec init: propose fingerprint acks for test-fixture secrets instead of a tests/ glob

## Summary
Semgrep `PartialParsing` on valid bash marks the whole Semgrep scanner as `error`, so the run is incomplete.

## Repro (0.21.1, Semgrep 1.177.0)
Two valid scripts (`bash -n` passes):
- `TO=${1:?usage: ./send.sh +E164 [approved|session]}` → "Syntax error … `|` was unexpected"
- a heredoc containing JSON (`cat > out/body.json <<J … J`)

`coverage.json` → `{"kind": "scanner", "detail": "semgrep: error"}`.

## Suggested fix
Treat `PartialParsing` / per-file syntax errors as a per-file limitation listed in coverage (the file was partially analysed), not a scanner-level execution error, as long as Semgrep itself exited normally. Related in spirit to #139 (errors hiding coverage), but here the error over-states the failure.
issues.title: Semgrep PartialParsing on valid bash marks the scanner as error (incomplete run)

issues.body:
## Summary
On a hand-rolled Node `http` router, `websec emit-context` states the auth scheme as a fact ("auth: jwt (bearer)") although the app has no JWT, and reports "1 route". The SessionStart block then primes every agent session with a wrong auth model. The briefing does warn that route discovery is incomplete, but the emit-context block does not carry that caveat.

## Repro (0.21.1)
App: `server.mjs` dispatches with `if (path === '…' && req.method === '…')`; auth is an HMAC request signature (`X-Hub-Signature-256`), signed one-time tokens and `HttpOnly` cookie sessions; one route uses `Authorization: Bearer <api key>` (not a JWT).
`websec emit-context .` → `Attack surface: 1 route(s) · auth: jwt (bearer)`.

## Expected
When route coverage is flagged incomplete (`surface-coverage` warning), emit-context should say so in the block, and mark the auth scheme as a low-confidence guess (or omit it). A bearer header alone should not imply JWT.
issues.title: emit-context states a guessed auth scheme (jwt) as fact on a hand-rolled router

## Summary
The `surface` source-flow extractor hits `LimitReached` ("JS assignment expression budget exceeded") on an ordinary 460-line ES module, and the run is marked incomplete (`coverage.gaps`: `{"kind": "extractor", "detail": "surface", "execution": true}`). Every gated run then exits 3.

## Repro (0.21.1)
Zero-dependency Node.js app; `lib/acme.mjs` is ~460 lines of plain functions (DynamoDB access, validation). `FACTS.json` → `surface.assigned_flow.errors: [{"file": "lib/acme.mjs", "kind": "LimitReached", "detail": "JS assignment expression budget exceeded"}]`; `sql_flow` has no errors.

## Expected
Either the budget fits a file of this size, or the overrun is reported as a per-file limitation that does not fail completeness when every other file completed.

## Suggested fix
- Make the budget configurable (CLI flag or config file), and/or
- Degrade a per-file `LimitReached` to a visible limitation for that file instead of an extractor-level execution gap.
issues.title: surface extractor LimitReached on a ~460-line JS module fails completeness for the whole run

- **An explicit `--graph <missing>` was silently ignored.** It is now an execution gap. Graphs get their own 64 MiB read cap; real graphify graphs exceed the 2 MB source cap.
- **A failing OWASP Noir read as absent.** The run now reports the failure (`routes.noir` plus a `route_engine` gap), and `doctor` has a route-engine section.

### Exit-code contract (0 clean · 1 findings · 2 usage · 3 incomplete)
- Usage errors exit `2`, not `1`. This covers a bad target, `dynamic`/`calibrate` argument errors, and malformed JSON inputs.
- `dynamic` gates on dynamic evidence only, and a confirmed leak wins over an incomplete run.
- `calibrate` that measured nothing exits `3`.
- `attest` never projects a partial run.
- `gate` outside a git repo without `--only` exits `3`.

### Suppression and misc
- **`.websec-ignore` path patterns** now match path components. During the transition, findings matched only by the old substring rule stay suppresse

issues.body:
## Summary
`--exclude` does not reach Checkov's own traversal. Findings under excluded paths are post-filtered, but Checkov **parsing errors** on excluded files still set the scanner outcome to `error`, which lands in `coverage.gaps` and makes every gated run exit 3 (incomplete).

## Repro (websec-validator 0.21.1, Checkov 3.3.19)
1. A repo with a gitignored `out/` folder holding two arbitrary JSON files (API response dumps).
2. `websec run . --scan --exclude out --fail-on high`
3. `coverage.json` → `{"kind": "scanner", "detail": "checkov: error", "execution": true}`; `scanners/checkov.json` → `terraform_plan` `parsing_errors: [".../out/connector.json", ".../out/ctpl.json"]`.

Same result with `--exclude 'out/**'`, and with `out/` listed in `.websec-ignore`.

## Cause
`scanners.py` `_checkov()` builds `checkov -d <target> --compact -o json …` with no path exclusion; the `_matches_excludes` post-filter only drops findings, not parsing errors.

## Suggested fix
- Pass `--skip-path <exclude>` for each `--exclude` / scope entry (Checkov supports it).
- When deciding the Checkov outcome, ignore `parsing_errors` whose path matches an exclude.

## Impact
Any repo with excluded non-IaC JSON can never get a complete gated run, so `--require-complete` / `--fail-on` exit 3 forever.
issues.title: --exclude does not reach Checkov: parsing errors on excluded files make every gated run incomplete

Closes #101.

Two false negatives in the `command-injection` sink, both silent.

**1. `os.popen` was missing** from the alternation while `os.system` was present. `subprocess.Popen` does not cover it — that alternative requires the literal `subprocess.` prefix. Added, with `subprocess.getoutput`/`getstatusoutput` (same always-shell class).

**2. The `shell=False` guard is file-level**, so one safe `subprocess.run(argv, shell=False)` anywhere in a module suppressed the whole file's finding — including a tainted `os.popen`/`os.system`. Those take a command *string*, have no argv form, and cannot be made safe by any keyword argument. The guard now stands down when an always-shell sink is present.

Without (2), (1) is inert in any realistic module mixing a safe call with a dangerous one.

    return subprocess.run(["ls", "-la"], shell=False, capture_output=True).stdout

@app.route("/ping")
def ping():
    return os.popen("ping -c1 " + request.args.get("host")).read()
```

issues.body:
Surfaced while triaging the bot-PR backlog. PR #84 *claimed* this fix in its changelog but its diff contained no source change, so the finding would have been discarded with the rest of the duplicate cluster. Recording it here so it is not lost.

## The gap

`SINKS["command-injection"]` in `src/websec_validator/extractors/surface.py:49` matches `os.system` and `subprocess.{run,call,check_output,Popen}` but **not `os.popen`**, which is equally injectable.

## Reproduction

```python
@app.route("/ping")
def ping():
    host = request.args.get("host")
    return os.popen("ping -c1 " + host).read()   # NOT detected

@app.route("/ping2")
def ping2():
    host = request.args.get("host")
    return os.system("ping -c1 " + host)         # detected
```

```
NO MATCH  return os.popen("ping -c1 " + host).read()
MATCH     return os.system("ping -c1 " + host)
```

Note `subprocess.Popen` does not cover it — that alternative requires the literal `subprocess.` prefix.

## Why it matters

A missed sink is the worst failure mode for this tool; the precision work so far has deliberately been about down-tiering noisy signals, never about removing coverage. This is the opposite direction — pure false negative.

## Fix sketch

Add `os\.popen` to the alternation. Worth auditing the same list for other stdlib exec paths (`commands.getoutput`, `popen2`, `subprocess.getoutput`) at the same time, and adding a `tests/test_pentest_regressions.py` case per sink added — the test-count floor in CI will then hold that coverage in place.

Related: #73 proposed a `surface.py` change for this but bundled a 30MB `.deb` and 13 scratch `test_repro*.py` files, so it is held.
issues.title: command-injection sink regex misses os.popen (false negative)

The reflective layer synthesizes the expressions an action-body statement writes at its own slots as elements the statement owns: an assignment's target and value, a loop's conditions, a `for` loop's collection, an `if` condition, the target of a `perform` or `terminate`. ## What and why

`\r` in a string literal or an unrestricted name (`"a\rb"`, `'a\rb'`) was accepted and decoded silently, although it is an escape only the pilot's grammar admits. It is still accepted and still read as U+000D, and each spelling is now reported as `nonstandard-notation` on the two-character escape: a warning by default, an error under `-strict` through that code's existing escalation in `NonstandardNotationPass`.

### Model and observed behaviour

```sysml
package P {
    part def Pt;
    part 'cr\rx' : Pt;
    attribute s = "a\rb";
}
```

The model checks clean, under `-validate -strict` too: `\r` is accepted in an unrestricted name and in a string literal with no diagnostic, and is read as a carriage return (U+000D).

### What the specification requires

KerML 1.1 Beta 2 §8.2.2.3, Note 2: "Table 4 shows the meaning of the allowed escape sequences." Table 4 (Escape Sequences) lists seven:

| Escape Sequence | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `\'` | Single Quote |
| `\"` | Double Quote |
| `\b` | Backspace |
| `\f` | Form Feed |
| `\t` | Tab |
| `\n` | Line Terminator |
| `\\` | Backslash |

`\r` is not among them. §8.2.2.5 gives `STRING_VALUE` the same `ESCAPE_SEQUENCE` ("ESCAPE_SEQUENCE is specified in 8.2.2.3"), so the same holds for string literals.

### Reference implementation

The pilot's grammar admits `\r` in both terminals (`KerMLExpressions.xtext`, pilot 2026-09):

```
terminal UNRESTRICTED_NAME returns Ecore::EString:
	'\'' ('\\' ('b' | 't' | 'n' | 'f' | 'r' | '"' | "'" | '\\') | !('\\' | '\''))* '\'';

terminal STRING_VALUE returns Ecore::EString:
	'"' ('\\' ('b' | 't' | 'n' | 'f' | 'r' | '"' | "'" | '\\') | !('\\' | '"'))* '"';
```

and its exporter gives `declaredName` `cr` + U+000D + `x` for the name above. `source.IsEscapeChar` follows that grammar.

### Proposed

Keep accepting and decoding `\r`, so what the pilot accepts still parses, and report it through the existing `nonstandard-notation` warning (`internal/check/passes/nonstandard_notation.go`) — in an unrestricted name and in a string literal alike, with the strict-conformance escalation that warning already has. issues.body:
When the Pilot's examples are parsed as one model (195 files), GetElementProperties answers no element of the model if any one document:

- has an error diagnostic, for example `Dynamics.sysml` ("cannot bind a value of dimension L^4·M^2·T^-5 to a feature typed by AccelerationValue"), or
- declares a top-level name that another document also declares. The Pilot's training material has four such pairs, e.g. `training/17. Control/Camera.sysml` and `examples/Camera Example/Camera.sysml`.

The answer for every element is then the same message, for example:

> cannot convert the declaration of Camera at …/training/17. Control/Camera.sysml:1:1: its id lands on the same IRI as Camera at …/examples/Camera Example/Camera.sysml:1:1, which another document declares, and merging two elements into one subject would be a different model

The reason given for the duplicate case makes sense. What makes it hard to use is the scope: one document affects the whole model. For a workspace of many files (an editor, a CI check over a repository), being able to read the elements of the other documents would help a lot. That could mean keeping the affected document out of the element form, or answering its elements with the error while the rest stay readable.

For reference, these documents are the ones OpenSysML reports errors in. The Pilot reports no error for any of them:

- `examples/Analysis Examples/Dynamics.sysml`: the dimension check above
- `examples/Simple Tests/PartTest.sysml`: "p1 participates in a specialization cycle"
- both Annex A vehicle files: `vehicle_b` is hidden by two imports that bring distinct elements of that name
- our `C30-accept.sysml`: a syntax error on `entry … then …`

Each of these may be worth a look on its own. We're happy to open separate issues if that's more convenient.

Found while building the census in #2028. In the census, such documents are left out for OpenSysML and listed under "Corpora".

## What and why

Fixes #2343.

The runtime computes coordinate frames and coordinate transformations, but the wire `Value` had no arm for either, so a posed part's `coordinateFrame` or a frame's `transformation` reached every consumer as an unsupported null.

`Value` gains two output-only arms, `coordinate_frame = 24` and `coordinate_transformation = 25`:

- **`CoordinateFrame`**: name, declaring usage, type, object, `dimensions`, one `MeasurementRef` per axis, the scale of a measurement scale (unit and `QuantityValueMapping`), and the transformation that places it.

- The arms are gated by the new `coordinate_frame_values` capability; a service without it answers the unsupported null as before.

## Summary

The engine evaluates coordinate frames and transformations
(`instance_coordinate_frames`), but the wire `Value` oneof has no arm for them.
`internal/frontend/protoconv` answers `ValCoordinateFrame`/
`ValCoordinateTransformation` with `UnsupportedShown`, so an inspector reports

the engine's internal types:

  repeated double matrix; … }` — the transform between two frames.

## Summary

The service has a `RunSweep` RPC that answers a table of run rows for a parameter
sweep. Every other client wraps it. `client/opensysml` has no `RunSweep` method at
all; a caller can only reach a sweep indirectly through `RecordRun`.

`docs/reference/client-parity.md` contradicts itself: "Every client exposes all 31
RPCs ... as typed calls", while the Open gaps table says "the package has no typed
`RunSweep` wrapper at all" (estimate about one day).

## Service contract (already implemented)

`api/proto/sysml.proto`:

`RunSweepRequest`: `model_hash`, `symbol_id` (FQN of an analysis case or calc,
definition or usage), `subject_symbol_id`, positional `arguments`, named
`named_arguments`, `ranges` (`SweepRange`: `parameter`, `start`, `end`, `step`),
`samples` (draw uniformly; 0 steps; above 0 needs a seed and refuses a range with
a step), `seed`, `engine`.

`RunSweepResponse`: `rows` (`SweepRow`: `inputs`, `outputs`, `verdicts`,
`elapsed_micros`, `error`, `failure_reason`, `evaluations`), `parameters`,
`sampled`, `seed`, `error`, `diagnostics`, `failure_reason`, `instances`,
`engine`, `strength`, `bounds`.

The handler is `internal/frontend/grpc/sweep.go:29`; it requires
**`CapabilityVerification`** (not `runs`), and already checks `ctx.Err()` per
table at `:143`. A pre-run failure is a 200 with `RunSweepResponse.error` +

- `client/opensysml/client.go` `Client`: `RunAction`/`RunMonteCarlo` (`RunRuns`)

- `client/opensysml/runs.go:284` — `runRowsFromProto` already decodes

Fixes #2198.

## What and why

`GetElementProperties` (`element_properties` in the clients) and the `api-json` element form answered `Feature::type` with a feature's written typing alone when the feature also subsets or redefines a typed feature:

```sysml
part def Owner {
    part q : T;
    part pBoth : V :> q;   // type was [V]; the Symbol API and the pilot answer [V, T]
}
```

Two causes, both below the surfaces:

- **`internal/semantic/metamodel` (`featureTypeConforms`)**: `deriveFeatureType` collects the own and the inherited typings and then drops the ones another candidate already specializes. That redundancy check could only answer for two source symbols, so on the graph-backed Structure it reported "unknown" and the rule fell back to the stated typing. It now walks the Structure's own specializations where an element has no symbol, and still uses `semantics.Model.Conforms` where both do.

No compliance row moves.

OpenSysML `develop` at `a159469093`, `bin/sysml-grpc` from `make build-grpc`, Python client from `client/python` of the same commit.

### Description

Go to Definition on an imported part definition behaves differently in a SysML notebook cell and a `.sysml` file containing the same model text. The notebook navigates to the enclosing package declaration in the imported file rather than to the part definition.

### Steps to reproduce

1. In a workspace, create a SysML file declaring a package containing a part definition.
2. In a SysML notebook cell, import the package with a wildcard and declare a part definition that specializes the imported part.
3. Invoke Go to Definition on the imported part name in the notebook cell.
4. Repeat on the same reference in an equivalent `.sysml` file.

### Expected

Both requests navigate to the imported part definition.

### Actual

The notebook request returns the imported file URI with a zero-length range on the package declaration (zero-based line 0). The equivalent `.sysml` request returns the range of the part definition (zero-based line 83). Hover identifies the referenced part definition in both cases. The traces show that the incorrect notebook location is returned in the `textDocument/definition` response.

- VS Code with Jupyter, connected to Ubuntu via WSL
- OpenSysML extension: `0.12.2-nightly-20261109-ddc5b7a632`
- Language server version: v0.12.1

The notebook also has a `%load` command for the imported file; its model cell separately contains the import. The issue was observed on the existing workspace model; it has not been independently reproduced with a minimal model.

`require b.closes;` on `subject b : Budget`, where `Budget` declares `assert constraint closes : Closes { in capability = allotment; in demand = estimate; }`, could not be evaluated: `sysml -satisfy` reported `operator '*' is not defined for a sequence and a Rational` instead of a verdict.

## What and why

### Problem

`GetSymbol` and `GetElementProperties` take one string that is "a qualified name or an element id". Generated ids (`Col__V__c_pend0` for an unnamed connector end, `Owner::@3` for an unnamed member) are legal declared names too, so a declaration could shadow the element an id was reported for: an id taken from `childIds` or `members` did not always resolve to the element it described, and clients could not join the Symbol API, `GetElementProperties` and the api-json/RDF export by id.

### Change

Generated ids keep their spelling. The request says which kind of string it carries, mirroring the SysML v2 API's separation of `@id` from `qualifiedName`:

```proto
enum LookupKind {
  LOOKUP_KIND_UNSPECIFIED = 0;     // legacy: qualified name first, then id
  LOOKUP_KIND_QUALIFIED_NAME = 1;  // a name resolves only as a name
  LOOKUP_KIND_ELEMENT_ID = 2;      // an id resolves only as an id
}
```

The model checks clean, and the element declared `''` is treated as unnamed:

|---|---|---|

So an empty name can be written by the encoder but is not read back by any reader of name text.

This predates #2214 / #2241, which changed what the characters between the quotes denote but not the handling of there being none.

KerML 1.1 Beta 2 §8.2.2.3: `UNRESTRICTED_NAME = single_quote ( NAME_CHARACTER | ESCAPE_SEQUENCE )* single_quote` — the repetition admits no characters at all, and Note 1 makes the represented name "the characters within the single quotes", here the empty string. ### To decide

1. Is `''` a declared name (the empty string) or the absence of one? The pilot says the former.
2. If it is a name: `declaredName` becomes `""`, the element gets a qualified name and a name-derived id, and the name-text readers accept `''`.
3. If it is not: say so where the parser drops it, and consider a diagnostic, since the notation was written.

## What and why

Fixes #2243.

Every run of `go run -C tools ./cmd/hideo-suite` printed Python tracebacks from the suite's own `mdk_version.py` (once per reader) and `report.py`, whether the baseline reproduced or not, which buried the ratchet's verdict in the daily `oracle-reproduction.yml` log. Both scripts belong to the stage `run-all.sh` runs after the readers: it records each MDK's version and tabulates the suite's cross-MDK report, and it needs a `SysMLv2-Pilot-Implementation` checkout beside the suite. That report is not the ratchet's verdict, and the ratchet deliberately needs neither the pilot nor Java.

`tools/referee/hideo` now runs the four readers itself instead of calling `run-all.sh`:

## What and why

`TestFormattingDiffIsCheaperThanFormatting` compared two wall-clock measurements, so the same tree could pass or fail with the runner's load. The property it protected — computing the LSP formatting edits must not dominate the formatter's own pass — was also not true at scale: `formatEdits` ran `model.DiffLines`, a shortest-edit-script search whose cost grows with the square of the lines that differ. On the largest standard-library file with every line changed the search took about 0.6 of the formatter's time; on eight copies of it, 1.4 times.

The formatter only changes whitespace, splits lines and adjusts blank runs, so once `regroupLines` has joined the split lines, the non-blank lines pair off in order and only the blank runs between them can differ in length. `formatEdits` now uses that:

- `regroupLines` reports whether the lines paired off.
- When they did, `blankRunHunks` produces the hunks in one pass over both line lists. A shortened run is one hunk over the whole run (so any selected line of it may be the one dropped, as the widening step did before); a lengthened run is an insertion after it.
- Otherwise `searchHunks` runs the search as before, widening included.

The timing test is replaced by `TestFormattingDiffIsOnePassOverTheDocument`: on the largest library file, for both `keepLineBreaks` settings, the lines pair off, the search is never called, the edit count is bounded by the lines plus blank-run hunks, and the edits reproduce the formatter's output. The corpus sweep (`checkFormattingEdits`) asserts zero searches for every fixture as well. The ratio is reported, not asserted, by `BenchmarkFormattingEdits` in `tests/perf` (`diff/format` metric, at one and eight copies of the file).

### What happened, and what you expected instead

`TestFormattingDiffIsCheaperThanFormatting` (`internal/frontend/lsp/formatting_test.go`) failed the `Go tests (rest grpc)` job of a pull-request run on a change that touches neither `internal/frontend/lsp` nor `internal/syntax/format`:

```
formatting_test.go:546: 150364 bytes: format 3.080798ms, diff 4.758803ms
formatting_test.go:548: diff took 4.758803ms, formatter 3.080798ms; the diff must not dominate
--- FAIL: TestFormattingDiffIsCheaperThanFormatting (0.39s)
```

The test formats the largest standard-library file and asserts `diffTime <= formatTime`, each being the best wall-clock time of 20 rounds. A unit test should give the same verdict for the same tree; this one compares two wall-clock measurements of a few milliseconds each, and on the pull-request tier (no `-race`) the two are close enough that runner noise decides the outcome.

Figures the test logged on recent runs of the `PR` workflow:

| Run | Tier | format | diff | diff below format by | Verdict |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 43558193796 | pull request | 3.08 ms | 4.76 ms | (diff 54% above) | **fail** |
| 43543663647 | pull request | 3.70 ms | 3.60 ms | 3% | pass |
| 43486038945 | pull request | 2.72 ms | 2.57 ms | 6% | pass |
| 43554860783 | pull request | 3.43 ms | 3.18 ms | 7% | pass |
| 43552161684 | pull request | 4.79 ms | 4.19 ms | 13% | pass |
| 43545839203 | pull request | 2.77 ms | 2.17 ms | 22% | pass |
| 43547363573 | merge queue (`-race`) | 58.21 ms | 15.96 ms | 73% | pass |
| 43550372755 | merge queue (`-race`) | 87.76 ms | 28.61 ms | 67% | pass |

So on the pull-request tier the assertion holds by 3–22% in the passing samples. Under `-race` the margin is wide, but only because the race detector slows the formatter far more than the diff, so that tier does not measure the property either. The test already skips the comparison under coverage instrumentation for the same reason (the two packages are instrumented differently).

## What and why

`GetSymbol` now exposes the two ends of a connection, interface or binding usage as child symbols of kind `connectorEnd`, each carrying the feature or feature chain it references. The ends are the ones the semantic model already holds (`Model.OwnedConnectorEnds`, the same symbols `GetElementProperties` reflects as `connectorEnd` → `ownedReferenceSubsetting` → `referencedFeature`); nothing is minted for the Symbol API.

## What and why

Fixes #2202.

A symbol's members left out every unnamed member inherited from the standard library, and reported a binding connector under a kind (`bindingUsage`) that names no metaclass, so a caller selecting members by metaclass could not find `bind a = b;`.

## What and why

Fixes #1532

The DOT form wrote a typing edge as `arrowhead=onormaldotdot`. Graphviz chains the shapes of an arrowhead along the edge, so that is a hollow triangle followed by two full-size dots in a row behind it. The notation's `definition` figure sets two small dots beside the line, one each side, just behind the triangle's base. Those are the two discrepancies the reporter still saw on v0.12.0: dot placement and dot size.

No arrowhead, and no other DOT attribute, sets a shape beside an edge relative to its direction: `headlabel` is one text per end and typing edges already use it, and a second invisible edge carrying the other dot is routed apart from the first or bends it. So the dots are drawn after layout:

- `internal/ir/view/dot.go` writes a typing edge as `arrowhead=empty, class=definition`. Graphviz copies the class to the edge's SVG group.
- `view.DrawDOTGlyphs` (new, `internal/ir/view/dot_glyph.go`) reads a Graphviz SVG, finds the triangle of each `edge definition` group and adds two circles placed from that triangle: centres 0.43 of its length behind the base and 0.36 off the line, radius 0.17, in the edge's colour and opacity. Those are the proportions of the standard's `definition.svg` (triangle 11 long, dots of radius 1.86 centred 4.74 behind the base and 4 off the line). The tip is found as the corner opposite the shortest side, so it holds for any edge direction, `arrowsize`, and for `dot`, `neato -n` and `neato -n2` drawings.
- `internal/doc/docpdf/graphviz.go` applies it to every SVG it has Graphviz draw. That one drawer serves the Jupyter kernel's `%viz` and `%render`, `%render-document` at the prompt, `sysml -render-document` (HTML, Markdown, PDF) and the language server.

Reporter's model, `%viz A::APart A::APort A::part1 A::part2`, drawn by Graphviz 16.1:

## Problem

OpenSysML has no per-element client API shaped like the KerML/SysML abstract syntax.
A client that wants `inheritedFeature`, `connectorEnd`, `relatedFeature`, `directedFeature`,
`portDefinition`, `payloadType`, `subjectParameter`, `entryAction`, `isComposite`, the
`FeatureValue` behind a feature, the operands of an expression, … has three routes and none
of them answers per element over gRPC:

- `GetSymbol` (`SymbolInfo`) is a curated surface: id, name, kind, metadata map, owned
  `child_ids`, `attributes`, type/multiplicity/specializations and, since #1974, `members`.
  Each metamodel property it lacks is a new field, a new proto message and four client
  bindings (#1974, #1978, #1979, #1981, #1983, #1992, #1993, #1994 each add one or two).
- `Query` admits exactly the 22 queryable properties of the SysML v2 API & Services
  projection (`internal/semantic/query` `PropertyNames`): `@id`, `@type`, `body`,
  `declaredName`, `declaredShortName`, `documentation`, `elementId`, `general`, `isAbstract`,
  `isIndividual`, `language`, `locale`, `multiplicityLower`, `multiplicityUpper`, `name`,
  `owner`, `qualifiedName`, `satisfiedRequirement`, `satisfyingFeature`, `shortName`,
  `textualRepresentation`, `type`. Anything else is `INVALID_ARGUMENT: unknown query property`.
- `Convert` to `api-json` exports the whole model as API element JSON with the derived
  properties completed, but that is a model-level export, not an element read.

> This is a feature request. The issue form points feature requests to Discussions, but
> Discussions are not enabled on this repository, so it is filed as an issue.

### What happened, and what you expected instead

```sysml
part def Car {
    part engine : Engine;          // composite (owned) part
    ref part driver : Person;      // reference part
}
```

Whether a part is owned or only referenced is central to walking a structure: a bill of
materials, a mass roll-up, or a containment tree has to include `engine` and skip `driver`. From
Python the two are indistinguishable:

| Route | `engine` | `driver` |
|---|---|---|
| `Symbol.kind` | `partUsage` | `partUsage` |
| `Symbol.metadata` | `{type, visibility}` | `{type, visibility}` |
| `Symbol.facts()` | no composite/reference field | same |
| `Car.parts()` | listed | listed |
| `model.query(select=["isComposite"])` | `InvalidRequestError: unknown query property "isComposite"` (`isAbstract` and `isIndividual` are queryable) | same |
| reflection `isComposite` / `isReference` | `True` / `False` ✔ | `False` / `True` ✔ |
| api-json `isComposite` | `true` ✔ | `false` ✔ |

## What and why

Closes #2092.

Hovering an element showed a previous element's `doc` instead of its own, across closing braces and into the standard library (hovering `Anything` showed the `Base` package's doc). Two defects, one behind the other:

1. **Parser.** The `/* ... */` body of a `doc`, `comment` or `rep` was recorded as pending leading trivia in `Parser.fill` and stayed there after `takePendingComment` handed it to the annotation as its body, so the next declaration parsed, at any nesting depth, received it as its `LeadingTrivia`. `takePendingComment` now drops the consumed body from the pending trivia (`dropPendingTrivia`). The checkpoint/restore path (`trivLog`) needs no change: a restore replays the trivia and the pending-comment state together, and the re-parse consumes and drops the body again (covered by `TestAnnotationBodyStaysOutOfTriviaAcrossBacktracking`).
2. **Language server.** Hover (declaration and reference paths), completion item documentation and, through the shared hover, the MCP `hover` tool read only `LeadingTrivia`. They now read the element's owned `doc` bodies, in declaration order, through the new `Workspace.DocumentationOf`, a locked wrapper over `semantics.Model.DocumentationOf` (the `Element::documentation` reader the model already uses), followed by the `//` and `//* ... */` notes written directly above the declaration.

Per the maintainer's decision on the issue, a bare `/* ... */` above a declaration is an anonymous `Comment` owned by, and about, the enclosing namespace: it is no longer shown as the following declaration's hover or completion documentation. It remains leading trivia, so `%print` still writes it out before the declaration.

Other readers of `LeadingTrivia`: the REPL's `%print` (`declarationSpan`) only needed the parser fix (it started its output at the leaked body); `astcodec` and the symbol snapshot serialize whatever the parser attached and need no change.

## What and why

Closes #2067.

An exploration reports one witness per outcome, and outcome identity observes only the subject machine, so when two linearizations differ only inside a nested machine (`sys.m.run` through `viaA` or through `viaB`) they collapse into one outcome and the run through `viaB` leaves no trace in the report: `exploreQueue.fold()` kept the first run's context and `p.release()` dropped the rest before anything read them. Regression suites that cache explored samples need the complete set of states a sample's runs entered to know which samples a changed transition can affect.

The runtime now keeps a per-run **coverage collector** on `Context` (`internal/exec/runtime/coverage.go`), fed at the two hooks that already exist — the `stateVisits` append in `state_executor.go` and the transition trace-record site — independent of `-trace` and retaining no trace records. Each entry is keyed by the owning object, the machine and the state path, deduplicated within a run and counted once per run. It is captured and restored with the snapshot like `coverageGaps`, so a check's rewinds do not lose or double-count it.

- **Exploration**: `exploreQueue.fold()` folds every run's coverage before `p.release()` into `Exploration.Coverage`, which lists `States` and `Transitions` as `CoverageEntry{Path, Declaration, Runs}`. ## What and why

Fixes the two symbol-side bugs of #2028 (closes #2028) at their root in the semantics layer, so the Symbol API, `GetElementProperties`, the api-json export and the REPL agree.

- `semantics.parametersOf` inherited no parameters from a behavior with more than one general, so `Calculations::Calculation :> Action, Evaluation` had no result parameter: a `calc def`'s `return` redefined nothing, `VerificationCase::verdict` never reached `Evaluation::result`, and the library result leaked into `members`, `directedFeature`, `feature` and `inheritedFeature`. Each general's unredefined parameters are now inherited (KerML 1.1 §7.4.7.2, §8.3.3.1), a parameter redefining by position masks the general parameter at its position (§8.4.4.6), and an inherited redefiner masks the whole chain it redefines. The metamodel's structural parameter table follows the same rule and asks the semantic model for a library parameter's positional redefinitions.
- A parameter its clause leaves nameless is identified by the name of the parameter its position redefines (§8.2.4, §8.3.3.3 `Feature::effectiveName`/`namingFeature`): `Performances::BooleanEvaluation`'s `return : Boolean` is `Performances::BooleanEvaluation::result` (the pilot's id `bca3d873-…`) instead of a minted `BooleanEvaluation/Feature[0]`, and a constraint def lists it as `result`. New `Model.QualifiedNameOf`/`PositionallyNamed` feed the identity catalog, the api-json/RDF writers and symbolfacts.

issues.body:
### Model and observed behaviour

```sysml
package P {
    port def Cmd;
    part x { port cmdIn : ~Cmd; }
}
```

The derived-property census (`go run -C tools ./cmd/derived-census`) lists `ConjugatedPortTyping::conjugatedPortDefinition` as **silent**: ours answers empty on every one of its 64 carriers across the corpus roots while the pilot answers a value on all 64 (`internal/semantic/metamodel/derived_census_baseline.json`, `silent` list; `docs/project/derived-property-census.md` table).

Cause: `rules.go` serves the rule with a basis only ("redefines FeatureTyping::type as a ConjugatedPortDefinition"), so it falls through to `structureRelationshipProperty` in `internal/semantic/metamodel/structure_rules.go`, whose generic `case "conjugatedPortDefinition"` answers `structureRelationshipOwner(element, "ConjugatedPortDefinition")` — the *owning* type, which is `PortConjugation::conjugatedPortDefinition`'s derivation. A `ConjugatedPortTyping` is owned by the port usage, never by a `ConjugatedPortDefinition`, so the answer is always empty. The `case "ConjugatedPortTyping"` branch of the structure rules handles `portDefinition` only.

### What the specification requires

SysML v2.1 Beta 2 §8.3.12.3 (ConjugatedPortTyping): `conjugatedPortDefinition : ConjugatedPortDefinition {redefines type}` — "The ConjugatedPortDefinition that is the type of the typedFeature of this ConjugatedPortTyping." ## What and why

Fixes #2003
Fixes #2005

`%check` and `%explain` passed no pins for a constraint or requirement target (`Session.solveQueriesWith` only called `solve.FixedFor` on the part/definition branch), so a derived declared value such as `attribute y : Real = x * 2.0;` was left free there and `%check CheckDerived::k` answered `sat` with `x = 0.0, y = 11.0`, while the same model on a part answered `unsat`. They also treated a literal bound with `=` (`attribute limit : Real = 1.0;`) like `default 1.0`, so the solver could pick `limit = -1.0` for a feature the model binds at all times.

- `runtime.EffectiveFeature.Binds` reports whether the value was written with `=` rather than `default` or `:=`, read from the declaration that wrote it (`DefaultDecl`), so an inherited `=` and a `:>> limit = 1.0` over a default bind while a redefined `default` does not.
- `solve.Pin.Bound` carries that on every declared pin `Fixed` produces (derived pins included).
- The REPL's `fixedFor`, for any target with no object to read — part, constraint, requirement or satisfaction — keeps the pins that are bound or derived and leaves the rest free (`modelBound` in `repl/check.go`). The part branch no longer has its own `FixedFor` call, so `default` and `:=` values on a part are free under `%check` too, which is what the reference now says.
- A derived value written with `default` (`attribute y : Real default x * 2.0;`) is a default like any other and stays free under `%check`; only an equation written with `=` is asserted (`CheckDerived::kd` in the REPL test).
- `solve.FixedFor` tells the features it gathers apart by declaration and redefinition chain, not by name: a constraint's own feature named like one of its owner's is another feature, fixed as declared rather than to what the owner's object holds under that name; a feature redefining one of the owner's (`attribute :>> a = 7.0;`) is that feature's nearest declaration, fixed to its own value where it writes one — so `%check` answer

> This issue was written with AI help. The model and the reproduction were run against the version below.

### What happened

An accept action used as a state's entry, do or exit action is a syntax error:

```sysml
package P {
    attribute def Sig;
    port def SigPort;
    state def S {
        port p : SigPort;
        state s {
            entry accept a : Sig via p;
        }
    }
}
```

```python
import opensysml
m = opensysml.loads(SRC)
m.ok            # False
m.diagnostics   # expected an action, an action reference or '{' after 'entry'
```

`do accept a : Sig via p;` and `exit accept a : Sig via p;` fail the same way, with `after 'do'` and `after 'exit'`. Other performed actions in the same position are accepted: `entry send new Sig() via p;` and `entry action a;` both load.

Because the parse fails, the whole model is unusable. Nothing else in the document can be read.

### Expected

The model loads, and the state's entry action is an `AcceptActionUsage`. The SysML v2 textual grammar allows an accept node in this position:

```
EntryActionMember : StateSubactionMembership =
    MemberPrefix kind = EntryActionKind ownedRelatedElement += StateActionUsage
StateActionUsage : ActionUsage =
    EmptyActionUsage ';' | PerformedActionUsage ActionBody
PerformedActionUsage : ActionUsage =
      {PerformActionUsage} PerformActionUsageDeclaration
    | {AcceptActionUsage} AcceptNodeDeclaration
    | {SendActionUsage} SendNodeDeclaration
    | {AssignmentActionUsage} AssignmentNodeDeclaration
```

`do` and `exit` use the same `StateActionUsage`.

For comparison, the SysML v2 Pilot Implementation (0.64.0-SNAPSHOT, commit `378a8700c`) and sysml-toolkit (v0.11.3) both accept the model. Both report the entry, do and exit actions as `AcceptActionUsage`.

### Version

OpenSysML `develop` at `1a8e4927dc` (2026-11-05), built locally: `sysml-grpc` v0.12.0-402-g1a8e4927dc, Python client from `client/python`. The Go API (`client/opensysml`) reports the same diagnostic.

## What and why

A connector end written as a feature chain (`connect a.inner.p to b.p`, `interface supplier ::> powertrain.tank.fuelOut`) made the connector's `relatedFeature`, `sourceFeature` and `targetFeature` the chain's last link in the reflective model, and made the API element form and Turtle state nothing at all for it. issues.body:
> This issue was written with AI help. The model, the reproduction script and its output are
> attached and were run against sysml-grpc v0.12.0-262-gc86932321 (develop at c86932321).

### The ruling

`docs/project/spec-compliance.md`, connector-ends row (marked ✅ Faithful):
"`relatedFeature`/`sourceFeature`/`targetFeature` of the connector stay the chain tips."

### Why it is wrong

KerML v1.1 Beta 2, §8.3.4.5.3 Connector, derives these properties from the ends' reference
subsettings:

> **deriveConnectorRelatedFeature** — The relatedFeatures of a Connector are the referenced
> Features of its connectorEnds.
> `relatedFeature = connectorEnd.ownedReferenceSubsetting->select(s | s <> null).subsettedFeature`
>
> **deriveConnectorSourceFeature** — The sourceFeature of a Connector is its first relatedFeature (if any).
>
> **deriveConnectorTargetFeature** — The targetFeatures of a Connector are the relatedFeatures other than the sourceFeature.

For an end written `powertrain.tank.fuelOut`, the end's ReferenceSubsetting subsets the feature
the chain denotes as a whole (KerML 8.3.3.3.9). The same spec-compliance row says so itself: "A
relationship target written as a feature chain … is the chaining feature the chain denotes as a
whole … whose `chainingFeature` is the chain's features in order". OpenSysML reflects that
correctly for the end:
`connectorEnd#(1).ownedReferenceSubsetting.referencedFeature.chainingFeature` is
`[vehicle::powertrain, Powertrain::tank, Tank::fuelOut]`. Following the derivation above,
`relatedFeature` must therefore be that chain feature, but OpenSysML answers `Tank::fuelOut`.
The row's two statements contradict each other through the derivation.

The tip also fails a constraint of the same section:

### Model and observed behaviour

Send actions nested in an action usage:

```sysml
part def Monitor {
    port alarmPort : AlarmPort;
    part display;
    action supervise {
        action notifyVia send new Alarm(3) via alarmPort;   // payload + sender
        action notifyTo send new Alarm(5) to display;       // payload + receiver
    }
}
```

Both are reported as ordinary actions that say nothing about what they send or where:

| Route | `notifyVia` / `notifyTo` |
|---|---|
| Python `Symbol` | `kind='actionUsage'`, `metadata={'visibility': 'default'}`, no `child_ids`, no children |
| `model.query` `@type` | `ActionUsage` |
| reflection, `last(X.metadata)` | `Metaobject(…, metaclass_id='SysML::Systems::ActionUsage')`; `.payloadArgument` → `ActionUsage declares no feature payloadArgument` |
| api-json `@type` | `SendActionUsage` ✔ (since #942) |

A client therefore cannot tell a send from any other action, let alone find its payload type
(`Alarm`) or its target port or part. The only route is api-json, and there the arguments are in
OpenSysML-specific keys (see the end of this issue).

The same happens for a send directly in an action def, in a part def, or as a state's `entry`
action, so it is not specific to nesting. An *unnamed* `send …;` is in addition missing from
`children()` altogether, which is #1960.

```shell
$ python repro.py          # loads model.sysml with opensysml.loads() over sysml-grpc
## notifyVia: send new Alarm(3) via alarmPort
[BUG ] notifyVia: Symbol kind is a send action
       observed: 'actionUsage'
[BUG ] notifyVia: Symbol exposes the payload and the sender
       observed: {'metadata': {'visibility': 'default'}, 'child_ids': [], 'children': []}
       expected: 'payload new Alarm(3) and sender alarmPort'
[BUG ] notifyVia: query @type is SendActionUsage
       observed: 'ActionUsage'
[BUG ] no

## What and why

Fixes #1959

A gRPC `Instance` carried only `id`, `type_symbol_id` and `feature_values`, so a Python client could not tell which part holds an object or by which usage path the graph reached it. - **Every path to it.** A new `InstancePaths` RPC (`runtime.Context.PathsTo`, `grpc/instancepaths.go`) lists every root-relative path to an object named by instance id or by path, from every held root, aliases through connector ends and reference usages included; library-derived collections are not separate paths and a path visits no object twice.         connect supplier ::> powertrain.tank.fuelOut
             to consumer ::> powertrain.engine.fuelIn;
}
```

`model.instantiate("InterfaceEnds::vehicle")` gives `vehicle.fuelLine.supplier` as the same
`Instance` (`id` 5) as `vehicle.powertrain.tank.fuelOut`.

But an `Instance` carries only `id`, `type_symbol_id` and its feature values (the gRPC `Instance`
message has nothing else). So starting from `fuelLine.supplier`, a client cannot ask which part
owns this port, or by which path (`vehicle.powertrain.tank.fuelOut`). The only way is to walk the
whole instance tree from the root and search for the id.

Would it make sense for an instance to report the object and feature that hold it, or its
usage path from the instantiated root? For example, `Instance.owner` / `Instance.path` in the
client, backed by fields on the `Instance` message. One complication is that an object can be
held by more than one feature, as here: `fuelLine.supplier` and `powertrain.tank.fuelOut` are the
same object. So "the path" probably means the composite owner chain, with the referencing
features listed separately.

## What and why

Fixes #1960
Fixes #1963

`Symbol.children()` in the Python client silently dropped every unnamed member of a scope, and a `#M` prefix annotation had no symbol at all:

- `SymbolInfo.child_ids` identified each member by `Index.GetFQN`, which for an unnamed member is the owner's name plus an empty segment (`UnnamedChildren::Controller::`), so every unnamed member of a scope collapsed to one malformed, duplicated id that `GetSymbol` could not resolve, and the client skipped a child whose lookup failed without saying so.
- In `symbols/builder.go` a `#M` prefix on a definition or usage only got its body scope built; no `MetadataUsage` symbol was registered, so it was missing from `model.query`, `child_ids`, `children()` and every other scope-driven surface, while the API JSON export and reflection already wrote it as an owned `MetadataUsage` of the annotated element.

What changed:

- `symbolfacts.Context` gains `Identity`/`Lookup` over a lazily derived `Positional` table (`export.PositionalIdentities`, the same names the query API reports): `child_ids` and `SymbolInfo.id` use the qualified name of a named member and the positional id (`Owner::@3`, `Owner::@3::wheel`) of an unnamed one; a member no id reaches (a body-local declaration) is left out instead of being listed under an id nothing answers. `GetSymbol`, `Evaluate` (context/subject) and `Instantiate` resolve positional ids. The derivation lives in the exporter, which the REPL core and `sysml-core` may not link (`TestREPLCoreLinksNoTranslatorOrTransport`, the core wasm budget), so `symbolfacts` takes it through `RegisterPositional`, registered by the new `symbolfacts/positional` package that the gRPC service and the REPL's positional extension import; the JSON-RPC core shares the same context, so `sysml` agrees with the service, while the bare `sysml-core` build (no exporter) lists named children only. `Index.QualifiedIdentity` moves from `semantic/query` to `semantic/symbols` for the same reason.

## What and why

Fixes #1929. Since 0.12.0 a feature valued by an expression carries the order-dependence marker of everything its expression reads, through features so valued in turn (`footprintBuilder.boundValue`). The guard against a cyclic binding was the stack of bindings being read, so a feature reached along many paths of such features was expanded once per path: in the reporter's N mutually referencing features (through `if` branches a run never takes as much as through taken ones) that is ~(N−1)! expansions — N=9 took 4 s, N=10 30 s, N=11 minutes, with no diagnostic — and a diamond of derived features re-read on two paths is 2^depth. `ExecuteAction` on an action usage performed with no arguments ignored the usage's own `in` values. For

### The ruling

docs/project/spec-compliance.md, the redefinition row: "A redefining feature's declared type need not conform to the redefined feature's type … OpenSysML still reports the unrelated-type case as `redefinition-type-mismatch`, an extension, because a redefinition typed by two unrelated types is almost always a slip — but as a **warning**, so no conforming model is rejected" (marked ⚠️ approximate).

The ruling's own premises leave the warning without a basis. A `bind` declared inside an `interface def`, an interface usage body, or a `connection def` had no effect on instances: only a `bind` written directly by the containing part was consulted (#1857). With

## What and why

Fixes #1776.

### The rule

A requirement check is `Requirements::RequirementConstraintCheck::result = allTrue(assumptions()) implies allTrue(constraints())` (SysML v2 §7.21.2; `Requirements.sysml`). A subject that fails an `assume constraint` therefore *satisfies* the requirement, whatever its `require constraint`s read: `false implies …` is true. The value read of `result`, the subrequirement check (`subrequirementHoldsAt`) and the solver (`solve/translate.go` `assertedCondition`, ¬(A ∧ ¬R)) already judged it that way; the condition evaluator did not.

### The old behavior

`runtime/condition.go` `evaluateConditions` evaluated an assumption and then acted only on `cond.Required && !holds`. A false assumption was a no-op, so the check degraded to `allTrue(constraints())`: on the issue's model, `satisfy levelOk by off` (`off.enabled = false`, `off.level = 5`) was reported as `Required condition evaluated to false: t.level == 1`, while `attribute r = offReq.result;` read `true`. Mirror bug: `assert not requirement nrOff : LevelOk { subject t = off; }` *held*, though `not (false implies …)` is false.

### The fix

`judgeConditions` (what `evaluateConditions` now wraps) settles a requirement-kind check (`conditionCheck.isRequirementCheck()`: requirement, satisfaction, objective) on the first condition that fails — `conditionCheck.decidedBy` — and `conditionCheck.failedCondition` is the one place that says what that failure means: a required condition failing is the violation (or exactly what a negated element asserts, as before); an assumption failing makes the check hold vacuously, and makes a negated check fail with a violation naming the assumption. `evaluateStepsConditions` (a body stating steps) reuses the same two helpers. Assumptions are judged before required conditions whatever order the body declares them in (`conditionCheck.assumptionsFirst`): `implies` reads its consequent only once its antecedent holds (KerML `ControlFunctions::implies`),

## Symptom

Reading `%features` (or any surface that walks the held object's `subparts`) of an object whose part definition declares a `timeslice part` fails with an occurrence-lifetime error instead of listing the portion: the timeslice is reported as holding itself as a portion.

## Reproducer

```sysml
package Repro {
    part def P {
        timeslice part cruise;
    }
    part p : P;
}
```

```text
$ sysml repro.sysml
sysml> %instantiate p
sysml> %features p
Instance: Repro::p (ID: 1)
Features:
  cruise = Instance(ID: 2)
    ...
    subparts: <error: occurrence lifetime does not admit the change: cruise #2 would hold cruise #2, a whole it is a portion of, as a portion of itself>

```

The same error shows in `examples/relay-probe-demo` (`%instantiate mission` then `%features mission`, under `relay.cruise`). Replacing `timeslice part cruise` with `part cruise` lists `subparts = []` cleanly.

## Expected

`cruise` is a portion of the `P` instance (a `timeslice` of it), so `p.subparts` lists it and `cruise.subparts` is empty — no attempt to hold the timeslice under itself, no error in the listing.

`cruise.subparts` is an error value: `occurrence lifetime does not admit the change: cruise #2 would hold cruise #2, a whole it is a portion of, as a portion of itself`. The portion is being redirected into the whole it is a portion of when the derived `subparts` of the timeslice itself is read.

## What was wrong

`stores/auth.js` checks the BetterTTV account against the platform user once, when the module loads, and reads `getCurrentUser().id` without a null check. On YouTube the platform user is only set once the chat input renders, which is usually after that check. So the check threw `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'id')` and never ran again. The extension stayed signed out with valid credentials stored, and signing in again "worked" (the popup authorized and closed) but changed nothing. That matches the report, including it later starting to work, since whether it breaks depends on timing. The same throw happens on Twitch or YouTube when you're logged out of the platform, so a sign in there also failed with no feedback.

## Changes

- **Auth sync waits for the platform user.** With no platform user the sync leaves you signed out without throwing, then runs again on `user.updated` once the platform user loads or changes. A sync that finishes after a newer sign in, sign out or platform user is discarded, and `waitForUserSync` waits for any sync that replaces the one it's waiting on.
- **Sign in is gated on being logged in to the platform.**
  - User Settings: the Sign In button is disabled, with a tooltip: "Log in to Twitch to sign in to BetterTTV." (YouTube on YouTube).
  - The "Sign In Required" modal that features open keeps its own content, adds the same line, and disables its Sign In button.
  - `executeSignIn` refuses to start without a platform user.
- **Account mismatch:** once the check can actually run, the existing mismatch modal from #8329 shows. A mismatch now also clears any stale `user`.

## Testing

Tested on Twitch with the dev build. I used a temporary local switch (not committed) that either hid the Twitch user or set it 5s late to imitate YouTube's timing:

- **Platform user hidden:** the Sign In button is disabled, the tooltip shows, and clicking it does nothing. Choosing a username effect opens
